resources.title: The repo's own `00_CONCEPTS.md` and `05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md`

b.s: The project's own notes, written by the people who built it. They explain what the helper is for and how the pieces fit together, like the instruction sheet that comes in a toy box.

Two documents inside this repository. The concepts file explains the ideas behind the first model, including the math of the logistic regression, in plain language. The plan file describes how the PeMS sensor data and the 511 incident feed will be combined into one training table. Read them once now, even if half of it is unclear, and again after phase 4, when all of it will make sense.

Read them like a map of the project. `00_CONCEPTS.md` explains the sigmoid, cross-entropy and gradient descent that lesson 7 rebuilds. `05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md` sets out the stages, the label definition, the join rules between incidents and stations, and the time-zone warning that lessons 3 to 5 elaborate. Write down every term you do not understand; that list is your study plan for the next three phases.

Project documentation is a primary source: it records decisions and their reasons, and it goes stale the moment code diverges from it. Compare the plan with the flowchart document (`21_PLAN_M1_TRAFFIC_MODEL.md`) and list what changed and why: the forward-shifted targets, the train-only profile, the second label, the missing real-time feed. That diff is a lesson in how plans evolve when they meet data.

Read them critically. The original plan paired features at t with the label at t, and computed the profile on all history; both are design errors that would have produced flattering numbers. Finding such issues in a design document before code exists is a core research and engineering skill; practice it by writing a one-page review of `05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md` as if it were a submission.

Design documents are where most of the leverage in an ML project lives, and most teams write them badly. The exercise at your level is to write the version a team could execute: explicit interfaces between stages, success criteria with numbers, risks with owners, and what would make you stop. Use these two files as the before, and the flowchart plan as a partial after.

The project's own documents. The concepts file explains the first model: how events become a training table, what logistic regression computes, and how gradient descent fits it. The plan file specifies how PeMS detector data and 511 incidents are cleaned, labelled, joined, featurized, split and evaluated.

items: The v1 model: a grid of road × hour × weekend cells, each labelled 1 if any incident ever occurred there. Features are hour (scaled to 0–1), a weekend flag and one-hot road indicators; the model is a logistic regression trained by hand-written gradient descent.

Logistic regression in the concepts file: score z = w·x + b, probability p = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), loss = −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)], gradient (p − y)·x, update w ← w − η·gradient. Lesson 7 rebuilds this.

The plan's pipeline: download PeMS 5-minute files and station metadata; clean (timezone to UTC, sanity bounds, short-gap fill, Fremont station filter); label slow episodes from a speed profile; join incidents by route, direction and distance; engineer lag, rolling, neighbor, calendar and incident features; split chronologically; train baselines, logistic regression, trees and an MLP; evaluate with standard metrics and lead time.

The plan's cautions: the timezone step is mandatory and easy to get wrong; PeMS column layout must be verified against a real file; the label threshold should be versioned in filenames; class weighting when positives are rare.

What the flowchart plan changed: targets shifted forward by the horizon, a train-only profile, a second absolute label, weather and static features, LightGBM as production, calibration and thresholds, a serving loop and monitoring, and the admission that no real-time speed feed exists yet.

b.s:
p = sigmoid(x @ weights + bias)
loss = -mean(y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p))
weights -= lr * X.T @ (p - y) / n

items: Read a design document as a hypothesis about data you have not seen yet; the first real file will change it.
The v1 model is a lookup table shaped like a model; its value is teaching the mechanics.
The plan's later revisions are the record of what evaluation discipline caught.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (MIT)

b.s: A short free class about the tools programmers use every day but nobody teaches: the typing window, the magic notebook, and how to make the computer do boring jobs for you.

MIT students made a course about the things regular classes skip: the shell, editors, git, debugging, command-line tools, and automating tasks. Eleven lectures with notes and exercises, all free. Do the shell, editors and git lectures during phase 0.

The lectures on the shell and shell tools, on editors (Vim), on data wrangling (pipes, grep, sed, awk), on git, and on debugging and profiling are directly useful. The git lecture's model of commits as a graph is the best short explanation there is; the data-wrangling lecture teaches you to inspect a PeMS file without Python.

Its value is the mental models: the shell as a programming environment, git as a content-addressed graph, profiling before optimizing. The exercises are small and worth doing; the notes are good references for the flags you forget.
A compact syllabus of practitioner tooling that most graduate students still lack; its debugging and profiling lecture is a fair summary of how to approach a slow or wrong pipeline stage.

For onboarding engineers and researchers alike, this is the shortest path to shared tooling literacy; its lecture on metaprogramming (build systems, testing, continuous integration) is the bridge to the engineering phase.

Eleven one-hour lectures with notes and exercises on the tools around programming: the shell, shell scripting, editors, data wrangling with command-line tools, command-line environments, version control, debugging and profiling, metaprogramming (build systems, dependencies, testing), security, and a potpourri.

items: Shell basics: how the shell finds programs through `PATH`, quoting and expansion, redirection, and why permissions (`chmod`, `sudo`) block scripts silently.

Shell scripting: variables, functions, exit codes (`$?`), `&&` and `||`, command substitution `$(cmd)`, `for` loops, `find`, `xargs`, and shebangs. The lecture's advice: use the shell for glue, Python for logic.
Editors: the Vim lecture teaches modal editing and why an editor you can drive without the mouse pays off; whichever editor you use, learn its search, multi-cursor and integrated terminal.

Data wrangling: `sed` substitutions, regular expressions (character classes, anchors, groups), `awk` for columns, `sort | uniq -c | sort -nk1`, `paste`, `bc`, and building a one-line analysis of a log file. Directly applicable to a PeMS file.
Command-line environment: job control (`&`, `Ctrl-Z`, `fg`, `bg`), terminal multiplexers (tmux), aliases and dotfiles, SSH keys and port forwarding for remote machines.

Version control: git's data model as a directed acyclic graph of commits over trees of blobs; the staging area; branches as references; merging and conflicts; `git bisect` to find a bad commit; `git stash`.

Debugging and profiling: print debugging versus logging levels, debuggers (`pdb`), `strace`-style system tracing, static analysis (linters, type checkers), CPU profilers and flame graphs, memory profilers, and `time` versus wall-clock.
Metaprogramming: build systems (`make` with targets and dependencies), semantic versioning, lock files, continuous integration, and testing vocabulary (unit, integration, regression, mocking).
Security: hashes, key derivation, symmetric and asymmetric encryption at a user's level, SSH keys, password managers, and why secrets never go in repositories.

cat log | grep 'Error' | sed -E 's/.*station=([0-9]+).*/\1/' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nk1 | tail
make all   # a Makefile target with dependencies runs only what changed
git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good v1.0; # test, mark, repeat

A Makefile with dependencies is the simplest correct pipeline runner.
Profile before optimizing and bisect before guessing.

resources.title: Elements of AI (University of Helsinki)

b.s: A gentle online course that explains what artificial intelligence is and is not, with pictures and simple quizzes, made for everyone.

A free course from the University of Helsinki, no math required: what AI means, how problems are solved by search, how probability handles uncertainty, what machine learning is, how neural networks work, and what AI does to society. About thirty hours, spread over a couple of weeks. A good first map before the phases begin.

Do it in the first week for the vocabulary and the big picture: the difference between rules and learning, why probability matters, what a neural network does in outline, and why AI's effects are a social question. The chapter on machine learning is a preview of phase 4 with no code.
It is deliberately non-technical; use it to calibrate how you explain the course to others, and note where it simplifies (it treats learning as fitting without discussing evaluation).
A model of public education about a technical field: careful about hype, honest about uncertainty, and concrete about societal effects.
Worth knowing as the reference for what a general audience can be expected to understand about AI, which matters when you write for policy makers or the public.

A non-technical introduction in six chapters: what AI is, problem solving by search, real-world AI and probability, machine learning, neural networks, and the implications of AI. Each chapter has short readings and exercises.

items: Defining AI: it is not one thing; useful distinctions are narrow versus general, autonomy versus adaptivity, and the observation that once something works we stop calling it AI. The Turing test and the Chinese room as framing arguments.

Search and games: a problem as states and actions, breadth-first and depth-first search, and game trees with the minimax idea; why exhaustive search fails as branching grows and heuristics are needed.
Probability: odds and probabilities, Bayes' rule with a medical-test example (base rates matter), naive Bayes for spam filtering; the point that uncertainty is handled by arithmetic, not intuition.

Machine learning: supervised (labelled examples), unsupervised (structure without labels) and reinforcement (rewards) learning; nearest neighbors and linear regression as first models; overfitting as memorization; the need for held-out evaluation.
Neural networks: neurons as weighted sums with a squashing function, layers, the idea of training by adjusting weights, and what deep networks do with images.

Implications: prediction versus explanation, bias in data becoming bias in decisions, the limits of current systems (no common sense, brittle outside training data), and the questions society should ask.

b.s: P(disease | positive) = P(positive | disease) P(disease) / P(positive)

items: AI is a set of methods with limits, not a mind; know which method is being used.
Base rates decide what a positive test means; the same logic runs through every alert this course builds.
Overfitting and biased data are the two failure modes a non-expert should be able to name.

phases.title: Python that does work

b.s: Read and write the collector scripts fluently, test them, and never be confused by a clock.

items: Variables, numbers, strings, lists, dicts, sets, tuples; `if`, `for`, `while`; functions, arguments, return values, scope.
Modules and imports, files, CSV and JSON, exceptions, `requests`, `argparse`, f-strings, comprehensions.
Dates and time zones with `datetime` and `zoneinfo`; what UTC is and why the log stores it.
The debugger, print-debugging with intent, and `pytest` for small functions.
What a PeMS row and a 511 event actually measure.

items.title: Python: from variables to functions to files

b.s: Read and write the kind of Python the collectors are made of: data structures, functions, files, JSON and CSV.
Python is a language for telling the computer what to do, one line at a time.
A variable is a box with a name. A list is a row of boxes. A function is a recipe you can use again and again without rewriting it.
Type `name = 'Sam'` and then `print('Hi', name)`. Change the name and run it again.
Types: numbers, strings, lists, and dictionaries, which are lookup tables from names to values, perfect for a JSON event. Booleans are true or false.

`if` decides, `for` repeats, `def` makes a function with inputs and an output. Files are opened, read line by line, and written. CSV and JSON are text with rules, and Python's `csv` and `json` modules read them for you.
Read `data/fremont_events_log.csv` with the `csv` module and count rows per `event_type` using a dictionary. Print the counts sorted from largest to smallest.

The skills inside `02_collect_events.py`: `requests.get(url, params=...)` and `.json()`; dictionary access with `.get()` so a missing key does not crash; list comprehensions to filter events; f-strings; `with open(...)`; `argparse` for `--bootstrap`; `try/except` around the network call; `datetime` with `timezone.utc`.
Modules and the `if __name__ == '__main__':` guard, so a file can be both a script and something another script imports.
Style that pays off in pipelines: small functions with one job, names that say what a variable holds, and no clever tricks.
Rewrite `flatten_event()` from its docstring without looking at the original, then run both on three real events and compare the outputs field by field.

Python's data model: everything is an object; mutability (lists versus tuples), identity versus equality, and references, so a list inside a dictionary is shared, not copied. Scope (local, enclosing, global, built-in) and closures.

Iterators and generators (`yield`) let you stream a large file without loading it, which is the pattern stage 5 needs. `pathlib` for paths, type hints and `dataclasses` for records, and the standard library's breadth: `collections.Counter`, `itertools`, `functools`.
Performance: Python loops are slow, so vectorize with numpy and pandas, and profile with `cProfile` before optimizing anything.
Write a generator that yields only Fremont rows from a gzipped PeMS file, line by line, and measure its peak memory with `tracemalloc`. Compare with reading the whole file.

The interpreter: CPython compiles to bytecode; the global interpreter lock means threads do not speed up CPU-bound code, so use processes or vectorized libraries; reference counting plus a cycle collector manage memory; C extensions such as numpy are the escape hatch.

Packaging with `pyproject.toml`, entry points and wheels. Testing strategy: unit tests for pure functions, fixtures for I/O, property-based tests for parsers. Concurrency for I/O: `asyncio` for polling several endpoints with a rate limiter.
Convert the poller to `asyncio` with an explicit rate limiter and prove, by logging, that it makes exactly the same requests in the same order.

In production ML, Python is the glue, not the engine: the arithmetic runs in C, C++ or Metal kernels reached through numpy, PyTorch and Arrow. The engineering concerns are dependency hygiene across a fleet, reproducible numerics, typed interfaces at module boundaries, and knowing when a hot loop should move to a compiled extension.
Python's flexibility is why ML iteration is fast and why production systems need contracts, schemas and tests to survive it.
Find the one function in the pipeline whose cost dominates, implement it twice (pandas and polars), benchmark both on a real file, and write down which you would ship and why.

b.q: Why `event.get('severity')` rather than `event['severity']`?

a.s: Some 511 events lack the key. `.get` returns None instead of raising, so one odd event does not stop the poll.

b.q: What does the `if __name__ == '__main__'` guard do?

a.s: It runs the block only when the file is executed directly, so another script can import its functions without triggering a poll.

items.title: Tests, debugging and time zones

b.s: Prove small pieces work, find out why they do not, and never be confused by a clock again.
A test is a tiny check that asks 'does this still work?' and answers yes or no. Debugging is being a detective when the answer is no.
When it is lunchtime in California it is dinnertime in London. Computers avoid the mix-up by writing times in one shared clock called UTC.
Find out what time it is right now in a city far away. How many hours different is it?
`pytest` runs every function whose name starts with `test_` and reports which passed. A good test builds a tiny fake input, such as five made-up events, and checks the exact output.
Debugging: read the error message from the bottom up, print the values you assumed were true, and shrink the input until the bug is obvious.
A naive time has no zone attached and is ambiguous; an aware time carries its zone. Store and compute in UTC; convert to California time only to display.
Write `test_event_touches_fremont` with one event inside the bounding box and one outside, run `pytest`, then break the function on purpose and watch the test fail.
Test anatomy: arrange, act, assert. Fixtures for shared setup, `parametrize` to run one test over many cases, `pytest -x -q` to stop at the first failure.
Debugging tools: `breakpoint()`, the VS Code debugger, and `logging` instead of print for scripts that run unattended.

Time in Python: `zoneinfo.ZoneInfo('America/Los_Angeles')`, `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, `astimezone()`, ISO 8601 strings ending in `Z`. Daylight saving removes an hour in March and repeats one in November; pandas exposes the choice through `ambiguous` and `nonexistent`.
Write a test that localizes 2026-11-01 01:30 to America/Los_Angeles and shows why `ambiguous` must be specified.

Testing data code: golden files (a stored known-good output) for pipelines, property checks (row counts preserved, no NaN in keys), and boundary cases (daylight saving, empty files, a day with one station). Test doubles for the network so tests run offline.
Debugging as hypothesis testing: form a guess, find the cheapest experiment that could refute it, and bisect the pipeline when the wrong number appears far from its cause.
Time semantics: instants versus wall-clock times, offsets versus zones (a zone has rules, an offset is a number), the epoch, and why `datetime.utcnow()` is a trap (it returns a naive object).
Build the 100-row fixture for `10_clean_pems.py` that includes a daylight-saving boundary and a station boundary, and write the three tests that use it.

Testing ML systems: data tests (schema, ranges, distributions), model tests (a training run on a fixture reaches a minimum average precision; shifting every timestamp by a week changes nothing), and pipeline tests on a golden day. Nondeterminism from seeds, thread counts and the GPU causes flakiness, so pin what you can and tolerate what you must.
Debugging statistical code is different: the failure is a wrong number, not a crash. Sanity baselines and synthetic data with known answers are the instruments.
The tz database changes when governments change rules; pin `tzdata`. The ambiguous hour is a real loss of information, not a formatting problem.
Write an invariance test that shifts all timestamps by seven days and asserts the feature table is identical except for the calendar columns.

Verification at scale: continuous integration on every change, contract tests between pipeline stages, canaries on live data, and the uncomfortable fact that most production ML failures are data failures that no unit test caught.
Time in distributed systems: clock skew, event time versus processing time, watermarks in stream processors, and the point-in-time discipline that makes training match serving.
Research threads: metamorphic testing for ML, and executable data contracts.
Specify the contract between `10_clean_pems.py` and `13_feature_engineering.py` as executable assertions, and decide which assertions should stop the pipeline and which should only warn.

b.q: Why test with fake events rather than the live API?

a.s: Speed, determinism and no network. The API changes; your fixture does not, so a failure means your code changed.

b.q: Why store UTC and convert only for display?

a.s: UTC has no daylight saving, so arithmetic on it is safe. Local time has a missing hour and a repeated hour every year.

items.title: The data: detectors, five-minute rows, incidents

b.s: Know what a PeMS row and a 511 event actually measure, how much of them there are, and where the numbers lie.
Under the road there are little wires that feel cars driving over them, like a doorbell mat that rings when you step on it.
Every five minutes the wires write down how many cars went by and how fast they were going. Another helper, called 511, writes down when there is a crash and where.
We collect both into two big lists. The lists are the food our helper learns from.
Count the cars that pass your window for one minute and write the number down. Do it again a few minutes later. The numbers change; that is data.

PeMS is California's collection of those road sensors. Each sensor is a 'station'. Every 5 minutes a station makes one row: the time, the station number, how many cars passed (flow), how full the road was (occupancy, the share of time a car was sitting over the sensor), and the average speed.
One day of the Bay Area district is about 1.3 million rows in a text file with no column names. We only care about the roughly 100 stations in Fremont on I-880, I-680 and SR-84.

511.org lists incidents: crashes, stalls, roadwork, each with a time, a road name and a map point. Our collector asks 511 every 15 minutes 'what is happening?' and saves anything near Fremont into a spreadsheet-like file.
The two lists look different: one is a steady drumbeat of numbers, the other is a scattered log of events.
Open `data/fremont_events_log.csv` in a spreadsheet. Sort by `created`. Which hour of the day has the most incidents? Which road?

Three quantities per station per 5 minutes. Flow: vehicles counted. Occupancy: the fraction of time the loop was covered, which stands in for how dense the traffic is. Speed: miles per hour, sometimes measured directly with a pair of loops and sometimes estimated from flow and occupancy with an assumed vehicle length.

The fundamental diagram links them: as density rises, flow rises until the road reaches capacity, then flow falls as the road jams. That is why occupancy matters and not just speed; a road at 60 mph with heavy occupancy is about to break down.

Timestamps in the file are California local time with no zone attached. We convert them to UTC and handle the two daylight-saving switches, where one hour repeats in November and one is missing in March.
Incidents arrive as JSON with `created` and `updated` times, but our poller only looks every 15 minutes, so a short stall can be missed entirely and every start time is fuzzy by up to 15 minutes.
Sketch the fundamental diagram: flow on the vertical axis, density on the horizontal. Mark free flow, capacity and jam. Where on the curve is 'slow'?

Detector physics decides the error model. Single-loop stations infer speed from flow and occupancy through a per-station 'g-factor' (effective vehicle length), so speed error grows at low flow and when truck mix changes. PeMS also imputes missing samples from neighboring stations and history and reports the share of real samples as `% Observed`; aggregate columns are flow-weighted across lanes.

Volume arithmetic: about 100 stations × 288 steps × 365 days is 10.5 million rows a year; at 5 float32 columns that is 210 MB in memory, and with 60 feature columns about 2.5 GB. Memory is rows × columns × bytes, and dtype choices decide whether two years fit a 16 GB machine.

Time semantics: `tz_localize('America/Los_Angeles')` must be told what to do with the ambiguous hour (fall back) and the nonexistent hour (spring forward); the plan drops the ambiguous hour rather than guess.

The 511 feed is an event stream sampled every 15 minutes, so incident start and end times are interval-censored. `created` is when CHP logged the report, which lags the physical event by an unknown, skewed delay.
Compute the memory of a year of features as rows × columns × 4 bytes. Then compute the same for float64 and for a naive pandas pipeline that holds three copies during a groupby-shift.

Write the measurement model: observed speed = true speed + detector noise + imputation error, where imputation is itself a model of neighbors and history. Imputed rows are therefore correlated with neighboring stations' values, which leaks spatial information into what looks like an observation and flatters any spatial model evaluated on them.

Spatial sampling sets what is predictable. Station spacing of 0.3 to 0.6 miles and backward-forming shock speeds around 10 to 15 mph (kinematic wave theory) mean a jam crosses one station every two to four minutes, so a 30-minute horizon corresponds to roughly two to six stations of upstream propagation.

Temporal aggregation at 5 minutes filters the high-frequency dynamics; the data cannot resolve a 90-second stall. The incident covariate has measurement error of its own: reporting delay, missing geography, unknown severity, and a selection effect, since incidents are reported more readily when congestion is already visible.
Estimate how many stations upstream a queue's tail passes in 30 minutes at a 12 mph shockwave with half-mile spacing, and what that implies for the value of two-hop versus five-hop neighbor features.

Sensor networks in production mix fixed loops, radar and probe data, and the fixed loops come with known pathologies: g-factor drift, chattering detectors, lane-assignment errors. In a district it is normal for a fifth to a third of detectors to be unhealthy at any time, so a serious pipeline carries a detector-health model as a component in its own right, and the imputation mask becomes a feature rather than an embarrassment.

Probe data introduces the privacy layer: on-device aggregation, differential privacy on segment speeds, and coverage that is a function of device share. The statistical problem becomes estimating a segment speed from a biased, sparse sample and propagating that uncertainty.

Here the binding constraint is not modelling but data availability: a 305-second rate limit and a one-day publication lag. Recognizing that a project is data-bound rather than model-bound is most of senior judgment.

Research threads: learned spatio-temporal imputation (graph recurrent imputation networks) against the risk that the downstream model learns the imputer; representing incidents as a marked point process joined to a regular grid; and asynchronous multi-rate sensor fusion.

Design a detector-health score from `% Observed`, flow-occupancy consistency against the station's own fundamental diagram, and agreement with neighbors. Say how you would validate it without ground truth.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

These are terminal commands, not Python. Open the Terminal app, change into the Traffic1 folder with `cd`, and type each line followed by return. The PeMS files arrive gzipped, a compression format whose files end in `.gz`; `zcat` prints a gzipped file's contents decompressed, without writing an uncompressed copy to disk.

The vertical bar `|` is a pipe: it sends the output of the command on its left into the command on its right. `head -3` keeps only the first three lines, so the first command shows three raw rows and nothing more. Never open a 200 MB file in a text editor; peek at it like this.

The second command counts columns. `head -1` keeps one line; `tr ',' '\n'` translates every comma into a line break, so each field lands on its own line; `wc -l` counts lines. The answer is the number of columns in a row, which is far more than the twelve documented ones because PeMS repeats a block of columns for every lane.
Look at a raw file before you trust any description of it.

zcat data/pems_raw/d04_text_station_5min_2026_03_02.txt.gz | head -3
zcat data/pems_raw/d04_text_station_5min_2026_03_02.txt.gz | head -1 | tr ',' '\n' | wc -l

items: `zcat file.txt.gz | head -3` — decompress and show the first three raw rows
`zcat file.txt.gz | head -1 | tr ',' '\n' | wc -l` — take one row, put each comma-separated field on its own line, count the lines: the column count

b.s: Now the same file in Python. A CSV is a text table with one row per line and commas between fields; the PeMS file is a CSV with no header line, so pandas has to be told the column names. `pd.read_csv` reads it, and it can read a gzipped file directly.

The arguments: `header=None` says the first line is data, not names; `usecols=range(12)` keeps the first twelve columns and ignores the per-lane repeats; `names=cols` gives those twelve columns the names in the list `cols`; `nrows=100_000` stops after a hundred thousand rows, which is enough to look at and keeps memory small. Python allows the underscore inside a number for readability.

The names follow the PeMS documentation: `ts` the timestamp text, `station` the detector id, `district` the Caltrans district (4 is the Bay Area), `fwy` the freeway number, `dir` the direction, `lane_type` mainline or ramp, `length` the stretch of road the station represents, `samples` how many raw sensor samples went into the five-minute row, `pct_obs` the percentage of the row that was actually observed rather than filled in, and `flow`, `occ`, `speed` the three measurements: vehicles counted, fraction of time the sensor was covered, and average speed in miles per hour.

`describe()` computes count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and maximum for every numeric column; `.T` transposes the table so columns become rows, easier to read. `nunique()` counts distinct values, here how many stations appear.
Read the first twelve columns for a hundred thousand rows and describe them.

import pandas as pd
cols = ["ts","station","district","fwy","dir","lane_type","length","samples","pct_obs","flow","occ","speed"]
df = pd.read_csv("data/pems_raw/d04_text_station_5min_2026_03_02.txt.gz", header=None,
                 usecols=range(12), names=cols, nrows=100_000)
print(df.describe().T)
print(df.station.nunique(), "stations in the first 100k rows")

items: `cols = [...]` — the twelve documented column names, in file order
`pd.read_csv(path, header=None, usecols=range(12), names=cols, nrows=100_000)` — read a hundred thousand rows of the first twelve columns, naming them
`print(df.describe().T)` — a summary of every numeric column: is speed between 0 and 100, is pct_obs often below 50
`print(df.station.nunique(), ...)` — how many distinct stations appear in this slice

b.s: A day has 24 × 12 = 288 five-minute slots, so a station that reported every slot has 288 rows. `groupby("station")` splits the table into one group per station; `.size()` counts rows in each group; `.describe()` summarizes those counts. If the minimum is far below 288, some stations are missing rows, and lesson 3 will have to put the gaps back on the grid.
This is the general pattern for questions of the form 'how many per something': group, then count.
Count rows per station. A healthy station has 288 per day.
print(df.groupby("station").size().describe())

items: `df.groupby("station").size()` — rows per station
`.describe()` — min, median, max of those counts; a healthy file shows 288 everywhere

b.s: The `ts` column is text such as `03/02/2026 00:05:00`, in California local time. Text cannot be compared or subtracted, so it must be parsed into a real datetime. `pd.to_datetime` does that; `format="%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S"` tells it the layout (month, day, four-digit year, hour, minute, second), which is faster and safer than guessing.

A timezone is the rule that maps a local clock reading to a moment in the world. California uses Pacific time, which shifts by an hour twice a year for daylight saving time (DST). On the spring night one hour of clock time does not exist; on the autumn night one hour happens twice. `tz_localize("America/Los_Angeles", ...)` attaches the Pacific rule; `ambiguous="NaT"` says that a repeated autumn hour should become NaT (not a time, the datetime version of NaN) rather than a guess; `nonexistent="shift_forward"` says a spring clock reading that never happened should move forward to the next real moment. `.dt` is the accessor that gives datetime methods on a column.

`tz_convert("UTC")` then turns every moment into Coordinated Universal Time, the single clock that has no DST. All storage in the course is in UTC; local time is recomputed only when a feature needs the hour of day.
Parse the local timestamp and convert to UTC with explicit DST handling.

ts = pd.to_datetime(df.ts, format="%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S")
df["timestamp"] = ts.dt.tz_localize("America/Los_Angeles", ambiguous="NaT", nonexistent="shift_forward").dt.tz_convert("UTC")

items: `pd.to_datetime(df.ts, format=...)` — text to datetime, with the layout stated
`.dt.tz_localize("America/Los_Angeles", ambiguous="NaT", nonexistent="shift_forward")` — declare the readings to be Pacific local time and decide what to do with the two DST edge cases
`.dt.tz_convert("UTC")` — express every moment on the one clock the course stores

b.s: The incident log is the CSV that `02_collect_events.py` appends to every time it polls the 511 service, the Bay Area traffic information feed. Polling means asking a server for its current list on a schedule. Each row of the log is one incident as seen at one poll, with `created` (when the incident was first reported), `updated` (when its details last changed) and `pulled_at` (when this program fetched it).

`parse_dates=[...]` tells `read_csv` to turn those three columns into datetimes as it reads. Subtracting two datetime columns gives a column of durations; `describe()` then shows how long, typically, an incident had already existed before this collector saw it. That delay is a fact of life for the live model: an incident cannot help a prediction until it has been reported and pulled.
Open the incident log and look at the gap between `created` and `pulled_at` for a few rows. That gap is the reporting and polling delay you will live with.

ev = pd.read_csv("data/fremont_events_log.csv", parse_dates=["created","updated","pulled_at"])
print((ev.pulled_at - ev.created).describe())

items: `pd.read_csv("data/fremont_events_log.csv", parse_dates=[...])` — load the incident log with real datetimes
`(ev.pulled_at - ev.created).describe()` — how long between an incident's creation and our seeing it: the reporting plus polling delay

b.q: Why does occupancy matter if you already have speed?

a.s: Speed alone cannot tell a nearly empty road from a dense one moving at the same speed. Occupancy stands in for density, and density is what predicts breakdown.

b.q: What does `% Observed` = 20 mean for a row?

a.s: Only a fifth of the samples in that 5 minutes were real; the rest of the row was filled in by PeMS's imputer. Treat the row as missing for labels and carry the fraction as a feature.

b.q: Why can the poller miss an incident entirely?

a.s: It samples the feed every 15 minutes; an event that is created and cleared between two polls never appears. Start times are also only known to within one poll.

items: 'The file has headers.' It does not; column order must be verified against the documentation on a real file.
'Speed is measured.' Often it is estimated from flow and occupancy with an assumed vehicle length.
'Incidents are the labels.' They are inputs. The label comes from the detectors.

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, chapters 1–13 and 16–18

b.s: A friendly book that teaches Python by making the computer do chores for you, like renaming lots of files at once or reading a spreadsheet. It is free to read on the internet, and every chapter ends with something useful you made.

Al Sweigart's book starts from zero: numbers, text, lists, dictionaries, functions, and then practical chapters on files, spreadsheets, CSV and JSON, and the web. Chapters 1 to 13 are the language basics; 16 to 18 cover CSV and JSON, time and scheduling, and sending email and text messages, which are close to what our collector script does. Type every example rather than copying it, and do the practice projects at the end of the chapters.

The best first Python book because every chapter ends in a program that does something real. For this project the payoff chapters are 9 and 10 (reading, writing and organizing files), 13 (spreadsheets), 16 (CSV and JSON, the two formats the pipeline lives on), and 17 (time and scheduling, which the poller needs). After it you can read `02_collect_events.py` end to end and change it with confidence. Its style, small scripts with clear names, is the right style for pipeline code.

Its limits are exactly what the official tutorial and later phases fill: little on the data model (mutability, references), nothing on numpy, and almost nothing on testing. Use it for fluency and for the habit of automating anything you do twice, then move on. The chapter on debugging (chapter 11 in the current edition) is the one to reread when you are stuck on a stage 5 bug at midnight.

Pedagogically it works through immediate utility, and that is the model for how to bring domain experts (a traffic engineer, a city planner) onto a data project: give them a script that saves them an hour on day one. If you already program, skip it yourself; recommend it to collaborators and write the project-specific chapter it lacks, 'automating the PeMS download and cleaning'.

The book's persistence as the default beginner text, across editions and free online, reflects a fact about ML teams: the bottleneck is often basic scripting fluency among the people who understand the domain. Building that capability across a team is a higher-leverage act than most modelling work, and this book is the cheapest tool for it.

Python from zero through practical programs. Part 1 (chapters 1 to 6) is the language: expressions, flow control, functions, lists, dictionaries, strings. Chapters 7 to 13 cover regular expressions, files, organizing files, debugging, web scraping and spreadsheets. Chapters 16 to 18 cover CSV and JSON, time and scheduling, and sending messages.

items: Expressions and types: integers, floats, strings; variables as names bound to values; `input()` and `print()`; converting with `int()`, `str()`, `float()`.
Flow control: booleans and comparisons, `if`, `elif`, `else`; `while` with `break` and `continue`; `for` over `range()`; importing modules; `sys.exit()`.
Functions: `def`, parameters, `return`, `None`, keyword arguments, local versus global scope, and exception handling with `try` and `except`.

Lists: indexing and slicing, `len`, `append`, `insert`, `remove`, `sort`, list concatenation, `in`, multiple assignment, references versus copies (the cause of many surprises), and tuples as immutable lists.
Dictionaries: key-value pairs, `keys()`, `values()`, `items()`, `get()` with a default, `setdefault()`, nested structures, and pretty printing; a 511 event is exactly this shape.
Strings: escape characters, raw and multiline strings, methods (`upper`, `strip`, `split`, `join`, `startswith`, `isdigit`), f-strings, and justifying text.
Regular expressions: `re.compile`, groups, `|`, `?`, `*`, `+`, `{n}`, character classes, `^` and `$`, `findall`, `sub`, and greedy versus non-greedy; used here to parse road names such as 'I-880 N'.
Files: paths with `pathlib`, `open` in read, write and append modes, `with` blocks, reading lines, and the `shelve` and `json` modules for saving data.
Debugging: raising exceptions, tracebacks, assertions, logging with levels and to files, and the debugger's step, over and continue.
CSV and JSON: `csv.reader` and `DictReader`, writing with `csv.writer`, `json.loads` and `json.dumps`, and reading a web API's JSON into dictionaries.
Time: `time.time()`, `time.sleep()`, `datetime` objects, `timedelta` arithmetic, `strftime` and `strptime`, running programs on a schedule, and launching other programs.

b.s:
import csv, json
with open('data/fremont_events_log.csv', newline='') as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
counts = {}
for r in rows:
    counts[r['event_type']] = counts.get(r['event_type'], 0) + 1
import re
m = re.search(r'(I-\d+|SR-\d+)\s*([NSEW])?', 'Collision on I-880 N')
route, direction = m.group(1), m.group(2)

items: Lists and dictionaries are the two structures most data code is made of; know their methods cold.
A `with open(...)` block, `csv.DictReader` and `json.loads` cover the project's file needs.
Regular expressions are a small language; learn groups and character classes and you can parse most text fields.

b.s: Write a script that reads the incident log with `csv.DictReader`, parses route and direction from `road_names` with a regular expression, and prints counts per route and direction.

resources.title: The official Python tutorial, sections 3–9

b.s: The instruction book written by the people who make Python. It is for looking things up when the friendly book did not say.

Sections 3 to 9 cover numbers and strings, control flow (`if`, `for`, `while`, functions), data structures (lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples), modules, reading and writing files, errors and exceptions, and classes. It is terser than Sweigart and assumes you will experiment. Read a section when you meet that topic in the code, then try its examples in the interpreter.

The tutorial is the authoritative short version of the language: how `for` really works (iterators), how arguments are passed to functions, what a module is and how imports find it, how exceptions propagate up the call stack, and what a class is. Read it once fully after Sweigart, then keep the language reference for details. Section 5 on data structures and section 7 on input and output are the ones the pipeline code exercises most.

This is where the data model becomes precise: mutable versus immutable objects, `is` versus `==`, how comprehension scope works, `*args` and `**kwargs`, `with` statements and context managers, and the exception hierarchy. Pair it with the library reference pages for `collections`, `itertools`, `pathlib` and `dataclasses`, which are the standard-library tools a clean pipeline uses.

Beyond the tutorial, the language reference and the PEPs are where design rationale lives: PEP 8 for style, PEP 484 and successors for typing, PEP 20 for the philosophy. Reading a few accepted and rejected PEPs teaches how language decisions are argued with evidence, which is a useful model for arguing design decisions in your own project.

For a team the tutorial's value is as the shared baseline that code-review standards can point to. Beyond it, the investment that turns research code into production code is static typing (mypy or pyright on every module), packaging, and a linter configuration checked into the repository so style is never a review comment.

The language as its authors describe it: informal introduction (numbers, strings, lists), control flow (if, for, range, break, functions, argument forms, lambda, docstrings), data structures (list methods, comprehensions, tuples, sets, dictionaries, looping techniques), modules and packages, input and output (formatting, files, JSON), errors and exceptions, and classes.

items: Numbers and strings: integer and float arithmetic, `//` and `%`, string indexing and slicing (strings are immutable), and lists as mutable sequences.
Control flow: `for` iterates over any iterable; `range` produces numbers lazily; `else` on loops runs when no `break` occurred; `match` statements for structural matching; `pass` as a placeholder.

Functions in depth: default values evaluated once (the mutable-default trap), keyword and positional-only arguments, `*args` and `**kwargs`, unpacking argument lists, lambda expressions, docstrings and annotations.

Data structures: `list.sort` versus `sorted`, list comprehensions and nested ones, `del`, tuples and packing, sets and their operations, dictionaries and `dict()` construction, `enumerate`, `zip`, `reversed`, `sorted` in loops, and comparison chaining.
Modules: a module is a file; `import` runs it once; `__name__ == '__main__'`; the module search path; packages as directories with `__init__.py`; `from package import name`.
Input and output: f-strings and `format`, `repr` versus `str`, reading and writing files with `with`, `read`, `readline`, iteration over lines, `json.dump` and `json.load`.
Errors: syntax errors versus exceptions, `try`, `except` with specific types, `else`, `finally`, raising, exception chaining, user-defined exceptions, and cleanup with `with`.

Classes: namespaces and scopes (the LEGB rule), class and instance attributes, methods, inheritance, `super()`, private names by convention, iterators (`__iter__`, `__next__`), and generators with `yield` for lazy sequences.
Iterables and generators are how Python streams large files; use them instead of reading everything.
Mutable defaults, references shared between names, and integer versus float division are the classic traps.
Catch specific exceptions and let the rest crash loudly.

The Learn courses are a funnel into Kaggle competitions. Their pedagogy, tiny graded steps, is effective for syntax and weak for design and debugging, the two skills that decide whether a pipeline survives. Use them accordingly and move on quickly.

Kaggle as a platform matters more than this course. It is where tabular machine-learning practice evolved: gradient-boosted ensembles, feature engineering, leakage detection, and careful validation. Reading winning solutions' write-ups for time-series competitions is a research-adjacent habit that this course is the first step toward.

resources.title: The `zoneinfo` and `datetime` documentation

b.s: The instructions for the part of Python that knows about clocks, dates and the different times in different places.

`datetime` handles dates and times; `zoneinfo` knows the time zones of the world. Read the section that explains aware versus naive times (aware means the time knows its zone), then the examples that convert a time from one zone to another. That is the whole trick behind storing every time in UTC.

The key pages: `datetime.datetime` (aware versus naive, `astimezone`, `isoformat`, `fromisoformat`), `timedelta` for arithmetic, and `zoneinfo.ZoneInfo`. Read the aware-versus-naive section twice, because most time bugs are a naive time mistaken for a UTC one. Then learn the pandas equivalents, `tz_localize` and `tz_convert`, which apply the same ideas to a whole column at once.

The docs explain `fold`, the attribute that distinguishes the first and second occurrence of the repeated hour when daylight saving ends. That is how Python represents the November ambiguity that pandas exposes as the `ambiguous` argument. Understanding fold makes the cleaning stage's choice to drop the ambiguous hour a deliberate decision rather than a default.

Time zone rules come from the IANA database through the `tzdata` package and change when governments change rules, so pin the version. The docs' note that naive datetimes are interpreted as local time is a trap on servers set to UTC, and `datetime.utcnow()` returning a naive object is a second trap that the docs now warn about. Both have caused real outages.

Time handling is a recurring production failure class across the industry. The documentation is the specification; the engineering answer is a house rule (UTC everywhere, aware objects only, conversions at the edges) enforced by a linter rule and a test, so the specification never has to be reread under pressure.

Two standard-library modules. `datetime` provides `date`, `time`, `datetime`, `timedelta`, `timezone` and `tzinfo`, with parsing, formatting and arithmetic. `zoneinfo` provides `ZoneInfo`, IANA time zone objects that apply daylight-saving rules.

items: Aware versus naive: a naive datetime has no `tzinfo` and no fixed meaning; an aware one has a zone or offset. Comparing or subtracting a naive and an aware datetime raises an error, which is a feature.

Constructing: `datetime(2026, 3, 8, 1, 30)`, `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` (never `utcnow()`, which is naive), `datetime.fromisoformat('2026-04-12T16:42:00+00:00')`, `datetime.strptime(text, '%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S')` for PeMS's format.

Zones: `ZoneInfo('America/Los_Angeles')` from the IANA database (installed with `tzdata` on systems without one). `dt.replace(tzinfo=zone)` attaches a zone to a naive time; `dt.astimezone(zone)` converts an aware time.

Daylight saving: in spring an hour does not exist (02:00 to 03:00 local); in fall an hour repeats. Python represents the repeated hour with the `fold` attribute (0 for the first occurrence, 1 for the second). Attaching a zone to a naive time in the repeated hour picks `fold=0` unless told otherwise.

Arithmetic: `timedelta(minutes=5)`, `dt + timedelta(...)`, differences give `timedelta` with `.total_seconds()`. Arithmetic on aware datetimes across a DST boundary is done in UTC internally, so it is correct.
Formatting: `isoformat()` produces ISO 8601 (`2026-04-12T16:42:00+00:00`); `strftime` with format codes; `%z` for the offset and `%Z` for the zone name.
pandas mirrors this: `tz_localize` attaches a zone to a naive column (with `ambiguous` and `nonexistent` arguments), `tz_convert` converts an aware column.

b.s:
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
LA = ZoneInfo('America/Los_Angeles')
local = datetime.strptime('11/01/2026 01:30:00', '%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S').replace(tzinfo=LA)   # ambiguous!
utc = local.astimezone(timezone.utc)
second = local.replace(fold=1).astimezone(timezone.utc)   # one hour later

items: Work in UTC with aware objects; convert to local only for display.
Never call `utcnow()`; call `now(timezone.utc)`.
The repeated November hour is real ambiguity; decide explicitly what to do with it.
