phases.lives: Everything this asks for has been explained above: the lessons and topics for the ideas, the walkthroughs for the code, the books and courses for depth. The glossary at the end defines any word that is still new.

phases.title: The math the model uses
phases.meta: weeks 3–11, alongside phases 1 and 3 · ≈60 h · builds stage 3 from a blank file

b.s: Follow every symbol in `00_CONCEPTS.md` and `03_train_from_scratch.py`, and derive the update rule yourself.

items: Linear algebra: vectors, dot product, matrix times vector, matrix times matrix, transpose, norms; what `x @ weights + bias` computes for a whole batch.
Calculus: the derivative as a slope, the chain rule, partial derivatives and the gradient; derivatives of the sigmoid and the log.
Probability: random variables, Bernoulli and normal distributions, expectation, variance, conditional probability and Bayes; the logistic function as a probability.
Statistics: mean, median and percentiles, sampling, the law of large numbers, confidence intervals, what a p-value is and is not, correlation versus causation.
Putting it together: binary cross-entropy from maximum likelihood, and its gradient for logistic regression, then the same lines in the code.

items.title: Linear algebra: vectors, dot products, matrices

b.s: See a row of features as a vector, a batch as a matrix, and a model's score as one multiplication.
A vector is a list of numbers that belong together, like three apples and two pears written as (3, 2). Adding two lists means adding the matching numbers.
A dot product is 'multiply the pairs and add them up'. That is how we mix clues with how much each clue matters.
Compute (2, 3) · (1, 4). Multiply the first numbers, multiply the second numbers, add the two results.
Vectors can be arrows or lists; they have a length and a direction. The dot product x·w = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + … is large when two vectors point the same way.
A matrix is a grid of numbers. Multiplying a matrix by a vector does many dot products at once, one per row. That is how a whole batch of rows gets scored in one line of code, `X @ w`.
With X = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and w = (1, −1), compute X @ w by hand. You should get two numbers.
Shapes must match: an n×d matrix times a d×k matrix gives n×k. The transpose flips rows and columns; the identity leaves things unchanged. Geometrically, a matrix is a linear map.
The dot product equals |x||w|cos θ, so it measures alignment. The set of points where w·x + b = 0 is a line or a plane, which is the decision boundary of a linear model.
In numpy: `@` for products, `.T` for transpose, and broadcasting for adding a bias to every row.
Write the logistic regression score for a whole batch as one matrix product and check the shape of the result against the number of rows.

Vector spaces, linear independence, rank and column space. Projections and least squares through the normal equations XᵀX w = Xᵀy. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors, symmetric matrices and the spectral theorem, the singular value decomposition and principal components.

Positive semidefinite matrices matter here because the Hessian of the logistic loss is one, which is what makes the loss convex. Conditioning explains why standardizing features speeds up gradient descent.
Compute the Hessian Xᵀ diag(p(1 − p)) X for a small X and show it is positive semidefinite by checking vᵀHv ≥ 0 for random v.

Matrix calculus: gradients of quadratic forms and the chain rule in matrix form. Graph Laplacians and spectral graph convolution (the Chebyshev filters in STGCN), random-walk matrices in diffusion convolution (DCRNN), and the power method.
Numerical linear algebra: floating point, stability, and why you never invert a matrix when you can solve a system.
Build the normalized adjacency for the Fremont road graph, compute its eigenvalues, and interpret the smallest ones in terms of connected pieces of road.

Linear algebra is the compute substrate: BLAS and LAPACK, the Accelerate framework on Apple silicon, matrix-multiply throughput as the number that sets training speed, and the distinction between bandwidth-bound and compute-bound kernels. Mixed precision is a linear-algebra decision.
Randomized linear algebra (sketching) for large least-squares problems; tensor decompositions for spatio-temporal data.
Measure GFLOP/s of `X @ W` on the M1 CPU and on MPS for several sizes, plot both curves, and explain their shapes.

b.q: Why does `X @ w` compute every row's score?

a.s: Each row of X dotted with w is one row's weighted sum; the product does all rows in one operation.

b.q: What does a positive semidefinite Hessian buy you?

a.s: Convexity. Every local minimum is global, so gradient descent cannot get stuck.

items.title: Calculus: derivatives, the chain rule, gradients

b.s: Know why stepping against the gradient reduces the loss, and derive the one gradient every model in this course uses.
A derivative tells you how fast something changes, like how steep a hill is right where you are standing.
If you want to reach the bottom, you step downhill. Learning is stepping downhill on the 'mistake' hill.
Draw a hill. Mark where it is steep and where it is flat. Where would a ball roll fastest?
The slope of a line is rise over run. The derivative is the slope of a curve at one point. If the function goes up when x goes up, the derivative is positive.
The chain rule: if y depends on u and u depends on x, then the change in y per x is the change in y per u times the change in u per x.
Gradient descent: move x a little against the slope and repeat.
For f(x) = x², the derivative is 2x. Start at x = 3 with step size 0.1. Take three steps of x ← x − 0.1 · 2x and watch x shrink toward 0.

Rules: power, product, chain. Derivatives of eˣ and ln x, and the sigmoid's own derivative σ′ = σ(1 − σ). Partial derivatives when there are several inputs, and the gradient as the vector of them; it points uphill.
The update rule w ← w − η∇L. Applied to one row's cross-entropy, the derivative with respect to the score z is p − y, which is the term at the heart of lesson 7.
Differentiate the one-row cross-entropy with respect to z and confirm you get p − y for y = 1 and for y = 0.

Multivariable calculus: Jacobians, the chain rule as a product of Jacobians (which is exactly backpropagation), Taylor expansion to second order (the Hessian), convexity from the Hessian, and Lagrange multipliers for constraints.

Optimization: gradient descent converges under a Lipschitz gradient with a step size bounded by the inverse of the Lipschitz constant; momentum as a heavy ball; why the learning rate that works depends on the scale of the features.
Derive the backward pass of a one-hidden-layer network as a chain of Jacobian-vector products, and count the multiplications.

Automatic differentiation: forward mode versus reverse mode, and why reverse mode suits many parameters and one loss. Non-smooth points (ReLU, subgradients). Stochastic gradients as unbiased estimators with variance, convergence rates for convex, strongly convex and non-convex objectives, second-order methods and their scaling limits, natural gradient.
Implement reverse-mode automatic differentiation for scalar operations (a small micrograd) and use it to train lesson 7's model to the same weights.

Differentiable programming as a paradigm: implicit differentiation through optimization layers, differentiating through simulators (a differentiable traffic model), gradient estimators for discrete decisions, and the numerics of mixed precision.
Sketch how you would differentiate through a kinematic-wave traffic simulator to fit its parameters to PeMS data, and what would make the gradient uninformative.

b.q: Why the negative gradient?

a.s: The gradient points toward increasing loss. Learning wants the opposite direction.

b.q: What is backpropagation in one sentence?

a.s: The chain rule applied in reverse order along the computation graph, reusing intermediate results.

items.title: Probability and statistics: distributions, medians, likelihood

b.s: Speak the language the labels, the metrics and the loss are written in.
Probability is how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (always). Flip a coin many times and about half come up heads.
Statistics is looking at lots of numbers and finding the typical one and how spread out they are.
Flip a coin twenty times and count the heads. Is it exactly ten? Is it close?
Random variables and distributions: a coin has two outcomes, a die six, and speeds spread out in a bell-like shape. Mean, median and mode are three kinds of 'typical'; the median resists outliers.
Spread: range and standard deviation. Percentiles: the 85th percentile speed is the speed that 85 % of readings fall below.
Conditional probability: the chance of slow given rain is not the chance of slow.
From a list of twenty speeds, find the median and the 85th percentile by sorting.
Bernoulli, binomial and normal distributions; expectation and variance and their rules; independence. Bayes' rule with a traffic example: P(crash | slow) is not P(slow | crash).
The law of large numbers, sampling variability and confidence intervals. Correlation is not causation: rain and incidents both cause slowness, so incidents and rain correlate.

The likelihood is the probability of the data given the parameters. Maximum likelihood picks the parameters that make the data most probable, and for a yes-or-no outcome that is exactly the cross-entropy loss.
Simulate a thousand coin flips with p = 0.3 in Python and plot the running fraction of heads. Watch it settle.

Probability spaces and random variables formally; joint, marginal and conditional distributions; expectation as an integral; the central limit theorem. Estimators and their bias, variance and consistency; maximum likelihood and its asymptotics; hypothesis tests and the misuse of p-values; the bootstrap; Bayesian inference as prior times likelihood.
The statistical view of learning: regression estimates E[y | x], classification estimates P(y = 1 | x), and the bias-variance decomposition explains why simpler models sometimes win.
Derive the maximum-likelihood estimate of a Bernoulli p, then show that the cross-entropy loss is the negative log-likelihood of the logistic model.

Dependence: stochastic processes, stationarity, autocorrelation and effective sample size; time series as dependent data. Robust statistics and the median's breakdown point. Quantile regression and the pinball loss. Proper scoring rules and calibration as a conditional-expectation property. Exchangeability and conformal prediction. Causal inference basics: confounding and the difference between P(y | do(x)) and P(y | x).
Compute the effective sample size of one station's speed series from its autocorrelation and compare it with the raw row count.

Statistics for ML at scale: high-dimensional inference, concentration inequalities and generalization bounds; sequential experiments (bandits, switchbacks) with interference; Bayesian deep learning and its approximations; uncertainty with guarantees (conformal, PAC-Bayes); causal machine learning under shift.
Write the estimand for 'the effect of an alert on travel time' and list the assumptions needed to identify it from logged data.

b.q: Why is the profile a median and not a mean?

a.s: A few outage days with speed 0 or an imputed 70 would drag a mean; the median ignores them.

b.q: What does the likelihood measure?

a.s: How probable the observed data are under a candidate model. Maximizing it picks the model that explains the data best.

items.title: Logistic regression from scratch: the math the model runs on

b.s: Derive, implement and check the training loop that every later model generalizes: weighted sum, sigmoid, cross-entropy, gradient step.
Imagine a seesaw. Each clue pushes it one way ('slow!') or the other ('fine'). Some clues are heavy, like a crash just ahead, and some are light, like a Tuesday.

Learning means finding out how heavy each clue should be. We look at lots of old days, and every time the seesaw tips the wrong way we make the wrong clues a bit lighter and the right clues a bit heavier.
Guess a friend's favorite color. When you are wrong, change your guess a little toward what they said, not all the way. Keep going until you are right most of the time.
Give each clue a weight, a number. Add up clue × weight for every clue, plus one extra number called the bias. That total is the score.
Squash the score into 0 to 1 with an S-shaped curve called the sigmoid, so it reads as a probability: a big positive score becomes nearly 1, a big negative score nearly 0, and zero becomes 0.5.

To learn the weights, take an old row, compute the probability, compare with what really happened (1 or 0), and nudge each weight a small step in the direction that would have made the guess better. Do that thousands of times and the weights settle.
One clue: 'speed dropped in the last 15 minutes' is 1 or 0. Weight 2, bias −1. Compute the score and the sigmoid for both clue values. Which one says 'probably slow'?

Score z = w·x + b. Probability p = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). Loss for one row, the cross-entropy: −[y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)], which is small when confident and right and huge when confident and wrong.

The gradient is surprisingly clean: ∂loss/∂w = (p − y)·x and ∂loss/∂b = (p − y). The sigmoid's derivative is p(1 − p), and the chain rule cancels it against the log's derivative, leaving error times input.
The update is w ← w − η (p − y) x with a small learning rate η. That line is the whole of `03_train_from_scratch.py`; everything in lesson 9 is this with more layers.
Take x = (1, 0.5), y = 1, w = (0, 0), b = 0, η = 0.1. Compute p, the gradient, and the new w and b. Then compute p again with the new weights and confirm it moved toward 1.

Logistic regression is maximum likelihood for a Bernoulli outcome with a logit-linear mean. The negative log-likelihood is convex in (w, b) (its Hessian X^T diag(p(1 − p)) X is positive semidefinite), so gradient descent with a suitable step reaches the global optimum; L2 regularization is a Gaussian prior and gives the MAP estimate.

Standardizing features conditions the problem; the safe learning rate scales inversely with the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian. Mini-batch SGD trades noise for speed; Adam is unnecessary for a convex problem but harmless.

Without regularization the first-order conditions force the mean predicted probability to equal the observed rate, so the model is calibrated in-sample given an intercept. The decision boundary is a hyperplane; interactions must be built by hand.
Derive the gradient from the negative log-likelihood using the chain rule through σ, and show from the stationarity condition on the intercept that the mean residual is zero at the optimum.

As a generalized linear model, logistic regression uses the canonical link of the Bernoulli family, which is why the gradient has the score-residual form and why iteratively reweighted least squares (Fisher scoring) converges in a few steps. The MLE is asymptotically normal, giving Wald and likelihood-ratio tests, and quasi-complete separation sends coefficients to infinity unless regularized.

Class reweighting is a prior shift: multiplying positive weights by r shifts the learned intercept by about ln r and destroys calibration; undo it with a log-odds offset before reporting probabilities.

Logistic regression is a one-layer network with sigmoid output; softmax is its multiclass form; the maximum-entropy view derives the same model from moment constraints. Its limits are representational, not statistical.
Show that reweighting positives by a factor r changes the asymptotic log-odds by ln r, and derive the correction that restores calibration to the original prevalence.

At scale the same model appears as sparse high-dimensional logistic regression in click-through prediction, trained with distributed SGD or L-BFGS, feature hashing, and per-coordinate learning rates; it persists in production for latency, interpretability and calibration properties that deeper models lack.

The loss lives on in every network as binary cross-entropy with logits, computed through log-sum-exp for numerical stability. Recent theory clarifies what gradient descent does on this loss: on separable data it converges in direction to the maximum-margin classifier (Soudry et al., 2018), which is why early stopping acts as regularization.

Open questions of practical weight: the interaction between class reweighting, calibration and decision thresholds under label shift, and generalization for linear classifiers in the interpolating regime.

State and sketch the proof that gradient descent on logistic loss over linearly separable data converges in direction to the max-margin solution, and explain what it implies for the choice of stopping time.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

Logistic regression is the simplest model that outputs a probability: multiply each feature by a weight, add them up, add a bias, and squash the sum into 0 to 1. Before any such model, features are standardized: each column has its mean subtracted and is divided by its standard deviation, so every column is centred on zero with a spread of about one. Without this a column measured in vehicles per five minutes (hundreds) would swamp a column measured as a fraction (0 to 1), and gradient descent would crawl.

The trap is the same as in lesson 4: the mean `mu` and standard deviation `sd` are computed from the training rows only and then applied to validation and test. `+ 1e-6` keeps a constant column from dividing by zero. `fillna(0)` puts missing values at the mean, a neutral choice. `to_numpy(np.float32)` converts the DataFrame into a plain numpy matrix `X` (rows × features) of 32-bit floats, and the target into a vector `y`, because the hand-written math below works on arrays, not tables. `feats` is a short list of features chosen to keep this lesson readable; `incident_active` is the 511 flag from stage 7.
Standardize with training statistics only.

feats = ["speed_lag_0", "speed_lag_3", "speed_roll_mean_30", "down1_speed", "incident_active", "min_sin", "min_cos"]
mu, sd = tr[feats].mean(), tr[feats].std() + 1e-6
Xtr = ((tr[feats] - mu) / sd).fillna(0).to_numpy(np.float32); ytr = tr.y_30.to_numpy(np.float32)
Xva = ((va[feats] - mu) / sd).fillna(0).to_numpy(np.float32); yva = va.y_30.to_numpy(np.float32)

items: `feats = [...]` — seven features for a readable first model
`mu, sd = tr[feats].mean(), tr[feats].std() + 1e-6` — training mean and spread per column
`Xtr = ((tr[feats] - mu) / sd).fillna(0).to_numpy(np.float32); ytr = ...` — standardized training matrix and its targets
`Xva = ((va[feats] - mu) / sd)...` — validation standardized with the training statistics, never its own

b.s: Three functions, each a few lines. `sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z))` turns any number into a probability: large positive z gives nearly 1, large negative nearly 0, zero gives 0.5. `np.exp` is e raised to a power, applied to a whole array at once. `X @ w` is matrix multiplication: for each row of X, the sum of feature times weight, giving one number per row; `+ b` adds the bias.

The loss is a single number that says how wrong the model is on a batch: cross-entropy, also called log loss. For a row with true label 1 it is −log p, which is near zero when p is near 1 and huge when p is near 0; for label 0 it is −log(1 − p). `np.mean` averages over rows. `np.clip(p, 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)` keeps p away from exactly 0 or 1 so that the logarithm never becomes infinite.

The gradient is the direction in which the loss rises fastest, one number per weight. For this loss and this model it has a famously simple form: the prediction error `e = p - y`, multiplied by the features and averaged. `X.T @ e / len(y)` computes that for every weight at once (`X.T` is the transposed matrix); `e.mean()` is the gradient for the bias. Training will step the weights against this direction.
The model, the loss and the gradient in eight lines.

items: `def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))` — any number to a probability
`p = np.clip(sigmoid(X @ w + b), 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)` — the model's probability per row, kept away from 0 and 1
`return -np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))` — cross-entropy: average penalty for confident wrong answers
`e = p - y` — the error per row
`return X.T @ e / len(y), e.mean()` — gradient for the weights and for the bias

b.s: A gradient formula derived on paper can be wrong by a sign or a factor, and training will still run, only badly. The numerical gradient check compares the formula with a brute-force estimate: nudge one weight up by a tiny amount `eps`, measure the loss, nudge it down, measure again, and divide the difference by 2·eps. That is the slope of the loss along that weight, computed with no calculus at all.

`np.zeros(n, np.float32)` makes a weight vector of zeros; `w.copy()` makes an independent copy so nudging `wp` does not change `w`. Only the first five thousand rows are used because the check is slow (one loss evaluation per weight per side). `np.max(np.abs(num - gw))` is the largest disagreement across all weights; with float32 arithmetic it should be around 1e-5 or below. If it is 0.1, the gradient is wrong; go back to step 2.
Check the gradient numerically before trusting it.

w = np.zeros(Xtr.shape[1], np.float32); b = 0.0
gw, gb = grad(w, b, Xtr[:5000], ytr[:5000])
eps = 1e-4; num = []
for j in range(len(w)):
    wp = w.copy(); wp[j] += eps; wm = w.copy(); wm[j] -= eps
    num.append((loss(wp, b, Xtr[:5000], ytr[:5000]) - loss(wm, b, Xtr[:5000], ytr[:5000])) / (2 * eps))
print(np.max(np.abs(np.array(num) - gw)))     # should be ~1e-5 or smaller

items: `w = np.zeros(...); b = 0.0` — start with all weights zero
`gw, gb = grad(w, b, Xtr[:5000], ytr[:5000])` — the formula's gradient on a small batch
`wp[j] += eps; wm[j] -= eps` — the same weights with one entry nudged up and down
`num.append((loss(wp, ...) - loss(wm, ...)) / (2 * eps))` — the brute-force slope for weight j
`print(np.max(np.abs(np.array(num) - gw)))` — the worst disagreement; should be tiny

b.s: Gradient descent is the training loop: compute the gradient, step the weights a little in the opposite direction, repeat. The step size is the learning rate `eta` (η); 0.1 is reasonable for standardized features. Mini-batch means each step uses a random slice of rows (4096 here) rather than all of them: cheaper per step and, in practice, better.

An epoch is one pass through the training rows. `rng.permutation(n)` shuffles the row numbers so each epoch sees the rows in a new order; `range(0, len(idx), 4096)` walks through them in slices; `j = idx[i:i + 4096]` is one batch's row numbers, and `Xtr[j]` selects those rows. `w -= eta * gw` is the update. After each epoch the validation loss and average precision are printed: the loss should fall and then flatten, and the average precision should rise above the baselines from lesson 6. If validation gets worse while training keeps improving, the model is overfitting and you should stop earlier.
Mini-batch gradient descent with a validation check every epoch.

items: `rng = np.random.default_rng(0); eta = 0.1` — repeatable shuffling; the learning rate
`idx = rng.permutation(len(ytr))` — a new random order every epoch
`j = idx[i:i + 4096]; gw, gb = grad(w, b, Xtr[j], ytr[j])` — one mini-batch and its gradient
`w -= eta * gw; b -= eta * gb` — step against the gradient
`print(epoch, loss(w, b, Xva, yva), ap(yva, sigmoid(Xva @ w + b)))` — validation loss and average precision after each pass

b.s: scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression` is the same model with a tested implementation. It always adds regularization, a penalty on large weights controlled by `C`; setting `C=1e6` makes the penalty negligible so the two fits are comparable. `max_iter=1000` gives its solver enough iterations to converge. `.fit(X, y)` trains; `sk.coef_[0]` are the learned weights.

`np.round(x, 3)` rounds to three decimals for printing. The two weight vectors should agree to a couple of decimals. If they do not, the usual causes are too few epochs, a learning rate that is too large, or a bug the gradient check would have caught. Once they agree you have earned the right to use the library and know what it is doing.
Compare with scikit-learn on the same matrix; the two should agree closely.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
sk = LogisticRegression(C=1e6, max_iter=1000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(np.round(sk.coef_[0], 3)); print(np.round(w, 3))

items: `sk = LogisticRegression(C=1e6, max_iter=1000).fit(Xtr, ytr)` — the library's fit with regularization effectively off
`print(np.round(sk.coef_[0], 3)); print(np.round(w, 3))` — its weights beside yours

b.q: Why cross-entropy and not squared error?

a.s: Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model and is convex in the weights; squared error on a sigmoid output is not convex and its gradient vanishes when the model is confidently wrong.

b.q: What does the bias do?

a.s: It sets the probability when all features are zero (after standardization, the average row). Without it the model cannot match the base rate.

b.q: Why does the gradient check matter if the code is short?

a.s: A sign error or a missing division by n produces a loop that still decreases the loss slowly, and you would never know. Finite differences catch it in one line.

items: 'A bigger learning rate learns faster.' Past a limit set by the curvature it diverges; the loss goes up, not down.
'The weights say which feature matters most.' Only after standardization, and only for the linear part; correlated features share weight arbitrarily.
'Logistic regression is obsolete.' It is the calibration-friendly baseline every other model must beat, and it is inside every neural network's output layer.

resources.title: Khan Academy: Linear algebra, Differential calculus, Statistics and probability

b.s: Video lessons and practice questions that teach math one small step at a time, with a friendly voice, and you earn points for practicing.

Three free courses, each made of short videos and exercises that get harder as you improve. Linear algebra is about vectors and grids of numbers, calculus is about slopes and how things change, and statistics is about averages, spread and chance. Do the exercises after every video; the videos alone will not stick.

Use them selectively rather than front to back. In linear algebra: vectors, dot products, matrix multiplication. In differential calculus: derivatives, the chain rule, and then the multivariable course's unit on partial derivatives and the gradient. In statistics: distributions, the normal curve, sampling, and probability rules including conditional probability. Skip nothing with the word gradient in it; that is the heart of lesson 7.

Khan is remedial in depth but excellent for gaps, and its mastery system is spaced repetition, which is why it works. Pair each unit with the corresponding chapter of Mathematics for Machine Learning to see the same idea at university level, and use Khan's diagnostics to find the specific skill that is rusty rather than redoing a whole subject.

Its limitation is proof and abstraction: it teaches computation, not why the computation is right. For that, Mathematics for Machine Learning and 3Blue1Brown. It remains the fastest way to rebuild one specific skill, such as partial derivatives, in an evening before you need it.

For a research group, mastery-style practice is an underrated onboarding tool for people arriving from adjacent fields. Its per-skill diagnostics let you prescribe precisely (three units, one evening) instead of sending someone away for a semester.

Three self-paced courses with videos and mastery exercises. Linear algebra: vectors, linear combinations, matrices, transformations, and eigenvalues. Differential calculus: limits, derivatives, rules, chain rule, applications; the multivariable course adds partial derivatives and the gradient. Statistics and probability: data displays, summary statistics, probability rules, random variables, distributions, sampling, confidence intervals, tests, and regression.

items: Vectors: arrows with magnitude and direction, or lists of numbers; addition, scalar multiplication, linear combinations and span; the dot product a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = |a||b|cos θ measures alignment; length is √(a·a).

Matrices as transformations: multiplying a matrix by a vector maps space; columns are where the basis vectors land; matrix multiplication composes transformations; the identity does nothing; the inverse undoes; determinant is the area scaling factor (zero means collapse).

Systems and rank: row reduction solves Ax = b; rank counts independent columns; null space and column space; eigenvectors are directions a transformation only stretches, eigenvalues the stretch factors.
Limits and derivatives: the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient, as slope of the tangent, as instantaneous rate; differentiability implies continuity.
Differentiation rules: power, constant multiple, sum, product, quotient, and chain rule d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) g′(x); derivatives of eˣ, ln x, sin, cos; implicit differentiation.

Applications: increasing and decreasing, critical points, maxima and minima, concavity and the second derivative, optimization word problems; the gradient in several variables as the vector of partial derivatives, pointing uphill.
Describing data: mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range, variance and standard deviation (population versus sample), percentiles, histograms and box plots, outliers.

Probability: sample spaces, addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), independence, Bayes' theorem, combinatorics; random variables, expected value, variance, binomial and geometric distributions.

Normal distribution and sampling: z-scores, the empirical rule, the central limit theorem, sampling distributions of means and proportions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and their errors, chi-square and regression basics.

b.s:
a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = |a||b| cos θ
d/dx σ(x) = σ(x)(1 − σ(x)) where σ(x) = 1/(1+e^{−x})
Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])²;   P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)
z = (x − μ)/σ;  CI = x̄ ± z* · s/√n

items: The dot product and matrix-vector product are the whole arithmetic of a linear model.
The chain rule is the whole arithmetic of backpropagation.
Conditional probability and the sampling distribution are the whole arithmetic of evaluation.

b.s: Do the mastery challenges for dot products, the chain rule and conditional probability, then derive the sigmoid's derivative and Bayes' rule on paper without notes.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; do the exercises, skip nothing marked 'gradient'

resources.title: 3Blue1Brown: Essence of linear algebra, Essence of calculus

b.s: Videos with beautiful moving pictures that show what math looks like, so arrows and slopes become things you can see instead of just numbers.

Two YouTube series by Grant Sanderson. The linear algebra one shows vectors as arrows and matrices as ways of stretching and turning space. The calculus one shows slopes and areas built from tiny pieces. Watch each video, then pause and redraw the picture yourself on paper; the drawing is where it sinks in.

Watch the linear algebra series before matrix homework: it turns matrix multiplication into composing transformations, the determinant into a scaling factor, and eigenvectors into directions that do not turn. The calculus series makes the chain rule and the derivative of e to the x intuitive rather than memorized. Neither replaces practice; both make practice make sense.

The series supply the geometric intuition textbooks omit: the dot product as projection, the derivative as a local linear approximation, change of basis as a change of viewpoint. That intuition is what you will lean on when reading about singular value decomposition, principal components and Jacobians, and when debugging a shape error in a matrix product.

Sanderson's method, visual first and symbols second, is a model for explaining your own work. His later videos on neural networks and on the Fourier transform extend the same approach to topics you meet in phases 6 and 8, and his video on backpropagation is the one to show someone who has read the equations and still does not see it.

The channel is evidence that rigorous intuition scales to millions of viewers. For someone who will teach and present, the animation library he built (manim) is also a practical tool for figures in talks, and his explanations of attention are a good benchmark for how clearly a research idea can be communicated.

Two animated video series. Linear algebra (16 videos): vectors, linear combinations and span, linear transformations and matrices, matrix multiplication as composition, determinants, inverse matrices and rank, non-square matrices, dot products and duality, cross products, change of basis, eigenvectors and eigenvalues, abstract vector spaces. Calculus (12 videos): the essence of calculus, the derivative paradox, derivative formulas through geometry, chain and product rules, exponentials, implicit differentiation, limits, integrals, the fundamental theorem, higher-order derivatives, Taylor series.

items: A vector is an arrow from the origin; its coordinates are how far along each basis arrow. Span is everything reachable by scaling and adding; linear dependence means an arrow adds nothing.

A linear transformation keeps grid lines parallel and evenly spaced and fixes the origin; it is fully described by where the basis vectors land, and those landing spots are the matrix's columns. Matrix-vector multiplication is 'apply the transformation'.

Matrix multiplication is composition: apply the right matrix first, then the left; that is why order matters. The determinant is the factor by which area (or volume) scales, negative when orientation flips, zero when space collapses.

Inverse and rank: the inverse undoes a transformation when the determinant is nonzero; rank is the dimension of the output; the null space is what gets squashed to zero; solving Ax = b is asking which vector lands on b.

Dot product and duality: projecting one vector onto another; a 1×n matrix is a linear function to the number line, and every such function is a dot product with some vector, which is why w·x is the natural form of a linear model.
Eigenvectors stay on their own line under the transformation; eigenvalues are their stretch factors; diagonalizing means choosing eigenvectors as the basis so the transformation becomes pure scaling.

Calculus: area under a curve built from thin rectangles; the derivative as the ratio of tiny changes; geometric derivations of d(x²) = 2x dx and d(1/x); the chain rule as nested tiny changes; the product rule as the change in area of a rectangle.
Exponentials: eˣ is its own derivative because its rate of change is proportional to itself; other bases scale by ln; implicit differentiation for relations; limits and ε-δ intuition.

Integration and Taylor series: the fundamental theorem links accumulation to slope; the second derivative as curvature; Taylor series approximate functions with polynomials from derivatives at one point, which is the second-order expansion used in Newton's method and in XGBoost's split gain.

b.s:
A(u + v) = Au + Av;  A(cu) = c·Au
(AB)v = A(Bv);  det(AB) = det(A) det(B)
Av = λv for an eigenvector v
d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) g′(x);  f(x + h) ≈ f(x) + f′(x)h + ½ f″(x)h²

items: A matrix is a transformation; its columns say where the basis lands; multiplication is composition.
A derivative is a tiny ratio; the chain rule multiplies tiny ratios along a path, which is backpropagation.
Taylor's second-order approximation is what boosting and Newton's method use to choose a step.

b.s: After each video, redraw its central picture from memory, then write the corresponding numpy expression and check it on a small example.

resources.lives: video · free · an afternoon each · free; the intuition the exercises lack

resources.title: Immersive Linear Algebra (Ström, Åström, Akenine-Möller)

b.s: An online book where the pictures move. You drag arrows around and the math updates, so you can feel what adding arrows and stretching space means.

A free web book with interactive figures in every chapter: vectors, dot products, matrices, determinants, and what a matrix does to a picture. Play with each figure until the text makes sense. It pairs well with the 3Blue1Brown videos; the videos show you, this lets you touch.

Work through chapters 2 to 6 (vectors, dot product, vector product, matrices, determinants) alongside Khan Academy exercises. The interactive matrix figures make the row-times-column rule and the idea of a transformation concrete, which is what you need to read `X @ w` and the neighbor-mixing matrices without hesitation.

The interactive treatment of change of basis and of the determinant as a volume factor supports the geometric view of eigenvectors and of the singular value decomposition. Use it as the intuition layer under Mathematics for Machine Learning's chapter 2 to 4.

It stops before numerical linear algebra and before spectral graph theory; its value is the mental imagery. For the graph operators in lesson 10 you will need the algebraic view as well, but a picture of what a matrix does to a set of points is what you will actually use when a shape bug appears.
A good example of what interactive explanation can do for a technical topic; if you write explanatory material for a team, this and Distill are the reference points for the medium.

An interactive online book: introduction, vectors, the dot product, the vector product, Gaussian elimination, the matrix, determinants, rank, linear mappings, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors, each with figures you manipulate.

items: Vectors: geometric (arrows) and algebraic (coordinates) views, addition, scaling, length, unit vectors, and the interactive figure that shows a linear combination sweeping a plane.
Dot product: definition, projection of one vector onto another, the angle between vectors, orthogonality, and decomposition into parallel and perpendicular parts, all shown live as you drag arrows.
Vector product: the cross product's direction and magnitude, its use for normals and areas, and its non-commutativity.
Gaussian elimination: solving linear systems by row operations, the meaning of no solution, one solution and infinitely many, with interactive steps.
The matrix: as a table, as a transformation, matrix-vector and matrix-matrix products, transpose, identity and inverse, and the interactive figure showing a matrix deforming a picture.
Determinants: as scaling of area and volume, sign as orientation, properties under row operations, and the link to invertibility.
Rank and mappings: column space, null space, rank-nullity, and linear mappings between spaces; projection and rotation as examples.
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors: the interactive figure where you drag a vector until it lands on its own line; the characteristic equation; diagonalization; symmetric matrices' orthogonal eigenvectors.

b.s:
proj_b(a) = (a·b / b·b) b
det[[a, b], [c, d]] = ad − bc
A = Q Λ Qᵀ for symmetric A (orthogonal eigenvectors)

items: Projection is the geometric meaning of the dot product and of least squares.
The determinant tells you whether a transformation loses a dimension.
Symmetric matrices have orthogonal eigenvectors, which is why covariance matrices and PCA behave.

b.s: Use the eigenvector figure to find both eigenvectors of a symmetric 2×2 matrix by dragging, then confirm them with numpy's `eigh`.

resources.lives: interactive · free · a few evenings · free, interactive; touch what the videos show

resources.title: Seeing Theory (Brown University)

b.s: A website that shows chance with little animations: you flip coins, roll dice and watch the results pile up into shapes.

Free, in the browser, with six chapters: basic probability, compound probability, distributions, frequentist inference, Bayesian inference and regression. Each idea has an animation you control. Spend an evening on it before Think Stats and the distribution shapes will already be familiar.

Its chapters on the central limit theorem, confidence intervals and Bayesian inference give the pictures behind lesson 6's bootstrap and lesson 11's calibration. The regression chapter animates least squares, which is the ancestor of every loss you will minimize.

Use it as a visual glossary while reading Blitzstein or Mathematics for Machine Learning chapter 6: when a definition is opaque, find its animation. It does not replace derivations, but it shortens the time between reading a definition and believing it.
Its coverage is introductory by design; its role for you is teaching, not learning. When explaining calibration or intervals to a non-specialist, its animations are the fastest bridge.
Another instance of explanation as interactive design; worth knowing when you brief a product team on what a confidence interval is not.

Six interactive chapters: basic probability (chance events, expectation, variance), compound probability (set theory, counting, conditional probability), probability distributions (random variables, discrete and continuous, central limit theorem), frequentist inference (point estimation, confidence intervals, bootstrap), Bayesian inference (Bayes' theorem, likelihood, prior to posterior), and regression (least squares, correlation, analysis of variance).

items: Chance events: a probability is a long-run frequency; the coin-flip animation shows the proportion of heads converging to p.
Expectation and variance: expectation as the balance point of a distribution; variance as average squared distance from it; dice animations show both.
Compound events and conditioning: Venn diagrams for union and intersection, counting with permutations and combinations, and conditional probability as restricting to a smaller sample space.

Random variables and distributions: discrete (Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, Poisson) and continuous (uniform, normal, exponential, beta) with adjustable parameters; the central limit theorem animation piles sample means into a bell.

Frequentist inference: point estimates with their sampling variability; confidence intervals drawn many times, most containing the truth; the bootstrap resampling from the data to estimate variability.
Bayesian inference: prior, likelihood and posterior updated as data arrive, shown as changing curves; the effect of a strong or weak prior.
Regression: the least-squares line as the one minimizing squared vertical distances, correlation as the strength of linear association, and analysis of variance as partitioning variability.

b.s:
E[X] = Σ x P(X = x);  Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²]
P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
posterior ∝ likelihood × prior

items: A confidence interval is a procedure that captures the truth a stated fraction of the time; no single interval has a probability.
The bootstrap estimates variability by resampling; block it for dependent data.
Bayesian updating is multiplication of prior and likelihood, renormalized.

b.s: In the confidence-interval animation, run 100 intervals at 90 % and count how many miss; then do the same with the bootstrap on one station's daily mean speed.

resources.lives: interactive · free · an evening · free, interactive; probability you can see

resources.title: Introduction to Probability (Blitzstein, Hwang) and Stat 110

b.s: A book and a set of video classes about chance, taught by a professor who explains coin flips and dice with stories and jokes.

Joe Blitzstein's Harvard course Stat 110 is free on YouTube, and the book with Jessica Hwang is free as a PDF. It covers probability from counting through random variables, expectation, conditional probability and the famous distributions, with lots of worked problems. It goes slower and deeper than Khan Academy.

The chapters on conditional probability and Bayes' rule, on expectation and variance, and on the normal and Bernoulli distributions are the ones the project uses. The book's habit of checking answers by simulation in R (translate to Python) is exactly the computational stance of Think Stats. The strategic practice problems are excellent.

This is the standard first rigorous probability course: it is careful about what a random variable is, why conditioning is the heart of probability, and how the named distributions relate (the 'distribution family tree'). Its treatment of the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem makes the bootstrap and confidence intervals of lesson 6 intelligible.

Blitzstein's stories (the 'fundamental bridge' between probability and expectation, symmetry arguments, indicator random variables) are problem-solving tools that reappear in analysis of algorithms and in variance calculations for estimators. The later chapters on Markov chains are the background for lesson 10's state-space view and for reinforcement learning.

Stat 110 is a model of pedagogy for a technical subject; its problem sets are the reference bank for probability interviews and qualifying exams alike. For research that leans on concentration inequalities and dependence, this is the base layer beneath the measure-theoretic course you take later.

A full first course: probability and counting; conditional probability; random variables and distributions; expectation; continuous random variables; moments; joint distributions; transformations; conditional expectation; inequalities and limit theorems; Markov chains; Markov chain Monte Carlo; Poisson processes.

items: Counting and the naive definition: probability as favorable over total outcomes when outcomes are equally likely; the multiplication rule, binomial coefficients, sampling with and without replacement, the birthday problem; the general definition via axioms.

Conditional probability is the soul of statistics: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B); Bayes' rule; the law of total probability; independence versus conditional independence; classic paradoxes (Monty Hall, Simpson) as exercises in careful conditioning.

Random variables: distributions through PMFs and CDFs; Bernoulli, binomial, hypergeometric, discrete uniform, geometric, negative binomial, Poisson; indicator random variables as a counting tool; the 'fundamental bridge' between probability and expectation: P(A) = E[I_A].

Expectation: linearity holds always, even for dependent variables, which solves many problems by decomposition into indicators; variance and its properties; the law of the unconscious statistician for E[g(X)].

Continuous random variables: PDFs, the uniform, normal (with the 68–95–99.7 rule), exponential (memoryless) distributions; universality of the uniform (inverse-CDF sampling); moment generating functions.

Joint distributions: joint, marginal and conditional distributions; covariance and correlation; the multinomial; the multivariate normal; transformations and convolutions; order statistics; the beta and gamma families and their conjugacy with binomial and Poisson.
Conditional expectation: E[Y|X] as the best predictor; Adam's law E[E[Y|X]] = E[Y]; Eve's law Var(Y) = E[Var(Y|X)] + Var(E[Y|X]), which is the decomposition behind bias-variance intuition.
Inequalities and limits: Markov, Chebyshev, Jensen, Cauchy-Schwarz; the weak and strong laws of large numbers; the central limit theorem and why sample means are approximately normal.

Markov chains: transition matrices, stationary distributions, reversibility; Markov chain Monte Carlo (Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs) as sampling from a distribution you can only evaluate up to a constant, the computation behind Bayesian inference in the final phase.

b.s:
P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B)
E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always;  Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y)
E[Y] = E[E[Y|X]];   Var(Y) = E[Var(Y|X)] + Var(E[Y|X])
Beta(a, b) prior + Binomial(n, k) data → Beta(a + k, b + n − k) posterior

items: Condition carefully; most probability errors are conditioning errors.
Linearity of expectation plus indicators solves what brute force cannot.
Conjugate updates (Beta-Binomial) are the simplest Bayesian model, and Eve's law is bias-variance in disguise.

resources.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong), chapters 2–7

b.s: A big free book about the math inside learning machines. It is for looking things up, not for reading from the first page to the last.

A university textbook, free as a PDF. Chapters 2 to 7 are linear algebra, geometry, matrix decompositions, vector calculus, probability, and optimization. When a lesson mentions a word you do not know, find it in the index and read that section. The pictures and worked examples are good; the exercises are hard and worth trying.

Use it as the reference after Khan Academy and 3Blue1Brown. Chapter 5 on vector calculus explains gradients and the chain rule in the form machine learning uses; chapter 6 covers distributions, expectations and Bayes; chapter 7 explains gradient descent and convexity. Do the exercises for chapters 5 and 7; they are the two chapters that lesson 7 and lesson 9 lean on.

The book's second half applies the math: work chapter 9 on linear regression fully to see maximum likelihood, maximum a posteriori and Bayesian regression in one place, then chapter 10 on principal components for the decomposition view. Its notation matches most ML papers, which makes it the bridge from courses to the literature.

Coverage stops before measure-theoretic probability and before optimization theory proper (convergence rates, duality in depth). For those, Boyd and Vandenberghe on convex optimization and a graduate probability text. It is the right prerequisite for Murphy's Probabilistic Machine Learning, and its exercises are a reasonable self-test before that book.

As a reference for writing, it fixes consistent notation for gradients, Jacobians and distributions that reviewers recognize. Its free availability makes it the safe citation for prerequisites in a paper or an internal design document, and its chapter on optimization is a compact refresher before reading anything on second-order methods.

The mathematical foundations in one notation: linear algebra (systems, vector spaces, independence, basis, rank, linear mappings, affine spaces), analytic geometry (norms, inner products, projections, rotations), matrix decompositions (determinant, eigendecomposition, Cholesky, SVD, matrix approximation), vector calculus (gradients, Jacobians, chain rule, backpropagation, automatic differentiation, higher-order derivatives, linearization), probability and distributions (discrete and continuous, sum and product rules, Bayes, Gaussians, conjugacy, exponential family, change of variables), and continuous optimization (gradient descent, constrained optimization, Lagrange duality, convex optimization).

items: Vector spaces and mappings: vectors as elements of a space closed under addition and scaling; linear independence, basis and dimension; a linear mapping is represented by a matrix once bases are chosen; kernel and image; change of basis.

Geometry: norms (Euclidean, Manhattan), inner products generalizing the dot product, lengths and angles, orthogonality, orthonormal bases, and orthogonal projections onto subspaces, with the projection matrix P = B(BᵀB)⁻¹Bᵀ; least squares as projection.

Decompositions: determinant and trace, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization of symmetric matrices, Cholesky for positive definite matrices, the singular value decomposition A = UΣVᵀ for any matrix, and the Eckart-Young theorem: the best rank-k approximation truncates the SVD (the basis of PCA).

Vector calculus: partial derivatives, the gradient as a row vector of partials, Jacobians of vector-valued functions, the chain rule as Jacobian products; gradients of matrix expressions; backpropagation as reverse-mode automatic differentiation along a computation graph; the Hessian and second-order Taylor expansion.

Probability: random variables, sum and product rules, Bayes' theorem, means and covariances, the Gaussian's marginals and conditionals in closed form, conjugate priors, the exponential family, sufficient statistics, and change of variables for transformed densities.

Optimization: gradient descent and step size, momentum, stochastic gradient descent, constrained optimization with Lagrange multipliers, duality, convex sets and functions, linear and quadratic programs, and why convexity makes local optima global.

For Gaussian (x, y): p(x|y) is Gaussian with mean μ_x + Σ_xy Σ_yy⁻¹ (y − μ_y)

items: The SVD is the universal decomposition: PCA, least squares and low-rank approximation are all views of it.
Backpropagation is the chain rule for Jacobians, evaluated in reverse.
Gaussians are closed under marginalizing and conditioning, which is why they appear everywhere from least squares to Gaussian processes.

resources.title: Think Stats (Downey)

b.s: A free book that teaches statistics by playing with real numbers in Python, instead of only formulas.

Allen Downey's book uses real data and Python code from the first chapter: distributions, averages, spread, probability, and how to tell whether a difference is real or just chance. Free online. Run the code as you read; each chapter's exercises use the same data, so you build up a small toolkit.

The approach is computational: build a distribution from data, compute a percentile, run a simulation instead of memorizing a formula. That is exactly how the profile (a median per slot) and the bootstrap (resampling days) work in this project. The chapters on distributions, probability, estimation and hypothesis testing are the core; the one on correlation is a good antidote to reading too much into a scatter plot.

Downey's simulation-first stance, resampling for confidence intervals and permutation tests for differences, is the modern practical approach and maps directly onto the block bootstrap for average-precision intervals. The treatment is light on theory; pair with chapter 6 of Mathematics for Machine Learning for the formal side.

Compare its resampling viewpoint with classical inference and understand when each is valid: the bootstrap fails for dependent data unless it resamples blocks, which is why lesson 6 bootstraps over days. Downey's Think Bayes is the natural next book for the uncertainty track in phase 8.

The book is an argument that computation has changed how statistics should be taught, and it is right. For someone designing evaluation methodology, its emphasis on effect sizes and simulation over p-values is the correct instinct, and its examples are a template for the kind of small, honest analysis that should accompany every metric in a report.

Exploratory data analysis in Python: distributions (histograms, PMFs, CDFs), probability mass and density, modelling distributions (exponential, normal, lognormal, Pareto), relationships between variables (scatter, correlation), estimation (bias, sampling distributions), hypothesis testing by simulation (permutation tests), linear least squares, regression, time series analysis, and survival analysis.

items: Distributions: the histogram counts, the PMF normalizes, the CDF answers 'what fraction is below x' and makes comparisons easy; percentiles and quantiles read off the CDF; the median and interquartile range are robust summaries.

Modelling: fitting analytic distributions and checking with probability plots; the exponential for waiting times, the normal for sums, lognormal and Pareto for skewed quantities such as incident durations.
Relationships: scatter plots with jitter and transparency, covariance, Pearson correlation for linear association, Spearman for monotone, and why correlation does not imply causation.

Estimation: an estimator's bias and its sampling distribution; the standard error as the spread of estimates over hypothetical repeated samples; simulation to see it; confidence intervals from percentiles of simulated estimates.

Hypothesis testing by simulation: choose a test statistic, simulate the null (permutation or resampling), compute the fraction of simulated statistics at least as extreme (the p-value); the same recipe covers means, proportions and correlations; power and the danger of many tests.

Least squares and regression: minimizing squared residuals, coefficients, R², residual plots, and multiple regression with control variables; the point that a regression coefficient is an association, not an effect.
Time series: decomposition into trend and seasonality, moving averages, serial correlation and autocorrelation, and why naive tests overstate significance for correlated data.
Survival analysis: hazard and survival curves for durations, which fit incident clearance times and episode lengths.
Plot the CDF before the histogram; comparisons and percentiles live there.
Simulate the null and count; that is what a p-value is.
Autocorrelated data need block resampling, or every test is overconfident.

b.s: Compute and plot the CDF of speed for one station on weekdays versus Sundays, then test the difference in medians with a permutation test that permutes whole days, not rows.

resources.title: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra (Strang), OpenCourseWare

b.s: Video lessons by a beloved professor who explains grids of numbers with a chalkboard and a lot of enthusiasm.

Gilbert Strang's MIT course, free on OpenCourseWare with videos, notes and problem sets. It covers vectors, matrices, solving equations, the four fundamental subspaces, projections, determinants, eigenvalues and singular values, in a way that makes the ideas feel concrete. Watch the first ten lectures alongside Khan Academy.

Lectures 1 to 4 (vectors, elimination, matrix multiplication), 14 to 16 (projections and least squares), and 21 to 22 (eigenvalues) are the ones the course needs. Strang's picture of the four subspaces is the mental model behind least squares, which is the ancestor of every loss function you will minimize.

Strang teaches through geometry and examples rather than proofs; his treatment of least squares, of positive definite matrices and of the singular value decomposition is exactly the linear algebra of regression, of the Hessian's convexity argument, and of principal components.

The later lectures on positive definiteness, similar matrices and the SVD connect to optimization and to spectral graph methods; his companion course on matrix methods for data analysis continues into machine learning directly.
A canonical course; for research communication, Strang's habit of stating the idea in one sentence before any symbol is the standard to aim for.

Thirty-four lectures: geometry of linear equations, elimination, matrix multiplication and inverses, factorization A = LU, transposes and permutations, vector spaces and subspaces, the null space and Ax = 0, Ax = b, independence, basis and dimension, the four fundamental subspaces, orthogonality, projections, least squares, Gram-Schmidt, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, differential equations, Markov matrices, symmetric matrices, positive definite matrices, similar matrices, the SVD, linear transformations, change of basis, and applications.

items: Two pictures of Ax = b: rows as planes intersecting, columns as a combination of column vectors landing on b; solvability is whether b is in the column space.
Elimination and LU: row operations as multiplication by elementary matrices; pivots; A = LU records the elimination; inverses exist when elimination finds n pivots.

The four subspaces: column space and null space of A, row space and left null space; their dimensions (rank r, n − r, r, m − r); the row space and null space are orthogonal complements. This is the map that explains every least-squares and regression fact.

Projections and least squares: projecting b onto the column space gives the closest solvable problem; the normal equations AᵀA x̂ = Aᵀb; the projection matrix A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ; fitting a line by least squares; orthonormal bases and Gram-Schmidt make it stable.
Determinants: properties (sign flips on row swap, linear in each row, zero for dependent rows), cofactors, and the formula det = product of pivots.
Eigenvalues: Ax = λx, the characteristic polynomial, diagonalization A = SΛS⁻¹, powers Aᵏ = SΛᵏS⁻¹ for difference equations and Markov chains, and the steady state of a Markov matrix.

Symmetric and positive definite matrices: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors (A = QΛQᵀ), positive definiteness tests (all pivots, all eigenvalues, all leading determinants positive, xᵀAx > 0), and the connection to minima of quadratic functions, which is why a positive definite Hessian means a convex bowl.
The SVD: A = UΣVᵀ from the eigenvectors of AᵀA and AAᵀ; it exposes the four subspaces and orders directions by importance, which is principal components.
Linear transformations and change of basis: a matrix depends on the bases chosen; similar matrices represent the same transformation; the best basis is eigenvectors or singular vectors.

AᵀA x̂ = Aᵀb;  P = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ
A = QΛQᵀ (symmetric);  xᵀAx > 0 for all x ≠ 0 ⇔ positive definite
A = UΣVᵀ;  columns of V are eigenvectors of AᵀA

items: Least squares is projection onto the column space; regression is linear algebra.
Positive definite means a bowl; that is the link between linear algebra and optimization.
The SVD orders the directions in data by variance; PCA is its application.

b.s: Fit speed in 30 minutes as a linear function of four lag features by solving the normal equations with numpy, and compare with `np.linalg.lstsq` and with a projection computed from an orthonormal basis.

resources.title: OpenIntro Statistics

b.s: A free statistics textbook with lots of real examples, written so that anyone can follow it.

A free, openly licensed introductory statistics book with videos and exercises: data collection, summarizing data, probability, distributions, inference with confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, and regression. Slower and more thorough than Khan Academy on inference.

The chapters on probability, on distributions, and on inference (sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and their misuse) give the statistical grounding that lesson 6 assumes. Its regression chapters preview the regression topic.

OpenIntro is careful about experimental design and about what a p-value is, which most machine-learning material glosses. Read it for the inference vocabulary and for its treatment of confounding, then Blitzstein for the probability depth.
It is introductory by design; its value is a correct foundation for the language of uncertainty that the evaluation and causal-inference topics build on.
An openly licensed textbook maintained by a nonprofit, usable in teaching without restrictions; its treatment of study design is what you will point a product team to when they propose an evaluation.

An introductory statistics text with data and code: introduction to data (observations, variables, sampling, experiments), summarizing data (numerical and categorical), probability (rules, conditional probability, random variables, continuous distributions), distributions of random variables (normal, geometric, binomial, negative binomial, Poisson), foundations for inference (point estimates, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing), inference for categorical data, inference for numerical data (t-tests, ANOVA), introduction to linear regression, and multiple and logistic regression.

items: Data and design: cases and variables, numerical and categorical types, observational studies versus experiments, confounding, random sampling versus random assignment, and why only experiments support causal claims.
Summaries: distributions' shape, center and spread; robust statistics; contingency tables and conditional proportions; the danger of comparing groups without accounting for their composition.

Probability: disjoint events, the general addition rule, independence, conditional probability from tables, Bayes' theorem by tree diagrams, random variables' expectation and variance, and linear combinations of random variables.

Named distributions: the normal with z-scores and percentiles, binomial with its normal approximation, geometric and negative binomial for waiting, Poisson for counts per interval, which is the natural model for incidents per hour.

Inference foundations: the sampling distribution of a proportion or mean, the standard error, the central limit theorem's conditions, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests with null and alternative, the p-value, significance level, type 1 and type 2 errors, and the distinction between statistical and practical significance.

Categorical and numerical inference: one and two proportions, chi-square goodness of fit and independence, one-sample and paired t-tests, two-sample comparisons, power and sample size, and ANOVA with its multiple-comparison problem.

Regression: fitting a line, residuals, correlation, conditions for inference on the slope, outliers and leverage; multiple regression with indicator variables, adjusted R², model selection; logistic regression as regression for a binary outcome, its odds-ratio interpretation and diagnostics.
Design decides what can be concluded; random assignment supports causation, random sampling supports generalization.
A p-value measures surprise under the null, not the probability the null is true.
Logistic regression coefficients are log odds ratios; that is how to read the weights of lesson 7.

b.s: Model hourly incident counts on I-880 as Poisson, check whether the variance exceeds the mean (overdispersion), and fit a logistic regression of 'slow at 5 pm' on rain and weekday, interpreting each coefficient as an odds ratio.
