phases.title: Data handling, files and SQL
phases.meta: weeks 8–15 · ≈60 h · builds stage 5 for real

b.s: Build stage 5, the cleaning stage, on a real PeMS file inside 2 GB, and be as fluent in SQL as in pandas.

items: numpy: arrays, dtypes, broadcasting, memory layout; why float32 halves everything.
pandas: Series and DataFrame, indexing, `groupby`, `merge`, time indexes, `shift`, `rolling`, `resample`, categoricals, `read_csv` with `chunksize`, Parquet through pyarrow.
Time zones and daylight saving in practice; data quality: missingness, bounds, duplicates, gaps, PeMS's `% Observed`.
SQL: `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, window functions; DuckDB over Parquet; when a database beats files.
Plotting with matplotlib; reading a plot before trusting a number. Measuring memory and time; polars as a second tool.
The domain data sources: PeMS, 511, Open-Meteo, and what each actually measures.

items.title: Cleaning: from a giant text file to a tidy table

b.s: Turn 200 MB of headerless text a day into a small, correct, gap-free table without ever loading the whole file.
The road sensors send a huge messy pile of numbers, like a toy box with everything dumped in at once.
Cleaning means putting each toy in its bin, throwing out the broken ones, and noticing when a piece is missing so we do not pretend it is there.
When it is done, the pile is a neat shelf where we can find anything fast.
Sort a pile of mixed building blocks by color. Count each color. Set aside any broken piece. Which color had the most?
One day's PeMS file is about 200 MB of text. We read it a chunk at a time so it never fills the memory, and we keep only the Fremont stations, which throws away about 97 % of the rows straight away.

Then we convert the times to a common clock (UTC), throw out impossible numbers such as a speed of 250 mph, mark rows that PeMS mostly made up as missing, and fill short gaps of up to 15 minutes by repeating the last value.
We also make sure every station has a row for every 5-minute slot, even if it is blank, so that 'six rows ago' always means 'thirty minutes ago'.
Finally we save the result in Parquet, a format that stores each column separately and loads in a fraction of a second.
In a spreadsheet, write 24 hourly temperatures. Delete two of them. What is a fair way to fill the holes? Now delete ten in a row. Is filling still fair?

Nine steps. Build the station registry from the metadata file: freeway, direction, postmile, coordinates, lanes, and from the postmile order, each station's upstream and downstream neighbor. Read each gzip in chunks with only the 12 columns you need. Filter to registry station ids inside each chunk. Convert timestamps to UTC with explicit daylight-saving handling. Apply bounds (speed 0 to 100, occupancy 0 to 1, flow up to 3000 per lane). Blank rows with `% Observed` under 50. Forward-fill gaps of at most three steps, within a station only. Reindex every station onto the full 5-minute grid. Write monthly Parquet files in float32.
Why float32: it halves memory and disk, and speed to a hundredth of a mile per hour is more precision than the detector has.
Why the full grid: later, a lag of six rows must mean exactly thirty minutes. If a row is missing, positional shifts silently become the wrong time.
Compute the bytes for 10 million rows × 5 columns at float64 and at float32. Then look up how much memory your machine has and see how many years of each would fit.

The principles are those of any data pipeline: idempotence (re-running yields identical output), streaming over in-memory, columnar storage with predicate pushdown, dtype economy, and validation at the boundary (assert the schema, the value ranges, and 288 rows per station-day).

Daylight saving is the classic correctness trap. `America/Los_Angeles` has a nonexistent hour in March and a repeated hour in November. `ambiguous='NaT'` drops the repeated hour rather than mislabelling half of it; `nonexistent='shift_forward'` handles the spring gap deterministically.

Forward fill must be grouped: `df.groupby('station_id').ffill(limit=3)` so that one station's last value never bleeds into the next station's first missing row. The reindex to the full grid must happen before any positional operation.
Testing: a fixture of a hundred rows that includes a DST boundary, a station boundary and a `% Observed` failure. If the fixture passes, the whole year is likely right; if it fails, you saved a day.
Write a pytest that constructs two stations with a gap at the boundary and asserts that forward fill does not cross it. Make it fail first by removing the groupby.

Imputation is inference. A zero-order hold assumes the process is locally constant; linear interpolation uses the next observed value and therefore looks ahead, which is inadmissible for features at serving time but harmless for cleaning history if labels never use imputed rows. Decide per column which rule applies and write it down.

Missingness mechanism matters: a power outage is missing completely at random; a loop that fails under heavy, stop-and-go traffic is missing not at random, correlated with exactly the state you want to predict. Dropping such rows biases the positive rate downward; filling them biases speed upward.
The registry's neighbor chain assumes a line. Interchanges (I-880 with SR-84, I-680 with Mission) break it; those need explicit edges or the graph model inherits a wrong prior.

Classify each failure cause (power outage, loop failure under congestion, PeMS server outage, roadwork removing a station) by missingness mechanism and state the direction of bias each induces in label prevalence.

At scale this stage is a streaming system with schema evolution, late and corrected data, backfills and lineage. The design that survives is layered: raw is immutable and content-hashed (the manifest in this plan), cleaned is a pure function of raw plus code version, features are a pure function of cleaned. Any month can then be rebuilt bit for bit, which is what makes an evaluation trustworthy a year later.

Detector health deserves a model of its own, with the imputation mask exposed downstream as a feature. On unified-memory hardware the cleaning stage is memory-bandwidth-bound long before it is compute-bound; profile with real files rather than reasoning about big-O.

Research threads: learned spatio-temporal imputation versus the downstream model learning the imputer; treating the observation mask as data; and reproducible backfills when the upstream provider re-publishes a corrected day.
Design the backfill procedure for a corrected PeMS day: what is recomputed, what is invalidated (features, models, logged metrics), and how the manifest records it.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

The meta file is PeMS's list of every station in district 4 with its location and role; it is tab-separated, so `sep="\t"` tells `read_csv` that the delimiter is a tab, not a comma. A registry is the course's word for the small, curated table of the stations the model uses, built once and saved.

Filtering to Fremont is a chain of boolean tests joined with `&` (and), each wrapped in parentheses because pandas needs that. `Fwy.isin([880, 680, 84])` keeps the three freeways through Fremont. `Latitude.between(...)` and `Longitude.between(...)` keep the box around the city. `Type == "ML"` keeps mainline detectors and drops ramps and HOV lanes. `.copy()` makes an independent table so later edits do not warn about modifying a slice.

Neighbors: PeMS gives every station a postmile, `Abs_PM`, its distance along the freeway. Sort by freeway, direction and postmile and the stations line up in driving order. `groupby(["Fwy", "Dir"]).ID.shift(1)` then gives, within each freeway-direction, the station one position earlier in the list: the upstream neighbor, the one traffic comes from. `shift(-1)` gives the downstream neighbor, the one traffic goes to. `to_parquet` saves the registry.
Build the registry once from the meta file and derive neighbors from postmile order.

meta = pd.read_csv("data/pems_meta/d04_text_meta_2026_03_01.txt", sep="\t")
fre = meta[(meta.Fwy.isin([880, 680, 84])) & meta.Latitude.between(37.447, 37.612)
           & meta.Longitude.between(-122.075, -121.888) & (meta.Type == "ML")].copy()
fre = fre.sort_values(["Fwy", "Dir", "Abs_PM"])
fre["upstream_id"]   = fre.groupby(["Fwy", "Dir"]).ID.shift(1)
fre["downstream_id"] = fre.groupby(["Fwy", "Dir"]).ID.shift(-1)
fre.to_parquet("data/pems_meta/fremont_stations.parquet")

items: `meta = pd.read_csv(..., sep="\t")` — load the station list, tab-separated
`fre = meta[(...isin...) & (...between...) & (...between...) & (...== "ML")].copy()` — keep mainline stations on 880, 680 and 84 inside the Fremont bounding box
`fre.sort_values(["Fwy", "Dir", "Abs_PM"])` — order stations along each freeway in each direction
`fre.groupby(["Fwy", "Dir"]).ID.shift(1)` — the previous station along the road: upstream
`...shift(-1)` — the next station along the road: downstream
`fre.to_parquet("data/pems_meta/fremont_stations.parquet")` — save the registry for every later stage

b.s: A day's PeMS file is about 200 MB compressed and several gigabytes as a DataFrame, more than a 16 GB Mac can spare while other things run. Streaming means reading a file in pieces and keeping only what you need from each piece. `chunksize=200_000` makes `read_csv` return an iterator: instead of one table, a sequence of tables of two hundred thousand rows each, one at a time.

`keep = set(fre.ID)` turns the registry's station ids into a set, a collection built for fast 'is this in there' tests. Inside the loop, `chunk[chunk.station.isin(keep)]` keeps the rows whose station is a Fremont station, a few percent of each chunk, and `parts.append` stores that small piece in a list. `pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)` glues the pieces into one table and renumbers the rows. Peak memory is one chunk plus the kept rows, never the whole file. `path` is the day's filename from step 2.1; `cols` is the column list from lesson 2.
Stream one day, keeping only registry stations in each chunk.

keep = set(fre.ID)
parts = []
for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, header=None, usecols=range(12), names=cols, chunksize=200_000):
    parts.append(chunk[chunk.station.isin(keep)])
day = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)

items: `keep = set(fre.ID)` — the registry ids as a set for fast membership tests
`for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, ..., chunksize=200_000):` — read the file two hundred thousand rows at a time
`parts.append(chunk[chunk.station.isin(keep)])` — keep only Fremont rows from this chunk
`day = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)` — one table of the day's Fremont rows

b.s: Three cleaning rules, all applied with `.loc`, pandas' way of selecting rows and columns by label and assigning to them. `day.loc[mask, "speed"] = np.nan` sets the speed to missing for every row where the mask is true.

The timestamp conversion is the same three-part chain as lesson 2.4, wrapped in parentheses so it can be split across lines. Bounds: a speed below 0 or above 100 miles per hour is a sensor fault, not a fact, so `~day.speed.between(0, 100)` (the tilde means not) picks the impossible rows and blanks them. Imputed rows: `pct_obs` is the share of a five-minute row that came from real observations; PeMS fills the rest in with estimates. Below 50 percent the row is more guess than measurement, so speed, occupancy and flow are all blanked. Blanking with NaN rather than deleting keeps the row on the time grid.
Convert time, apply bounds, blank imputed rows.

day["timestamp"] = (pd.to_datetime(day.ts, format="%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S")
    .dt.tz_localize("America/Los_Angeles", ambiguous="NaT", nonexistent="shift_forward").dt.tz_convert("UTC"))
day.loc[~day.speed.between(0, 100), "speed"] = np.nan
day.loc[day.pct_obs < 50, ["speed", "occ", "flow"]] = np.nan

items: `day["timestamp"] = (pd.to_datetime(...).dt.tz_localize(...).dt.tz_convert("UTC"))` — text to Pacific to UTC, as in lesson 2
`day.loc[~day.speed.between(0, 100), "speed"] = np.nan` — impossible speeds become missing
`day.loc[day.pct_obs < 50, ["speed", "occ", "flow"]] = np.nan` — mostly-imputed rows lose all three measurements

b.s: Every later stage assumes that each station has exactly one row per five-minute slot, in order, with no gaps: the full grid. Missing rows must be added as NaN, not skipped. An index in pandas is the row labels; a MultiIndex is a two-level index, here (station, timestamp). `pd.MultiIndex.from_product` builds every combination of the station list and the timestamp list: N stations × 288 slots.

`pd.date_range(start, periods=288, freq="5min", tz="UTC")` makes the 288 slot timestamps; `day.timestamp.min().floor("D")` is midnight UTC of the day in the file. `set_index([...])` makes station and timestamp the row labels; `rename_axis` gives the levels the names the rest of the course uses; `reindex(grid)` reorders onto the full grid, inserting NaN rows for any missing slot.

Forward fill (`ffill`) copies the last known value into the following NaN slots, and `limit=3` stops after three slots (fifteen minutes) so a dead detector does not keep reporting a stale speed for hours. `groupby(level="station_id")` makes the fill stay inside one station, so a value never leaks from the end of one station into the start of the next. Finally `astype(float32)` stores the three measurements as 32-bit floats, half the memory of the default 64-bit, which is plenty of precision for a speed.
Reindex onto the full grid per station, then forward-fill within station.

grid = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([sorted(keep), pd.date_range(day.timestamp.min().floor("D"), periods=288, freq="5min", tz="UTC")],
                                  names=["station_id", "timestamp"])
tidy = day.set_index(["station", "timestamp"]).rename_axis(["station_id", "timestamp"]).reindex(grid)
tidy[["speed", "occ", "flow"]] = tidy.groupby(level="station_id")[["speed", "occ", "flow"]].ffill(limit=3)
tidy = tidy.astype({"speed": "float32", "occ": "float32", "flow": "float32"})

items: `grid = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([stations, slots], names=["station_id", "timestamp"])` — every station × every five-minute slot of the day
`tidy = day.set_index(["station", "timestamp"]).rename_axis([...]).reindex(grid)` — put the rows on that grid, with NaN where a slot is missing
`tidy[...] = tidy.groupby(level="station_id")[...].ffill(limit=3)` — carry each station's last reading forward for up to three slots
`tidy = tidy.astype({... "float32"})` — halve the memory of the measurement columns

b.s: `assert` is Python's way of saying 'this must be true, stop with an error if not'. It is the cheapest safety net there is: an assertion that fails at the end of a stage is far better than a silent wrong file used by every later stage. Here it checks that every station really has 288 rows after reindexing; the `.all()` says the test must hold for every station.

`reset_index()` turns the two index levels back into ordinary columns, because Parquet stores columns, and `to_parquet` writes the day's tidy table into the month file (in the real script the days are concatenated first). Also log how long the stage took and how much memory it used; lesson 12.5 gives the line that does it. Checks like range and row counts belong before every write, never after.
Validate before writing: 288 rows per station, values in range, and log memory and seconds.

assert (tidy.groupby(level="station_id").size() == 288).all()
tidy.reset_index().to_parquet("data/pems_processed/2026-03.parquet")

items: `assert (tidy.groupby(level="station_id").size() == 288).all()` — stop if any station is not on the full daily grid
`tidy.reset_index().to_parquet("data/pems_processed/2026-03.parquet")` — write the tidy table with station and timestamp as columns

b.q: Why filter inside each chunk rather than after concatenating?

a.s: Concatenating first means holding the whole district-day in memory, about 1.3 million rows and every column. Filtering per chunk keeps the peak under a few hundred megabytes.

b.q: What goes wrong if you forward-fill without grouping by station?

a.s: The last value of station A fills the first missing rows of station B, inventing data that looks real and is completely wrong.

b.q: Why drop the ambiguous November hour instead of resolving it?

a.s: Half of those rows belong to the first 1 am and half to the second; the file does not say which. Guessing mislabels an hour of data every year; dropping loses one hour per year, honestly.

items: 'Parquet is just a faster CSV.' It is columnar and typed; the dtypes you write are the dtypes you get back, and only the columns you ask for are read.
'Filling gaps is harmless.' Every fill is a model; a fill that looks ahead leaks the future into features.
'Cleaning is a one-off.' It is the stage that runs on every new day forever, and the one whose silent errors are costliest.

items.title: SQL and databases: where data usually lives

b.s: Ask questions of a database in SQL, know when a database beats files, and never be stuck because the data is not a CSV.
Most numbers in the world live in databases, which are like giant well-organized filing cabinets.
SQL is the way you ask the cabinet questions: 'show me every crash on I-880 in March, biggest first.' The cabinet answers with a table.
Think of a question you could ask about the incident list, like 'which road had the most crashes?' Say it as a sentence starting with 'show me'.

A database stores tables (rows and columns) and lets many programs read and write them safely. SQL is the language for questions: `SELECT` picks columns, `WHERE` filters rows, `GROUP BY` counts or averages per group, `ORDER BY` sorts, and `JOIN` combines two tables that share a key, like events and stations.
SQLite is a database in a single file with no server; DuckDB is one built for analysis and can query Parquet files directly. Both come free with Python.
Load `fremont_events_log.csv` into DuckDB and run: `SELECT road_names, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY road_names ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 5`.

The core of SQL in one afternoon: `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` with aggregates, `HAVING`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, inner and left `JOIN`, subqueries, and `CASE`. Window functions (`LAG`, `AVG() OVER`) compute lags and rolling means inside the database, which is stage 8 in another language.
Schemas and keys: a primary key identifies a row, a foreign key links tables, an index makes lookups fast. Types matter: store timestamps as timestamps, not text.
When to use what: files (Parquet) for a pipeline that rebuilds from raw; a database when several programs share live data, need transactions, or need fast lookups by key.
Rebuild the lag-3 speed feature with a window function in DuckDB over one month of Parquet and check it equals the pandas version row for row.

The relational model: relations, keys, normalization (and when to denormalize for analytics), the difference between OLTP (many small transactions) and OLAP (large scans and aggregates), and why columnar engines such as DuckDB dominate the second.

Query execution: how a planner turns SQL into scans, joins and aggregates, why indexes help lookups but not scans, and how to read an `EXPLAIN` plan. Transactions and ACID guarantees; concurrency and isolation levels in one paragraph.

From Python: `duckdb.sql()` over DataFrames and Parquet, `sqlite3` in the standard library, SQLAlchemy for a server database. A feature pipeline can be written entirely in SQL over Parquet, which is often faster and easier to audit than pandas.
Write the profile computation (median speed per station, slot and day type on training rows) as one SQL query in DuckDB and compare its runtime and memory with the pandas version.

Data modelling for ML: point-in-time correctness expressed as `AS OF` joins, slowly changing dimensions for station metadata that changes when detectors are replaced, and event tables versus state tables. Lakehouse formats (Parquet with a table layer) as the current default for analytical data.

Query optimization matters at scale: predicate pushdown, partition pruning, join ordering. The same pipeline can run on DuckDB on one machine and on a distributed engine (Spark, BigQuery) with mostly the same SQL, which is the argument for writing transformations in SQL.

Design a schema for the pipeline's data (raw, cleaned, features, predictions, monitoring) with keys and partitioning, and write the `AS OF` join that attaches the latest station metadata valid at each timestamp.

At scale, data platforms are the substrate of ML: streaming ingestion, table formats with time travel, feature stores backed by both an offline warehouse and an online key-value store, and governance (lineage, access control, retention). The hard problems are consistency between offline and online views and reproducibility of training sets from a warehouse that changes.
Research and engineering overlap in query engines for ML (vectorized execution, GPU databases) and in declarative feature definitions compiled to both batch and streaming.
Specify how the training table for one model version could be reconstructed bit for bit from the warehouse a year later, and what the warehouse must guarantee for that to be possible.

b.q: When does a database beat Parquet files?

a.s: When several programs share live data, when you need transactions, or when you need fast lookups by key. A rebuild-from-raw pipeline is happier with files.

b.q: What does a window function give you that GROUP BY does not?

a.s: A value per row computed over neighboring rows, such as the previous value or a rolling average, without collapsing the rows.

resources.title: Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition (McKinney), chapters 4–8 and 10–11

b.s: A book by the person who invented pandas, the tool that turns big tables of numbers into things you can sort, count and draw.

Wes McKinney created pandas and wrote this book about it. Chapters 4 to 8 teach numpy and pandas basics: arrays, tables, reading files, cleaning messy values, and combining tables. Chapters 10 and 11 teach grouping and time series, which this project uses everywhere. It is free online; do the examples with the project's own data instead of the book's.

The essential chapters for stages 5 and 8: 5 (pandas basics), 7 (cleaning: missing data, duplicates, transformations), 8 (merging and reshaping), 10 (groupby, the split-apply-combine that builds the speed profile), and 11 (time series: resampling, shifting, rolling windows, time zones). Do chapter 11 twice; every lag, rolling mean and DST fix in this pipeline comes from it.

The book explains pandas' model (index alignment, dtypes, categoricals) so you can predict behavior instead of guessing. Understanding index alignment prevents the silent misjoins that plague feature engineering, and the numpy chapter's broadcasting and vectorization are the reason loops are avoided. Its appendix on advanced numpy is worth reading before lesson 9's hand-written backward pass.

Its limits are scale and the newest tooling: little on Arrow-backed dtypes, nothing on polars or out-of-core processing. Read the pandas documentation on Copy-on-Write and Arrow strings, and the polars guide, to see where the ecosystem is heading. The book's groupby chapter remains the clearest explanation of split-apply-combine in print.

pandas' design decisions (label alignment, mutable frames, Python-level groupby) explain its performance ceiling and why Arrow-native tools win the cleaning stage while pandas keeps the analysis stage. McKinney's later work on Apache Arrow is the continuation of the story, and understanding both is what lets you choose a tool per stage rather than per habit.

numpy basics (chapter 4), pandas basics (5), data loading and file formats (6), cleaning and preparation (7), wrangling: join, combine, reshape (8), data aggregation and group operations (10), and time series (11).

items: numpy arrays: homogeneous, typed (`dtype`), n-dimensional; creation, arithmetic elementwise, broadcasting rules (trailing dimensions of size 1 stretch), indexing and slicing return views, boolean masks select, fancy indexing copies; universal functions, `where`, aggregations along an axis, sorting, unique; random number generation. Vectorization replaces loops.

pandas objects: `Series` (values plus an index) and `DataFrame` (columns sharing an index). Indexing with `loc` (labels) and `iloc` (positions); alignment: arithmetic between objects lines up on index labels and produces NaN where they differ; reindexing; sorting; descriptive statistics; `value_counts`; correlation.

Loading: `read_csv` with `sep`, `header=None`, `names`, `usecols`, `dtype`, `parse_dates`, `chunksize` (an iterator of DataFrames for files too large for memory), `nrows`; writing with `to_csv`; JSON, Parquet (`read_parquet`, `to_parquet` with pyarrow), and databases through SQLAlchemy.

Cleaning: missing data (`isna`, `dropna`, `fillna` with values, methods and limits), duplicates, `map` and `replace`, renaming, binning with `cut` and `qcut`, outliers with boolean masks, permutation and sampling, dummies with `get_dummies`, string methods on `.str`, regular expressions in columns, and categorical dtype for memory and speed.

Wrangling: hierarchical indexing, `merge` (inner, left, outer, on keys, with suffixes and validation), `join`, `concat` along axes, `combine_first`, reshaping with `stack`, `unstack`, `pivot` and `melt`.

Group operations: `groupby` splits by keys, applies a function, and combines; aggregations (`sum`, `mean`, `size`, custom with `agg`), transformations that return same-shaped results (`transform`, which is how a per-station lag is built), `apply` for arbitrary functions, group-wise fills, quantile analysis, and pivot tables and cross-tabulations.

Time series: `Timestamp`, `DatetimeIndex`, parsing, generating ranges with frequency strings (`'5min'`, `'D'`), shifting (`shift` by positions or by frequency), time zones (`tz_localize`, `tz_convert`), periods, resampling (downsample with aggregation, upsample with fill), rolling and expanding windows with `min_periods`, exponentially weighted windows, and moving-window correlations.

b.s:
for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, header=None, usecols=range(12), names=cols, chunksize=200_000):
    parts.append(chunk[chunk.station.isin(keep)])
df['speed_lag_3'] = df.groupby('station_id').speed.shift(3)
prof = tr.groupby(['station_id','daytype','slot']).speed.median()
df.set_index('timestamp').groupby('station_id').speed.rolling('30min').mean()

items: Alignment on the index is pandas' defining behavior; know it or your joins will silently misalign.
`groupby(...).transform` and `shift` inside groups are the two operations feature engineering is built from.
Chunked reading, categoricals and float32 are how a 16 GB machine handles a year of data.

b.s: Implement stage 5's cleaning on one district-day with chunked reading, then compute per-station lag-1 and rolling-30-minute means with groupby, and verify a random row by hand.

resources.lives: book · free · weeks · free online; the pandas book by pandas's author

resources.title: pandas user guide: Time series and date functionality

b.s: The manual page for the part of pandas that understands dates, times and clocks.

One long page in the pandas documentation. It shows how to make a range of 5-minute timestamps, shift values forward and back, compute rolling averages, and convert between time zones. Read it with a notebook open and try each example on one station's data from the project.

The sections you need: date ranges and frequency strings (`freq='5min'`), shifting, `rolling` windows, `resample`, and the time-zone section covering `tz_localize`, `tz_convert`, and the `ambiguous` and `nonexistent` arguments. This page is where the daylight-saving behavior in stage 5 is specified, so read that section with the November example in front of you.

Understand the difference between a positional shift and a time-based shift, and why the full-grid reindex in stage 5 makes them agree. Also the exact semantics of `rolling`: windows are right-aligned by default, `center=True` looks ahead and is therefore forbidden for features, and `min_periods` controls when the window starts producing values.

The guide documents edge behaviors (periods versus timestamps, offsets, business-day calendars) that matter for holiday and weekday features, and the performance notes on tz-aware columns. Read the Copy-on-Write page alongside; it changed chained-assignment semantics and quietly breaks old code.

The precise semantics of window operations are what point-in-time correctness rests on. For an engineering organization the right move is to encode them once in a feature library with tests rather than rereading the guide per project, and to treat any window parameter as part of the model's versioned configuration.

Everything pandas does with time: parsing and constructing timestamps, date ranges and frequencies, indexing by time, shifting and lagging, time zones, resampling, periods, and the related pages on window operations.

items: Timestamps and ranges: `pd.Timestamp`, `pd.to_datetime` with `format` for speed and safety, `pd.date_range(start, periods, freq='5min', tz='UTC')`; frequency aliases (`min`, `h`, `D`, `W`, `MS`) and anchored offsets.
Indexing: partial string indexing (`df.loc['2026-03']`), slicing by time, `at_time`, `between_time`, `first`, `last`; the index must be sorted for slices to be efficient.
Shifting: `shift(n)` moves values by n rows (positional; only a time shift if the grid is complete); `shift(freq='5min')` moves the index instead; `diff` for changes.

Time zones: naive versus aware; `tz_localize('America/Los_Angeles', ambiguous=..., nonexistent=...)` where `ambiguous` accepts `'raise'`, `'NaT'`, `'infer'` or a boolean array, and `nonexistent` accepts `'raise'`, `'NaT'`, `'shift_forward'`, `'shift_backward'`; `tz_convert('UTC')`; arithmetic in UTC.

Resampling: `resample('5min')` then an aggregation (`mean`, `sum`, `first`) to downsample, or `asfreq` and `ffill` to upsample; `origin` and `label` control bin edges; resampling groups by time the way `groupby` groups by key.

Windows: `rolling(window)` by count or by time offset (`'30min'`), `min_periods`, `center` (which looks ahead; never for features), `expanding`, `ewm` with `span` or `halflife`; aggregations, `apply`, and windowed correlation.
Periods and offsets: `Period` for spans (a month), `PeriodIndex`, conversions, and `DateOffset` arithmetic for business calendars and holidays; `pandas.tseries.holiday` for custom calendars.
Performance: keep the index sorted, prefer vectorized datetime accessors (`dt.hour`, `dt.dayofweek`), and avoid Python-level `apply` on datetimes.

b.s:
ts = pd.to_datetime(df.ts, format='%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S').dt.tz_localize('America/Los_Angeles', ambiguous='NaT', nonexistent='shift_forward').dt.tz_convert('UTC')
grid = pd.date_range(day, periods=288, freq='5min', tz='UTC')
s.rolling(6, min_periods=3).mean()   # trailing 30 minutes on a 5-minute grid

items: `shift` is positional; the full grid is what makes it a time shift.
`ambiguous` and `nonexistent` are not optional for a US time zone; choose and document.
Trailing windows only; `center=True` leaks the future.

b.s: Localize and convert one November week, reindex to the full grid, and prove with an assertion that every station has exactly 288 rows per day after the DST change.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; the `shift` and `rolling` semantics live here

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Pandas, Data Cleaning, Data Visualization

b.s: Three short online lessons about sorting tables, tidying up messy numbers, and drawing charts from them.

Browser lessons with instant grading. Pandas: selecting, grouping and summarizing tables. Data Cleaning: missing values, scaling, parsing dates, fixing inconsistent text. Data Visualization: line charts, bar charts and histograms with the seaborn library. About an afternoon each; do them between chapters of McKinney.

They rehearse exactly the operations of stage 5 (missing data, parsing dates, deduplication) and the plots you will make of a station's day and week. Their datasets are small and tidy compared with a PeMS file, so treat them as syntax practice and then confront the real 200 MB file, where the same operations need chunking and care.

Use them for the mechanics and then go to the source: the matplotlib documentation for control over figures, and a book such as Fundamentals of Data Visualization (Wilke, free online) for how to design a plot that communicates. Learn to read a plot before trusting a metric; the fundamental-diagram scatter and the daily speed line should become habits.

The visualization course stops at defaults. The skills that matter for this project are diagnostic plots: reliability diagrams, lead-time histograms, per-station error maps, and autocorrelation plots. Build a small plotting module for the project so every evaluation produces the same figures.

Visualization is a research instrument, not decoration. A reliability diagram or a lead-time distribution communicates what a table of metrics hides, and the habit these courses seed, plotting before concluding, is worth more than their content. Wilke's book and Tufte remain the references for the design side.

Pandas: creating, reading and writing; indexing, selecting and assigning; summary functions and maps; grouping and sorting; data types and missing values; renaming and combining. Data Cleaning: handling missing values, scaling and normalization, parsing dates, character encodings, inconsistent data entry. Data Visualization: line charts, bar charts and heatmaps, scatter plots, distributions, plot types and custom styles, and a final project.

items: Selecting: `iloc` by position, `loc` by label, conditional selection with boolean expressions and `isin`, assignment to columns.
Summaries and maps: `describe`, `mean`, `unique`, `value_counts`; `map` and `apply` to transform; vectorized arithmetic between columns.
Grouping and sorting: `groupby` with `size`, `agg` of several functions, multi-index results and `reset_index`, `sort_values` by one or more columns.

Types and missing values: `dtype` and `astype`, NaN detection with `isnull`, `fillna` with a value or a strategy, `replace`; decide whether a value is missing because it does not exist or was not recorded, which is the `% Observed` question.

Cleaning dates and text: `pd.to_datetime` with an explicit format, detecting rows that fail to parse, character encodings for legacy files, and fixing inconsistent categories with normalization and fuzzy matching.
Scaling versus normalization: scaling changes the range (min-max), normalization changes the shape (Box-Cox); when each is appropriate and when neither is (tree models).

Visualization with seaborn: `lineplot` for time, `barplot` and `heatmap` for categories and matrices, `scatterplot`, `regplot`, `lmplot`, `swarmplot`, `histplot` and `kdeplot` for distributions, `jointplot`; choosing a plot by the question.

b.s:
df.groupby('station_id').speed.agg(['mean', 'median', 'count'])
sns.lineplot(data=one_day, x='timestamp', y='speed')
sns.heatmap(profile.pivot(index='station_id', columns='slot', values='speed'))

items: Decide what a missing value means before filling it.
Parse dates with an explicit format and inspect the rows that fail.
Choose the plot from the question: distribution, relationship, comparison or change over time.

b.s: Make three plots of one station: a day line, a weekday-versus-Sunday distribution, and a station-by-slot heatmap of the profile; write one sentence each about what they show.

resources.lives: course · free · an afternoon each · free, short

resources.title: The polars user guide, first three chapters

b.s: The manual for a newer, faster tool that does the same job as pandas: turning big tables into answers.

Polars is a table library written in the Rust language. It is often several times faster than pandas and uses less memory, which matters on a 16 GB machine. The first chapters cover expressions (how you describe what you want), selecting and filtering rows, and grouping. Do stage 5 once in pandas and once in polars, and time both.

Its model differs from pandas: expressions instead of index alignment, lazy evaluation where `scan_csv` plans the whole query and runs it once, strict dtypes, and no index. For streaming a district-day file and keeping a hundred stations, the lazy scan with a filter is exactly right and runs in a few seconds where pandas takes twenty.

Learn the lazy API and streaming collection, and understand why immutability and the absence of an index make parallel execution straightforward. Interoperation goes through Apache Arrow, so `to_pandas` and `from_pandas` are cheap or zero-copy for most dtypes, which lets you use polars for the heavy stage and pandas for analysis without friction.

Polars represents the Arrow-native, query-optimized direction of data tooling, alongside DuckDB. For pipelines it is the better default; for ad hoc analysis pandas still has the larger ecosystem. Know both and choose per stage; the guide's chapter on the query optimizer explains why the same operation costs so differently.

The performance gap is architectural (columnar memory, SIMD, multithreading, query optimization) rather than incidental, and on unified-memory hardware both libraries end up limited by memory bandwidth. Benchmark on the real file before choosing, and note that the decision is per stage: the cleaning stage is a query, the modelling stage is not.

Getting started (installation, reading, selecting, filtering, grouping), concepts (data types, data structures, contexts: select, filter, with_columns, group_by; expressions; lazy versus eager), and expressions (basic operators, column selection, casting, strings, aggregation, missing data, window functions, folds, lists, user-defined functions, and the streaming API).

items: Data model: a DataFrame of typed columns with no index; strict dtypes; `pl.read_csv`, `pl.read_parquet`, `pl.scan_csv` and `pl.scan_parquet` for lazy frames.

Contexts and expressions: `select` picks and computes columns, `filter` keeps rows, `with_columns` adds columns, `group_by(...).agg(...)` aggregates; expressions (`pl.col('speed').mean()`) are composable and run in parallel; no row-by-row Python.

Lazy evaluation: a `LazyFrame` builds a query plan; `collect()` optimizes (projection and predicate pushdown, common subexpression elimination) and executes; `explain()` shows the plan; `collect(streaming=True)` processes in chunks for data larger than memory.

Expressions in depth: arithmetic and comparisons, `when/then/otherwise`, casting, string namespace (`str.contains`, `str.extract`), temporal namespace (`dt.hour`, `dt.replace_time_zone`, `dt.convert_time_zone`), null handling (`fill_null`, `forward_fill` with a limit inside `over`), and window functions with `over('station_id')` that compute per-group values without collapsing rows.
Joins and reshaping: `join` (inner, left, outer, asof for nearest-time matching, which is the incident and weather join), `concat`, `pivot` and `unpivot`.
Time series: `group_by_dynamic` for time windows, `rolling` with time-based windows, `shift` inside `over`, and time zone handling in the temporal namespace with explicit ambiguity handling.
Interop: `to_pandas`, `from_pandas`, Arrow zero-copy where dtypes allow, and writing Parquet with compression and row groups.

b.s:
q = (pl.scan_csv(path, has_header=False, new_columns=cols)
       .filter(pl.col('station').is_in(keep))
       .select(cols[:12]))
day = q.collect(streaming=True)
df.with_columns(pl.col('speed').shift(3).over('station_id').alias('speed_lag_3'))
df.with_columns(pl.col('speed').rolling_mean(window_size=6, min_periods=3).over('station_id'))

items: Expressions plus lazy plans are why polars is fast; write the query, let the engine order it.
`over` is the per-group window that replaces `groupby(...).transform`.
The asof join is the right tool for attaching the latest weather or metadata to each timestamp.

b.s: Redo stage 5 with `scan_csv`, a filter and a streaming collect; then build the lag and rolling features with `over` and compare timing and peak memory with pandas.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; do stage 5 once in each

resources.title: SQLBolt, interactive SQL lessons

b.s: A website where you type questions to a pretend filing cabinet and it answers right away, with hints when you get stuck.

Free, in the browser, about twenty short lessons: selecting rows, filtering, sorting, joining two tables, counting and averaging, and changing data. Each lesson has a few exercises against a tiny database. Two evenings and you can read most SQL.

Work through lessons 1 to 12 (queries, filters, joins, aggregates) and 13 to 18 (inserting, updating, creating tables). Then repeat the aggregate lessons in DuckDB on the incident log, where the questions are real: incidents per road per hour, longest-lasting events, roads with the most unknown-severity events.

It teaches syntax, not the relational model; pair it with a page on normalization and keys, and with `EXPLAIN` in DuckDB to see what a query does. Its exercises are single-table or two-table; practice multi-join and window-function queries on the project's data afterward.

Sufficient for reading analytics SQL; insufficient for schema design, transactions and performance, which come from a database textbook or the documentation of the engine you use. Its value is speed: fluency in a weekend.
For a team, a shared minimum of SQL fluency is what makes feature definitions reviewable by analysts and engineers alike; an interactive tutorial is the cheapest way to reach it.

Eighteen lessons plus extras: SELECT queries, constraints (WHERE with comparison, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN), filtering and sorting (DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET), multi-table queries with JOINs, outer joins, NULLs, expressions, aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY, HAVING), order of execution, inserting, updating, deleting, creating and altering tables, dropping tables, and subqueries and unions.

items: SELECT and WHERE: choose columns, filter rows with `=`, `<>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `LIKE` with `%` wildcards; combine with `AND` and `OR`.
Sorting and limiting: `DISTINCT` for unique values, `ORDER BY col ASC|DESC`, `LIMIT n OFFSET m` for pagination.

Joins: `INNER JOIN t2 ON t1.key = t2.key` keeps matching rows; `LEFT JOIN` keeps all left rows with NULLs where unmatched; the incident-to-station join and the station-to-registry join are exactly this.
NULLs and expressions: `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`, arithmetic and string expressions in SELECT with `AS` aliases.
Aggregates: `COUNT(*)`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`; `GROUP BY` to aggregate per group; `HAVING` to filter groups after aggregation (WHERE filters rows before).
Order of execution: FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT; knowing it explains why you cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE.
Modifying data: `INSERT INTO ... VALUES`, `UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE` (always with WHERE), `DELETE FROM ... WHERE`; schema: `CREATE TABLE` with types and constraints, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP TABLE`.
Subqueries and unions: a query inside `IN (...)` or in FROM; `UNION` to stack results; correlated subqueries as a prelude to window functions.

b.s:
SELECT road_names, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events WHERE severity = 'MAJOR' GROUP BY road_names HAVING n > 5 ORDER BY n DESC;
SELECT e.event_id, s.station_id FROM events e JOIN stations s ON s.fwy = e.fwy AND s.dir = e.dir;

items: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups; the order of execution explains the rest.
A LEFT JOIN keeps what you started with; an INNER JOIN silently drops the unmatched.
Never UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE.

b.s: In DuckDB over the incident log, find the ten hours of the week with the most incidents on I-880, and the share of events with unknown severity per road.

resources.lives: interactive · free · a weekend · free; SQL fluency in a weekend

resources.title: DuckDB documentation, the Python API and SQL reference

b.s: The manual for a small, fast database that lives inside your program and can read the project's files directly.

DuckDB is a free analytical database that runs inside Python with no server. Its documentation shows how to query CSV and Parquet files with SQL in one line, how to hand results to pandas, and the full list of SQL functions including window functions for lags and rolling averages.

Read the Python API page (`duckdb.sql`, `read_parquet`, `to_df`), the window-functions page, and the page on the `ASOF` join, which attaches the latest weather or metadata valid at each timestamp. Then rewrite one feature (lag-3 speed) as a window function and check it against pandas.

DuckDB is a vectorized, columnar, single-node engine with a query optimizer; its documentation on the execution model and on out-of-core processing explains why it handles a district-day file in seconds within a few hundred megabytes. Its Parquet reader does predicate pushdown and partition pruning, which is what stage 5 needs.

The engine is the local counterpart of cloud warehouses; SQL written for it moves to them with small changes. Its extensions (spatial, JSON, httpfs) let the whole pipeline be expressed as SQL over files, which is easier to audit and version than pandas code.

Embedded analytical engines changed what one machine can do; their documentation is also a compact account of modern query execution. For a lead, DuckDB is the argument that the cleaning and feature stages should be declarative.

The Python API (connections, querying DataFrames and files, results to pandas or Arrow, relations), the SQL reference (statements, data types, expressions, functions, window functions, aggregates, samples), the data-import pages (CSV, Parquet, JSON, partitioned files, globbing), and the guides (performance, out-of-core, ASOF joins, time zones).

items: Embedded and columnar: `import duckdb`; `duckdb.sql('SELECT ...')` runs against files by name (`read_parquet('data/pems_processed/*.parquet')`) or against DataFrames in scope; results convert with `.df()` or `.arrow()`; a persistent database is one file.

Reading files: CSV with `read_csv` and auto-detection (or explicit `columns`, `header=false`, `delim`), gzip transparent; Parquet with projection and predicate pushdown and Hive-style partitions; globs over many files; `DESCRIBE` and `SUMMARIZE` to inspect.

Types and time: `TIMESTAMP`, `TIMESTAMPTZ`, `INTERVAL`; `strptime` for PeMS's format; `timezone('America/Los_Angeles', ts)` conversions; `date_trunc`, `time_bucket` for 5-minute bins; the ICU extension for zone rules.

Window functions: `LAG(speed, 3) OVER (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY ts)`, `AVG(speed) OVER (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`, `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `QUANTILE_CONT` as an aggregate for medians; `QUALIFY` to filter on window results.
ASOF join: `ASOF JOIN weather ON ts >= weather.ts` attaches the latest weather reading at or before each row, and with `PARTITION BY` per station; the correct way to join metadata valid at a time.
Aggregates and grouping sets: `GROUP BY ALL`, `median`, `quantile`, `mode`, `arg_max`, `list` aggregates, `FILTER (WHERE ...)` clauses, `PIVOT` and `UNPIVOT`.

Performance and memory: `SET memory_limit`, `SET threads`, out-of-core sorting and grouping to temp files, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to see the plan and timings, writing Parquet with `COPY ... TO ... (FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY (month))`.

b.s:
duckdb.sql("""
  SELECT station_id, ts, speed,
         LAG(speed, 3) OVER w AS speed_lag_3,
         AVG(speed) OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS speed_roll_mean_30
  FROM read_parquet('data/pems_processed/*.parquet')
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY ts)
""").df()
SELECT station_id, daytype, slot, median(speed) AS profile_speed FROM cleaned WHERE ts <= '2026-08-31' GROUP BY ALL;
SELECT * FROM rows ASOF JOIN weather ON rows.ts >= weather.ts;

items: Query files directly; a year of Parquet is one `read_parquet` glob.
Window functions with PARTITION BY station are lags and rolling means in SQL.
ASOF joins are the point-in-time join that feature stores are built around.

b.s: Write the whole of stage 6 (profile, ratio, three-step label) as one DuckDB query over the monthly Parquet files and check its label prevalence per hour against the pandas version.

resources.title: PeMS documentation and the Clearinghouse (Caltrans)

b.s: The website where the road sensor numbers come from, with pages that explain what each column of numbers means.

PeMS is Caltrans's system that collects data from the freeway sensors. After you log in, the Clearinghouse page lets you download one file per day for a district, and the help pages explain the columns: timestamp, station, flow, occupancy, speed, and how many of the samples were real. Read the help page for the 5-minute station data before touching a file.

The documentation describes the `station_5min` layout (no header row; timestamp, station id, district, freeway, direction, lane type, station length, samples, percent observed, total flow, average occupancy, average speed, then per-lane columns) and the meta file that gives each station's location and postmile. It also explains that PeMS imputes missing data and how the percent-observed column reports it. Confirm every claim against a real file; the documentation has drifted from the files before.

Understand the data provenance: loop detectors report raw 30-second counts and occupancy, the district servers aggregate to 5 minutes, speed is often estimated for single-loop stations, and the imputation algorithm fills gaps from neighbors and history. That chain determines the error model in lesson 2 and the cleaning rules in lesson 3.

PeMS's imputation and its detector-health diagnostics are documented in Caltrans reports and in the traffic-engineering literature (Chen, Kwon, Rice, Skabardonis and Varaiya's work at Berkeley). Reading those explains what percent observed means statistically and why imputed rows correlate with neighbors.

PeMS is also the source of the public benchmark datasets (PEMS-BAY, PeMSD4, PeMSD8) used across the spatio-temporal literature, which makes it a rare case where your production data and the research benchmarks share a lineage. The rate limits and login are the practical constraint; a data-sharing agreement or a bulk export is what a real deployment would negotiate.

The Performance Measurement System: what detectors report (30-second counts and occupancy per lane), how PeMS aggregates to 5 minutes, hours and days, how it estimates speed for single-loop stations, how it imputes missing data and reports the share observed, the station metadata, and the Clearinghouse's file types (station 5-minute, hourly, daily, meta, incidents from CHP).

items: Detectors: inductive loops (and radar or magnetometers) count vehicles and measure occupancy (fraction of time occupied); double loops measure speed directly; single loops estimate it from flow and occupancy with an effective vehicle length (the g-factor) that PeMS calibrates per station.
Aggregation: raw 30-second samples become 5-minute rows; flow sums, occupancy averages, speed averages flow-weighted across lanes; the timestamp is the start of the interval.

Station 5-minute file layout (verify on a real file): timestamp, station id, district, freeway, direction, lane type (ML mainline, OR on-ramp, FR off-ramp, HV HOV), station length, samples, percent observed, total flow, average occupancy, average speed, then per-lane samples, flow, occupancy, speed and observed; no header.

Imputation: when detectors fail, PeMS fills values from neighboring lanes, neighboring stations and historical profiles; `% Observed` says what fraction of the lane-points were real; detector health diagnostics flag stuck, chattering and dead detectors.

Metadata: station id, freeway, direction, district, county, city, state and absolute postmile, latitude and longitude, station length, type, number of lanes, and name; postmile order defines upstream and downstream along a route.

Clearinghouse: one file per district per day for station 5-minute data; meta files per district; download requires a free account; the interface is a web form and rate limited, which the Selenium collector respects.
Related products: CHP incidents, lane closures, and performance measures (VMT, VHT, delay) computed from the same data; the public benchmark datasets in traffic research derive from PeMS.

b.s:
speed_est ≈ flow / (occupancy × (1 / g))   # single-loop estimate, g = effective vehicle length
observed_frac = pct_obs / 100;  treat rows with observed_frac < 0.5 as missing for labels

items: Speed is often estimated, and imputed rows are not observations; `% Observed` is the column that tells you which is which.
Postmiles, not coordinates, define the road graph.
The layout in the documentation must be checked against a real file before a parser is trusted.

b.s: Download one district-day and the meta file; confirm the column count and the meaning of columns 8 to 12 by checking that total flow equals the sum of per-lane flows on a few rows.

resources.title: Open-Meteo, historical weather API documentation

b.s: A free website that tells you what the weather was, hour by hour, for any place, so we can know whether it rained when the road got slow.

Open-Meteo is a free weather API with no sign-up. Its historical endpoint returns hourly values (rain, temperature, wind, visibility) for a latitude and longitude going back decades, and its forecast endpoint returns the next days. The documentation page builds the request URL for you as you tick boxes.

For stage 8, request hourly precipitation for Fremont's coordinates over the training period and join it on the UTC hour. For the live loop, use the forecast endpoint, because at prediction time only a forecast exists. The docs list every variable and its units; note that historical data come from reanalysis models, not from a rain gauge in Fremont.

Understand the difference between reanalysis (a model's reconstruction of past weather from observations) and forecasts, and why training on reanalysis while serving on forecasts is a mild train-serve skew that you should measure (compare forecast and reanalysis precipitation on the same hours).

The point-in-time question from lesson 5 applies: the correct training feature is the forecast that would have been available at t, which Open-Meteo also archives (previous-runs endpoints). Whether the extra fidelity matters for a binary rain feature is an experiment worth an afternoon.

Weather is the cheapest exogenous signal with a real effect on traffic. In a production system the questions become licensing, latency, and fallbacks when the provider is down; Open-Meteo's open model is a useful default and its terms are worth reading before shipping.

A free weather API: the historical (archive) endpoint with hourly and daily variables from reanalysis models back to 1940, the forecast endpoint with hourly forecasts and past days, the request builder, variable lists with units, time zone handling, and terms of use.

items: Requests: GET with `latitude`, `longitude`, `start_date`, `end_date`, `hourly=precipitation,rain,temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m,visibility`, `timezone=UTC`; the response is JSON with parallel arrays of times and values.

Historical data: derived from reanalysis (ERA5 and higher-resolution regional models), gridded at kilometers, so a value is an area estimate, not a gauge reading in Fremont; hourly resolution; units are metric by default.

Forecast data: the forecast endpoint gives the coming days hourly and can include `past_days`; forecasts are model runs that update; for point-in-time training features the previous-runs endpoint archives what a forecast said at the time.

Variables for traffic: precipitation and rain (mm per hour), visibility, wind speed, temperature; derived flags such as `is_raining = precipitation > 0.2 mm`; daily summaries for calendar-level features.
Joining: align on the UTC hour (`timestamp.floor('h')`) with a left join onto the 5-minute grid; for the live loop use the forecast issued before the prediction time.
Limits and terms: free for non-commercial use with fair-use rate limits; commercial use requires a subscription; cache responses locally (a year of hourly values is small).

b.s:
https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive?latitude=37.55&longitude=-121.98&start_date=2026-01-01&end_date=2026-12-31&hourly=precipitation,visibility&timezone=UTC
wx['hour'] = pd.to_datetime(wx.time, utc=True); df['hour'] = df.timestamp.dt.floor('h'); df = df.merge(wx, on='hour', how='left')

items: Reanalysis is a model's reconstruction; treat it as an area estimate.
Train on what serving will have: the forecast, not the realized weather.
Cache; the whole training period is a few megabytes.

resources.title: 511 SF Bay Open Data, traffic API documentation

b.s: The rules for asking the 511 helper about crashes and roadwork, so our program can ask politely and understand the answer.

511.org publishes traffic events (incidents, roadwork, closures) through an API that follows a standard called Open511. You register for a free key, then request events as JSON. The documentation lists the fields (id, type, severity, roads, geography, created, updated) and the limits on how often you may ask.

Read the events endpoint documentation next to `02_collect_events.py`: which query parameters exist (`status`, bounding box), what each field means, and the request quota. Note which fields are optional; missing geography and unknown severity are normal, which is why lesson 7's join handles them.

Open511 is an open specification for road events; reading the spec explains the field semantics that the 511 docs assume, including how `created` and `updated` relate to an event's life and how multiple roads are represented. The quota defines the sampling interval of your incident stream and therefore its censoring.

Event feeds are the interface between human reporting (CHP dispatch) and your model; their delay and severity encoding are measurement properties you should estimate rather than assume. Compare the feed with CHP's own incident page for a day to see what the API drops.

Public-sector data APIs are governed by terms and by quotas that shape what a product can promise; at scale, direct feeds from agencies or probe-based incident detection replace polling. The Open511 standard is also a small lesson in how interoperability specifications succeed or fail.

The 511 SF Bay open data portal: registering for a token, the traffic events API following the Open511 specification (events resource, filters, pagination, formats), the fields of an event, the road and geography sub-objects, the status lifecycle, rate limits, and the transit APIs alongside.

items: Access: request a free API token; include it as `api_key` on every request; the specification documents request quotas per token and asks for attribution.

The events resource: `GET /traffic/events?api_key=...&format=json` returns a list of events with `id`, `status` (ACTIVE or ARCHIVED), `event_type` (INCIDENT, CONSTRUCTION, SPECIAL_EVENT, ROAD_CONDITION, WEATHER_CONDITION), `severity` (MINOR, MODERATE, MAJOR, UNKNOWN), `headline`, `description`, `created`, `updated`, `schedule`, `roads` (a list with `name`, `from`, `to`, `direction`, `state`), and `geography` (a GeoJSON Point or LineString).
Filtering: by status, by bounding box (`bbox`), by road name, by jurisdiction, by event type, by severity, and by time; pagination with `offset` and `limit`; formats JSON and XML.

Lifecycle: an event is created when reported, updated as details change, and archived when cleared; `updated` is the last edit time, not necessarily the clearing time; short events may never appear to a 15-minute poller.

Open511: an open specification for road event data used by several agencies; its field semantics (statuses, event types, schedule recurrence) are defined there, and reading it explains fields the portal's page glosses.
Data quality: geography may be missing or coarse; severity is often UNKNOWN; road names follow conventions (`I-880 N`) that need parsing; timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC or with offset.

b.s:
GET https://api.511.org/traffic/events?api_key=KEY&format=json&status=active
roads: [{'name': 'I-880 N', 'direction': 'N', 'from': 'Mission Blvd', 'to': 'Dixon Landing Rd'}]

items: The feed is a sampled event stream; what you see depends on how often you ask.
`created` is report time and `updated` is edit time; neither is the physical start or end.
Parse roads and directions defensively; the fields are text written by people.

b.s: Poll the active endpoint every 5 minutes for a day, record first-seen and last-seen per event id, and compare those windows with the `created` and `updated` fields.

resources.title: Python Data Science Handbook (VanderPlas)

b.s: A free book that shows how to use Python to look at data: sorting it, summarizing it, and drawing pictures of it.

Jake VanderPlas's book, free online as notebooks: IPython, numpy, pandas, matplotlib and an introduction to scikit-learn. The numpy and pandas chapters are a good second explanation next to McKinney; the matplotlib chapter is the clearest short guide to plotting in Python.

Read the numpy chapter for broadcasting and vectorized operations, the pandas chapter for grouping and time series, and the matplotlib chapter before making the station plots. Its scikit-learn chapter is a preview of phase 4 with clear examples of the fit-predict pattern.

Its explanations of numpy's memory model and of pandas' index alignment complement McKinney's; the visualization chapter's coverage of matplotlib's object model is what you need to make consistent figures for the evaluation report.
The book predates Arrow-backed pandas and polars; its scikit-learn chapter is introductory. Its lasting value is the clear treatment of the numerical stack's fundamentals.
A widely used free reference; a good default recommendation for engineers moving from another language to Python's data stack.

IPython and Jupyter (help, magics, profiling), numpy (arrays, ufuncs, aggregations, broadcasting, boolean masks, fancy indexing, sorting, structured arrays), pandas (objects, indexing, operations, missing data, hierarchical indexing, concat and merge, aggregation and grouping, pivot tables, strings, time series, high-performance eval and query), matplotlib (line, scatter, errorbars, density and contour, histograms, legends, colorbars, subplots, annotation, ticks, styles, 3-D, geographic, seaborn), and machine learning with scikit-learn (the API, hyperparameters and validation, feature engineering, naive Bayes, linear regression, SVMs, random forests, PCA, manifold learning, k-means, Gaussian mixtures, kernel density, and worked applications).

items: IPython: `?` and `??` for help and source, tab completion, `%timeit` and `%prun` for timing and profiling, `%debug` after an exception.

numpy in depth: dtypes and memory, views versus copies, broadcasting rules with diagrams, boolean masking and counting, fancy indexing for gathering and scattering, `argsort` and partial sorts, structured arrays.

pandas in depth: index objects, `loc`/`iloc`, ufuncs preserving indexes, alignment, `None` versus `NaN`, hierarchical indexing for panel data (station by time), `concat` and `merge` with all join types, `groupby` with `aggregate`, `filter`, `transform`, `apply`, pivot tables, vectorized string methods, time series with resampling and rolling, and `eval`/`query` for speed.

matplotlib's object model: figure and axes, `plt.subplots`, styling lines and markers, error bars, `contour` and `imshow`, histograms and 2-D histograms, legends and colorbars, annotation, tick customization, style sheets, and seaborn's statistical plots on top.

scikit-learn's API: estimator objects with `fit`, `predict`, `transform`; data as a features matrix and a target array; the train-test split; validation curves and learning curves to diagnose bias and variance; grid search; feature engineering (categorical encoding, text features, derived features, imputation, pipelines).

Model tours: naive Bayes for text, linear regression with basis functions and regularization, support vector machines with kernels, random forests and their ensembles, PCA for dimensionality reduction and noise filtering, manifold learning for visualization, k-means and Gaussian mixtures for clustering, kernel density estimation, and applications (face detection, digits).

b.s:
%timeit df.groupby('station_id').speed.shift(3)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3)); ax.plot(day.timestamp, day.speed); ax.set(ylabel='mph', title='Station 400001, 2026-03-02')
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve

items: Learn the object model of matplotlib once and every figure becomes controllable.
Validation and learning curves are the diagnostic pictures for bias and variance.
The scikit-learn API is three verbs; everything composes from them.

resources.title: Fundamentals of Data Visualization (Wilke)

b.s: A free book about drawing pictures of numbers so that people understand them, with lots of examples of bad pictures made good.

Claus Wilke's book, free online, is about the design of plots rather than any one tool: which chart for which question, color, axes, legends, and the mistakes that mislead. Read the chapters on visualizing amounts, distributions and time series, then look at your own plots differently.

Its chapters on visualizing uncertainty, on time series, and on the principle of proportional ink apply directly to the evaluation report: reliability diagrams, lead-time histograms and daily speed lines. The chapter on color explains why a sequential scale is right for one thing and wrong for another.

Wilke's rules (avoid unnecessary 3-D, order categories meaningfully, show uncertainty honestly) are the review checklist for every figure you publish; its discussion of small multiples is how to show a hundred stations at once.
Pair it with the literature on perception (Cleveland and McGill) that it draws on; its guidance on uncertainty visualization is the practical counterpart of the calibration and interval topics.
A free, rigorous, tool-agnostic reference for figures in papers and reports; the standard to hold a figure to before a talk.

Part 1, from data to visualization: aesthetics and data types, coordinate systems and axes, color scales, amounts, distributions, proportions, x-y relationships, geospatial data, uncertainty. Part 2, principles of figure design: proportional ink, overplotting, color use and misuse, redundant coding, multi-panel figures, titles and captions, tables, balancing data and context, larger axis labels, avoiding line drawings, not going 3-D. Part 3, miscellaneous: file formats, choosing software, telling a story.

items: Aesthetics map data to position, shape, size, color, line type; data types (quantitative, ordinal, categorical, date, text) decide which mappings are legitimate; log and sqrt axes for skewed data; polar coordinates rarely.

Color: sequential scales for ordered quantities, diverging for values around a center, qualitative for categories; colorblind-safe palettes; color as a highlight, not decoration; never encode more than a handful of categories by hue.
Amounts: bars from zero, dot plots when the baseline is meaningless, grouped and stacked bars, heatmaps for two categorical axes and a quantity (the station-by-slot profile).

Distributions: histograms and density plots (bin width and bandwidth matter), empirical cumulative distributions for comparison, quantile-quantile plots, boxplots, violins, ridgeline plots for many groups (a distribution per hour).
Proportions and relationships: pie charts rarely, stacked bars, mosaic plots; scatter with transparency and jitter, bubble charts, paired data, correlograms, and connected scatter for time.

Uncertainty: error bars with a stated meaning, confidence bands, graded bands, hypothetical outcome plots; show the distribution rather than a bar with a whisker when you can; the reliability diagram and the interval coverage plot belong here.

Principles: the amount of ink should be proportional to the data; avoid overplotting with transparency, contours or binning; redundant coding (color plus shape) for accessibility; small multiples with shared axes for comparison; a title says the finding, a caption says what is plotted; do not use 3-D for 2-D data.

b.s:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 5, sharex=True, sharey=True)   # small multiples, one station each
ax.fill_between(t, lo, hi, alpha=.2)   # a band, with its meaning stated in the caption

items: Choose the scale by the data type and the color scale by the data's structure.
Show distributions and uncertainty as shapes, not as bars with whiskers.
The title states the finding; the caption states the encoding.

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Intro to SQL, Advanced SQL

b.s: Two short online lessons about asking questions of a giant table of data, with answers checked as you type.

Kaggle's SQL courses run against real public datasets in BigQuery from the browser. Intro to SQL covers select, where, group by, order by, and joins; Advanced SQL covers joins in depth, analytic (window) functions and nested data. An afternoon each.

Do Intro to SQL after SQLBolt and Advanced SQL's window-functions lesson before rewriting the lag feature in DuckDB. The window-functions lesson is the same idea as `shift` and `rolling` in pandas, expressed in SQL.
The courses use a cloud warehouse, which shows what large-scale analytical SQL feels like (partitioning, cost of scans); the ideas transfer to DuckDB unchanged.
Their coverage of nested and repeated fields previews the semi-structured data you meet in event streams such as the 511 feed.
A free, practical introduction to warehouse SQL for a team that needs analysts and engineers to share feature definitions.

Intro: getting started with BigQuery and SQL, SELECT/FROM/WHERE, GROUP BY/HAVING/COUNT, ORDER BY, AS and WITH (common table expressions), and joining data. Advanced: JOINs and UNIONs in depth, analytic (window) functions, nested and repeated data, and writing efficient queries.

items: Warehouse basics: datasets and tables, schemas with types, previewing rows, estimating a query's scanned bytes before running it (cost awareness).
Core clauses: SELECT and WHERE with types and dates, aggregations with GROUP BY and HAVING, ORDER BY with dates, `EXTRACT` for parts of a timestamp, and aliases.
CTEs: `WITH name AS (SELECT ...)` to stage intermediate results, which keeps multi-step feature queries readable; joins on keys with table aliases.
Joins and unions: inner, left, right, full outer; UNION ALL versus UNION; joining more than two tables; self-joins.

Analytic functions: `OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN ...)`; `LAG`, `LEAD`, `FIRST_VALUE`, `RANK`, `ROW_NUMBER`, running totals and moving averages; the exact machinery of lag and rolling features.
Nested and repeated fields: STRUCT and ARRAY columns, `UNNEST` to flatten, which is how the 511 event's `roads` list would be stored in a warehouse.
Efficiency: select only needed columns, filter early, avoid `SELECT *`, use partitions, and read the query plan.
CTEs make feature queries readable; window functions make them possible.
Nested fields are unnested with UNNEST; event lists become rows.
Scan less; column pruning and partition filters decide cost.

resources.title: Select Star SQL

b.s: A free online book that teaches you to ask a database questions by working through one real story from start to finish.

An interactive SQL book, free and without sign-up, that uses one real dataset throughout and builds up to real questions. Four chapters, about half an hour each. Do it after SQLBolt for a project-shaped practice run.

Its single-dataset design mirrors how you will work with the traffic data for months; the chapters on aggregation and on joins are the operations of the profile computation and the incident join. Its final chapter asks questions that need several steps, which is where SQL fluency is tested.
The book is short and stops before window functions; pair with DuckDB's documentation for those. Its emphasis on reading the data before querying is the right habit.
Useful mostly as a teaching resource; its narrative approach is a good model for a project-specific SQL primer.
A small, well-made open resource; the kind of thing to fork and adapt to a team's own dataset for onboarding.

An interactive book in four chapters over one dataset (Texas death-row records): beazley (SELECT, WHERE, LIMIT, basic filters), hierarchy (aggregations, GROUP BY, HAVING, counting and averaging), harder (CASE, subqueries, joins, NULL handling), and the story (composing several steps to answer a real question), with exercises checked in the browser.

items: Reading before querying: look at the columns, their types, and a few rows; ask what one row means.
Filtering and projecting: SELECT chosen columns, WHERE on text and numbers, `LIKE` patterns, `LENGTH` and string functions, `LIMIT` for inspection.
Aggregation: `COUNT`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` over groups; `GROUP BY` one or several columns; `HAVING` on aggregates; `ORDER BY` an aggregate.
Conditional logic: `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` to bucket values (a severity code from text) or to count conditionally with `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
Subqueries and joins: a query in FROM or WHERE, joining a table to an aggregate of itself, and the reasoning about NULLs in comparisons and aggregates.
Composing a story: chaining steps, checking intermediate results, and stating the assumptions the query makes about the data.

b.s: SELECT road, SUM(CASE WHEN severity = 'MAJOR' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS major, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY road;

items: Bucket with CASE; count conditionally with SUM over CASE.
Every aggregate query hides an assumption about NULLs; make it explicit.
Compose in steps and inspect each.

phases.title: Classical machine learning, the core

b.s: Labels, the incident join, baselines, logistic regression, gradient boosted trees, calibration, and honest row-level evaluation.

items: The supervised setup: features, target, train, validation, test, and why three. Overfitting, bias and variance, regularization, early stopping.
Metrics: confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, the precision-recall curve and average precision, ROC-AUC, log loss, Brier score, reliability diagrams; why accuracy lies under imbalance.
Leakage in its three forms: target, temporal, group. Class weighting.
Linear and logistic regression with scikit-learn; decision trees; random forests; gradient boosting and what `num_leaves`, `learning_rate` and `min_data_in_leaf` do; categorical handling.
Feature engineering as hypothesis-making; feature importance and SHAP values.
Isotonic and Platt calibration; choosing a threshold from a curve.

items.title: Labels: what does 'slow' mean?

b.s: Define the target precisely, compute it without leaking, and understand that the definition decides what the model can mean.
How do we know a road is slow? We compare it with how it usually is.
If cars usually zoom at 65 and today they crawl at 30, that is slow. If they always crawl at five o'clock, that is just five o'clock.
So the helper first learns what 'usual' looks like for every road and every time of day, and then notices when today is different.
Is it cold today? Compared with what: yesterday, summer, or winter? Notice that the answer changes with what you compare to.

For every station and every 5-minute slot of the day, separately for weekdays and weekends, we find the typical speed by taking the median of all the days we have. The median is the middle value when you line the numbers up, so a couple of crazy days do not drag it around the way an average would.
Then 'slow' means today's speed is below 60 % of that typical speed. A slow episode is three slots in a row that are slow, fifteen minutes, so one odd reading does not count.
That definition has a surprise inside it: the evening rush hour, which is slow every day, is not 'slow' by this rule, because slow is normal then. The rule finds unusual slowness.
Line up these speeds: 62, 64, 65, 12, 66, 63, 65. Find the median and the mean. Which one is a better 'typical'? Why?

Three formulas. profile(s, slot, daytype) = median of speed over training days. ratio = speed / profile. is_slow = ratio < 0.6, and label = 1 when is_slow holds for three consecutive steps, the window ending at the row's own time.

Two design choices with consequences. Relative to profile: the label flags unusual slowness, so recurrent congestion is invisible to it. Absolute (speed below 35 mph for three steps): the label flags congestion itself, rush hour included. The plan computes both and makes you pick.

Details that matter: 5-minute slots instead of hours, because a 4 pm median mixes free flow at 4:00 with a jam at 4:55; and free-flow speed is better measured as the station's 85th percentile than as a median, which is why the plan adds `ratio_ff` too.
Make up one day of speeds for a station with a 5 pm rush hour. Compute both labels by hand. Where do they disagree, and which one would a driver want?

The label is a deterministic function of the series and an estimated profile, so the profile is part of the model. Estimating it on all data lets the test period influence training labels: target leakage through the label definition. The profile must be fit on training timestamps only and stored as an artifact.

Quantile estimation: the median has a 50 % breakdown point and, for n days per cell, a standard error near 1.25 σ/√n; with eight weeks of weekdays that is n ≈ 40, so smoothing across neighboring slots trades a little bias for a useful variance reduction, and cells below 20 samples fall back to the hourly median.

Consecutive-run labels: label_t = Π_{k=0..2} is_slow_{t−k}. For horizon h = 3 steps, the label at t + 3 depends on speeds at t + 1, t + 2, t + 3 and does not touch the features at t. Prevalence is a steep function of the 0.6 cutoff and the run length; sweep both once and freeze them in the filename.
Show that for a horizon of two steps the label window at t + 2 would include the row at t itself, overlapping the feature `speed_lag_0`, and explain what that does to a naive evaluation.

Label design is a modelling decision. The relative label approximates conditional anomaly detection; the absolute label approximates a level target. They induce different class balance, different predictability (recurrent congestion is calendar-predictable, non-recurrent is not), and different product semantics, and a model good at one can be useless at the other.

Alternatives keep more information: regress the speed ratio with a pinball loss and derive probabilities from quantiles; or model episode onset as a point process with covariates and predict hazard. Both avoid the brittle 3-step run and make horizon coherence natural.

Errors-in-variables: detector noise near the 0.6 boundary is heteroscedastic (single-loop speed error grows at low flow), so label noise is concentrated exactly where the decision is made. And because the profile pins the training positive rate near a quantile by construction, real seasonal shifts in congestion are masked in the training window.
