b.s: Using the ROC and precision-recall essays as guides, plot both curves for the LightGBM model and explain in two sentences why they tell different stories at 5 % positives.

resources.lives: interactive · free · an hour per essay · free; visual essays on precision, ROC, cross-validation and more

resources.title: StatQuest with Josh Starmer (YouTube)

b.s: Videos with silly songs and simple drawings that explain how learning machines work, one small idea at a time.

A YouTube channel where each video explains one idea, such as what a decision tree is or how logistic regression works, with drawings and a short song. Watch the videos on decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting and logistic regression during phase 4; they are slow, clear and free.

StatQuest's series on gradient boosting (four videos) walks through fitting trees to residuals step by step with numbers, which is exactly lesson 8's mechanism. The videos on ROC and AUC, on cross-validation and on bias and variance give the pictures behind lesson 6. The logistic regression series covers maximum likelihood and the meaning of the coefficients.

The channel's strength is tracing a computation with small numbers until it is obvious; use it to check your understanding of a derivation rather than as a source of the derivation. Its XGBoost series covers the second-order split gain, which is the LightGBM math in lesson 8's higher levels.

It stops at intuition and worked examples, which is the right place for a video; the formal accounts are in ISLP and ESL. When you teach, its pattern (a concrete numeric example before any symbol) is worth stealing.

A reminder that clarity is a research skill; the channel's popularity among practitioners reflects a gap textbooks leave, and it is the resource to hand to a stakeholder who wants to know what a boosted tree actually does.

Hundreds of short videos, each one concept: statistics fundamentals (mean, variance, distributions, p-values, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, maximum likelihood), machine learning fundamentals (bias and variance, cross-validation, confusion matrices, sensitivity and specificity, ROC and AUC), linear models (regression, R², logistic regression series, regularization with ridge, lasso and elastic net), trees (decision trees, regression trees, random forests, AdaBoost, gradient boost series, XGBoost series), support vector machines, PCA and clustering, neural networks and backpropagation, and more.

items: Maximum likelihood: pick the parameters that make the observed data most probable; for a normal, the sample mean and variance; for logistic regression, the coefficients that maximize the product of predicted probabilities of the observed classes.

Logistic regression series: fitting a line to log odds, the S-curve back in probability, maximum likelihood instead of least squares, R² analogues and p-values for coefficients, and the meaning of each coefficient.

Bias and variance, cross-validation: bias as inability to capture the true relationship, variance as sensitivity to the training set; k-fold cross-validation to compare methods; the confusion matrix, sensitivity (recall) and specificity, ROC by sweeping thresholds and AUC to compare models.
Regularization: ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero to reduce variance; lasso can zero them (feature selection); elastic net mixes; λ chosen by cross-validation.

Trees and ensembles: building a classification tree with Gini impurity and a regression tree with squared residuals; random forests with bootstrapping plus random feature subsets and out-of-bag error; AdaBoost's weighted stumps; gradient boost for regression (fit trees to residuals, scale by a learning rate) and for classification (residuals of log odds, leaf values from the sum of residuals over the sum of p(1 − p)); XGBoost's similarity scores, gain, pruning by γ, regularization λ, and the second-order derivation.
Support vector machines: the maximal margin classifier, soft margins, and the kernel trick (polynomial, radial) computing high-dimensional dot products cheaply.
PCA and clustering: PCA step by step with singular value decomposition, scree plots and loadings; k-means and hierarchical clustering with distance choices.
Neural networks: a chain of weighted sums and activations, the chain rule for backpropagation worked with actual numbers, gradient descent step by step.

b.s:
Gradient boost (classification): leaf value = Σ residuals / Σ p(1 − p)
XGBoost similarity = (Σ residuals)² / (Σ p(1 − p) + λ);  gain = sim_L + sim_R − sim_root
Ridge: minimize Σ (y − ŷ)² + λ Σ βⱼ²

items: Boosting's leaf values come from residuals divided by curvature; XGBoost's gain is the same idea with regularization.
Regularization trades a little bias for a lot of variance.
Sensitivity and specificity, precision and recall: know which pairs move together.

b.s: Follow the gradient boost classification videos with pencil and paper on eight rows of traffic data: compute the initial log odds, the residuals, one tree's leaf values, and the updated predictions.

resources.lives: video · free · hours, as needed · free; one idea per video, worked with numbers

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Intro to ML, Intermediate ML, Feature Engineering

b.s: Three short online lessons: build your first learning machine, make it better, and invent better clues for it.

Intro to ML builds a decision tree and then a random forest on a table of house prices. Intermediate ML covers missing values, categorical columns, pipelines, cross-validation and XGBoost, a cousin of LightGBM. Feature Engineering covers finding useful columns, creating new ones, and encoding categories. Quick, practical, and graded as you go.

They give you working code for the exact tools of phase 4 (imputation, categorical handling, gradient boosting with early stopping) in an afternoon. Their cross-validation is shuffled, which is fine for house prices and wrong for traffic; keep lesson 6 in mind and do not copy that part.

The Feature Engineering course's target-encoding lesson is a leakage hazard for time series: encode out-of-fold in time or skip it. Its mutual-information lesson is a useful quick screen for which features carry signal. Intermediate ML's pipeline lesson is the pattern to adopt for the feature module.

The courses reflect Kaggle's tabular culture: gradient-boosted trees, engineered features, and careful validation. The competition write-ups they link to are the richer resource; reading three winning solutions for a time-series competition teaches more about leakage and validation than any course.

Kaggle's tabular consensus (boosted ensembles, careful validation, feature engineering over architecture) has been stable for a decade, and understanding why, which Grinsztajn and colleagues studied systematically, is more valuable than any single course and directly justifies LightGBM as this project's production model.

Intro: how models work, basic data exploration, your first model (decision tree), model validation, underfitting and overfitting, random forests. Intermediate: missing values, categorical variables, pipelines, cross-validation, XGBoost, data leakage. Feature Engineering: what is feature engineering, mutual information, creating features, clustering with k-means, principal component analysis, target encoding.

items: First model: choose a target and features, `DecisionTreeRegressor().fit(X, y)`, predict, and validate on held-out data with mean absolute error; the difference between training and validation error.
Under and overfitting: control tree size with `max_leaf_nodes`; sweep and pick by validation error; random forests average many trees and usually beat a single tree without tuning.
Missing values: drop columns, impute (mean), or impute plus an indicator column; compare by validation score.
Categoricals: drop, ordinal encode, or one-hot (for low cardinality); handle categories unseen in training.
Pipelines and cross-validation: bundle preprocessing and model; `cross_val_score` for a more reliable estimate; the note that folds should respect groups and time when the data have them.
XGBoost: gradient boosting with `n_estimators`, `learning_rate`, `early_stopping_rounds` on a validation set, and `n_jobs`.
Leakage: target leakage (features that become available after the target) and train-test contamination (preprocessing fit on all data); examples and how to detect them.

Feature engineering: mutual information as a first screen for relevance (captures any dependence, is univariate); creating features by arithmetic, counts, breaking down strings and group transforms; k-means cluster labels and distances as features; PCA components and loadings as features; target encoding with smoothing, fit on a separate fold to avoid leakage.

b.s:
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
mi = mutual_info_classif(X, y, discrete_features=False)
target encoding: enc(c) = (n_c · mean_c + m · prior) / (n_c + m)

items: Validation error, not training error, chooses the model.
Leakage is the most common cause of a too-good score; target encoding and preprocessing are where it hides.
Mutual information is a screen; the model decides what matters.

b.s: Compute mutual information between each feature and `y_30`, then implement target encoding of `station_id` out-of-fold in time and check whether it improves validation AP over LightGBM's native categorical handling.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free

resources.title: LightGBM documentation: Parameters, Parameters Tuning

b.s: The instruction sheet for the tree-building program, with all of its knobs and what each one does.

Two pages of the LightGBM documentation. The first lists every parameter with a one-line meaning; the second is a guide to which knobs to turn for speed, for accuracy, or to stop the model memorizing. Read the tuning page before you change anything, and change one thing at a time.

Know these entries: `objective`, `num_leaves`, `min_data_in_leaf`, `learning_rate`, `feature_fraction`, `bagging_fraction` with `bagging_freq`, `lambda_l2`, `max_bin`, `is_unbalance`, `categorical_feature`, and early stopping. The tuning page explains leaf-wise growth and why `num_leaves` and `max_depth` interact, which is the single most common source of overfitting in LightGBM.

Read the Features page too: the histogram algorithm, gradient-based one-side sampling, exclusive feature bundling, and native categorical handling explain where the speed and the memory footprint come from. The Python API page's `Dataset` semantics (`free_raw_data`, `reference` for consistent binning between train and validation) prevent subtle bugs.

The documentation is terse on interactions among regularizers; the LightGBM paper (Ke et al., 2017) and the XGBoost paper (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) supply the algorithms and the second-order split gain. Monotone constraints and linear trees are documented options directly relevant here, and the parameter aliases are a known source of silent misconfiguration.

Documentation quality is a production concern. Parameter aliases have caused silent misconfigurations in real systems; the fix is a team configuration schema that validates parameters before training. At scale, also read the distributed-training and GPU pages to understand what changes when the data no longer fits one machine.

Parameters: core (objective, boosting type, learning rate, number of leaves, threads, device), learning control (max depth, min data in leaf, feature and bagging fractions, lambda L1 and L2, min gain to split, early stopping, categorical handling, monotone constraints, linear trees), I/O (max bin, categorical feature specification), objective-specific (is_unbalance, scale_pos_weight, quantile alpha), and metrics. Parameters Tuning: leaf-wise growth, tuning for speed, for accuracy, and against overfitting.

items: Leaf-wise growth: LightGBM grows the leaf with the largest loss reduction first, which converges faster than level-wise but overfits small data unless `num_leaves` and `min_data_in_leaf` are controlled; `max_depth` limits the worst case.

Core parameters: `objective` (`binary`, `regression`, `quantile`, `lambdarank`), `learning_rate` (0.05 to 0.1 typical with early stopping), `num_leaves` (31 default; 63 for millions of rows), `num_threads` (physical cores), `seed`.

Regularization: `min_data_in_leaf` (hundreds for large data), `min_sum_hessian_in_leaf`, `lambda_l1`, `lambda_l2`, `min_gain_to_split`, `feature_fraction` (0.7 to 0.9), `bagging_fraction` with `bagging_freq`, `extra_trees`, `path_smooth`.
Histograms: `max_bin` (255 default) trades accuracy for speed and memory; `min_data_in_bin`; the histogram subtraction trick makes sibling leaves cheap.

Categoricals: declare with `categorical_feature`; LightGBM sorts categories by gradient statistics to find optimal partitions; `cat_smooth`, `cat_l2`, `max_cat_to_onehot`; high-cardinality categories can overfit, so raise `min_data_per_group`.
Imbalance: `is_unbalance=true` or `scale_pos_weight`; both change calibration, so recalibrate afterward; `pos_bagging_fraction` for sampling.

Constraints and shapes: `monotone_constraints` per feature with a method (`basic`, `intermediate`, `advanced`); `linear_tree` fits linear models in leaves for extrapolation; `interaction_constraints`.
Early stopping and metrics: `early_stopping_round`, `metric` (`average_precision`, `auc`, `binary_logloss`, `l1`, `quantile`), `first_metric_only`; validation sets share bins through `reference`.

Tuning guide: for speed use bagging, feature fraction, fewer bins, `max_bin`; for accuracy use larger `max_bin`, smaller learning rate with more rounds, more leaves, more data; against overfitting use smaller leaves, larger `min_data_in_leaf`, bagging and feature fraction, regularization, `max_depth`, `extra_trees`.

params = dict(objective='binary', metric='average_precision', learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=63, min_data_in_leaf=200,
              feature_fraction=0.8, bagging_fraction=0.8, bagging_freq=1, lambda_l2=1.0, max_bin=255, is_unbalance=True, num_threads=8, seed=0)
monotone_constraints = [-1 if f == 'down1_speed' else 0 for f in feats]   # P(slow) non-increasing in downstream speed

Categoricals are handled natively; declare them and regularize high-cardinality ones.

resources.title: The boosting papers: Friedman (2001), XGBoost (2016), LightGBM (2017)

b.s: Three papers, written years apart, about a way of learning that builds many small decision trees, each fixing the mistakes of the ones before. The later papers made it much faster.

Friedman's 2001 paper invented gradient boosting: fit a small tree to what the current model gets wrong, add it with a small weight, repeat. XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) made it fast and added a smarter way to choose splits. LightGBM (Ke and colleagues, 2017) made it faster still with histograms and by growing the most useful leaf first. Reading the abstracts and the pictures is enough at this stage.

Friedman's paper defines boosting as gradient descent in the space of functions and derives the algorithm for several losses, including the logistic loss this project uses. XGBoost's paper introduces the second-order split gain and the regularized objective. LightGBM's paper explains gradient-based one-side sampling and exclusive feature bundling, the two tricks behind its speed. Read them in order, one per week, after lesson 8.

Work through the derivations: the functional gradient view, the second-order Taylor expansion leading to the leaf-weight formula, and the histogram algorithm's memory footprint. Then map every LightGBM parameter to the equation it controls. This is the fastest route from tuning by folklore to tuning by understanding.

Compare the three on regularization (shrinkage, subsampling, leaf constraints), on categorical handling, and on the assumptions their speed tricks make (GOSS biases the gradient sample). The papers are also a study in how systems contributions (histograms, cache-aware access) can matter as much as algorithmic ones.

Together they explain why boosted trees are the default for tabular problems in industry and why their implementations converge; the open research is in uncertainty (natural-gradient and probabilistic boosting), in monotone and shape constraints, and in hybrids with neural representations.

Friedman's 'Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine': boosting as steepest descent in function space, with algorithms for squared error, absolute error, Huber loss, and binary and multiclass logistic loss, plus shrinkage and subsampling. Chen and Guestrin's 'XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System': the regularized objective, second-order approximation, split finding (exact and approximate with weighted quantile sketch), sparsity-aware splits, and the system design (cache-aware blocks, out-of-core). Ke et al.'s 'LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree': histogram-based learning, gradient-based one-side sampling (GOSS) and exclusive feature bundling (EFB), with leaf-wise growth.

items: Function-space gradient descent: we want F minimizing E L(y, F(x)); at step m, compute the negative gradient of the loss at each training point, g_i = −∂L(y_i, F(x_i))/∂F(x_i); fit a base learner h (a regression tree) to the g_i; take a step F ← F + ρ h with ρ by line search; for squared loss g_i are residuals, for logistic loss g_i = y_i − p_i.

Tree-specific refinements: fit one step size per leaf (each leaf minimizes the loss over its region); shrinkage ν scales each tree's contribution (small ν with more trees generalizes better); stochastic gradient boosting subsamples rows each iteration.

XGBoost's objective: L = Σ l(y_i, ŷ_i) + Σ_trees Ω(f), with Ω(f) = γT + ½λ‖w‖² (T leaves, leaf weights w); second-order Taylor expansion with per-row gradient g_i and Hessian h_i gives optimal leaf weight w* = −Σg/(Σh + λ) and objective −½ Σ_leaves (Σg)²/(Σh + λ) + γT.
Split gain: gain = ½ [ (Σg_L)²/(Σh_L + λ) + (Σg_R)²/(Σh_R + λ) − (Σg)²/(Σh + λ) ] − γ; a split is kept if gain > 0; pruning happens naturally through γ.

Finding splits: exact greedy enumerates sorted values; the approximate algorithm proposes candidate thresholds from weighted quantiles (weights h_i); sparsity-aware learning learns a default direction for missing values, which is why NaN is fine.
System design: column blocks in compressed sorted format, cache-aware prefetching, out-of-core computation with block compression and sharding; parallel and distributed training.

LightGBM's histogram algorithm: bin feature values (max_bin), build histograms of gradient sums per bin in O(data × features), find splits over bins in O(bins × features), and compute a child's histogram by subtraction from the parent's.

GOSS: keep all rows with large gradients (they matter more) and a random sample of small-gradient rows, upweighted to keep the gradient estimate unbiased; EFB: bundle mutually exclusive sparse features into one to cut the feature count; leaf-wise growth with depth limit.

b.s:
g_i = −∂L(y_i, F(x_i))/∂F;  for logistic loss with p = σ(F): g_i = y_i − p_i, h_i = p_i(1 − p_i)
w*_leaf = −Σ_{i∈leaf} g_i / (Σ_{i∈leaf} h_i + λ)
gain = ½ [G_L²/(H_L + λ) + G_R²/(H_R + λ) − (G_L + G_R)²/(H_L + H_R + λ)] − γ

items: Boosting is gradient descent where the step is a tree; the residual is the gradient.
Second-order boosting turns leaf values and split gains into closed forms with gradient and Hessian sums.
Histograms, sampling and bundling are why LightGBM handles ten million rows in minutes.

b.s: Implement second-order gradient boosting for logistic loss with depth-2 trees in numpy using the leaf-weight and gain formulas, train it on one month of features, and compare its validation AP with LightGBM at the same number of trees.

resources.title: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data? (Grinsztajn, Oyallon, Varoquaux, 2022)

b.s: A paper where scientists tested many learning machines on lots of tables of numbers and found that the tree-based ones usually won.

A research paper that compared gradient-boosted trees, random forests and several neural networks on 45 table datasets. Trees won most of the time, and the paper tries to explain why: tables have columns with different meanings and scales, and trees handle that naturally. It is the evidence behind choosing LightGBM as this project's production model.

Read the abstract, the benchmark figure and the section on why trees win: networks are biased toward smooth functions while real tables have sharp thresholds; uninformative columns hurt networks more; and rotating the feature space (which networks are indifferent to) destroys the meaning of columns. Each point maps to a design choice in stage 9.

The paper is a careful benchmark with tuned baselines, which is rarer than it should be. Note its scope (medium-sized datasets, no time or graph structure) and what that leaves open for this project: the spatial structure is the one place a network has an argument, which is why the challenger is a graph model, not an MLP.

Follow-up work on tabular deep learning (attention-based tabular models, tree-inspired networks) chips at the gap without closing it. The methodological lesson is about benchmark design: the choice of datasets and tuning budget decides the headline, so read the appendix before the abstract.

A rare example of a negative-result benchmark shaping practice. For a lead deciding on architecture, it is the citation that ends the argument for tabular problems, and its limitations define exactly where an argument remains.

A benchmark of 45 tabular datasets (medium size, numerical and mixed features, classification and regression) comparing tuned gradient-boosted trees and random forests with tuned MLPs, ResNet-style networks and tabular transformers, with a fixed hyperparameter-search budget; then three controlled experiments explaining why trees win.

items: Benchmark design: datasets curated to be truly tabular (heterogeneous columns, not too easy, not tiny), balanced accuracy for classification and R² for regression, and a random search over hyperparameters with the same budget per model, reported as performance versus number of search iterations.

Result: tree-based models (XGBoost, gradient boosting, random forests) beat the neural models on most datasets with medium data, especially with mixed numerical and categorical features; the gap narrows with more data and more tuning but does not close in their regime.

Finding 1, smoothness: networks are biased toward smooth functions; smoothing the target (Gaussian kernel) hurts trees more than networks, showing trees exploit irregular, threshold-like target functions that tabular data often have.

Finding 2, uninformative features: removing uninformative features barely hurts trees but helps networks; adding random features hurts networks more; MLP-like models are less robust to useless columns.

Finding 3, rotation invariance: rotating the feature space (mixing columns) does not affect MLPs but destroys the meaning of columns, and trees, which are not rotation-invariant, suffer; the natural basis of tabular data carries information that rotation-invariant learners ignore.

Implications: for tabular data, prefer tree ensembles unless there is structure (images, sequences, graphs) or very large data; feature selection helps networks; and inductive bias, not capacity, explains the gap.

b.s: balanced accuracy = (TPR + TNR)/2;  budget-matched random search over hyperparameters

items: Inductive bias explains the gap: trees fit irregular targets, ignore useless columns and keep the column basis.
The result is for medium tabular data; the traffic graph structure is the one argument for a network here.
Report benchmarks with tuning budgets; the headline depends on them.

b.s: Replicate finding 2 on the traffic features: add ten random columns and compare the drop in validation AP for LightGBM and for the MLP.

resources.title: Interpretable Machine Learning (Molnar), the SHAP chapter

b.s: A free book about asking a learning machine why it said what it said, and getting an answer you can understand.

Christoph Molnar's online book explains ways to understand models. The SHAP chapter shows how to split one prediction into a contribution from each clue, so you can see that 'downstream speed dropped' pushed the model toward slow and 'Sunday' pushed it away. Read the chapter, then make the plots on the project's own model.

SHAP values come from game theory: each feature's fair share of the difference between this prediction and the average prediction. For tree models there is an exact and fast algorithm, TreeSHAP. The chapter explains the plots you will make in stage 9: the summary plot (which features matter overall), dependence plots (how a feature's effect changes with its value), and force plots (one prediction explained).

Understand what SHAP does and does not say: it attributes the model's output, not the world's causes; correlated features share credit in ways that depend on the method; and global importance from mean absolute SHAP differs from split-gain importance. The chapter's section on caveats is the important part, and the neighboring chapters on partial dependence and permutation importance give alternatives.

Read alongside the original papers (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; the TreeSHAP paper, 2020) and the critiques concerning feature dependence and off-manifold evaluation. Use SHAP for debugging features and for per-station failure analysis, where it excels, and resist presenting it as a causal story about traffic.

Interpretability in products is a communication and accountability tool as much as a technical one. SHAP's computational cost at scale and its misuse as causal explanation are both live issues, and Molnar's book is the best neutral survey to hand to a product partner or a regulator before a discussion about what the model 'thinks'.

Shapley values (the game-theory definition, properties, estimation) and SHAP: the definition as an additive feature attribution method, KernelSHAP, TreeSHAP, and the global explanations built from many local ones (feature importance, summary plots, dependence plots, interaction values, clustering), with advantages and disadvantages.

items: Shapley value: for a prediction f(x), the contribution of feature j is the average, over all orderings of features, of the change in prediction when j is added to the features already present; it satisfies efficiency (contributions sum to f(x) − E[f]), symmetry, dummy and additivity, and is the only attribution with those properties.

Estimation: exact Shapley values need 2^p coalitions; Monte Carlo sampling of orderings approximates them; absent features are replaced by values from the data (marginal expectation), which creates unrealistic combinations when features are correlated.

SHAP as additive attribution: φ₀ + Σ φ_j = f(x); KernelSHAP fits a weighted linear model over coalitions with a specific kernel so the coefficients are Shapley values; TreeSHAP computes exact values for tree ensembles in polynomial time by walking the trees and tracking subset weights.

Global views: mean absolute SHAP per feature as importance; the summary (beeswarm) plot showing each feature's SHAP values colored by feature value, which reveals direction and spread; dependence plots of SHAP against feature value with interaction coloring; SHAP interaction values; clustering rows by SHAP vectors.

Caveats: SHAP explains the model, not the world; correlated features share credit in a way that depends on the background distribution; marginal versus conditional expectations differ; interventional TreeSHAP versus path-dependent; explanations can be gamed; computation cost for KernelSHAP is high.

Practical use here: debugging (a feature with a suspicious SHAP direction indicates leakage or a bug), per-station failure analysis (which features drive misses), and communication (a force plot for one alert).

b.s:
φ_j = Σ_{S ⊆ F∖{j}} |S|!(p − |S| − 1)!/p! [f(S ∪ {j}) − f(S)]
f(x) = φ₀ + Σ_j φ_j  (efficiency)
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model); sv = explainer.shap_values(X); shap.summary_plot(sv, X)

items: Shapley values are the unique fair split of a prediction among features; SHAP computes them for models.
They attribute the model's output, not causes; correlated features blur the picture.
Use them to debug and to explain single predictions, not to rank causes.

b.s: Compute TreeSHAP for the 30-minute model on a rainy weekday afternoon and on a dry Sunday; compare the top five contributing features and check that they sum to the logit difference from the base value.

resources.title: scikit-learn user guide: Model evaluation, Probability calibration

b.s: The manual pages that explain how to score a learning machine, and how to make its confidence honest.

Two pages of the scikit-learn documentation. Model evaluation lists every scoring function (precision, recall, average precision, log loss, Brier score) with its formula and an example. Probability calibration explains reliability curves and the two fixes, Platt scaling and isotonic regression. Read them with the functions open in a notebook.

For lessons 6 and 11 the functions are `average_precision_score`, `precision_recall_curve`, `brier_score_loss`, `log_loss`, `calibration_curve` and `IsotonicRegression`. The guide's examples show the pitfalls directly: ROC curves that look fine under imbalance, and calibration measured on training data that looks perfect and means nothing.

The evaluation page is a compact textbook on metrics with definitions and references; the calibration page explains the calibration-refinement decomposition and why calibration must be fit on held-out data. Note that `CalibratedClassifierCV` uses shuffled cross-validation by default, which is wrong for time series; fit isotonic regression manually on the chronological validation split instead.

scikit-learn's implementations are the de facto standard, so knowing their exact conventions (how ties are handled in average precision, the interpolation choices in the precision-recall curve, the binning strategies in `calibration_curve`) matters when comparing your numbers with a paper's.

The guide is also a model of documentation: definitions, references, examples, and caveats in one place. Your team's metric library should meet that bar, with the label definition and the split protocol versioned alongside the metric code so a number can always be traced to how it was computed.

Model evaluation: the `scoring` parameter and scorer objects; classification metrics (accuracy, balanced accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, precision-recall curve and average precision, ROC and AUC, log loss, Brier score, Matthews correlation, confusion matrix, classification report, multiclass and multilabel averaging); regression metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE, R², pinball loss); clustering metrics; dummy estimators as baselines. Probability calibration: calibration curves (reliability diagrams), `CalibratedClassifierCV` with sigmoid and isotonic methods, and guidance on which classifiers are miscalibrated and why.

items: Scorers: `scoring='average_precision'` in cross-validation and search; `make_scorer` for custom metrics with `greater_is_better` and `needs_proba`; metrics functions take `y_true, y_pred` or `y_score`.
Threshold metrics: confusion matrix; precision, recall, F-beta with `average` options for multiclass (`macro`, `micro`, `weighted`); balanced accuracy for imbalance; `classification_report`.

Ranking metrics: `precision_recall_curve` (returns precision, recall, thresholds) and `average_precision_score` (a step-wise area, no interpolation); `roc_curve` and `roc_auc_score`; the guide's warning that ROC-AUC can be optimistic under heavy imbalance and precision-recall is more informative.
Probabilistic metrics: `log_loss` (needs clipped probabilities), `brier_score_loss` (mean squared error of probabilities), both proper scoring rules that reward calibration and refinement.
Regression metrics: `mean_absolute_error`, `mean_squared_error` (and RMSE), `mean_absolute_percentage_error`, `r2_score`, `mean_pinball_loss` for quantiles, `d2_pinball_score`.
Baselines: `DummyClassifier(strategy='prior')` and `DummyRegressor` produce the no-skill references every model must beat; the guide recommends reporting them.

Calibration: `calibration_curve(y, p, n_bins, strategy='uniform'|'quantile')` gives mean predicted probability and observed fraction per bin; well-calibrated models track the diagonal; naive Bayes pushes toward 0 and 1, SVMs and boosted trees are sigmoid-shaped miscalibrated, random forests pull toward the middle.

Calibrating: `CalibratedClassifierCV(estimator, method='sigmoid'|'isotonic', cv=...)` fits the calibration map on held-out folds; sigmoid (Platt) assumes a logistic distortion and works with little data; isotonic is nonparametric and needs more data; calibration must never be fit on training predictions; with time series, provide a chronological split or calibrate manually.

b.s:
p, r, thr = precision_recall_curve(y, s); ap = average_precision_score(y, s)
frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y, p, n_bins=10, strategy='quantile')
IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds='clip').fit(p_val, y_val)

items: Average precision for ranking under imbalance; Brier and log loss for probabilities; dummy estimators as the floor.
Calibration is measured with a reliability curve and fixed on held-out data.
Boosted trees need calibration; isotonic when validation has thousands of positives, Platt otherwise.

items.title: Regression: predicting a number, and the metrics that judge it

b.s: Predict the speed itself, not only whether it will be slow, and know how to score a numeric forecast.
Sometimes the question is not 'will it be slow?' but 'how fast will the cars go?' The answer is a number, like 32 miles per hour.
Guessing a number is called regression. You are right when your number is close, and you can measure how far off you were.
Guess how tall your friend is in centimeters, then measure. How far off were you? That distance is your error.

A regression model predicts a number from clues. The simplest is a line: speed in 30 minutes ≈ a + b × speed now. Fitting the line means choosing a and b so the guesses are as close as possible to what happened.

How close is close? Mean absolute error is the average distance between guess and truth. Root mean squared error punishes big misses more. R² says how much better you did than just guessing the average every time.
Take ten (speed now, speed 30 minutes later) pairs from one station and plot them. Draw the line you think fits best. Compute the average distance from the line to the points.

Linear regression minimizes the sum of squared errors; with several clues it is y ≈ w·x + b, fit by least squares. Metrics: MAE (robust, in mph), RMSE (sensitive to outliers), MAPE (percent, undefined at zero), R² (fraction of variance explained). Residual plots show where the model fails.

Regularization: ridge (L2) shrinks weights, lasso (L1) zeroes some, both fight overfitting when clues are many or correlated. Quantile regression predicts the 10th or 90th percentile instead of the mean, which is what a 'worst plausible speed' needs.
Trees and networks do regression too: LightGBM with `objective='regression'` or `quantile`, the same features as the classifier, a different target (`speed_t30`).
Train LightGBM to predict `speed_t30` and report MAE against persistence (speed now) and against the profile. Which stations have the largest errors, and at what hour?

Least squares as maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise; the normal equations and their geometry (projection onto the column space); Gauss-Markov; heteroscedasticity and why MAE or quantile losses are preferable when noise scales with level. Bias-variance for regression; ridge as a Bayesian prior; lasso and sparsity; elastic net.

Evaluation subtleties: RMSE decomposition into bias and variance, MASE (scaled by a naive forecast) for comparability across series, and the pinball loss for quantiles. Multi-output regression (three horizons at once) versus three models.
Show that minimizing squared error yields the conditional mean and minimizing absolute error yields the conditional median, and explain which the traffic product should report.

Generalized linear models unify regression targets (Gaussian, Poisson for counts such as flow, Gamma for positive skewed durations). Heteroscedastic and distributional regression (predict mean and variance, or full quantile sets) are the bridge to uncertainty. Regression under dependence: errors autocorrelated in time, spatially correlated across stations, and what that does to standard errors and to cross-validation.

Trees regress piecewise-constantly and cannot extrapolate; linear models extrapolate linearly and can be wildly wrong; networks are in between. Monotone and shape constraints in gradient boosting encode physics.

Fit a Poisson GLM to flow counts with calendar features and compare its calibration of predicted variance with a squared-error model. Then fit quantile boosting at 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 and check pinball loss and crossing.

Production forecasting is regression at scale: hierarchical targets, reconciliation across levels (station, route, city), distributional outputs for downstream optimization, and metrics chosen by the decision they serve (ETA error weighted by trips, not by rows). Research threads: distribution-free intervals for regression, multi-horizon coherence, and losses aligned with downstream utility.
Propose the regression target and metric for a route-level travel-time product built on station speeds, and say how station-level errors compound along a route.

b.q: Why is RMSE larger than MAE on the same data?

a.s: Squaring weights large errors more; RMSE is at least MAE and the gap grows with outliers.

b.q: What does R² = 0 mean?

a.s: The model does no better than predicting the mean every time. It can be negative when the model is worse than that.

items.title: Other classifiers and multiclass: k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, support vector machines, softmax

b.s: Know the rest of the classical toolbox, when each wins, and how two-class methods extend to many classes.

There are many ways to sort things into groups. One way: look at the things nearest to you and copy their label. Another: count how often each clue shows up in each group. Another: draw the widest possible gap between the groups.
Sort a pile of leaves into trees by looking at each leaf's closest match among leaves you already know. That is nearest neighbors.

k-nearest neighbors predicts by finding the k most similar past rows and voting. Naive Bayes multiplies the chance of each clue given each class, assuming clues are independent, which is naive but often works. A support vector machine finds the boundary with the widest margin between classes.
When there are more than two classes (light, moderate, heavy congestion), softmax turns scores into probabilities that add to one, and the loss is cross-entropy over all classes.
With five past rows labelled slow or fine and their speeds, classify a new row using k = 3 nearest neighbors by speed. Change k to 1 and 5; does the answer change?

k-NN: no training, all the cost at prediction; needs scaled features and a distance; works when similar inputs have similar outputs and data are plentiful. Naive Bayes: fast, works with counts and text, calibrates badly. SVM: maximize margin, use kernels to draw curved boundaries, strong on small clean data, slow on millions of rows.

Multiclass: one-vs-rest, one-vs-one, or native softmax (logistic regression and networks). Metrics generalize: per-class precision and recall, macro versus micro averages, the confusion matrix as the primary picture. Ordinal classes (light < moderate < heavy) deserve ordinal losses or a regression on the ratio.
Turn the speed ratio into three classes (above 0.8, 0.6 to 0.8, below 0.6) and train a softmax logistic regression; print the 3 × 3 confusion matrix and macro F1.

Bayes-optimal classification and what each method approximates: k-NN estimates the posterior locally (consistent as k grows with n, cursed by dimension); naive Bayes is a generative model with a factorized likelihood; the SVM is a large-margin discriminative model whose dual reveals the kernel trick and support vectors. Hinge loss versus logistic loss; kernels as inner products in a feature space; the representer theorem.
Softmax regression as the multinomial logit; its gradient generalizes p − y to a vector. Calibration in multiclass (temperature scaling). Cost-sensitive learning and thresholding per class.
Derive the dual of the soft-margin SVM and identify the support vectors; then show that kernel k-NN and kernel SVM use the same similarity in different ways.

Where each method still matters: k-NN as a retrieval baseline and in nearest-neighbor search at scale (approximate methods, vector databases); naive Bayes as a fast text baseline; SVMs in small-sample scientific settings and as the origin of kernel methods leading to Gaussian processes. Structured prediction and sequence labelling as multiclass over structured outputs.
Metric choice under class imbalance in multiclass, hierarchical classification, and label noise. The relation between margin theory (SVMs, boosting) and generalization.
Implement a kernelized ridge classifier and a linear SVM on the same features; compare margins and calibration, and explain why the boosted trees still win on this data.

Nearest-neighbor retrieval is now infrastructure (embeddings plus approximate search underlie retrieval-augmented systems and recommenders); kernel methods live on in theory (neural tangent kernels) and in Gaussian processes. The practical multiclass problems at scale are extreme classification (millions of labels) and hierarchical, cost-sensitive decisions.
Design an approximate nearest-neighbor index over per-station day embeddings to find 'days like today' as a forecasting baseline, and state its failure modes.

b.q: Why does k-NN need scaled features?

a.s: Distance mixes units; an unscaled flow in vehicles swamps a speed in mph, so the neighbors are chosen by one feature only.

b.q: What does softmax guarantee?

a.s: A vector of positive numbers that sum to one, so the outputs can be read as class probabilities.

items.title: Unsupervised learning: clustering, principal components and anomaly detection

b.s: Find structure with no labels: groups of similar stations or days, compact descriptions of many columns, and rows that look wrong.
Sometimes nobody tells you the answers, and you just sort things into piles that look alike. That is unsupervised learning: finding groups on your own.
It can also spot the odd one out, like the one sensor that says cars are going 200 miles per hour.
Dump out a box of buttons and sort them into piles however makes sense to you. Now find the button that fits no pile.
Clustering groups similar rows: k-means picks k centers and assigns each row to the nearest one, then moves the centers, and repeats. Days could cluster into 'normal weekday', 'holiday', 'crash day'.

Principal component analysis finds the few directions along which the data vary most, so sixty columns can be summarized by a handful. Anomaly detection flags rows far from everything else, which is how you catch a broken detector.
Take one station's daily speed profiles (288 numbers per day) for a month and run k-means with k = 3. Which days landed together? Look at the odd cluster.

k-means (choose k with the elbow or silhouette), hierarchical clustering (a tree of merges), DBSCAN (density, no k, finds noise). PCA: center, take the top eigenvectors of the covariance, project; explained variance tells how many to keep. Anomaly detection: distance from the profile, isolation forests, or reconstruction error.

Uses here: cluster stations by their weekly profile to find station types; PCA on the 288-slot daily profile to get a few 'shape' features; anomaly scores to flag detector faults before they poison training.
Run PCA on daily speed profiles across all stations and plot the first two components colored by weekday. What does component one measure?

Clustering as optimization (k-means as coordinate descent on within-cluster variance; Gaussian mixtures and EM as its probabilistic version), the meaning of a 'good' clustering (no ground truth; stability and downstream utility), and the curse of dimensionality for distances. PCA as the best low-rank approximation (Eckart-Young), its relation to the SVD, and its limits (linear, variance is not always signal). Nonlinear reduction (t-SNE, UMAP) for visualization only.
Anomaly detection formally: density estimation and its thresholds; one-class methods; the distinction between point, contextual and collective anomalies (a detector stuck at 65 mph is contextual).
Implement k-means and EM for a Gaussian mixture from scratch in numpy on the daily profiles, and show that k-means is the limit of EM as the variances shrink.

Representation learning as the modern form of unsupervised learning: autoencoders, contrastive methods, and the fact that most 'unsupervised' structure now comes from pretext tasks. Mixture models and latent-variable models for regime detection on the fundamental diagram; hidden Markov models for congestion states over time. Evaluation of unsupervised methods through downstream tasks and through stability under resampling.
Anomaly detection under distribution shift: what counts as anomalous changes with roadwork; contextual detection using the profile and neighbors.
Fit a hidden Markov model with three states to a station's speed and occupancy and compare the inferred states with the relative and absolute labels; where do they disagree?

Unsupervised structure at scale underlies embeddings, retrieval, and pretraining; the research frontier is in self-supervised objectives, in identifiability of latent variables, and in detection of anomalies and drift without labels in streaming systems. For sensor networks, unsupervised detector-health models are a product in their own right.
Propose a self-supervised pretraining task on unlabeled PeMS history for all of California and argue what representation it would learn and how you would test transfer to Fremont.

b.q: Why is there no accuracy for clustering?

a.s: There are no labels to compare with. You judge clusters by stability, by interpretability, and by whether they help a downstream task.

b.q: What does the first principal component of daily profiles usually capture?

a.s: Overall level, how slow or fast the whole day was. Shape differences come in the later components.

items.title: Hyperparameter tuning and model selection

b.s: Choose settings and models with a budget and without fooling yourself.

A learning machine has dials, like how many questions a tree may ask. Turning the dials changes how well it learns. Finding good dial settings is tuning, and you check each setting on a quiz the machine has not seen.
Set a kitchen timer to different times for cooking rice. Which time gives the best rice? That is tuning one dial.

Hyperparameters are settings you choose, not things the model learns: number of leaves, learning rate, how many lags to use. Tuning tries settings and keeps the best by the validation score. Grid search tries every combination; random search tries random ones and is usually better for the same effort.
The trap: if you try a thousand settings and pick the best on validation, the validation score is now too optimistic. That is why the test split stays untouched until the end.
Train LightGBM with learning rates 0.01, 0.05, 0.2 and leaves 15, 63, 255. Make a 3 × 3 table of validation AP. Is the best corner where you expected?

Search strategies: grid, random, Bayesian optimization (build a model of score versus settings and pick the most promising next point), and early-stopping-based methods such as successive halving that kill bad trials early. Tools: Optuna. Rules: tune few things (learning rate, leaves, min data in leaf, feature fraction), on the chronological validation split, with a fixed budget of trials, and log every trial.

Model selection is the same problem one level up: which model family to ship. Use the same validation protocol, compare against baselines, and prefer the simpler model unless the gain is clear and reproducible across folds.
Run 30 Optuna trials over four LightGBM parameters with early stopping, plot validation AP against trial number, and check how much the best trial beats the defaults.

Why random beats grid (most dials matter little, so sampling explores the important ones more densely); Bayesian optimization with Gaussian processes or tree-structured estimators; multi-fidelity methods (Hyperband). The selection bias of picking the maximum of many noisy scores, and nested cross-validation as the honest fix. Learning curves to decide whether more data or more capacity helps.
For time series: tuning on rolling-origin folds, reporting the spread, and re-tuning cadence when retraining monthly.
Simulate selecting the best of N random models with pure-noise validation scores and plot the expected 'best' score against N; then explain what nested cross-validation changes.

AutoML as automated pipeline search; its wins on benchmarks and its costs in compute and interpretability. Hyperparameter importance analysis (which dials mattered) as a research tool. Transfer of hyperparameters across tasks and scales, and scaling laws as principled tuning for large models. The reproducibility problem: reported gains within tuning noise.
Fit a functional ANOVA on your tuning trials to estimate each parameter's importance, and use it to prune the search space for the monthly retrain.

At scale, tuning is an engineering system: distributed trials, early stopping, warm starts from previous versions, and budgets set by cost. The research frontier includes learning-rate-free methods, tuning under distribution shift, and using scaling laws to extrapolate from small runs.
Design the tuning policy for the monthly retrain: what is re-tuned, what is inherited, how many trials, and the statistical test that decides whether the new configuration replaces the old.

b.q: Why does random search often beat grid search?

a.s: Most parameters matter little; random search spends its trials exploring more distinct values of the ones that matter.

b.q: Why must the test split stay untouched during tuning?

a.s: Any choice made by looking at a score on a split makes that score optimistic; the test split is the one score you never chose on.

items.title: Information theory in machine learning: entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, mutual information

b.s: See why cross-entropy is the loss, what KL divergence measures, and how mutual information screens features.
Information is surprise. If I tell you the sun rose today, that is no surprise, so little information. If I tell you it snowed in Fremont, that is a big surprise.
A learning machine is trying to be less surprised by what happens. Its score is how surprised it was.
Play twenty questions and count how many yes-or-no questions you need. Fewer questions means the answer carried less surprise.

Entropy measures how unpredictable something is: a fair coin has one bit of entropy, a coin that always lands heads has zero. Cross-entropy measures how surprised your model is by the truth: if you said 90 % slow and it was slow, small surprise; if you said 5 % and it was slow, big surprise.

Training minimizes the average surprise, which is exactly the cross-entropy loss of lesson 7. Mutual information measures how much knowing one thing (rain) reduces your uncertainty about another (slow).
Compute the surprise −log₂(p) for p = 0.9, 0.5 and 0.05. Notice how fast it grows as p shrinks.

Entropy H(p) = −Σ p log p. Cross-entropy H(p, q) = −Σ p log q is the expected surprise when the truth follows p and you predicted q. KL divergence KL(p‖q) = H(p, q) − H(p) is the extra surprise from using q instead of p; it is zero only when q = p and it is not symmetric. Minimizing cross-entropy over your model's q is minimizing KL to the truth.

Mutual information I(X; Y) = KL between the joint and the product of marginals; it is zero when independent and captures nonlinear dependence, which correlation misses. Decision trees choose splits by information gain, a drop in entropy.
Estimate the mutual information between each feature (binned) and `y_30` on one month; rank the features and compare the ranking with LightGBM's gain importance.

The source-coding theorem gives entropy its meaning (bits needed on average); cross-entropy is the cost of coding with the wrong distribution. Maximum likelihood equals cross-entropy minimization equals KL minimization. Proper scoring rules and the log score. Differential entropy and its caveats. Mutual information estimation from data is hard in high dimensions; binning and k-NN estimators.

Applications: the information bottleneck as a view of representation learning, entropy regularization, and the variational lower bound (ELBO) which is the KL machinery behind variational autoencoders.
Prove KL(p‖q) ≥ 0 with Jensen's inequality and derive the ELBO for a latent-variable model as a KL identity.

Information theory in learning theory: mutual-information generalization bounds, minimum description length and Occam, channel capacity as a limit on what noisy features can carry about a target. Rate-distortion as the theory of lossy compression, which is what representation learning does. Estimating mutual information with neural estimators and their pitfalls.
Bound the achievable average precision from the mutual information between the feature set and the target on a synthetic problem, and discuss why the bound is loose for real features.

Information-theoretic ideas organize much of modern ML: cross-entropy pretraining of language models, compression as a view of intelligence, and channel-capacity arguments about sensor networks (how much a detector network can tell you about a road). The research frontier includes information-theoretic accounts of generalization in overparameterized models and of what pretraining learns.

Estimate, from data, how much information about a station's speed in 30 minutes is carried by its own history versus by its neighbors versus by the calendar, and what that implies about the horizon at which each source dominates.

b.q: Why is cross-entropy the loss for classification?

a.s: It is the expected surprise of the truth under the model, which equals the negative log-likelihood; minimizing it moves the model's distribution toward the true one in KL divergence.

b.q: What does mutual information capture that correlation misses?

a.s: Any dependence, including nonlinear and non-monotone ones; correlation only measures linear association.

resources.title: scikit-learn user guide: Supervised and unsupervised learning

b.s: The manual for a big toolbox of learning methods, with a page for each tool that explains what it is for.

The scikit-learn user guide has one section per method: nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, support vector machines, linear models, clustering, principal components, anomaly detection. Each page explains the idea, shows the code, and links an example. Read the page for each method the week you meet it.

For the classical-ML phase: the pages on nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, support vector machines, linear models (ridge, lasso, logistic), clustering (k-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical), decomposition (PCA), novelty and outlier detection, and model selection (cross-validation, grid and random search, learning curves). Their examples are runnable on the project's features.

The guide is unusually good at stating each method's assumptions, complexity and pitfalls (for instance, k-means's sensitivity to scaling, or the meaning of the SVM's C). Read the 'tips on practical use' sections; they are the accumulated experience of the maintainers.

It is also a reference for evaluation and preprocessing (scalers, encoders, pipelines, `TimeSeriesSplit`). Its consistent API (fit, predict, transform) is the pattern every internal ML library ends up imitating, and the reason to prototype in scikit-learn before writing anything custom.

scikit-learn's documentation is a public good and a standard; its design decisions (no GPU, no deep learning, stability over novelty) are a deliberate scope that has kept it reliable for fifteen years, which is a lesson in library governance.

Supervised: linear models (OLS, ridge, lasso, elastic net, logistic, quantile, robust), kernel ridge, SVMs, SGD, nearest neighbors, Gaussian processes, naive Bayes, decision trees, ensembles (bagging, forests, boosting, stacking), multiclass and multioutput strategies, feature selection, semi-supervised, isotonic regression, calibration, neural networks. Unsupervised: Gaussian mixtures, manifold learning, clustering (k-means, affinity propagation, mean shift, spectral, hierarchical, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, OPTICS, BIRCH), biclustering, decomposition (PCA, kernel PCA, truncated SVD, dictionary learning, factor analysis, ICA, NMF, LDA), covariance estimation, novelty and outlier detection, density estimation.

items: Linear models: OLS minimizes ‖Xw − y‖²; ridge adds α‖w‖² (stable under collinearity); lasso adds α‖w‖₁ (sparse); elastic net mixes; `LogisticRegression` with `C` (inverse regularization), solvers and `class_weight`; `QuantileRegressor` with the pinball loss; robust regressors (Huber, RANSAC) for outliers.

SVMs: `SVC` with `C` and `kernel` (`linear`, `rbf` with `gamma`, `poly`); the margin, support vectors, and the cost of scaling to many rows (quadratic to cubic); `LinearSVC` for large linear problems; probabilities only via internal calibration.
Nearest neighbors: `KNeighborsClassifier` with `n_neighbors` and `weights`; algorithms (brute, KD-tree, ball tree) and when each is efficient; the need for scaling.
Naive Bayes: Gaussian, multinomial, Bernoulli, complement variants; fast, good for text, poorly calibrated.

Trees and ensembles: `DecisionTreeClassifier` criteria (Gini, entropy), `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, cost-complexity pruning `ccp_alpha`; `RandomForest` with `n_estimators`, `max_features`, out-of-bag score; `HistGradientBoosting` (histogram-based, native NaN and categorical support, early stopping, monotone constraints) as the built-in LightGBM-like learner; `StackingClassifier`.
Multiclass and outputs: one-vs-rest and one-vs-one wrappers; `MultiOutputClassifier`; `ClassifierChain`.
Feature selection: variance threshold, univariate tests, `SelectFromModel`, recursive feature elimination, sequential selection, all inside pipelines to avoid leakage.

Clustering: k-means (inertia, `n_init`, k-means++ initialization, mini-batch), hierarchical (linkage types, dendrograms, connectivity constraints), DBSCAN (`eps`, `min_samples`, noise label −1), HDBSCAN (varying density), spectral (graph Laplacian); evaluation with silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin, and against labels with adjusted Rand and mutual information.

Decomposition: PCA (explained variance ratio, whitening, randomized solver), kernel PCA, truncated SVD for sparse data, NMF for non-negative parts, ICA for independent sources; manifold methods (t-SNE, Isomap, UMAP outside sklearn) for visualization only.

Outliers and density: `IsolationForest`, `LocalOutlierFactor`, `OneClassSVM`, elliptic envelope; `KernelDensity` with bandwidth; Gaussian mixtures with `n_components`, covariance types and BIC for selection.

b.s:
Ridge: min ‖Xw − y‖² + α‖w‖²;  Lasso: min ½‖Xw − y‖² + α‖w‖₁
k-means: min Σ_k Σ_{x∈C_k} ‖x − μ_k‖²
silhouette(i) = (b_i − a_i)/max(a_i, b_i)

items: `HistGradientBoosting` is the in-library equivalent of LightGBM and supports NaN, categoricals and monotone constraints.
Choose clustering by data shape (density, hierarchy, spherical) and judge it by stability and use, not by one score.
Feature selection belongs inside the pipeline.

b.s: Cluster stations by weekly profile with k-means and with hierarchical linkage; compare silhouettes, plot the dendrogram, and check whether the clusters match freeway and direction.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; one page per method with its pitfalls

resources.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Python (ISLP), chapters 2–4 and 8

b.s: A famous textbook, free, that explains learning machines with pictures and real examples, written by teachers who invented some of the methods.

Written by statisticians, with Python labs. Chapter 2 explains what learning from data is and why a model can be too simple or too complicated. Chapter 3 is linear regression, chapter 4 is classification including logistic regression, and chapter 8 is trees, forests and boosting. Read a chapter, then do its lab in a notebook.

The clearest explanation anywhere of bias versus variance (chapter 2, with figures worth redrawing), of logistic regression as a model of probability (chapter 4), and of why boosting works by fitting small trees to what is left over (chapter 8). Its lab for chapter 8 uses the same scikit-learn calls you will make in stage 9.

ISLP is the practical face of The Elements of Statistical Learning. Add chapter 5 on cross-validation and the bootstrap, and chapter 6 on model selection and regularization; together with the core chapters they cover phase 4's theory. Its treatment of the bootstrap is the basis for lesson 6's block bootstrap, with the modification that blocks are days.

After ISLP, go to ESL for proofs and depth. ISLP's boosting section gives the additive-model view; combine it with Friedman's 2001 paper for the gradient view that LightGBM implements. Note where ISLP's examples assume independent rows and how each method's assumptions change under temporal dependence.

As a citation for standard methods and as a teaching text it is the reference, and its evolution from R to Python editions tracks the field's tooling. For research, its framing of methods as estimators with bias and variance you can reason about is the habit that distinguishes a careful ML engineer from a library user.

Chapter 2, statistical learning: what it is, prediction versus inference, parametric and nonparametric, the bias-variance trade-off, the classification setting and the Bayes classifier, k-nearest neighbors. Chapter 3, linear regression: simple and multiple, coefficient estimates and their accuracy, model fit, qualitative predictors, interactions, nonlinearity, potential problems, comparison with KNN. Chapter 4, classification: logistic regression, multinomial, generative models (LDA, QDA, naive Bayes), comparison, generalized linear models (Poisson regression). Chapter 8, tree-based methods: regression and classification trees, pruning, bagging, random forests, boosting, Bayesian additive regression trees.

items: The setup: Y = f(X) + ε; we estimate f for prediction or to understand which inputs matter; reducible versus irreducible error; parametric methods assume a form (linear), nonparametric do not (KNN) and need more data; flexibility versus interpretability.

Assessing accuracy: training MSE falls with flexibility but test MSE is U-shaped; expected test error = variance + bias² + irreducible noise; flexible methods have low bias and high variance; cross-validation estimates test error.

Classification: the error rate; the Bayes classifier assigns the most probable class and is the lower bound; KNN estimates conditional probabilities locally; small k is flexible (low bias, high variance).

Linear regression: least-squares estimates, standard errors and confidence intervals for coefficients, t-tests, R² and residual standard error; multiple regression and the F-test; qualitative predictors as dummies; interaction terms; polynomial terms; diagnostics for nonlinearity, correlated errors (time series!), heteroscedasticity, outliers, high leverage, and collinearity (VIF).

Logistic regression: the logit model log(p/(1 − p)) = β₀ + β₁x; maximum likelihood estimation; interpreting coefficients as changes in log odds; multiple logistic regression and confounding; multinomial for several classes.

Generative classifiers: model P(X | Y) and the prior, apply Bayes; LDA (shared covariance, linear boundary), QDA (separate covariances), naive Bayes (independent features); ROC curves and the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity; when each method wins.
Trees: recursive binary splitting to minimize RSS or Gini/entropy; cost-complexity pruning chosen by cross-validation; trees are interpretable but high variance.

Ensembles: bagging averages trees grown on bootstrap samples and out-of-bag error estimates test error; random forests decorrelate trees by sampling m of p predictors at each split; boosting grows trees sequentially on residuals with shrinkage λ, depth d and B trees chosen by cross-validation; variable importance; BART as a Bayesian ensemble.

b.s:
E[(y₀ − f̂(x₀))²] = Var(f̂(x₀)) + [Bias(f̂(x₀))]² + Var(ε)
log(p(X)/(1 − p(X))) = β₀ + β₁X
Boosting: f̂ ← f̂ + λ f̂ᵇ, where f̂ᵇ is a depth-d tree fit to the residuals r ← r − λ f̂ᵇ(x)

items: Test error is U-shaped in flexibility; the bias-variance decomposition says why.
Logistic coefficients are log odds ratios; generative classifiers model the inputs instead.
Boosting fits small trees to residuals slowly; shrinkage and the number of trees trade off.

b.s: Fit logistic regression, LDA and a random forest to the same traffic features on the chronological split; report AP and a ROC curve for each and explain the ordering using the chapter's arguments about bias and variance.

resources.lives: book · free · three weeks · now chapters 6 (regularization), 9 (SVMs) and 12 (unsupervised)

resources.title: Google's Clustering course

b.s: A free short class about sorting things into groups without being told the groups, like putting similar songs together.

A short free course from Google about clustering: how to measure similarity, the k-means algorithm step by step, how to check whether clusters are any good, and where clustering is used. A few hours. Do it before clustering the stations.

Its sections on similarity measures (why scaling matters), on k-means and its failure modes, and on interpreting and evaluating clusters are exactly the unsupervised topic's needs. The section on choosing k with the elbow and silhouette methods is practical.

The course is introductory and k-means-centric; pair it with scikit-learn's clustering guide for density-based and hierarchical methods, and with the Gaussian-mixture view for the probabilistic version.
Its emphasis on the similarity measure as the real modelling decision is correct and often skipped; for stations, the choice of profile distance decides the clusters more than the algorithm does.
A free, focused mini-course; useful as the standard reference when a team disagrees about what a clustering result means.

Clustering overview and workflow; similarity measures (manual and supervised, embeddings); k-means (algorithm, choosing k, advantages and disadvantages); interpreting results and evaluating cluster quality (cardinality, magnitude, downstream performance); and a summary with a worked example.

items: Uses of clustering: generalization (fill missing values from cluster mates), compression (represent by cluster id), privacy (aggregate), and exploration (structure); clustering is unsupervised, so quality is judged by use.

Similarity: prepare data (normalize numerical features, log-transform skewed ones, one-hot or embed categoricals); a manual similarity combines per-feature distances; a supervised similarity learns an embedding (an autoencoder) and measures distance in it; the similarity measure decides the clusters more than the algorithm.

k-means: choose k centroids, assign each point to the nearest, recompute centroids as means, repeat until assignments stop changing; it minimizes within-cluster squared distance; initialization matters (k-means++), so run several times; it assumes spherical clusters of similar size and is sensitive to outliers and scale.
Choosing k: plot total loss against k and look for the elbow; consider the use case; silhouette as a complementary measure; there is no single right k.

Interpreting: check cluster cardinality (sizes) and magnitude (sum of distances) for anomalies; examine features per cluster; verify that similar examples cluster together and dissimilar apart; test clusters in a downstream task.
Alternatives: density-based, hierarchical and distribution-based methods for non-spherical or nested structure.

b.s: assign: c_i = argmin_k ‖x_i − μ_k‖²;  update: μ_k = mean{x_i : c_i = k}

items: The similarity measure is the modelling decision; the algorithm is secondary.
Run k-means several times and compare; check cardinality and magnitude for oddities.
Judge clusters by what they are for.

b.s: Cluster stations by their standardized weekly speed profile with k = 3 to 8; plot loss against k, inspect cardinalities, and describe each cluster's typical week in one sentence.

resources.lives: course · free · a few hours · free; similarity, k-means and how to judge clusters

resources.title: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay)

b.s: A famous free book by a scientist who explained information, coding and learning as one big idea, with puzzles on every page.

David MacKay's textbook, free online, covers information theory (entropy, coding, compression), probabilistic inference, and machine learning (clustering, neural networks, Gaussian processes) as one subject. It is long; read chapters 1, 2 and 4 for entropy and coding, and the exercises are famously good.

Chapters 2 and 4 make entropy and the source-coding theorem concrete; chapter 22 on maximum likelihood and clustering connects to the unsupervised topic; chapter 36 previews decision theory. His writing style, with worked puzzles, rewards patience.

The book unifies coding, inference and learning through probability; its chapters on Bayesian inference, on model comparison (Occam's razor as a consequence of marginal likelihood) and on Gaussian processes are a second, deeper take on the Bayesian topic.

MacKay's treatment of the information-theoretic view of learning (chapters on inference and on neural networks as inference) is the intellectual background for variational methods and for the information bottleneck.
A classic, free, and still one of the best-written technical books in the field; its lectures (also free) are a model of teaching.

Part I, data compression: probability, entropy and inference; the source coding theorem; symbol codes; stream codes. Part II, noisy-channel coding: dependent random variables, the noisy-channel coding theorem, error-correcting codes. Part III, further topics in information theory. Part IV, probabilities and inference: an example inference task (clustering), maximum likelihood and clustering, exact marginalization, Laplace's method, model comparison and Occam's razor, Monte Carlo methods, variational methods, and decision theory. Part V, neural networks: single neurons, capacity, Hopfield networks, Boltzmann machines, supervised learning in multilayer networks, learning as inference, Gaussian processes, deconvolution. Part VI, sparse graph codes.

items: Probability and inference: the sum and product rules, Bayes' theorem as inference, likelihood, priors, and the argument that all inference is probability; the entropy of a distribution and Gibbs' inequality; information content as −log p.

Source coding: a source with entropy H can be compressed to about H bits per symbol and no fewer; Huffman codes for symbols, arithmetic coding for streams; the link to prediction: a good predictive model is a good compressor.

Noisy channels: mutual information as the information a received symbol gives about the sent one; channel capacity as the maximum over input distributions; error-correcting codes achieve rates up to capacity; a reading-level pass suffices for this course.

Clustering as inference: k-means as a hard assignment, soft k-means with responsibilities, and the connection to Gaussian mixtures and expectation-maximization; maximum likelihood versus Bayesian posteriors over parameters.

Model comparison: the evidence (marginal likelihood) automatically penalizes complexity, giving an Occam's razor without ad hoc terms; Laplace's method approximates the evidence with a Gaussian around the mode.

Monte Carlo and variational methods: importance sampling, rejection sampling, Metropolis, Gibbs sampling, slice sampling; variational free energy minimization as an alternative to sampling; these are the algorithms behind the Bayesian phase.

Neural networks as inference: a neuron as a probabilistic classifier, learning as maximizing a posterior, regularization as priors, error bars on predictions from the posterior, and Gaussian processes as the infinite-width limit of a network with a Bayesian prior.
Decision theory: expected utility; the point that a probability model plus a loss function yields the decision, which is exactly the alert threshold rule.

b.s:
H(X) = Σ p(x) log₂ (1/p(x));  I(X; Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y)
evidence P(D | M) = ∫ P(D | θ, M) P(θ | M) dθ
soft k-means: r_k(x) ∝ exp(−β ‖x − μ_k‖²)

items: Prediction and compression are the same problem; cross-entropy measures both.
The marginal likelihood is a built-in Occam's razor.
Sampling and variational methods are the two ways to compute Bayesian answers.

b.s: Implement soft k-means with a temperature parameter on the daily profiles, watch it become hard k-means as the temperature drops, and relate the responsibilities to a Gaussian mixture's posterior.

resources.lives: book · free · a semester, selectively · free; entropy, coding and learning as one subject

resources.title: StatQuest with Josh Starmer (YouTube)

b.s: Videos with silly songs and simple drawings that explain how learning machines work, one small idea at a time.

A YouTube channel where each video explains one idea, such as what a decision tree is or how logistic regression works, with drawings and a short song. Watch the videos on decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting and logistic regression during phase 4; they are slow, clear and free.

StatQuest's series on gradient boosting (four videos) walks through fitting trees to residuals step by step with numbers, which is exactly lesson 8's mechanism. The videos on ROC and AUC, on cross-validation and on bias and variance give the pictures behind lesson 6. The logistic regression series covers maximum likelihood and the meaning of the coefficients.

The channel's strength is tracing a computation with small numbers until it is obvious; use it to check your understanding of a derivation rather than as a source of the derivation. Its XGBoost series covers the second-order split gain, which is the LightGBM math in lesson 8's higher levels.

It stops at intuition and worked examples, which is the right place for a video; the formal accounts are in ISLP and ESL. When you teach, its pattern (a concrete numeric example before any symbol) is worth stealing.

A reminder that clarity is a research skill; the channel's popularity among practitioners reflects a gap textbooks leave, and it is the resource to hand to a stakeholder who wants to know what a boosted tree actually does.

Hundreds of short videos, each one concept: statistics fundamentals (mean, variance, distributions, p-values, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, maximum likelihood), machine learning fundamentals (bias and variance, cross-validation, confusion matrices, sensitivity and specificity, ROC and AUC), linear models (regression, R², logistic regression series, regularization with ridge, lasso and elastic net), trees (decision trees, regression trees, random forests, AdaBoost, gradient boost series, XGBoost series), support vector machines, PCA and clustering, neural networks and backpropagation, and more.

items: Maximum likelihood: pick the parameters that make the observed data most probable; for a normal, the sample mean and variance; for logistic regression, the coefficients that maximize the product of predicted probabilities of the observed classes.

Logistic regression series: fitting a line to log odds, the S-curve back in probability, maximum likelihood instead of least squares, R² analogues and p-values for coefficients, and the meaning of each coefficient.

Bias and variance, cross-validation: bias as inability to capture the true relationship, variance as sensitivity to the training set; k-fold cross-validation to compare methods; the confusion matrix, sensitivity (recall) and specificity, ROC by sweeping thresholds and AUC to compare models.
Regularization: ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero to reduce variance; lasso can zero them (feature selection); elastic net mixes; λ chosen by cross-validation.

Trees and ensembles: building a classification tree with Gini impurity and a regression tree with squared residuals; random forests with bootstrapping plus random feature subsets and out-of-bag error; AdaBoost's weighted stumps; gradient boost for regression (fit trees to residuals, scale by a learning rate) and for classification (residuals of log odds, leaf values from the sum of residuals over the sum of p(1 − p)); XGBoost's similarity scores, gain, pruning by γ, regularization λ, and the second-order derivation.
Support vector machines: the maximal margin classifier, soft margins, and the kernel trick (polynomial, radial) computing high-dimensional dot products cheaply.
PCA and clustering: PCA step by step with singular value decomposition, scree plots and loadings; k-means and hierarchical clustering with distance choices.
Neural networks: a chain of weighted sums and activations, the chain rule for backpropagation worked with actual numbers, gradient descent step by step.

b.s:
Gradient boost (classification): leaf value = Σ residuals / Σ p(1 − p)
XGBoost similarity = (Σ residuals)² / (Σ p(1 − p) + λ);  gain = sim_L + sim_R − sim_root
Ridge: minimize Σ (y − ŷ)² + λ Σ βⱼ²

items: Boosting's leaf values come from residuals divided by curvature; XGBoost's gain is the same idea with regularization.
Regularization trades a little bias for a lot of variance.
Sensitivity and specificity, precision and recall: know which pairs move together.
