resources.title: Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization (Bergstra, Bengio, 2012)

b.s: A paper that found that trying dial settings at random beats trying them in a neat grid, because only a few dials really matter.

Bergstra and Bengio showed that random search finds good hyperparameters faster than grid search for the same number of trials. The reason is in one figure: if only one of two dials matters, a grid wastes trials repeating the same values of the important one, while random search tries many different values. Free to read in the Journal of Machine Learning Research.

Read the introduction and the figure, then the experiments on neural networks. The lesson generalizes: budget your trials, sample them randomly (or with a smarter method), and look at which parameters actually moved the score.

The argument rests on low effective dimensionality of the hyperparameter response surface; the paper also introduces the use of quasi-random sequences. It is the foundation for later Bayesian and multi-fidelity methods, which improve on random search by modelling the response surface.
Compare with Hyperband and Bayesian optimization papers; random search remains the honest baseline that every tuning method must beat, and it parallelizes trivially.
A rare methodology paper that changed practice immediately; for a lead, its message is that a well-chosen search space and a fixed budget matter more than the search algorithm.

An empirical and theoretical case that random search over hyperparameters beats grid search for the same number of trials, on neural networks and deep belief networks, with an analysis based on low effective dimensionality and a discussion of quasi-random sequences and of the reproducibility of experiments.

items: The problem: hyperparameters (learning rate, layer sizes, regularization) are chosen by trial; grid search evaluates all combinations of a few values per dimension; the number of trials grows exponentially with dimensions.

Low effective dimensionality: on most problems, only a few hyperparameters matter, and which ones differ by dataset; a grid with k values per dimension tries only k distinct values of the important one, wasting the rest on repeats.

Random search: sample each hyperparameter from its own distribution independently; every trial has a distinct value for every dimension, so the important ones are explored densely; the experiments show equal or better results in a fraction of the trials.
Practical benefits: trials are independent and can run in parallel or be stopped and extended; a failed trial does not break the design; adding a new hyperparameter does not require restarting.
Quasi-random sequences: low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton) spread points more evenly than pure random, with a small extra gain.
Method: define sensible distributions (log-uniform for learning rates and regularization), fix a budget, run, and analyze which hyperparameters actually changed the score.

b.s: learning_rate ~ LogUniform(1e-3, 0.3); num_leaves ~ Uniform{15, …, 255}; min_data_in_leaf ~ LogUniform(20, 2000)

items: Random search is the honest baseline every tuner should beat.
Use log-uniform distributions for scale-like parameters.
Analyze the results to learn which parameters matter; that is more valuable than the best trial.

resources.title: Optuna documentation

b.s: The manual for a helper that tries dial settings for you, learns which ones look promising, and stops the bad tries early.

Optuna is a free Python library for hyperparameter search. You write a function that trains a model with settings drawn from ranges you define and returns the validation score; Optuna runs trials, favors promising regions, and can stop bad trials early. The tutorial pages get you running in an hour.

Read the tutorial (define an objective, create a study, optimize), the pruning page (early stopping of bad trials with LightGBM's callback), and the visualization page (parameter importance, optimization history). Use it to tune four LightGBM parameters with a budget of 30 trials on the chronological validation split.

Its default sampler is a tree-structured Parzen estimator, a Bayesian optimization method; the docs explain samplers and pruners so you can choose. Understand how to make trials reproducible (seeds), how to store studies (SQLite) and how to run trials in parallel on the Mac's cores.

Optuna's design (define-by-run search spaces, pluggable samplers) makes it usable for pipeline search, not only parameters; its parameter-importance analysis is a practical functional-ANOVA implementation for pruning the search space of a monthly retrain.

Tuning libraries are infrastructure; the questions at scale are distributed trials, warm starts across model versions, and integration with experiment tracking, all of which Optuna's docs address at a level worth reading before building your own.

Tutorial: the objective function and trials, samplers (TPE default, random, CMA-ES, grid), pruners (median, successive halving, Hyperband) with integration callbacks, multi-objective optimization, user attributes, saving and resuming studies with storage, distributed optimization, visualization (history, importance, parallel coordinates, slices, contours), and best practices for reproducibility.

items: Define-by-run: the objective function suggests values inside itself (`trial.suggest_float('lr', 1e-3, 0.3, log=True)`, `suggest_int`, `suggest_categorical`), builds and evaluates the model, and returns the score; conditional search spaces are natural.

Studies: `optuna.create_study(direction='maximize', sampler=..., pruner=..., storage='sqlite:///study.db', study_name=...)`; `study.optimize(objective, n_trials=30, timeout=...)`; `study.best_trial`, `best_params`, `trials_dataframe()`.
Samplers: TPE models good and bad regions with density estimates and samples where the ratio is favorable; random sampler as baseline; CMA-ES for continuous spaces; grid for exhaustive small spaces.

Pruning: report intermediate values (`trial.report(score, step)`) and stop unpromising trials (`trial.should_prune()`); the LightGBM integration callback reports each boosting round; median pruner and Hyperband implement successive halving.
Visualization and importance: optimization history, parameter importances (functional ANOVA), slice plots per parameter, parallel coordinates for interactions, and contour plots.
Reproducibility and scale: seed the sampler, log every trial's parameters and score, persist the study in a database to resume or to run trials in parallel processes on the Mac's cores.

b.s:
def objective(trial):
    params = dict(objective='binary', metric='average_precision', learning_rate=trial.suggest_float('lr', 1e-3, 0.3, log=True),
                  num_leaves=trial.suggest_int('leaves', 15, 255, log=True), min_data_in_leaf=trial.suggest_int('mdl', 20, 2000, log=True),
                  feature_fraction=trial.suggest_float('ff', 0.5, 1.0), num_threads=8, verbose=-1)
    m = lgb.train(params, dtr, 3000, valid_sets=[dva], callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100), optuna.integration.LightGBMPruningCallback(trial, 'average_precision')])
    return m.best_score['valid_0']['average_precision']

resources.title: Visual Information Theory (Olah)

b.s: A web page with pictures that explains what information is, using rectangles whose size shows how surprising something is.

Chris Olah's essay explains entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence with diagrams of code lengths: rare events need long codes, and using the wrong codebook wastes bits. It makes the cross-entropy loss feel like a real cost. Free, about an hour.

Read it before the information-theory topic; its diagrams show why cross-entropy is at least entropy, why KL is not symmetric, and what mutual information measures. Then redo its examples with the traffic label's base rate as the distribution.

The essay gives the coding interpretation that makes the theorems intuitive (the source-coding theorem as optimal code lengths); with it, the KL-based derivations in variational inference and the information bottleneck read naturally.
Olah's other essays (on neural network representations, on attention) are of the same quality; his work on interpretability is where the visual method meets research.
An example of explanation as research communication at its best; when you write for a broad technical audience, this is the standard.

A visual essay on information theory: optimal codes and code lengths, entropy, cross-entropy and its asymmetry, KL divergence, entropy and multiple variables (joint, conditional, mutual information), and the connection to machine learning.

items: Codes: to send messages about outcomes, give short codewords to frequent outcomes; a codeword of length L costs a fraction 1/2^L of the code space; the cheapest code assigns length −log₂ p(x) to outcome x.
Entropy: the expected code length under the optimal code, H(p) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x); it measures uncertainty in bits; uniform is maximal, certain is zero.

Cross-entropy: the expected length when you use a code optimized for q but events follow p, H(p, q) = −Σ p(x) log₂ q(x); always at least H(p); not symmetric, because the wrong code hurts differently in each direction.

KL divergence: the extra bits, KL(p‖q) = H(p, q) − H(p); zero only when the distributions match; the essay's rectangles show why it is asymmetric and why a code that ignores a possible event costs infinitely.

Multiple variables: joint entropy H(X, Y); conditional entropy H(Y|X) = H(X, Y) − H(X); mutual information I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X, Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X), the reduction in uncertainty about one from knowing the other; the Venn-like diagram of these quantities.

Machine learning: minimizing cross-entropy between labels and predictions minimizes the KL to the truth (the entropy of the truth is fixed); log loss is measured in nats; mutual information as a dependence measure for feature screening.

b.s:
H(p) = −Σ p log₂ p;  H(p, q) = −Σ p log₂ q;  KL(p‖q) = H(p, q) − H(p) ≥ 0
I(X; Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) = Σ p(x, y) log [p(x, y)/(p(x)p(y))]

items: Cross-entropy is the cost of the wrong codebook; minimizing it moves your model toward the truth.
KL is not a distance; the direction matters.
Mutual information is the reduction in surprise one variable gives about another.

b.s: Compute the entropy of the slow-episode label per hour of day, the cross-entropy of the LightGBM predictions, and the mutual information between the label and `down1_speed` binned into ten quantiles.

items.title: Jams move: sequences, neighbors and the road graph

b.s: See why a slowdown downstream predicts your station's future, and how models that read the road as a sequence and a graph exploit that.
When the front car in a line stops, the stopping spreads backwards, car by car, like a wave running down a slinky.
So if the road just ahead of you got slow, you will be slow soon. Our helper watches the road ahead to see the wave coming.
Line up toy cars and stop the first one. Watch how the 'stop' moves backwards along the line. Which car stops last?

Jams start at a bottleneck, a crash or a busy merge, and grow backwards against the direction of travel at roughly 10 to 15 mph. A station two miles upstream of a jam will be inside it in about ten minutes.

That is why the neighbor clues, especially the downstream station's speed, predict so well at 15 and 30 minutes, and why a model that looks at all the stations together, a 'graph' model, can learn the wave itself instead of being told about it.
A jam's tail moves backwards at 12 mph. How long until it reaches a station 3 miles upstream? What about 6 miles? Which horizon does each match?

Time series vocabulary: autocorrelation (speed now versus five minutes ago correlates at about 0.9), seasonality (daily and weekly), lags as features; persistence is strong precisely because autocorrelation is strong.

Space: the road is a line graph, and the registry's postmiles give each station an upstream and a downstream neighbor. A sequence model (GRU) reads the last 12 steps in order and keeps a memory; graph mixing lets each station's memory hear its neighbors' memories.

The physics: between two traffic states the boundary moves at w = Δflow / Δdensity. When a road goes from flowing to jammed, that slope is negative, a backward-moving wave, and its size sets how far ahead a station's future can be read from stations downstream.
Plot the autocorrelation of one station's speed for lags 1 to 48 (four hours). Describe the shape and say what it implies for the lag features.

Kinematic wave theory (Lighthill-Whitham-Richards): conservation ∂k/∂t + ∂q/∂x = 0 with a fundamental diagram q = Q(k). A discontinuity between states 1 and 2 moves at w = (q₂ − q₁)/(k₂ − k₁); in the congested branch w is about −10 to −15 mph, and queues discharge at capacity when the bottleneck clears.

Implication for prediction: the horizon over which a station's future is readable from its neighbors is roughly the distance to the nearest downstream disturbance divided by |w|. Beyond that, the calendar and incidents carry the signal.

Models along the ladder: ARIMA on one series, vector autoregression across stations, a GRU as a nonlinear state-space model, graph convolution as spatial smoothing with learned weights, and direct multi-horizon heads.
From one station's scatter of flow against occupancy, estimate capacity and the slope of the congested branch, and convert the slope into a shockwave speed in mph.

The spatio-temporal literature on PeMS data: DCRNN (diffusion convolution with forward and backward random-walk matrices on a directed graph, encoder-decoder GRU, scheduled sampling), STGCN (gated temporal convolutions with Chebyshev graph convolutions), Graph WaveNet (adaptive adjacency with dilated causal convolutions), then transformer variants. Benchmarks report MAE, RMSE and MAPE at 15, 30 and 60 minutes on METR-LA and PEMS-BAY.

The stable findings: gains over persistence grow with horizon; learned or adaptive graphs help; simple models are competitive at 15 minutes. The plan's two-hop mixing corresponds to a K = 2 diffusion step, and respecting wave direction (separate upstream and downstream weights) is a physically motivated inductive bias.
Implement diffusion convolution with the registry's directed adjacency and compare its validation average precision at 30 and 60 minutes with LightGBM's hand-made neighbor features.

City-scale graphs have hundreds of thousands to millions of segments with uneven probe coverage; practical systems use supersegments, embedding tables and hierarchy (the Google Maps ETA graph network is the public reference point), and update hidden states incrementally in streaming rather than recomputing windows.

Research threads: coupling learned models with simulators (cell transmission, microsimulation) for counterfactual questions such as rerouting a share of drivers; causal effects of incidents on propagation; transfer across cities; and wave physics as a regularizer in the loss.
Sketch a hybrid where the GRU predicts a residual over a kinematic-wave forecast, and argue where along the road and at which horizons the residual should carry the most signal.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

Autocorrelation is the correlation of a series with itself shifted by some lag: how much does speed now resemble speed k steps ago. `sid` is a station id you choose; `set_index("timestamp").speed` gives the speed series in time order; `interpolate(limit=3)` fills short gaps by drawing a straight line between neighbors, up to three steps, so the correlation is not broken by NaN. `s.autocorr(lag)` computes the correlation at one lag; the list comprehension collects lags 1 to 48 (four hours).

matplotlib is Python's plotting library; `plt.plot(x, y)` draws a line, `xlabel` and `ylabel` label the axes, `show()` displays it (in Jupyter the figure appears under the cell). The curve should start near 1 and decay: high for a few steps, still clearly positive at an hour. That decay is why lags are good features and why a 60-minute forecast is harder than a 15-minute one.
Autocorrelation of one station's speed.

items: `s = df[df.station_id == sid].set_index("timestamp").speed.interpolate(limit=3)` — one station's speed series, short gaps bridged
`acf = [s.autocorr(lag) for lag in range(1, 49)]` — correlation with itself at lags 1 to 48
`plt.plot(range(1, 49), acf); ...; plt.show()` — draw how memory fades with lag

b.s: The fundamental diagram is the one picture from traffic engineering everyone should know: flow (vehicles passing per interval) against occupancy (fraction of time the sensor is covered, a stand-in for density). At low occupancy flow rises with occupancy, since more cars pass; past a critical point the road is saturated, cars slow, and flow falls as occupancy climbs. Congestion is the falling branch.

`plt.scatter(x, y, s=2, alpha=.3)` draws one small, translucent dot per five-minute row, so dense regions look darker. A month of one station shows the triangle shape clearly, and the point where it turns over is that station's capacity. The model's `speed_ratio` and `occ` features are reading positions on this diagram.
The fundamental diagram from one month of one station.

x = df[df.station_id == sid]
plt.scatter(x.occ, x.flow, s=2, alpha=.3); plt.xlabel("occupancy"); plt.ylabel("flow per 5 min"); plt.show()

items: `x = df[df.station_id == sid]` — one station's month
`plt.scatter(x.occ, x.flow, s=2, alpha=.3)` — flow against occupancy, one dot per row

b.s: The graph needs to be numbers. `ids = list(reg.ID)` fixes an order for the N stations, and `pos` is a dictionary (a lookup table from key to value) from station id to its position 0 to N−1. `np.zeros((N, N), np.float32)` makes an empty N × N matrix. `reg.iterrows()` walks the registry one row at a time as `(index, row)` pairs; for each station with an upstream neighbor, the entry (station's position, neighbor's position) is set to 1, and likewise downstream. `pd.notna` guards the ends of each freeway, where a station has no neighbor on one side. The result is two directed adjacency matrices, the `A_up` and `A_down` that the `Mix` module of lesson 9.5 expects. With N around a hundred these matrices are tiny.
Directed adjacency matrices from the registry.

ids = list(reg.ID); pos = {i: k for k, i in enumerate(ids)}; N = len(ids)
A_up = np.zeros((N, N), np.float32); A_down = np.zeros((N, N), np.float32)
for _, r in reg.iterrows():
    if pd.notna(r.upstream_id):   A_up[pos[r.ID], pos[r.upstream_id]] = 1
    if pd.notna(r.downstream_id): A_down[pos[r.ID], pos[r.downstream_id]] = 1

items: `ids = list(reg.ID); pos = {i: k for k, i in enumerate(ids)}; N = len(ids)` — station order and id-to-position lookup
`A_up = np.zeros((N, N), np.float32); A_down = ...` — empty adjacency matrices
`for _, r in reg.iterrows(): ...` — for each station in the registry
`A_up[pos[r.ID], pos[r.upstream_id]] = 1` — mark its upstream neighbor, if it has one
`A_down[pos[r.ID], pos[r.downstream_id]] = 1` — and its downstream neighbor

b.s: A sequence model needs its input as a window: for each timestamp, the last twelve steps (one hour) for every station and every channel, where a channel is one measured or derived quantity. The six channels here are the speed ratio, occupancy, scaled flow, the incident flag and the two time-of-day circle coordinates. `pivot(index="timestamp", columns="station_id", values=chan)` turns the long table (one row per station per time) into a wide one (one row per time, one column per station per channel).

`to_numpy(np.float32).reshape(T, 6, N)` gives a three-dimensional array: time × channel × station. The list comprehension slices, for every t from 12 onward, the twelve rows before t; `np.stack` piles those slices into a four-dimensional array of shape (windows, 12, 6, N). Shapes are the whole difficulty of deep learning code; print `X.shape` and say each number's meaning out loud. Memory: a month is about 8,600 windows × 12 × 6 × N floats, a few hundred megabytes for N near a hundred, fine on 16 GB.
Windows of 12 steps × N stations × 6 channels, one per timestamp.

chan = ["speed_ratio", "occ", "flow_scaled", "incident_active", "min_sin", "min_cos"]
wide = df.pivot(index="timestamp", columns="station_id", values=chan)        # (T, 6*N)
X = np.stack([wide.to_numpy(np.float32).reshape(len(wide), len(chan), N)[t - 12:t] for t in range(12, len(wide))])  # (T-12, 12, 6, N)

items: `chan = [...]` — the six channels per station
`wide = df.pivot(index="timestamp", columns="station_id", values=chan)` — one row per timestamp, one column per station and channel
`wide.to_numpy(np.float32).reshape(len(wide), len(chan), N)` — time × channel × station
`X = np.stack([... [t - 12:t] for t in range(12, len(wide))])` — for each time, the hour before it: windows × 12 × 6 × N

b.s: A GRU (gated recurrent unit) is a recurrent network: it reads a sequence one step at a time, keeping a hidden vector that it updates at each step with learned gates deciding what to remember and what to forget. `nn.GRU(C, H, batch_first=True)` takes sequences of C-channel steps and produces H-dimensional hidden states; `batch_first` means the input shape is (batch, time, channel). `self.head = nn.Linear(H, 3)` turns a station's final hidden vector into three logits, one per horizon, so one network predicts 15, 30 and 60 minutes at once (multi-task).

In `forward`, `x` arrives as (batch, 12, 6, N). `permute(0, 3, 1, 2)` reorders the axes to (batch, N, 12, 6) and `reshape(B * N, T, C)` treats every station in every batch item as its own sequence, which is what a GRU wants. `self.gru(seq)[1][0]` is the final hidden state of each sequence; `reshape(B, N, -1)` puts the stations back together (−1 means 'work this dimension out'). Then two rounds of neighbor mixing with the adjacency matrices from step 3, and the head. The output, (batch, N, 3), is logits: apply a sigmoid and the calibration of lesson 11 before treating them as probabilities. Train it with the same loop as lesson 9.4.
A minimal spatio-temporal model.

items: `self.gru = nn.GRU(C, H, batch_first=True)` — reads each station's hour, step by step
`self.mix1 = Mix(H); self.mix2 = Mix(H); self.head = nn.Linear(H, 3)` — two rounds of neighbor mixing, then three horizon logits
`seq = x.permute(0, 3, 1, 2).reshape(B * N, T, C)` — every station becomes its own sequence
`h = self.gru(seq)[1][0].reshape(B, N, -1)` — final hidden state per station, regrouped by batch
`h = self.mix2(self.mix1(h, A_up, A_down), A_up, A_down)` — each station reads its neighbors, twice
`return self.head(h)` — logits for 15, 30 and 60 minutes, per station

b.q: Why is the downstream neighbor more informative than the upstream one for the next 30 minutes?

a.s: Queues grow backwards. A slow downstream station means the wave is heading toward you; a slow upstream station means it has already passed.

b.q: What limits how far ahead neighbors can help?

a.s: Distance to the disturbance divided by the wave speed. Beyond that horizon nothing on the road yet carries the information.

b.q: Why share the GRU across stations?

a.s: One set of weights sees a hundred times more data, and the dynamics of a queue are the same physics everywhere; station identity can be added as an embedding if needed.

items: 'Traffic is random.' Propagation is mechanical and fast to learn; what is hard is the onset of the first disturbance.
'The graph model replaces the physics.' It learns the physics from data; encoding wave direction helps it learn faster.
'Longer windows are better.' Beyond an hour the extra history mostly adds noise; the calendar carries the slow signal.

items.title: From scores to alerts: calibration, thresholds, lead time

b.s: Make the probabilities honest, choose when to warn, and measure the warning the way a driver would: how early, and how often wrongly.
Our helper says '70 % chance of slow'. If it says that a hundred times, it should be right about seventy of them. If it is only right forty times, its sureness is broken and we fix it.
Then we decide how sure it has to be before we shout 'slow!'. Shout too easily and people stop listening; shout too rarely and they get stuck.
Guess ten coin flips and say how sure you are each time. Keep score. Was your 'very sure' really more right than your 'not sure'?

Calibration means the probabilities are honest. We check by grouping predictions, all the 0.6-to-0.7s together, and counting how many really were slow. If the model is over-confident, we fit a correction curve, called isotonic regression, using data it did not train on.

Then the threshold. Warn at 0.3 and you catch more jams but cry wolf more; warn at 0.7 and the opposite. We pick the threshold that keeps, say, half of the warnings right, and we accept the recall that comes with it.
Lead time is the number of minutes between our first warning and the jam actually starting. That is the number a driver cares about.
Write ten predictions and what happened. Split them into two bins, below 0.5 and above. In each bin, compare the average prediction with the share that were slow.

Reliability diagram: bin rows by predicted probability, plot the observed share of positives per bin; the gap is calibration error. Two fixes fit on the validation split: Platt scaling (a sigmoid on the score) and isotonic regression (a monotone step function). Isotonic is more flexible and needs more data.

The threshold comes from the validation precision-recall curve at the precision the alert has to keep. Episode metrics: an episode begins at the first step of a run of label = 1; the alert is the first t in the two hours before that with p ≥ τ; lead = onset − alert; a false alarm is an alert not followed by an episode within 60 minutes, counted per station-day.
Trade-off: lower τ, longer lead and more false alarms. Plot lead time against false alarms per station-day for several τ and choose with the user in mind.
Make up a sequence of probabilities and labels over two hours. Compute the lead time and count false alarms at τ = 0.5 and τ = 0.3.

Proper scoring rules decompose into calibration and refinement; a model can rank perfectly and be badly calibrated, which is the tree-ensemble case. Isotonic regression is the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm and can overfit on a small validation set, so it needs thousands of positives; Platt scaling is safer with fewer.

Class reweighting shifts the prior, so calibrate after reweighting, on data with the true prevalence. Decision theory gives the threshold for calibrated probabilities: warn when p > C_FA / (C_FA + C_miss). Alerts are a policy, not a classifier: hysteresis (raise at τ_on, clear at a lower τ_off) prevents flapping, and the policy, not the model, is what gets evaluated on episodes.

Prove the cost-optimal threshold formula from expected cost and compute it for a false alarm costing 1 and a miss costing 4. Then explain why the formula is useless if the probabilities are not calibrated.

Three horizons produce three probabilities that can disagree; combine them into an expected time-to-slow or a hazard curve, or enforce monotone structure. Conformal methods give alert sets with distribution-free control of error rates over episodes, at the cost of exchangeability assumptions that time series violate and must be handled with weighting.

Calibration drifts and per-station calibration is noisy; hierarchical shrinkage toward the pooled map is the practical middle. Human factors from warning science: false-alarm ratios above roughly a half erode compliance, which sets a floor on the precision the policy must keep.

Formulate alerting as a sequential decision with a constraint on false alarms per station-day, and propose a policy with hysteresis that respects the constraint. Say how you would evaluate it on the test split.

In products, calibration and thresholds live in a policy layer separate from the model, versioned, and tested with real users; alert budgets are enforced globally and evaluated on outcomes rather than on precision.

Research threads: risk-controlling prediction sets (Angelopoulos, Bates and colleagues), calibration under covariate and label shift with unlabeled target data, and decision-focused learning where the model is trained for the policy's objective rather than for log loss.
Design an experiment that estimates the causal effect of an alert on a driver's reroute decision and travel time, given that alerts change the traffic other drivers experience.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

A boosted model's scores rank rows well but are not honest probabilities, especially with `is_unbalance` on. Calibration fixes that with a second, tiny model fitted on validation: it maps raw score to observed frequency. Isotonic regression is the standard choice: a step function that is only allowed to go up, fitted so that rows with higher raw scores get higher calibrated probabilities that match the positive rate actually seen. `IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds="clip")` handles scores outside the fitted range by clamping; `.fit(raw, truth)` fits, `.predict(raw)` maps.

The Brier score is the mean squared difference between the probability and the outcome, one number that rewards both good ranking and honest probabilities; lower is better. Print it before and after calibration; it should fall. Calibration is per horizon, so repeat for 15 and 60, and it uses validation rows, not training rows (which the model has already fitted) and not test rows (which must stay untouched).
Isotonic calibration on validation, per horizon.

from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression
iso = IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds="clip").fit(va.p_30, va.y_30)
va["q_30"] = iso.predict(va.p_30)
print("Brier raw", np.mean((va.p_30 - va.y_30) ** 2), "Brier calibrated", np.mean((va.q_30 - va.y_30) ** 2))

items: `iso = IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds="clip").fit(va.p_30, va.y_30)` — the monotone map from raw score to honest probability
`va["q_30"] = iso.predict(va.p_30)` — calibrated probabilities
`print("Brier raw", np.mean((va.p_30 - va.y_30) ** 2), "Brier calibrated", ...)` — should fall after calibration

b.s: The same threshold search as lesson 6.3, now on the calibrated scores `q_30`, and now written to be saved: `float(...)` turns numpy numbers into plain Python floats so they can go into a JSON file. The requirement is unchanged: at least half of alarms must be correct. Save `tau` per horizon into `models/calibration.json`; the live predictor in lesson 12 reads it. Changing the required precision later means rerunning only this step, not retraining.
Threshold at the required precision.

p, r, thr = precision_recall_curve(va.y_30, va.q_30)
ok = np.where(p[:-1] >= 0.5)[0]; tau = float(thr[ok[0]]); print("tau_30", tau, "recall", float(r[ok[0]]))

items: `p, r, thr = precision_recall_curve(va.y_30, va.q_30)` — the curve on calibrated scores
`ok = np.where(p[:-1] >= 0.5)[0]; tau = float(thr[ok[0]])` — the lowest threshold meeting the precision requirement
`print("tau_30", tau, "recall", float(r[ok[0]]))` — the threshold and the share of jams it catches

b.s: Drivers do not care about row-level scores; they care about whether they were warned before a jam started. An episode onset is the first row of a slow episode: the label is 1 now and was 0 in the previous row. `groupby("station_id").label.shift(1)` is the previous row's label within each station; `fillna(0)` treats the first row of each station as not slow; the `&` combines the two conditions. Sorting first is required, as always before shift. This is done on the test split, `te`, because this is the final, reported evaluation.
Episode onsets on the test split.

te = te.sort_values(["station_id", "timestamp"])
te["onset"] = ((te.label == 1) & (te.groupby("station_id").label.shift(1).fillna(0) == 0)).astype(int)

items: `te = te.sort_values(["station_id", "timestamp"])` — time order within each station
`te["onset"] = ((te.label == 1) & (prev label == 0)).astype(int)` — 1 at the first row of each slow episode

b.s: Lead time is how many minutes before an onset the first alert fired. First make the alert column: calibrated test scores at or above `tau`. Then, for each station (`groupby` again, `g` being one station's rows, `reset_index` renumbering them), find the rows where an episode starts (`on`), and for each such row `i` look at the window of the 24 rows before it (two hours; `g.loc[max(0, i - 24):i - 1]`). `hit` are the window rows that alerted; the lead is the distance from the first of them to the onset, times five minutes. If nothing alerted, the lead is NaN: a missed episode.

`pd.Series(leads)` makes the list a Series so that `notna().mean()` gives the share of episodes caught and `median()` the typical lead time in minutes. Report those two numbers together with the false-alarm rate from the next step; they are the model's real scorecard.
Lead time: first alert in the two hours before each onset.

te["alert"] = (iso.predict(te.p_30) >= tau).astype(int)
leads = []
for sid, g in te.groupby("station_id"):
    g = g.reset_index(drop=True); on = g.index[g.onset == 1]
    for i in on:
        w = g.loc[max(0, i - 24):i - 1]
        hit = w.index[w.alert == 1]
        leads.append((i - hit[0]) * 5 if len(hit) else np.nan)
leads = pd.Series(leads); print("episodes", len(leads), "caught", leads.notna().mean(), "median lead min", leads.median())

items: `te["alert"] = (iso.predict(te.p_30) >= tau).astype(int)` — 1 where the calibrated score crosses the threshold
`for sid, g in te.groupby("station_id"): ... on = g.index[g.onset == 1]` — each station's episode starts
`w = g.loc[max(0, i - 24):i - 1]; hit = w.index[w.alert == 1]` — the two hours before an onset, and the alerts in it
`leads.append((i - hit[0]) * 5 if len(hit) else np.nan)` — minutes from the first alert to the onset, or missed
`print("episodes", len(leads), "caught", leads.notna().mean(), "median lead min", leads.median())` — how many jams, how many warned, how early

b.s: A false alarm is an alert with no slow episode in the next hour. `fut` marks whether any of the next twelve rows (an hour) is slow: reversing the label series with `s[::-1]`, taking a rolling maximum over twelve rows, and reversing back turns a backward-looking window into a forward-looking one; `min_periods=1` lets it work near the end. This is one of the rare legitimate uses of future information, because it is evaluation, not a model input.

The false alarms are rows with `alert == 1` and `fut == 0`. Grouping them by station and by day (`timestamp.dt.floor("D")` drops the time of day) and taking `size()` counts them per station-day; dividing the total by the number of station-days gives the rate a driver would feel: how many wrong warnings per station per day. Below one is livable; several is not, whatever the average precision says.
False alarms per station-day.

te["fut"] = te.groupby("station_id").label.transform(lambda s: s[::-1].rolling(12, min_periods=1).max()[::-1])
fa = te[(te.alert == 1) & (te.fut == 0)].groupby([te.station_id, te.timestamp.dt.floor("D")]).size()
print("false alarms per station-day", fa.sum() / (te.station_id.nunique() * te.timestamp.dt.floor("D").nunique()))

items: `te["fut"] = te.groupby("station_id").label.transform(lambda s: s[::-1].rolling(12, min_periods=1).max()[::-1])` — 1 if any of the next hour's rows is slow
`fa = te[(te.alert == 1) & (te.fut == 0)].groupby([station, day]).size()` — false alarms per station per day
`print(fa.sum() / (stations × days))` — the average false-alarm rate per station-day

b.q: Why calibrate on the validation split and not on training?

a.s: The model has fit the training rows; its confidence there is meaningless. Calibration needs rows the model has not seen, and the test split must stay untouched for the final report.

b.q: What does a lead time of zero or negative mean?

a.s: The first alert came at or after the episode began: the model saw the jam, it did not foresee it. Expect that for crash-initiated episodes.

b.q: Why count false alarms per station-day and not per row?

a.s: A driver experiences alerts per trip, not per 5-minute row; a station firing twenty times in one hour is one bad hour, not twenty errors.

items: '0.5 is the natural threshold.' It is only right when a false alarm and a miss cost the same, which they never do.
'Calibration fixes ranking.' It is monotone; it changes the numbers, not the order.
'A high AP means useful alerts.' Only the episode metrics, lead time and false alarms, say that.

resources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, the Python edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), chapters 1–5, 7, 9

b.s: A free book about predicting the future from the past, by people who do it for a living, with lots of pictures of wiggly lines.

The standard forecasting textbook, free online, now with Python. Chapters 1 to 5 cover what forecasting is, how to draw time series, how to split a series into trend and seasonal parts, simple forecasting methods, and how to check whether a forecast is any good. Chapter 7 is regression with time features, chapter 9 is ARIMA. Read 1 to 5 fully and do the exercises.

Chapter 5's evaluation (training and test in time order, residual checks, accuracy measures) and its simple baselines (naive, which is persistence; seasonal naive, which is our profile rate) are the heart. Chapter 3's decomposition helps you see the daily and weekly cycles in a station's speed, and chapter 7's Fourier terms are the sine and cosine time features of lesson 5.

The book supplies the statistical forecasting vocabulary that ML-first people lack: stationarity, autocorrelation, exponential smoothing, ARIMA, and its 'time series cross-validation', which is the rolling-origin protocol lesson 6 uses. Chapter 9 shows why ARIMA is a linear model on lags with a principled error structure, which clarifies what a gradient-boosted model on lag features adds and gives up.

Compare its classical models with the ML approach: one ARIMA per series does not scale to a hundred stations with spatial dependence, and its hierarchical and global-model chapters bridge toward the global boosted and graph models used here. Its treatment of forecast intervals is the classical route to the uncertainty questions of phase 8.

Hyndman's wider work (the M4 and M5 forecasting competitions, hierarchical reconciliation, feature-based model selection) is the empirical forecasting literature. The M5 result, gradient-boosted models on lag features winning at scale, is direct evidence for this project's choice of LightGBM as the production model.

Getting started (what can be forecast, forecasting steps, the statistical perspective); time series graphics (plots, seasonal plots, scatterplots, lag plots, autocorrelation, white noise); time series decomposition (transformations, components, moving averages, classical and STL decomposition); time series features; the forecaster's toolbox (simple methods, fitted values and residuals, residual diagnostics, forecast distributions and prediction intervals, evaluating accuracy on training and test sets, time series cross-validation); regression models with time series features (trend, seasonality, dummies, Fourier terms, selecting predictors, forecasting with regression); ARIMA (stationarity and differencing, autoregressive and moving-average models, non-seasonal and seasonal ARIMA, estimation and order selection, forecasting).

items: What is forecastable: depends on how well the factors are understood, how much data exist, whether the forecast affects the outcome (it does, for traffic alerts), and the horizon; the steps: define the problem, gather information, exploratory analysis, choose models, use and evaluate.

Graphics: time plots, seasonal plots (each day overlaid, which shows the daily cycle in traffic), seasonal subseries plots, lag plots, and the autocorrelation function; trend, seasonality and cycles; white noise's ACF within ±2/√T.

Decomposition: Box-Cox transforms to stabilize variance; additive versus multiplicative components; moving averages to estimate trend; STL for robust decomposition with multiple seasonalities (daily and weekly).

Simple methods as baselines: mean, naive (last value, which is persistence), seasonal naive (same time last cycle, which is the profile), drift; residuals should be uncorrelated with zero mean; prediction intervals from residual variance; bootstrapped intervals.

Evaluation: point forecast errors (MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE scaled by a naive forecast's in-sample MAE); the training-test split in time; time series cross-validation (rolling origin) where each fold trains on data before its test point; evaluating forecast distributions with quantile and CRPS scores.

Regression with time features: linear regression on trend, seasonal dummies, holidays, Fourier terms (sin and cos pairs for a period, exactly the minute-of-day encoding), intervention dummies and lagged predictors; selecting predictors by AICc or cross-validation; ex-ante versus ex-post forecasts (you only have forecasts of predictors at forecast time, which is the weather point).

ARIMA: stationarity, differencing (and seasonal differencing) to reach it; AR(p) as regression on lags, MA(q) as regression on past errors, ARIMA(p, d, q); the ACF and PACF for identification; maximum likelihood estimation; order selection by AICc; seasonal ARIMA; forecasting and intervals; the point that ARIMA is a linear model on lags with a principled error structure.

b.s:
MASE = MAE / MAE_naive_in-sample
Fourier terms: sin(2πkt/m), cos(2πkt/m) for k = 1..K
ARIMA(p, d, q): (1 − Σ φ_i B^i)(1 − B)^d y_t = c + (1 + Σ θ_j B^j) ε_t

items: Naive and seasonal naive are the baselines; report MASE so skill is comparable across series.
Rolling-origin evaluation is the only honest one for time series.
Fourier terms encode seasonality for any model; the sine and cosine time features are this idea.

b.s: Decompose one station's speed with STL into daily and weekly components, then compare seasonal naive, a regression with Fourier terms and holiday dummies, and LightGBM on a rolling-origin evaluation with MASE.

resources.lives: book · free · three weeks · free online; the forecasting book

resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Time Series

b.s: A short online lesson about guessing what comes next in a line of numbers.

Six lessons on store sales data: the trend, seasonality using sine and cosine features, using past values as features (lags), combining two models, and forecasting several steps ahead with machine learning. About half a day, graded as you go.

Its lag-feature and Fourier-feature lessons are exactly our lags and the sine and cosine encoding of time. Its hybrid lesson, a simple model for the predictable part plus a boosted model for what is left, is a pattern to try here: profile plus a residual model.

Note how the course handles multi-step forecasting (direct versus recursive strategies) and where leakage hides in lag construction. Its examples are single series without spatial structure, so the neighbor features of lesson 5 and the graph models of lesson 10 are beyond it.

The hybrid idea generalizes to 'physics plus residual', which lesson 10's advanced prompt asks about, and its Fourier treatment of seasonality is the linear analogue of what a recurrent network learns. Short courses like this are where practitioner defaults come from, so know what they teach and where they stop.

The design principle it plants, decompose into predictable structure and a learned residual, is robust across production forecasters and is how a classical model can remain as a fallback when a learned model goes stale.

Linear regression with time series (time-step and lag features); trend (moving averages, polynomial trend, forecasting with trend); seasonality (seasonal plots, indicators, Fourier features, periodograms); time series as features (serial dependence, cycles, lag plots, choosing lags); hybrid models (residuals, combining a linear model and a boosted model); forecasting with machine learning (horizons, multistep strategies: multioutput, direct, recursive, DirRec).

items: Two kinds of features: time-dependent (a time-step counter, trend) and serially dependent (lags); a linear model on a time index fits trend, on lags fits autocorrelation.
Trend: moving-average smoothing to see it, deterministic trend features (linear, quadratic) from a `DeterministicProcess`, and the risk of extrapolating polynomials.

Seasonality: seasonal indicators (one-hot for weekday) for short periods; Fourier features (pairs of sin and cos at harmonics of the period) for long periods; the periodogram to pick how many harmonics.
Lags: partial autocorrelation to choose lags; lag plots to see nonlinearity; leading indicators as lagged exogenous series; the leakage risk when lags are computed after a target shift.

Hybrids: fit a linear model to trend and seasonality, then a second model (gradient boosting) to the residuals, because trees cannot extrapolate trend; feature-transforming versus target-transforming learners.

Multistep forecasting: define the forecast origin, horizon and lead; multioutput models predict all steps at once; the direct strategy trains one model per step (this project's choice); recursive feeds predictions back; DirRec combines; each has bias and variance trade-offs.

b.s:
y_{t+h} = f_h(y_t, y_{t−1}, …, x_t)   (direct strategy, one model per h)
residual = y − linear_trend_seasonal;  boost(residual)

items: Trend and seasonality by linear features, the rest by lags; hybrids let trees do what they are good at.
Choose the multistep strategy deliberately; direct is simplest and robust.
Lags are computed before, and never from, the shifted target.

b.s: Fit a hybrid of the profile (as the seasonal model) plus LightGBM on residual speed, and compare its 30-minute MAE with LightGBM on raw speed.

resources.lives: course · free · half a day · free; lag features and hybrids in an afternoon

resources.title: statsmodels documentation: one ARIMA fit on one station

b.s: A tool that fits an old but famous kind of forecast to a line of numbers. You try it once to see what it does.

statsmodels is a Python library for statistics. Fit an ARIMA model to one station's speed, look at its forecast for the next hour and at what it got wrong. The point is to know what ARIMA is and how it behaves, not to put it in the pipeline.

ARIMA(p, d, q) predicts a value from p past values, d differences, and q past errors. Fit it with `ARIMA(series, order=(2, 0, 1)).fit()`, forecast twelve steps, and compare with persistence. You will see a linear model on lags that does about as well as persistence at short horizons and drifts toward the mean at long ones.

Understanding ARIMA clarifies why lag features work and what a recurrent network adds: nonlinearity, exogenous inputs, and parameters shared across stations. SARIMAX adds seasonality and exogenous regressors, which is the classical way to include incidents and rain, and its diagnostics (residual autocorrelation) are useful for any model.

Vector ARIMA and state-space models with the Kalman filter are the classical route to multi-station forecasting, and their scaling limits are what motivated the graph deep-learning literature. statsmodels' state-space module is a good place to see the Kalman filter concretely before reading about recurrent models as nonlinear state-space models.

Classical models remain the interpretable baseline and a source of principled uncertainty that deep models lack. A production system often keeps a simple statistical model as the fallback when the learned model is stale or its inputs are missing, and statsmodels is where that fallback would be built.

The time-series analysis module: ARIMA and SARIMAX models (specification, fitting, diagnostics, forecasting), exponential smoothing, state-space models, unit root tests, ACF and PACF functions and plots, seasonal decomposition, and VAR models.

items: Specification: `ARIMA(endog, order=(p, d, q), seasonal_order=(P, D, Q, s), exog=...)`; `SARIMAX` for exogenous regressors (incidents, rain); trend terms.

Fitting and output: `.fit()` by maximum likelihood; the summary shows coefficients with standard errors, AIC and BIC, and diagnostic tests (Ljung-Box for residual autocorrelation, Jarque-Bera for normality, heteroscedasticity).
Diagnostics: `plot_diagnostics()` (standardized residuals, histogram, Q-Q plot, correlogram); `acf`, `pacf`, `plot_acf`, `plot_pacf` for identification; `adfuller` and `kpss` for stationarity.

Forecasting: `.forecast(steps)` and `.get_forecast(steps)` with `.conf_int()` for intervals; `predict` with dynamic forecasting; `.apply` to new data with fixed parameters for out-of-sample evaluation.
Decomposition and smoothing: `seasonal_decompose` and `STL`; `ExponentialSmoothing` (Holt-Winters) with additive or multiplicative seasonality.
State space: `UnobservedComponents` for local level and trend with seasonal terms; the Kalman filter underlying SARIMAX; `VAR` for several series jointly.

b.s:
m = ARIMA(s, order=(2, 0, 1)).fit(); print(m.summary()); fc = m.get_forecast(12); fc.predicted_mean, fc.conf_int()
sm.tsa.acf(s, nlags=48); plot_pacf(s, lags=48)

items: ARIMA diagnostics (residual ACF, Ljung-Box) are useful checks for any model's residuals.
SARIMAX is the classical way to add exogenous inputs.
Forecast intervals from ARIMA are model-based; compare their coverage with empirical ones.

b.s: Fit ARIMA(2,0,1) and SARIMAX with a rain regressor to one station's speed, forecast an hour, and compare MAE and interval coverage with persistence over a week of rolling forecasts.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; do it once to know what it is

resources.title: traffic-simulation.de and its model documentation (Treiber, Kesting)

b.s: A website where you can watch cartoon cars drive on a ring road, add a slow truck, and see a traffic jam appear from nowhere and travel backwards. The pages next to it explain why.

A free browser simulation by the authors of a well-known traffic textbook. You change the number of cars, the road shape and driver behavior, and watch jams form and move upstream. The site's documentation pages explain the models it runs (car-following and lane-changing) without needing the book.

Use the simulator to see lesson 10's ideas: the fundamental diagram, capacity, the backward-moving jam wave and its speed, and how an on-ramp creates a bottleneck. The documentation pages describe the Intelligent Driver Model and the kinematic-wave picture in enough detail to follow the equations.

The model documentation covers the Intelligent Driver Model and lane-changing rules with parameters and references to the open literature; the authors' papers (free preprints) supply the theory of the textbook. Together they give you the physical priors that justify monotone constraints and neighbor direction.
Use simulator-generated data for stress tests on regimes rare in the archive and as a baseline for physics-informed components; the source code of the simulation is open and readable.

Coupling learned forecasters with open simulators is where counterfactual evaluation starts; the site and its code are the practical entry, and the Intelligent Driver Model is simple enough to make differentiable.

An interactive microscopic traffic simulator with scenarios (ring road, on-ramp, off-ramp, road works, uphill grade, traffic lights, roundabout) and controls for inflow, truck fraction, driver parameters, and speed limits; documentation of the models it runs: the Intelligent Driver Model for car-following and MOBIL for lane changing, plus explanations of the traffic phenomena you can produce.

items: Car-following: each vehicle accelerates based on its own speed, the gap to the leader and the speed difference; the Intelligent Driver Model has a desired speed v₀, time headway T, minimum gap s₀, maximum acceleration a and comfortable deceleration b, and produces realistic gaps and stop-and-go waves.
Lane changing: MOBIL changes lanes when the changing vehicle gains acceleration and the disadvantage imposed on others is below a politeness-weighted threshold, with safety limits.

Phenomena to produce: free flow, capacity, breakdown at an on-ramp (a bottleneck), the jam propagating upstream at 10 to 15 mph against traffic, stop-and-go waves on the ring road with no bottleneck (instability from a small perturbation), capacity drop after breakdown, and the effect of speed limits and truck share.

Macroscopic reading: plotting flow against density from the simulation gives the fundamental diagram; the slope between congested states is the wave speed; the on-ramp scenario shows why a queue forms upstream of the merge.
Control experiments: ramp metering (limiting on-ramp inflow) delays or prevents breakdown; variable speed limits smooth waves; both are the setting for the reinforcement-learning control exercise.
Data generation: the simulator's source is open; run it headlessly to produce synthetic detector data for testing the forecaster on rare regimes.

b.s:
IDM: dv/dt = a [1 − (v/v₀)^δ − (s*(v, Δv)/s)²],  s* = s₀ + vT + vΔv/(2√(ab))
wave speed w = Δq/Δk between two traffic states

items: A jam needs only a bottleneck and enough demand; it then travels upstream at a nearly constant speed.
Stop-and-go waves can arise with no bottleneck at all; traffic is an unstable system near capacity.
Ramp metering works by keeping the mainline below breakdown density.

b.s: Run the on-ramp scenario, raise inflow until breakdown, measure how many seconds the jam's tail takes to move 500 m upstream, convert to mph, and compare with the shockwave speed estimated from one station's fundamental diagram.

resources.lives: interactive · free · an evening · free simulator and model docs; the physics of jams

resources.title: Kaggle: Store Sales, Time Series Forecasting competition

b.s: A practice contest with real store sales numbers where you guess future sales and get a score, for free.

A permanent beginner competition on Kaggle: predict daily sales for many products and stores from history, holidays and oil prices. You submit a file and get a score. It is the exercise for the time-series topic on data that is not traffic, and the public notebooks show many approaches.

Build lag and calendar features, a global gradient-boosted model, and a rolling-origin validation, then submit; read three public notebooks and note where they leak (features that use the future). The evaluation metric and the multi-series structure mirror the M5 findings.

Use it to practice global models across series, hierarchical structure (store, family), exogenous regressors and honest validation on a leaderboard; then compare your validation score with your leaderboard score to see selection bias in action.
Competitions are natural experiments about what works under a protocol; this one is small enough to iterate quickly and is a fair place to test a new idea before applying it to the traffic data.
A free, standing benchmark for time-series practice and for calibrating a newcomer's forecasting skill.

A getting-started competition: forecast daily unit sales for product families across Favorita stores in Ecuador for 16 days, using training sales, store metadata, oil prices, holidays and events, and transactions; evaluated by root mean squared logarithmic error; with a companion tutorial series and many public notebooks.

items: The data: a long table of date, store, family and sales; auxiliary tables for stores (type, cluster, city), oil price (a macro driver), holidays (national, regional, local, transferred), and transactions; the test period follows training.

Feature ideas: lags respecting the 16-day horizon (a lag of at least 16 days for direct models, or a recursive scheme), rolling statistics, calendar features (day of week, payday effects on the 15th and month end), holiday flags with regional matching, oil price and its lags, and store and family identifiers as categoricals.
Models: a global LightGBM across all series (target log1p sales); hybrids with a linear trend and seasonal model plus boosted residuals; per-family models; ensembles.
Validation: hold out the last 16 days of training as a validation window, and better, several such windows; compare validation RMSLE with the public leaderboard to see the gap.
Leakage traps in public notebooks: rolling features computed with the current day, target encodings fit on all data, and using test-period information (holidays are fine, sales are not).
The metric: RMSLE penalizes underprediction more than overprediction and handles zeros; it matches a log-transformed target.

b.s:
RMSLE = √( mean (log(1 + ŷ) − log(1 + y))² )
lag_16 = sales.groupby(['store','family']).shift(16)

items: Respect the horizon when building lags.
Use several validation windows and compare with the leaderboard to measure your own selection bias.
A log target plus a global boosted model is the strong, simple baseline.

resources.title: The M5 forecasting competition and its findings (Makridakis, Spiliotis, Assimakopoulos)

b.s: A big contest where thousands of people tried to predict how many of each thing a store would sell. The winners used the same kind of tree model we use for traffic.

M5 was a large forecasting competition on Kaggle in 2020 with real Walmart sales data, tens of thousands of series. The organizers later published what worked: gradient-boosted trees on lag features won, simple statistical methods were strong baselines, and combining models helped. The competition page and the summary papers are free.

Read the organizers' summary of the accuracy competition: the winning approaches, the role of cross-learning (one model across many series), and the evaluation metric. Then read one winner's write-up. The pattern, a global boosted model on lag and calendar features with careful validation, is this project's stage 9.

M5 is the largest public evidence for global models over per-series models, for boosted trees over classical methods at scale, and for the importance of the validation protocol (many teams overfit the public leaderboard). Its uncertainty track (quantile forecasts) connects to the uncertainty topic in the final phase.

The M-competition series (M1 through M6) is the empirical forecasting literature; read the M4 findings alongside M5 to see how the consensus moved from statistical ensembles to boosted global models, and what the organizers concluded about deep learning's role.

Competitions are natural experiments about what works under a fixed protocol; their limitations (leaderboard overfitting, no deployment costs) are as instructive as their results. For a forecasting team, M5's write-ups are the closest thing to a field manual.

The competition (42,840 hierarchical daily sales series from Walmart, 28-day horizon, accuracy track scored by weighted RMSSE across aggregation levels, uncertainty track scored by weighted scaled pinball loss over nine quantiles) and the organizers' papers on background, findings and the winning methods.

items: The data and hierarchy: items within departments within categories within stores within states; the metric averages performance across all levels with weights by dollar sales, so both bottom-level and aggregate forecasts matter.

Findings: gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM) on lag, rolling, calendar and price features dominated; cross-learning across series (one global model) beat per-series models; simple statistical methods were competitive baselines and useful ensemble members; combining models helped; external information (prices, events) mattered.

Validation: the public leaderboard's validation period misled many teams; those who validated on multiple time windows generalized better; the point about selection bias and rolling-origin evaluation.
Uncertainty track: quantile forecasts from boosted models and from distributional assumptions; empirical scaling from point forecasts worked; coverage was often poor at extreme quantiles.

Practical recipes: features such as lags at 7, 14, 28 days, rolling means and standard deviations, days since last sale, calendar and event flags, price changes; tweedie or Poisson objectives for intermittent counts; recursive versus direct strategies; ensembling over seeds and windows.
Limits: a competition metric is not a business objective; leaderboard overfitting; compute-heavy solutions; but the evidence for global boosted models on many related series is strong.

pinball(q) = mean( max(q(y − ŷ), (q − 1)(y − ŷ)) )

items: The perceptron and the multilayer perceptron; activations; loss functions; backpropagation for one hidden layer, by hand.

items.title: Neural networks and backpropagation, on the M1

b.s: Build a network by hand once, check its gradients, then let PyTorch do it on the Mac's GPU and know what changed.
A neural network is a lot of tiny seesaws stacked in layers. The first layer looks at the clues, the next layer looks at what the first layer said, and so on until the last one gives the answer.
When the answer is wrong, the 'oops' travels backwards through the layers so every seesaw adjusts a little. That is called backpropagation.
Play the whisper game down a line of friends. When the message comes out wrong, work backwards to find where it changed. That is what the network does with its mistake.

One layer computes weighted sums of its inputs, exactly like lesson 7, and then applies a simple bend: negatives become zero (ReLU). Stacking layers lets the network learn combinations of clues, such as 'raining AND rush hour', which a single seesaw cannot.
Training is the same loop as before: guess, compare, adjust. The adjusting uses the chain rule to pass the error back through every layer. PyTorch does that calculus for you.

The Mac mini has a small GPU. PyTorch can run the arithmetic there through a backend called MPS. For tiny networks the CPU is nearly as fast, because telling the GPU what to do costs more than the work.
Inputs a = 1, b = 2, weights 0.5 and −1, bias 0.2. Compute the weighted sum, then apply ReLU. Now flip the sign of the first weight and do it again.

Forward pass: h = ReLU(W₁x + b₁), p = σ(w₂·h + b₂). Loss: cross-entropy. Backward pass: ∂L/∂w₂ = (p − y) h; ∂L/∂h = (p − y) w₂; through ReLU multiply by 1 where the pre-activation was positive and 0 elsewhere; ∂L/∂W₁ = δ₁ xᵀ.

Optimizers: plain gradient descent, momentum, Adam (adaptive step per weight). Overfitting controls: early stopping, dropout, weight decay. Practical rules: standardize inputs, start with a learning rate of 1e-3, batches of a few hundred, and make sure the loss falls on a tiny subset before training on everything.
On the M1: `device = torch.device('mps')`, move the model and each batch with `.to(device)`, float32 only.
Implement the one-hidden-layer forward and backward pass in numpy and check every gradient with finite differences at ε = 1e-5. Do not move on until the largest difference is below 1e-6.

Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation on a computational graph: one forward and one backward pass give every parameter's gradient at a cost independent of parameter count. Initialization (He for ReLU, Xavier for tanh) keeps activations and gradients at unit scale; without it deep nets vanish or explode.

Batch and layer normalization stabilize training; Adam's bias correction matters in the first steps; warmup and cosine schedules are cheap wins. Early stopping on validation is the main regularizer for small tabular nets and is equivalent to L2 for linear models.

Engineering: keep the dataset on the device, batch in large chunks, avoid per-batch Python work. MPS specifics: fp32 and fp16, no fp64, `PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1` for unsupported ops, and a launch-overhead floor that makes tiny models CPU-competitive. Measure rows per second at batch 256 and 8192 on both devices before choosing.
Benchmark the MLP on CPU and MPS at batch sizes 256, 2048 and 8192; find the crossover and explain it in terms of kernel launch overhead versus arithmetic.

Overparameterized networks generalize for reasons still being mapped: the implicit bias of SGD, double descent, and flat minima are the working vocabulary. On tabular data of this size they rarely beat boosted trees (Grinsztajn et al., 2022) unless the data has structure the trees cannot see, which here is the spatial graph.

Sequence models: GRU and LSTM gating, truncated backpropagation through time, dilated temporal convolutions and attention. For traffic, DCRNN couples diffusion convolution on the road graph with a sequence-to-sequence GRU; STGCN alternates gated temporal convolutions with spectral graph convolutions; Graph WaveNet learns an adaptive adjacency. The plan's challenger, a shared GRU plus two rounds of neighbor mixing, is a stripped-down DCRNN.
Training recipe for the 12 × N × 6 windows: whole dataset in memory, batches of timestamps, positive class weight per horizon, early stopping on validation average precision.
Write the message-passing update h ← h + W_u h_up + W_d h_down as a matrix expression with directed adjacency matrices A_up and A_down, and relate two rounds of it to a K = 2 diffusion convolution.

On-device deep learning brings constraints that training clusters hide: Core ML export, fp16 on the Neural Engine, static shapes, a supported-operator list, energy per inference, and thermal throttling. The unified-memory model on Apple silicon removes copies between CPU and GPU but makes many workloads bandwidth-bound.
What transfers from the Mac mini to a cluster: recipes, evaluation discipline, and the habit of checking gradients; what does not: batch-size and learning-rate scaling laws.

Research threads: spatio-temporal transformers and adaptive graphs at city scale; physics-informed losses that respect kinematic wave direction; time-series foundation models used zero-shot against small specialized models; and uncertainty through deep ensembles, dropout at inference or conformal wrappers.
Outline the Core ML export path for the spatio-temporal net: which layers convert cleanly, how to handle a variable number of stations, and what you would measure on device before shipping.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) is logistic regression with a hidden layer in between: the inputs are multiplied by a weight matrix `W1` and shifted by `b1`, passed through ReLU (`max(z, 0)`, which zeroes negatives and is what lets the network bend), then multiplied by a second weight vector `w2` and squashed by the sigmoid. `H = 64` is the hidden width. Weights start small and random; the `sqrt(2 / d)` and `sqrt(1 / H)` scales (He and LeCun initialization) keep the signal from blowing up or vanishing.

`forward` computes the prediction and keeps the intermediate values needed for the backward pass. `backward` is backpropagation by hand: start with the output error `e = (p − y) / n`, get the gradient of the last layer (`h.T @ e`), push the error back through `w2` (`np.outer(e, w2)`), zero it where ReLU was off (`* (z1 > 0)`), and get the first layer's gradient (`dh.T @ X`). Each step is the chain rule from calculus applied to one layer. `X @ W1.T` uses the transpose so the shapes line up: rows × features times features × hidden.
The numpy MLP with a hand-written backward pass.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0); d, H = Xtr.shape[1], 64
W1 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / d), (H, d)).astype(np.float32); b1 = np.zeros(H, np.float32)
w2 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(1 / H), H).astype(np.float32); b2 = 0.0
def forward(X):
    z1 = X @ W1.T + b1; h = np.maximum(z1, 0); z2 = h @ w2 + b2; p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z2)); return z1, h, p
def backward(X, y):
    z1, h, p = forward(X); e = (p - y) / len(y)
    gw2 = h.T @ e; gb2 = e.sum()
    dh = np.outer(e, w2) * (z1 > 0)
    gW1 = dh.T @ X; gb1 = dh.sum(0)
    return gW1, gb1, gw2, gb2

items: `W1, b1, w2, b2 = small random matrices and zero biases` — the network's parameters, sensibly scaled
`z1 = X @ W1.T + b1; h = np.maximum(z1, 0)` — first layer, then ReLU
`z2 = h @ w2 + b2; p = sigmoid(z2)` — second layer, then a probability
`e = (p - y) / len(y); gw2 = h.T @ e; gb2 = e.sum()` — output error and the last layer's gradients
`dh = np.outer(e, w2) * (z1 > 0)` — error pushed back through w2 and the ReLU gate
`gW1 = dh.T @ X; gb1 = dh.sum(0)` — first layer's gradients

b.s: The same numerical check as lesson 7.3, on one weight of the first layer. `L` is the cross-entropy loss written as a one-line function. The entry `W1[3, 5]` is nudged up, the loss measured, nudged down by twice the amount, measured, and restored; the slope is compared with the backward pass's `gW1[3, 5]`. Sixty-four rows are enough. A disagreement near 1e-6 means the backward pass is right; try a second entry and one of `w2` before moving on. Every network you ever train relies on this check having been done by someone.
Gradient check on a few rows.

def L(X, y): p = np.clip(forward(X)[2], 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7); return -np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))
X0, y0 = Xtr[:64], ytr[:64]; gW1, gb1, gw2, gb2 = backward(X0, y0)
eps = 1e-4; i, j = 3, 5
W1[i, j] += eps; lp = L(X0, y0); W1[i, j] -= 2 * eps; lm = L(X0, y0); W1[i, j] += eps
print(abs((lp - lm) / (2 * eps) - gW1[i, j]))     # ~1e-6

items: `def L(X, y): ...` — the loss as a function of the current weights
`gW1, gb1, gw2, gb2 = backward(X0, y0)` — the analytic gradients
`W1[i, j] += eps; lp = L(...); W1[i, j] -= 2 * eps; lm = L(...); W1[i, j] += eps` — loss with one weight nudged up, then down, then restored
`print(abs((lp - lm) / (2 * eps) - gW1[i, j]))` — brute-force slope minus analytic gradient

b.s: PyTorch is the library that does the backward pass for you and runs on the GPU; install it with `pip install torch`. A tensor is PyTorch's array, like a numpy array but able to live on the GPU and to remember how it was computed so gradients can be derived automatically (autograd). On Apple silicon the GPU is reached through MPS (Metal Performance Shaders); `torch.device("mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu")` picks it when present. `.to(dev)` moves a model or tensor there.

`nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 1))` is the same network as step 1: a linear layer, ReLU, a linear layer with one output, the logit (the number before the sigmoid). AdamW is the optimizer, an improvement on plain gradient descent that adapts the step size per weight; `lr=1e-3` is its learning rate and `weight_decay=1e-4` a mild penalty on large weights. `BCEWithLogitsLoss` is cross-entropy that takes the logit directly, numerically safer than sigmoid then log; `pos_weight` up-weights the rare positives by the ratio of negatives to positives. `torch.tensor(Xtr, device=dev)` copies the training arrays to the GPU once.
The same network in PyTorch on MPS.

import torch, torch.nn as nn
dev = torch.device("mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu")
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 1)).to(dev)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
pos_w = torch.tensor([(1 - ytr.mean()) / ytr.mean()], device=dev)
lossf = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_w)
Xt, yt = torch.tensor(Xtr, device=dev), torch.tensor(ytr, device=dev)

items: `dev = torch.device("mps" if ... else "cpu")` — the Mac's GPU if PyTorch can see it
`net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 1)).to(dev)` — the same two-layer network, on the GPU
`opt = torch.optim.AdamW(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)` — the optimizer that will update the weights
`lossf = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_w)` — cross-entropy on logits, positives up-weighted
`Xt, yt = torch.tensor(Xtr, device=dev), torch.tensor(ytr, device=dev)` — training data as GPU tensors

b.s: The training loop in PyTorch has a fixed rhythm per batch: `opt.zero_grad()` clears the previous gradients, the forward pass computes the loss, `.backward()` computes every gradient by autograd, `opt.step()` updates the weights. `net.train()` and `net.eval()` switch modes (they matter for layers such as dropout; harmless here). `torch.randperm` shuffles, as `permutation` did in numpy; `.squeeze(1)` drops the trailing dimension so the output shape matches the targets.

Evaluation is wrapped in `torch.no_grad()` so PyTorch does not build the gradient bookkeeping for it; `torch.sigmoid` turns logits into probabilities; `.cpu().numpy()` brings the result back to numpy for scikit-learn's `ap`. Early stopping by hand: when validation average precision improves, save the weights with `torch.save(net.state_dict(), path)` and reset patience; when it has not improved for five epochs, stop. The `:=` operator assigns and tests in one expression. The saved file is the model you keep.
Train with early stopping on validation AP.

items: `perm = torch.randperm(len(yt), device=dev)` — a new order each epoch
`opt.zero_grad(); lossf(net(Xt[j]).squeeze(1), yt[j]).backward(); opt.step()` — clear, forward, backward, update: one batch
`with torch.no_grad(): pv = torch.sigmoid(net(...)).squeeze(1).cpu().numpy()` — validation probabilities without gradient bookkeeping
`if score > best: best, patience = score, 0; torch.save(net.state_dict(), "models/mlp_h30.pt")` — keep the best weights seen so far
`elif (patience := patience + 1) >= 5: break` — stop after five epochs without improvement

b.s: This step previews lesson 10. Suppose each station already has a hidden vector `h` of size H summarizing its last hour (a GRU, a recurrent network, produces that in lesson 10). Neighbor mixing lets each station read its neighbors' summaries. An adjacency matrix `A` is an N × N table of zeros and ones where entry (i, j) is 1 if station j is station i's neighbor; then `A @ h` gives, for each station, the sum of its neighbors' vectors, and in a directed road there are two: `A_up` for the upstream neighbor and `A_down` for the downstream one.

`nn.Module` is PyTorch's base class for a model piece; `__init__` creates the learnable parts, here two linear layers without bias that transform the upstream and downstream messages, and `forward` says how to compute the output. The `h +` is a residual connection: the station keeps its own summary and adds what it learned from its neighbors. This single module, applied twice, is a small graph neural network.
The spatio-temporal step: one round of neighbor mixing as matrix products.

items: `class Mix(nn.Module):` — a reusable model piece
`self.Wu = nn.Linear(H, H, bias=False); self.Wd = nn.Linear(H, H, bias=False)` — learnable transforms for upstream and downstream messages
`return h + self.Wu(A_up @ h) + self.Wd(A_down @ h)` — own summary plus transformed neighbor summaries

b.q: Why check gradients numerically when autograd exists?

a.s: For the numpy version, because a wrong backward pass still trains, just badly. For PyTorch, because the check teaches you what autograd is doing and catches a wrong loss or a detached tensor.

b.q: Why `BCEWithLogitsLoss` rather than a sigmoid followed by `BCELoss`?

a.s: It computes the loss from logits with log-sum-exp, which is numerically stable for large scores; sigmoid then log can underflow to −inf.

b.q: Why is the GPU barely faster for this network?

a.s: Each batch launches a handful of tiny kernels; the launch overhead is comparable to the arithmetic. Larger batches or larger models tip the balance toward MPS.

items: 'Deep learning needs a data center.' A 0.1 M-parameter network trains in an hour on a Mac mini; what needs a data center is a different problem.
'A network will beat the trees.' On this data, usually not; the graph structure is its one real advantage.
'Training loss going down means it works.' Validation AP is the only number that means it works.
