resources.title: 3Blue1Brown: Neural networks

b.s: Four videos with moving pictures that show what a neural network is and how it learns, using handwritten numbers as the example.

Watch them before Karpathy's course. They show a network as layers of numbers, what a weight and a bias do, what gradient descent means, and what backpropagation computes, all with animations of the digit-recognition example. Pause often and predict what the next picture will show.

The third and fourth videos derive backpropagation with the chain rule visually. Pause and write the equations yourself as they appear; then lesson 9's numpy implementation will feel like transcribing the pictures. The first video's description of a neuron as a weighted sum plus a squashing function is lesson 7 in one image.

The series builds intuition for the computation graph and for how gradients flow backward through it; after it, the formal Jacobian-chain view is easy. Its digit example is a plain multilayer perceptron, the same architecture as the numpy network in stage 9, and its remarks on what the hidden layers actually learn are a good caution against over-interpreting them.

Good for teaching; note what it simplifies (no batching, no optimizers beyond plain gradient descent, no regularization, no normalization). The newer videos on transformers and attention extend the same visual method to the models of phase 8, and are the shortest route to understanding attention geometrically.

Its visual language has become the standard for explaining networks to non-specialists. Reuse the logic of its diagrams when presenting the spatio-temporal network to a product team, and its treatment of what a layer 'sees' as a caution when someone asks what the model has learned.

Four core videos: what a neural network is (neurons, layers, weights, biases, activations, the digit example), how it learns (the cost function, gradient descent, the meaning of the negative gradient), what backpropagation is doing (intuition for which weights to nudge, averaging over examples, stochastic gradient descent), and backpropagation calculus (the chain rule on a chain of neurons, then on layers).

items: A network: an input layer of pixel activations (784 for a 28×28 digit), hidden layers, an output layer of 10 activations; each neuron's activation is a weighted sum of the previous layer's activations plus a bias, squashed (sigmoid in the video, ReLU in practice); the weights and biases are the parameters (about 13,000 for the example).

Layers as matrices: a layer computes a = σ(Wa_prev + b); the whole network is a chain of such steps; the hope that hidden layers detect edges and then shapes is not exactly what happens, which the video is honest about.

Learning: a cost is the squared difference between output activations and the desired one-hot output, averaged over examples; the parameters are a point in a high-dimensional space and the cost is a landscape; gradient descent moves downhill; the gradient's components say which parameters matter most.

Backpropagation intuition: for one example, the output error says which output activations should go up or down; each is influenced by its weights (in proportion to the previous activations), its bias, and the previous activations (in proportion to the weights); summing the desired changes over all outputs gives the desired change to the previous layer, and the process repeats backward; averaging over a batch gives the gradient; stochastic gradient descent uses mini-batches.

The calculus: for a chain of single neurons, the cost's sensitivity to a weight is the product of ∂z/∂w = a_prev, ∂a/∂z = σ′(z) and ∂C/∂a = 2(a − y); for layers, the same with sums over the next layer's neurons; the gradient vector collects all of these.
A network is a chain of matrix multiplications and squashes; learning is descending a cost landscape.
Backpropagation is the chain rule organized layer by layer, reusing sensitivities.
Mini-batches trade gradient accuracy for speed.

b.s: Redraw the four-neuron chain from the last video, write its three partial derivatives, and check them on numbers with a finite difference in numpy.

resources.title: TensorFlow Playground

b.s: A web page where you build a tiny brain by clicking, then press play and watch it learn to separate blue dots from orange dots.

A free browser toy: pick a dataset of dots, add layers and neurons, choose a learning rate, press play, and watch the network learn a boundary. You can see what each neuron detects. It makes the words in lesson 9 (layer, neuron, activation, learning rate) into something you can poke.

Use it to run the experiments lesson 9 describes: too high a learning rate diverges; too few neurons underfit the spiral; adding features (x², sin x) lets a small network solve what a bigger one struggles with; regularization smooths the boundary. Fifteen minutes here saves an hour of confusion later.

It visualizes the decision boundary and per-neuron activations for a two-input problem, which is the clearest demonstration of what hidden layers compute and why feature engineering and depth are partial substitutes for each other.
Its role for you is demonstration when teaching; it cannot show the high-dimensional effects (initialization statistics, batch norm) that matter in practice.
A reminder that a well-designed toy can carry a concept further than a lecture; it is the demo to open when a stakeholder asks what a neural network 'is'.

A browser neural network on four 2-D datasets (circle, exclusive-or, Gaussian clusters, spiral) with controls for features (x₁, x₂, squares, product, sines), hidden layers and neurons, activation (ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, linear), learning rate, regularization (L1, L2) and its rate, batch size, noise, and train-test ratio, with live visualization of each neuron's function and the decision boundary.

items: Linear limits: with only x₁ and x₂ as features and no hidden layer, the boundary is a line; the circle and spiral cannot be fit; adding x₁² and x₂² lets a linear model fit the circle, which is feature engineering.

Hidden layers: with raw features and one hidden layer of a few neurons, the network learns its own features; each neuron's panel shows a half-plane (ReLU) or a smooth ramp (tanh); the output combines them into curved boundaries.
Learning rate: too high and the loss oscillates or explodes; too low and it crawls; watch the training loss curve.
Activation: linear activations collapse the network to a linear model no matter the depth; ReLU trains fast; tanh gives smooth boundaries; sigmoid saturates.

Regularization: L2 shrinks weights and smooths the boundary; L1 zeroes some; too much underfits; noise in the data shows overfitting as a boundary that wraps around individual points, visible as a gap between training and test loss.

The spiral: hard for small networks; needs more neurons or engineered sine features; depth helps up to a point; a lesson in inductive bias and in why feature engineering and depth are partial substitutes.

b.s: neuron output = activation(w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b)

items: Hidden layers learn features; engineered features can replace them for simple structure.
The learning rate is the first dial to check when training misbehaves.
Regularization smooths the boundary; noise plus capacity produces overfitting you can see.

b.s: Fit the spiral three ways: raw features with two hidden layers, engineered sine features with no hidden layer, and raw features with L2 regularization; record the test loss of each and explain the differences.

resources.title: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero (Karpathy), micrograd and makemore

b.s: A programmer builds a tiny brain from scratch on video, typing every line, and explains each one as he goes.

Andrej Karpathy's free YouTube course. micrograd builds automatic differentiation, the machinery that computes gradients, in about a hundred lines of Python. makemore builds models that generate names, starting from counting letter pairs and ending with a small transformer. Code along in a notebook; pause and predict what each line does before he runs it.

micrograd is lesson 9's backward pass done generally: every operation records how to pass its gradient back, and the chain rule falls out. Build it, then use it to train lesson 7's logistic regression. makemore's early lessons teach the training loop, learning rates, initialization and batch normalization by showing failures happening on screen and fixing them.

The course's method (make the bug, watch it, fix it) teaches debugging networks better than any textbook. Its lesson on the statistics of activations and gradients is a practical tutorial on initialization and normalization. After micrograd, PyTorch's autograd is obvious rather than magical, and you will know what `requires_grad` and `backward` actually do.

makemore's progression to attention is the clearest path to understanding transformers, and the follow-up on building GPT completes it. For traffic the relevant carry-over is the sequence-modelling mindset and the training diagnostics: reading the loss curve, the gradient norms and the activation histograms before changing an architecture.

Karpathy's teaching sets the bar for from-scratch pedagogy, and his emphasis on reading gradients and activations is the diagnostic culture a research team should share. For a lead, the course is the fastest way to give a strong engineer without deep-learning background a working mental model in a week.

micrograd: a scalar-valued automatic differentiation engine and a tiny neural network library built from scratch, with the chain rule implemented as backward functions on a computation graph. makemore: a series building character-level language models on a list of names, from a bigram count model to a neural bigram, an MLP following Bengio et al., diagnostics of activations and gradients with batch normalization, a manual backward pass through the whole MLP, a WaveNet-like hierarchical model, and (in the follow-up) a GPT built from scratch.

items: micrograd: a `Value` object stores data, a gradient, the operation that produced it and its children; each operation defines a local derivative; `backward()` topologically sorts the graph and applies the chain rule in reverse, accumulating gradients; a neuron, layer and MLP are built from `Value`s; training is a loop of forward, zero grads, backward, update.

Bigram model: counts of next characters as a probability table; the negative log-likelihood as the training objective; the same model as a one-layer network with one-hot inputs and softmax outputs trained by gradient descent, showing that counting and learning coincide.

The MLP language model: embed characters into a small vector space, concatenate a context window, a hidden tanh layer, a softmax over the next character; mini-batches, learning-rate search by sweeping and watching the loss, train-validation-test splits, and overfitting versus capacity; visualizing the embedding space.

Activations and gradients: initialization scale matters (saturated tanh kills gradients; too-large logits give confident wrong initial predictions); Kaiming initialization; batch normalization to standardize pre-activations, its running statistics, and its interaction with biases; diagnostic plots of activation and gradient distributions and of the update-to-data ratio.

Manual backpropagation: deriving the backward pass through cross-entropy, linear layers, tanh, batch norm and the embedding by hand and matching PyTorch's autograd exactly; the exercise that makes autograd transparent.
Hierarchical models: fusing characters progressively with a tree of layers (WaveNet-style dilated structure), organizing code into PyTorch-like modules, and the importance of checking shapes.

GPT from scratch: tokenization, the bigram baseline, self-attention as a weighted average with learned weights (queries, keys, values, scaling, masking), multi-head attention, feed-forward blocks, residual connections and layer norm, and scaling up.

class Value: ... def __mul__(self, other): out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other), '*'); def _backward(): self.grad += other.data * out.grad; other.grad += self.data * out.grad
loss = −mean(log p[next_char]);  logits = h @ W2 + b2;  h = tanh(emb.view(-1, block*d) @ W1 + b1)
batchnorm: x̂ = (x − mean_batch)/√(var_batch + ε);  y = γ x̂ + β

items: Autograd is a graph of local derivatives applied in reverse; you can write it in a hundred lines.
Initialization and normalization decide whether training starts well; look at the activation statistics.
Attention is a data-dependent weighted average; everything else in a transformer is plumbing.

resources.title: PyTorch tutorials: Learn the Basics; the MPS backend notes

b.s: The official lessons for the tool that runs neural networks, plus a note about making it use the Mac's graphics chip so it goes faster.

Learn the Basics is eight short pages: tensors (grids of numbers), datasets, building a model, automatic gradients, the training loop, and saving. The MPS notes explain how to run on the Mac's GPU by setting the device to `mps`. Do the tutorial in a notebook and run each cell.

After it you can write lesson 9's PyTorch network: `nn.Module`, `DataLoader`, the training loop, `torch.no_grad()` for evaluation, and saving a `state_dict`. The MPS page lists the limits that matter on the Mac mini: float32 and float16 only, no float64, and an environment variable that lets unsupported operations fall back to the CPU.

Understand tensors' memory model (views versus copies, contiguity, in-place operations), the autograd graph and `requires_grad`, and why moving data to the device in large chunks matters more than any architectural choice for small models. Read the profiler tutorial to see where time actually goes on MPS; the answer is usually kernel launches, not arithmetic.

The advanced tutorials (custom autograd functions, `torch.compile`, distributed training) are the next layer. For this project, test whether `torch.compile` helps on MPS rather than assuming; support is uneven. The tutorials on saving and loading, and on reproducibility, are the ones that prevent embarrassment at handover.

PyTorch's eager, Pythonic design is why research iterates fast; its deployment story (TorchScript's decline, ExecuTorch, ONNX and Core ML export) is where production effort goes. Knowing both ends, and the operator-support gaps between them, is what lets you promise a model can ship on a device.

Learn the Basics: quickstart; tensors (creation, attributes, operations, bridging with numpy); datasets and dataloaders (built-in datasets, custom `Dataset`, `DataLoader` iteration); transforms; build the neural network (`nn.Module`, layers, `forward`, parameters); automatic differentiation (`autograd`, computational graphs, `requires_grad`, `backward`, disabling gradients); optimizing model parameters (hyperparameters, the training loop, loss functions, optimizers); save and load the model. The MPS notes: enabling the Metal backend on Apple silicon, checking availability, moving tensors and models, and limitations.

items: Tensors: like numpy arrays with device placement and autograd; `torch.tensor`, `zeros`, `rand`; `.shape`, `.dtype`, `.device`; indexing, joining, arithmetic, matrix multiply with `@`, in-place ops with a trailing underscore; `.numpy()` and `from_numpy` share memory on CPU.

Data: a `Dataset` implements `__len__` and `__getitem__`; a `DataLoader` batches, shuffles and iterates; for a tabular tensor already in memory, slicing by index permutations is faster than a DataLoader with Python overhead.

Models: subclass `nn.Module`, define layers in `__init__`, compute in `forward`; `nn.Sequential`, `nn.Linear`, `nn.ReLU`; `model.parameters()`; move with `.to(device)`; `model.train()` and `model.eval()` switch dropout and batch norm behavior.

Autograd: tensors with `requires_grad=True` record operations; `loss.backward()` computes gradients into `.grad`; gradients accumulate, so `optimizer.zero_grad()` each step; `torch.no_grad()` for inference; `detach()` to stop tracking.

Training loop: for each batch, compute predictions, loss (`nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss`, `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`), `backward`, `optimizer.step()`; validation loop under `no_grad` with `eval()`; hyperparameters (epochs, batch size, learning rate); optimizers `SGD`, `Adam`, `AdamW`.
Saving: `torch.save(model.state_dict(), path)` and `model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path))`; save the class definition alongside; checkpoints include optimizer state for resuming.

MPS: `torch.backends.mps.is_available()`, `device = torch.device('mps')`; supported dtypes are float32 and float16 (no float64); some operators are unimplemented and `PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1` routes them to the CPU; unified memory means no host-device copies but also a shared budget; small batches are launch-bound, so benchmark against the CPU.

net.eval()

Keep tensors on the device and batch large; Python overhead per batch dominates small models.
MPS is float32 only and launch-bound for tiny models; measure.

resources.title: Dive into Deep Learning (d2l.ai), chapters 3–5 and 9–10

b.s: A free online textbook where every idea comes with code you can run, about teaching computers using layers of simple math.

Chapters 3 to 5 cover linear and softmax regression and multilayer perceptrons with PyTorch code you can execute. Chapters 9 and 10 cover recurrent networks (RNN, GRU, LSTM) and how to train them well. Run the notebooks; each section ends with exercises that are worth doing.

Chapter 5's multilayer perceptron from scratch mirrors lesson 9's numpy network; chapter 9 explains why GRUs can remember and forget, which is the sequence half of the spatio-temporal network. The exercises about changing hidden size and learning rate are the experiments to actually run on the traffic data.

d2l's coverage of optimization (chapter 12), attention (chapter 11) and computational performance (chapter 13) is deeper than most books and free. Its consistent code style makes it easy to lift components, and its treatment of truncated backpropagation through time explains what a recurrent model can and cannot learn from a 12-step window.

Its graph-neural-network coverage is thin; use CS224W for that. Its attention chapters are the bridge to spatio-temporal transformers, and its chapter on computational performance (asynchrony, memory, multi-device) is the right background before profiling on unified memory.

A living, open textbook with code in several frameworks is itself a research-infrastructure achievement. Cite it for standard architectures, use its implementations as reference points when reproducing papers, and note its authors' choice to include the messy practical chapters most textbooks omit.

Chapter 3, linear neural networks for regression (linear regression, its implementation from scratch and concisely, generalization, weight decay). Chapter 4, linear networks for classification (softmax regression, the image classification dataset, implementations, generalization in classification, environment and distribution shift). Chapter 5, multilayer perceptrons (MLPs, implementation, forward and backward propagation, numerical stability and initialization, generalization, dropout, a Kaggle house-price example). Chapter 9, recurrent neural networks (sequences, text to sequence, language models, RNNs, implementation, backpropagation through time). Chapter 10, modern RNNs (LSTM, GRU, deep and bidirectional RNNs, machine translation data, encoder-decoder, sequence-to-sequence, beam search).

items: Linear regression as a network: the model, squared loss, minibatch stochastic gradient descent with learning rate and batch size, vectorization, the normal-distribution view of squared loss; from-scratch implementation with manual gradients, then `nn.Linear` and `MSELoss`.

Generalization and weight decay: training versus generalization error, model selection with validation, underfitting and overfitting versus capacity and data; L2 penalty as weight decay in the optimizer.

Softmax regression: one-hot targets, softmax outputs, cross-entropy loss and its gradient (softmax minus one-hot), the log-sum-exp trick for stability, accuracy as a metric; distribution shift (covariate, label, concept) and why test data may not match.

MLPs: hidden layers with nonlinear activations (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh) give universal approximation; forward propagation, the computational graph, backpropagation through it, and memory for stored activations.

Numerical stability: vanishing and exploding gradients from products of Jacobians, symmetry breaking by random initialization, Xavier initialization derived from keeping variances constant across layers; dropout as noise injection (zero units with probability p, scale by 1/(1 − p), off at test time).

Sequences: autoregressive models, the Markov assumption, tokenization and vocabularies, language modelling as next-token prediction, perplexity; RNNs with a hidden state h_t = φ(x_t W_xh + h_{t−1} W_hh + b), the character-level RNN from scratch, gradient clipping, truncated backpropagation through time and its analysis.

Gated RNNs: LSTM's input, forget and output gates with a memory cell; GRU's reset and update gates; why gates mitigate vanishing gradients; deep and bidirectional RNNs (bidirectional only when the whole sequence is available, never for forecasting).
Encoder-decoder: encoding a sequence to a state, decoding a sequence from it, teacher forcing during training, greedy versus beam search decoding, BLEU for evaluation.

resources.title: Understanding Deep Learning (Prince)

b.s: A newer big book about deep learning, free to read, with lots of clear pictures that show what each part of a network does.

Simon Prince's textbook (2023), free as a PDF with notebooks. It covers supervised learning, networks, training, measuring performance, regularization, convolutional and recurrent and transformer networks, graph networks, and generative models. It is more modern and more visual than the older Deep Learning book. Read the early chapters after phase 6.

Chapters 1 to 9 are the modern version of lesson 9: networks, loss functions, fitting, gradients and initialization, measuring performance, and regularization, each with figures that make the idea visible. Chapter 13 on graph neural networks covers the neighbor mixing of the spatio-temporal net. The notebooks let you run every figure.

Prince's treatment of why deep networks generalize, of the loss landscape, and of the transformer architecture is the clearest current textbook account, and it includes the recent empirical findings (double descent, scaling) that Goodfellow predates. Chapter 12 on transformers is the reading before lesson 8's attention material.

The chapters on generative models (VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion) are a compact, correct introduction with the math intact, and the chapter on ethics is unusually careful for a technical text. Use it as the reference when reading current papers.

A free, modern, rigorous textbook is a public good; it is the one to recommend to a new graduate student and the one to cite for standard architectures in the current idiom. Its figures are also the model for how to draw a network in a paper.

Chapters: introduction; supervised learning; shallow networks; deep networks; loss functions; fitting models; gradients and initialization; measuring performance; regularization; convolutional networks; residual networks; transformers; graph neural networks; unsupervised learning; generative adversarial networks; normalizing flows; variational autoencoders; diffusion models; reinforcement learning; why does deep learning work; deep learning and ethics.

items: Shallow and deep networks: a shallow network is a linear combination of ReLU-transformed linear functions, producing piecewise linear maps with regions; depth composes such maps and creates exponentially many regions per parameter; universal approximation with width, efficiency with depth.

Losses from maximum likelihood: choose a distribution over outputs (Gaussian gives least squares, Bernoulli gives binary cross-entropy, categorical gives softmax cross-entropy, others give robust or heteroscedastic losses); the network predicts the distribution's parameters.

Fitting: gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, momentum, Adam; learning-rate schedules and warmup; backpropagation derived for the general case with the forward pass storing activations; initialization that preserves variance (He), and the analysis of exploding and vanishing signals.

Measuring performance: noise, bias and variance; the double-descent curve; hyperparameter search; the importance of test sets; the curse of dimensionality and how real data lie on lower-dimensional manifolds.

Regularization: explicit (L2, early stopping), implicit (SGD's noise, larger learning rates), heuristic (ensembling, dropout, augmentation, transfer learning, multi-task, self-supervision), and the general picture of why regularized deep networks generalize.

Architectures: convolutions (invariance, equivariance, pooling, receptive fields, classic networks), residual connections (why depth trained poorly before them, batch and layer norm), transformers (dot-product attention, positional information, encoder and decoder, scaling, vision transformers), graph networks (adjacency, node embeddings, message passing, graph-level and node-level tasks, spectral and spatial views).

Generative models: GANs (minimax, mode collapse, Wasserstein), normalizing flows (invertible transformations and exact likelihoods), VAEs (the ELBO, reparameterization, posterior collapse), diffusion (forward noising, reverse denoising, the training objective, conditioning and guidance).

Reinforcement learning basics, the chapter on why deep learning works (loss landscapes, overparameterization, lottery tickets, adversarial examples) and the ethics chapter (bias, explainability, misuse, environmental cost).

deep network: y = φ_K ∘ … ∘ φ_1(x), each φ = ReLU(W h + b)
ELBO = E_q[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z))
attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d) V

Depth buys expressive piecewise-linear maps; normalization and residuals make depth trainable.
Generative families differ in how they make likelihood tractable: flows exactly, VAEs by bounds, diffusion by denoising, GANs not at all.

resources.title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders (fast.ai)

b.s: A free class where you train a real neural network on the very first day and only later learn all the details, like learning to ride a bike before studying how it works.

Jeremy Howard's course is top-down: you build working models first (on images, text and tables) and learn the theory as you need it. It uses the fastai library built on PyTorch. It is good for confidence and full of practical tricks that make training work.

Its tabular lessons (random forests first, then neural networks on tables) and its training tricks (a learning-rate finder, the one-cycle schedule) are directly usable in stage 9. The lesson on embeddings for categorical variables shows how to give station identity to a network, which is how the spatio-temporal net could learn per-station behavior.

The course's emphasis on iterating quickly and inspecting data is a counterweight to theory-first study, and its stated view that tree ensembles usually win on tabular data matches the evidence and this project's production choice. Its chapter on data ethics is short and worth the time for anyone whose model will issue alerts to drivers.

The fastai library's abstractions can hide details you need for a custom model such as the spatio-temporal network. Learn the ideas from the course, then implement in plain PyTorch. The course's lessons on collaborative filtering and on tabular embeddings are the clearest introduction to learned representations for categorical data.

fast.ai's research output (training-efficiency results, transfer learning for text) shows that practitioner-driven groups produce research results. Its philosophy of accessible deep learning shaped how many teams onboard engineers, and its lesson structure is a reasonable template for an internal course on this pipeline.

Lessons: getting started (a working image classifier in minutes, what ML is, transfer learning); deployment (data cleaning with the model, a web app); neural net foundations (from scratch: a linear model, then a network, SGD, the training loop); natural language (fine-tuning a language model then a classifier); from-scratch model (tabular, neural nets from foundations); random forests (bagging, out-of-bag, feature importance, partial dependence, tree interpretation); collaborative filtering (embeddings, dot products, biases, weight decay); convolutions (kernels, stride, padding, channels); data ethics; and the book's later chapters (ResNets, architecture details, training tricks, a CNN from scratch).

items: Top-down: train a state-of-the-art classifier first with a pretrained backbone and fine-tuning, then learn why it works; the argument that transfer learning is the default for images and text.

The training loop from foundations: parameters, predictions, loss, gradients (autograd), step, repeat; from a linear model on MNIST digits to a network with ReLU; mini-batches; the learning-rate finder (increase the rate until the loss explodes and pick a point before) and the one-cycle schedule.

Tabular: random forests as the first model (fast, robust, informative), out-of-bag error, feature importance by permutation, partial dependence plots, removing redundant features, extrapolation failure of trees and the test for out-of-domain data; then neural nets on tabular data with categorical embeddings; ensembling both.

Collaborative filtering: users and items as embeddings whose dot product plus biases predicts a rating; training with weight decay; interpreting embedding dimensions; the same idea gives station embeddings for the traffic net.
Text: tokenization, numericalization, language-model pretraining on the domain corpus, then fine-tuning a classifier (ULMFiT), which is the recipe for the incident headline classifier.

Convolutions: a kernel sliding over an image, stride and padding, channels, receptive fields, batch norm, and building a ResNet; the practical rules (start with a pretrained model, progressive resizing, test-time augmentation, mixup, label smoothing).
Ethics: feedback loops, bias, disinformation, and the responsibility of practitioners; checked in every project through questions about data provenance and affected people.

items: Start from a pretrained model whenever one exists; train from scratch only for tabular data or when you must.
The learning-rate finder and one-cycle schedule remove most guesswork from training.
Random forests are the fast, interpretable first model for tables; embeddings turn categories into geometry.

resources.title: A Gentle Introduction to Graph Neural Networks (Distill, 2021)

b.s: An article with pictures you can play with about learning from things that are connected, like friends in a group or roads in a city.

A free interactive article on Distill, a journal for clear explanations. It explains what a graph is, how information passes between connected nodes in a graph neural network, and what such networks can predict. Play with the interactive figures; they show messages moving along edges.

Read it before lesson 10's higher levels and before CS224W: it explains message passing (each node updates from its neighbors), pooling, and the design choices (how many layers, what to aggregate) with live figures. The road graph of this project is a small instance of what it describes.

The article's playground lets you change layers and aggregation and watch performance change, which is an intuition for over-smoothing and receptive field. Its taxonomy of graph tasks (node, edge, graph level) places station-level traffic prediction precisely.
It is deliberately introductory; the formal treatment (spectral versus spatial convolutions, expressiveness) is in CS224W and the survey literature. Its value is fixing the vocabulary before those.

Distill's format, interactive and peer-reviewed, is the high bar for explanatory writing in ML; this article and its companion on graph convolutions are what to point a collaborator to before a graph-learning discussion.

What a graph is and how to represent one (nodes, edges, global context; adjacency matrices and lists), where graphs appear (molecules, social networks, text and images as graphs), the kinds of tasks (graph-level, node-level, edge-level), the challenges of learning on graphs, the GNN as layers that update node, edge and global embeddings, message passing between neighbors, pooling for predictions, and an interactive playground plus a discussion of design choices (depth, aggregation, learned edges, attention).

items: Representation: a graph has node attributes, edge attributes and global attributes; adjacency lists scale better than dense matrices; node ordering must not matter (permutation invariance), which rules out treating the adjacency matrix as an image.

Tasks: predict a property of the whole graph (molecule toxicity), of each node (station is slow), or of each edge (road segment congestion); the traffic problem is node-level prediction on a fixed graph.

The simplest GNN: apply separate small networks to each node, edge and global vector, keeping the structure; predictions by a classifier on the updated node vectors; pooling (sum, mean, max) to move information between nodes and edges when one is missing.

Message passing: each node gathers its neighbors' vectors, aggregates them (sum or mean), and updates its own with a learned function; stacking k layers lets information travel k hops; this is graph convolution, and the neighbor mixing of the spatio-temporal net is one layer of it with directed neighbors.
Global context: a master node connected to everything, or a global vector updated from pooled nodes and edges, so distant nodes can communicate.

Design choices shown in the playground: number of layers, embedding dimension, aggregation function, and which attributes to pass; performance is not monotone in depth, since over-smoothing makes node embeddings indistinguishable.
Related ideas: graph attention (learned weights per neighbor), graph sampling and batching for large graphs, learned or inferred edges, and comparisons with sequences and images as special graphs.

b.s:
h_v ← UPDATE( h_v, AGGREGATE({ h_u : u ∈ N(v) }) )
with directed neighbors: h ← h + W_u (A_up h) + W_d (A_down h)

items: A GNN is repeated neighbor aggregation with learned update functions; depth equals hops.
Permutation invariance is the constraint that shapes every design.
More layers is not better past a few hops; over-smoothing sets in.

resources.title: DCRNN (Li et al., ICLR 2018) and STGCN (Yu et al., IJCAI 2018)

b.s: Two papers where scientists taught computers to predict traffic on real Californian roads, using the same kind of sensors we use.

Two research papers that started modern traffic forecasting. DCRNN treats traffic as something that spreads along the road (diffusion) and uses a recurrent network to follow it in time. STGCN uses convolutions over time and over the road graph instead. Both are tested on PEMS-BAY, which is Bay Area PeMS data like ours, at 15, 30 and 60 minutes ahead.

First pass: the abstract, figure 1, the results table (mean absolute error at 15, 30 and 60 minutes) and the datasets section. Note the baselines (historical average, ARIMA, vector autoregression, a plain LSTM) and how the gains grow with horizon. That table is your yardstick for the spatio-temporal network in stage 9.

DCRNN: diffusion convolution with forward and backward random-walk matrices on a directed graph, GRU cells whose matrix multiplies are replaced by graph convolutions, and a sequence-to-sequence architecture with scheduled sampling. STGCN: gated temporal convolutions sandwiching Chebyshev graph convolutions, with no recurrence. Work through each equation; the plan's spatio-temporal net is a two-hop diffusion GRU without the decoder.

Read critically: sensitivity to how the graph is built (a Gaussian kernel on road distance with a threshold), the evaluation protocol (12-step windows, masking missing values), and later critiques showing that simple baselines are competitive at short horizons. Graph WaveNet's adaptive adjacency is the natural next read.

These papers set the benchmark protocol the field still uses, and their limitations (fixed sensor sets, no incidents or weather, no transfer across networks) are the open problems. Reproducing them on the M1 with a reduced configuration and then adding incident and weather features to the same protocol is a publishable direction.

DCRNN, 'Diffusion Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network: Data-Driven Traffic Forecasting': models spatial dependency as a diffusion process on a directed graph, replaces the matrix multiplications in a GRU with diffusion convolutions, and uses a sequence-to-sequence architecture with scheduled sampling; evaluated on METR-LA and PEMS-BAY at 15, 30 and 60 minutes. STGCN, 'Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks: A Deep Learning Framework for Traffic Forecasting': stacks spatio-temporal blocks of gated temporal convolutions around a graph convolution, without recurrence, for faster training; evaluated on BJER4 and PeMSD7.

items: Problem setting: a sensor graph with N nodes and a weighted adjacency from road-network distances (a thresholded Gaussian kernel), a history of T steps of speed per node, predict the next T′ steps; metrics MAE, RMSE, MAPE at each horizon; baselines historical average, ARIMA with Kalman filter, VAR, SVR, feed-forward and LSTM networks.

Diffusion convolution: a random walk on the graph with transition matrix D_O⁻¹W (forward) and its reverse D_I⁻¹Wᵀ (backward); the diffusion convolution of a signal X with filter parameters θ sums powers k = 0..K−1 of both transition matrices weighted by θ, capturing upstream and downstream influence separately; K is the number of hops.

DCGRU: a GRU whose reset, update and candidate computations use diffusion convolutions instead of dense matrices, so the hidden state of each node is updated from its own history and its graph neighbors' states.

Sequence to sequence: an encoder DCGRU reads the history; a decoder DCGRU produces the T′ future steps; scheduled sampling feeds the decoder its own predictions with increasing probability during training to reduce exposure bias.

Results: DCRNN improves over baselines by larger margins at longer horizons; ablations show both the diffusion (spatial) and recurrent (temporal) components matter; the learned filters localize around each sensor along the road.

STGCN: each ST-Conv block is a temporal gated convolution (1-D convolution over time with a gated linear unit), a spatial graph convolution (spectral, with a Chebyshev polynomial approximation of order K, or a first-order approximation), and another temporal convolution; blocks stack and an output layer maps to the horizon; no recurrence means fast, parallel training.

Graph convolution in STGCN: the normalized Laplacian L = I − D⁻½WD⁻½; a spectral filter approximated by Chebyshev polynomials T_k(L̃) up to order K, giving K-hop localization; the first-order approximation reduces to a normalized adjacency multiplication.

Comparisons: STGCN trains faster and performs well at short and medium horizons; DCRNN handles direction through forward and backward walks; both assume a fixed known graph, which Graph WaveNet later relaxes.

b.s:
DCRNN: X ⋆_G f_θ = Σ_{k=0}^{K−1} ( θ_{k,1} (D_O⁻¹W)^k + θ_{k,2} (D_I⁻¹Wᵀ)^k ) X
DCGRU: r = σ(Θ_r ⋆_G [X_t, H_{t−1}] + b_r); u = σ(Θ_u ⋆_G [X_t, H_{t−1}] + b_u); C = tanh(Θ_C ⋆_G [X_t, r ⊙ H_{t−1}] + b_C); H_t = u ⊙ H_{t−1} + (1 − u) ⊙ C
STGCN block: Γ₁ ⋆_T ReLU( Θ ⋆_G (Γ₀ ⋆_T X) ),  Θ ⋆_G x ≈ Σ_k θ_k T_k(L̃) x

items: Diffusion convolution with forward and backward walks is how a model respects the direction of a road.
A graph-convolutional GRU is a GRU whose weights act along the graph; the traffic net is a small one.
Spectral (Chebyshev) and spatial (random-walk) convolutions both give K-hop locality; the choice is about direction and cost.

b.s: Implement the two-hop diffusion convolution with the registry's forward and backward transition matrices in PyTorch and use it inside a GRU cell; train on Fremont data and compare with the hand-made neighbor features at 60 minutes.

resources.title: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Nielsen)

b.s: A free online book that builds a tiny brain that reads handwritten numbers, and explains every piece as it goes.

Michael Nielsen's classic free book teaches neural networks through one running example, recognizing handwritten digits, with code you can run. It explains neurons, gradient descent, backpropagation, and why deep networks are hard to train, with clear pictures. Read chapters 1 to 3 before lesson 9.

Chapter 2 is the best written derivation of backpropagation; chapter 3 covers cross-entropy, regularization and initialization with experiments you can rerun; chapter 4 gives a visual proof that networks can approximate any function. The code is plain numpy, like lesson 9's.

Nielsen's four backpropagation equations and his discussion of the vanishing-gradient problem are the background for the initialization and normalization material; his universality chapter is the intuition behind the approximation theorems.
It predates modern architectures and optimizers, which is fine for its purpose: the foundations, explained better than most textbooks.
A free classic; still the recommendation for anyone who wants to understand backpropagation rather than call it.

Chapter 1, using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits (perceptrons, sigmoid neurons, architecture, gradient descent, a from-scratch implementation). Chapter 2, how the backpropagation algorithm works (notation, the four fundamental equations, proof, algorithm, code, why it is fast). Chapter 3, improving the way networks learn (cross-entropy cost, softmax, overfitting and regularization, weight initialization, hyperparameter choice, other techniques). Chapter 4, a visual proof that neural nets can compute any function. Chapter 5, why deep networks are hard to train (vanishing gradients). Chapter 6, deep learning (convolutional networks and recent progress).

items: Perceptrons and sigmoid neurons: a perceptron thresholds a weighted sum; a sigmoid neuron smooths the threshold so small weight changes cause small output changes, which makes learning by gradient possible; a network of layers; the digit task with 784 inputs, a hidden layer and 10 outputs.
Gradient descent: the quadratic cost, the gradient, the update rule, stochastic gradient descent with mini-batches and epochs; a 74-line numpy implementation that reaches about 95 % accuracy.

The four equations of backpropagation: the error at the output layer δ^L = ∇_a C ⊙ σ′(z^L); the error in terms of the next layer δ^l = ((w^{l+1})ᵀ δ^{l+1}) ⊙ σ′(z^l); the bias gradient ∂C/∂b = δ; the weight gradient ∂C/∂w^l_{jk} = a^{l−1}_k δ^l_j; the algorithm is a forward pass, an output error, a backward pass, and the gradient; it is fast because it computes all partial derivatives in one backward pass.

Improving learning: the cross-entropy cost avoids the learning slowdown of quadratic cost with sigmoids (its gradient is proportional to the error); softmax with log-likelihood; regularization (L2, L1, dropout, augmentation) against overfitting, with experiments; weight initialization with variance 1/n_in to avoid saturation; heuristics for learning rate, early stopping, schedules, and mini-batch size; momentum and other activations.

Universality: a visual argument that a hidden layer of sigmoid neurons can build step functions and bumps and therefore approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy; universality is about existence, not learnability.

Vanishing gradients: in deep sigmoid networks, gradients in early layers are products of terms smaller than one and shrink exponentially (or explode), so early layers learn slowly; the instability is inherent to gradient-based learning in deep chains and motivates ReLU, careful initialization and normalization.

Convolutional networks: local receptive fields, shared weights (feature maps), pooling; a network for digits reaching over 99 %; the chapter's tour of ensembles, dropout and augmentation, and the state of the field.

b.s:
δ^L = ∇_a C ⊙ σ′(z^L);  δ^l = ((w^{l+1})ᵀ δ^{l+1}) ⊙ σ′(z^l)
∂C/∂b^l_j = δ^l_j;  ∂C/∂w^l_{jk} = a^{l−1}_k δ^l_j
cross-entropy: C = −(1/n) Σ [y ln a + (1 − y) ln(1 − a)];  ∂C/∂w ∝ (a − y)

items: The four equations are backpropagation; memorize their shape and every framework becomes readable.
Cross-entropy fixes the sigmoid's learning slowdown; initialization and ReLU fix vanishing gradients.
Universality is an existence result; learnability and generalization are separate questions.

b.s: Implement the four equations for a one-hidden-layer network in numpy, train it on the traffic features, and confirm the gradients against finite differences and against lesson 9's implementation.

resources.title: The Little Book of Deep Learning (Fleuret)

b.s: A short free book, made to fit on a phone screen, that explains deep learning from start to finish in plain language.

François Fleuret's book is about 150 small pages, free, covering machine learning basics, efficient computation, training, the main model components, architectures, and applications. It is dense but readable; use it as a summary after the longer courses.

Read the chapters on training (losses, autoregressive models, optimization), on model components (layers, attention, normalization) and on architectures after lesson 9 to consolidate; its figures are precise and its notation consistent.
The book is a compact, rigorous map of the field; its chapter on efficient computation (GPUs, memory, batching) is the shortest correct account of why hardware shapes models.
Useful as a reference for definitions and as a checklist of what a current practitioner should know; its brevity makes gaps in your own understanding visible.
A free, expert summary; the kind of document to hand a strong engineer who needs the whole picture in a weekend.

Part I, foundations: machine learning (learning from data, basis function regression, under and overfitting, categories of models); efficient computation (GPUs, tensors); training (losses, autoregressive models, gradient descent, backpropagation, training protocols, the benefits of scale). Part II, deep models: model components (layers, linear, activations, pooling, dropout, normalizing, skip connections, attention, token embedding, positional encoding); architectures (MLP, convolutional networks, attention models). Part III, applications: prediction (image denoising, classification, detection, segmentation, speech recognition, text-image, reinforcement learning) and synthesis (text generation, image generation). A closing chapter on what is missing.

items: Foundations: a model is a parametric function; learning minimizes a loss on training data; generalization requires capacity matched to data; the categories of tasks (regression, classification, density modelling, generation).
Computation: tensors as the data structure, GPUs as parallel matrix engines, memory bandwidth as the bottleneck, and why batching matters.

Training: cross-entropy and its relatives; autoregressive factorization for sequences; stochastic gradient descent with momentum and Adam; backpropagation through the computational graph with stored activations; training protocols (validation, learning-rate schedules, early stopping) and the empirical benefits of scale (more data, more parameters, more compute improve smoothly).

Components: linear layers, convolutional layers (1-D and 2-D, stride, padding, dilation, transposed), activations (ReLU, GELU, and others), pooling, dropout, batch and layer normalization with their statistics, skip connections and why they help optimization, attention layers (query, key, value, multi-head, causal masking), token embeddings and positional encodings.

Architectures: the MLP; convolutional networks (LeNet, ResNet, and the receptive-field view); attention models (the transformer encoder and decoder, GPT as a decoder-only model, the vision transformer).

Applications: how each task is cast as a loss over a network's outputs (denoising as regression, detection with box regression and class heads, segmentation as per-pixel classification, speech with CTC, text-image with contrastive alignment, reinforcement learning with value networks) and how generation works (autoregressive sampling, diffusion).
What is missing: recurrent networks, GANs, graph networks, self-supervision, and the training details of large models, with pointers.

b.s:
autoregressive: p(x_1..x_T) = Π_t p(x_t | x_{<t})
layer norm: y = γ (x − μ)/σ + β over the feature dimension

items: Every architecture is a stack of a dozen component types; know the components and any diagram is legible.
Autoregressive factorization plus cross-entropy is how sequence generation is trained.
Skip connections and normalization are what make depth optimizable.

b.s: Read the components chapter, then list which components the spatio-temporal net uses and which it could add (layer norm, skip connections, attention over stations), and test one addition.

resources.lives: book · free · a weekend · free; the whole field in 150 small pages

resources.title: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks (Karpathy)

b.s: A checklist from an expert about how to train a learning machine without fooling yourself: start simple, look at the data, change one thing at a time.

A blog post with a step-by-step recipe: inspect the data first, build a tiny end-to-end pipeline, get baselines right, overfit a small batch on purpose, then regularize and tune. It is short, free and practical, and it prevents most beginner mistakes.

Apply it to the spatio-temporal net: verify the loss at initialization, overfit two batches, add complexity one piece at a time, and plot everything. Its list of things that silently go wrong (mismatched shapes, wrong learning rates, data leaks) is a debugging checklist.

The post's principle, that neural network training fails silently and so must be built incrementally with verification at each step, is the engineering discipline behind every successful training run; its specific checks are cheap and catch real bugs.
Read it with Karpathy's course on activations and gradients statistics; together they are the practical theory of training diagnostics.
A widely used piece of practitioner wisdom; for a lead, it is the shared protocol to require before anyone reports a result.

A blog post arguing that neural network training fails silently and must be built incrementally, with a step-by-step recipe: become one with the data; set up an end-to-end skeleton with dumb baselines; overfit; regularize; tune; squeeze out the juice.

items: Failure is silent: shapes broadcast wrongly, labels are off by one, learning rates are off by orders of magnitude, and the loss still goes down; only a disciplined process catches it.
Become one with the data: look at hundreds of examples, find duplicates, corrupt labels, imbalances, biases; think about what features a simple model would use; plot distributions and outliers.

Skeleton and baselines: fix the seed; simplify (no augmentation, no fancy schedules); verify the initial loss equals the expected value for random predictions (for binary cross-entropy at prevalence p, −[p log p + (1 − p) log(1 − p)]); initialize the final layer's bias to the base rate; build human and simple baselines; a model that predicts from inputs and one with inputs zeroed should differ; overfit one batch to zero loss; verify decreasing training loss with capacity; visualize exactly what enters the network just before it does; visualize prediction dynamics on a fixed batch; use backpropagation to chart dependencies (a loss on one example should produce gradients only for that example); generalize a special case first.

Overfit: get a model large enough to overfit the training set, then regularize; use the standard architecture for the domain; Adam with learning rate 3e-4 is a safe start; add complexity one piece at a time; disable learning-rate decay at first.

Regularize: more real data, augmentation, creative augmentation, pretraining, fewer inputs, smaller model, smaller batch, dropout (carefully with batch norm), weight decay, early stopping on validation; a larger model with early stopping often beats a small one.
Tune: random search over hyperparameters rather than grid; Bayesian optimization if you like; squeeze: ensembles, and train longer than you think.

b.s: initial BCE ≈ −[p log p + (1 − p) log(1 − p)] for prevalence p;  final bias = log(p/(1 − p))

items: Verify the loss at initialization and overfit one batch before anything else.
Add one thing at a time and keep a fixed batch to watch.
Regularize after you can overfit, not before.

b.s: Apply the recipe to the spatio-temporal net: check the initial loss against the prevalence formula, set the output bias to the base rate, overfit two batches, then add neighbor mixing and early stopping one step at a time with a log of each change and its effect.

resources.title: UvA Deep Learning Tutorials

b.s: A set of free lessons with code you can run that teach how to build learning machines with a popular tool called PyTorch.

The University of Amsterdam's deep learning course notebooks, free online: PyTorch basics, activation functions, initialization, optimization, transformers, graph neural networks, autoencoders, and more. Each notebook runs and explains as it goes. They fill gaps between the theory and the code.

The notebooks on initialization and optimization, on transformers and multi-head attention, and on graph neural networks are directly useful for lesson 9 and lesson 10's advanced levels; run them on the Mac (they are written for GPUs but work on CPU and MPS with smaller settings).

Their careful experiments (comparing initializations, optimizers, normalization) are the empirical version of the training material, and their graph neural network notebook implements message passing from scratch.
The tutorials on energy-based models, normalizing flows and autoregressive models are a bridge to the generative-model topic with working code.
A free, maintained set of reference implementations; useful when reproducing a paper and needing a correct baseline component.

Notebooks: introduction to PyTorch; activation functions; optimization and initialization; inception, ResNet and DenseNet; transformers and multi-head attention; graph neural networks; energy-based models; deep autoencoders; normalizing flows; autoregressive image modelling; vision transformers; meta-learning; self-supervised contrastive learning; plus a JAX track and guides on scaling.

Optimization and initialization: constant versus random initialization, variance analysis leading to Xavier and Kaiming, the effect of activation choice; SGD, momentum and Adam compared on a small model; learning-rate effects; the notebook's diagnostic plots of gradient norms per layer.
ResNets and friends: skip connections, bottlenecks, pre-activation blocks, DenseNet's concatenation, and what each does to optimization.

Transformers: scaled dot-product attention implemented from scratch, multi-head attention, the encoder block, positional encoding, learning-rate warmup and why it matters, and experiments on sequence tasks (reversing, set anomaly detection).
Graph neural networks: graph convolution as normalized adjacency multiplication, graph attention layers from scratch, node classification on Cora, and PyTorch Geometric usage.

Generative and self-supervised: autoencoders with latent visualization, normalizing flows with coupling layers, autoregressive PixelCNN, energy-based models with contrastive divergence, and SimCLR contrastive learning with augmentations and a linear probe.

resources.title: The training-recipe papers: Adam (Kingma, Ba, 2014), Batch Normalization (Ioffe, Szegedy, 2015), Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014)

b.s: Three papers that gave learning machines three tricks: a smarter way to take steps, a way to keep numbers in a comfortable range, and a way to make the machine not rely on any one part too much.

Three research papers behind the standard training recipe. Adam adapts the step size for each weight; batch normalization keeps activations in a stable range so training is faster and more forgiving; dropout randomly switches off neurons during training so the network cannot depend on any one. All free; read the abstracts and the main figures.

Read each after using the method: Adam's update rule and its bias correction, batch norm's normalization and its learned scale and shift, dropout's training and test-time behavior. The experiments show the effect sizes; note what each claims and what later work revised.

Understand Adam as a combination of momentum and per-parameter scaling; batch norm's effect on optimization (smoothing the loss landscape, later analyses argue) rather than the internal-covariate-shift story; dropout as approximate model averaging. Each has known failure modes worth knowing.

Together with later corrections (AdamW's decoupled weight decay, layer normalization for transformers, batch norm's issues at small batch size) they are the history of the training recipe; reading them teaches how empirical claims in ML get revised.
Canonical citations; for research, the interesting part is the gap between their stated explanations and the later understanding, which is a lesson in how the field learns.

Adam: an optimizer with per-parameter adaptive learning rates from exponential moving averages of the gradient and its square, with bias correction, convergence analysis and experiments. Batch normalization: normalizing each layer's inputs per mini-batch with learned scale and shift, its effect on training speed and on allowable learning rates, and inference with population statistics. Dropout: randomly dropping units during training to prevent co-adaptation, its interpretation as training an exponential ensemble, the weight-scaling rule at test time, and experiments across domains.

items: Adam's update: m_t = β₁m_{t−1} + (1 − β₁)g_t; v_t = β₂v_{t−1} + (1 − β₂)g_t²; bias-corrected m̂ = m_t/(1 − β₁ᵗ), v̂ = v_t/(1 − β₂ᵗ); θ ← θ − α m̂/(√v̂ + ε); defaults α = 1e-3, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε = 1e-8; the effective step is bounded by α and invariant to gradient scale; later AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient.

Why Adam: momentum smooths noisy gradients; dividing by the root of the second moment equalizes step sizes across parameters with different gradient scales; bias correction fixes the early steps when the averages start at zero.

Batch normalization: for each feature, normalize over the mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, then scale by γ and shift by β (learned); during inference use running averages of mean and variance; place before the nonlinearity; it allows higher learning rates, makes initialization less critical and regularizes slightly; the paper's 'internal covariate shift' explanation was later disputed in favor of loss-landscape smoothing.

Batch norm caveats: depends on batch size (small batches give noisy statistics), behaves differently in training and evaluation (`model.eval()` matters), interacts with dropout, and is unsuitable for sequence models where layer normalization is used.

Dropout: during training, each unit is kept with probability p (0.5 hidden, 0.8 inputs typical) and dropped otherwise; at test time, all units are kept and weights scaled by p (or inverted dropout scales at training time); the network cannot rely on specific co-adapted units; it approximates averaging over 2ⁿ thinned networks; experiments show consistent gains on vision, speech and text with larger models and longer training.

Practical combination: Adam(W) with a learning-rate schedule, normalization appropriate to the architecture, dropout tuned by validation; the three form the default recipe that most models still use in some form.

b.s:
Adam: θ_t = θ_{t−1} − α · m̂_t / (√v̂_t + ε)
BatchNorm: y = γ (x − μ_B)/√(σ_B² + ε) + β
Dropout (inverted): h ← h ⊙ mask / p, mask ~ Bernoulli(p)

items: Adam normalizes step sizes per parameter; its defaults work across most problems.
Batch norm stabilizes training but ties the model to batch statistics; use layer norm for sequences.
Dropout is ensemble averaging in disguise; scale correctly at test time.
