resources.title: Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch

b.s: A university class where students build a language model from the very bottom, including collecting and cleaning the text it learns from.

A Stanford course whose lectures and assignments are public. Students implement everything: the tokenizer, the model, the training system, data cleaning and evaluation. It is demanding and current, and its assignment write-ups are worth reading even if you do not do them all.

Watch the lectures on tokenization, on the transformer and its variants, and on data. The assignments show how much of a language model is engineering (systems, data pipelines) rather than architecture.

The course's systems assignments (efficient attention kernels, distributed training, mixed precision) are the practical version of the scaling topic; its data assignment (filtering, deduplication) is the part most courses skip and most products get wrong.

Compare its curriculum with the ultra-scale playbook and with the papers on data curation; together they are the current state of the art in how language models are built, at a level that lets you read the industrial reports.
The course is a snapshot of what a research lab considers foundational in 2026; for a lead, its assignments define what an engineer joining an LLM team should be able to do.

Lectures and assignments covering the full stack: tokenization (BPE from scratch); the transformer architecture and its modern variants (RMSNorm, rotary embeddings, SwiGLU, attention variants); training (optimizers, learning rate schedules, mixed precision, systems considerations); GPU kernels and performance (FlashAttention, Triton kernels); parallelism (data, tensor, pipeline); scaling laws and their use; data (crawling, filtering, deduplication, mixing); alignment (supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, RL for reasoning); evaluation and safety. Assignments: build a tokenizer and transformer, systems and kernels, scaling, data, alignment.

items: Tokenization from scratch: byte-level BPE training (count pairs, merge the most frequent, repeat), encoding and decoding, special tokens, pre-tokenization with regular expressions, and the effect of vocabulary size on sequence length and compute.

Architecture in 2026: pre-norm blocks with RMSNorm, rotary positional embeddings applied to queries and keys, SwiGLU feed-forward, grouped-query or multi-query attention for inference efficiency, no biases, tied or untied embeddings; the assignment builds all of it in PyTorch.

Training: AdamW with cosine schedules and warmup, gradient clipping, mixed precision with bfloat16, checkpointing, and the resource accounting of memory (parameters, gradients, optimizer state, activations) and FLOPs (≈ 6 × parameters × tokens for training).

Systems: profiling, memory-bound versus compute-bound kernels, FlashAttention's tiling to avoid materializing the attention matrix, writing a Triton kernel, and benchmarking; distributed training with data parallelism and sharded optimizer state, tensor and pipeline parallelism, communication costs.
Scaling laws: fitting loss against compute, parameters and tokens; using small runs to choose the size of a large run; the Chinchilla trade-off; the assignment estimates laws under a budget.

Data: what pretraining corpora contain, filtering for quality and safety, deduplication (exact and near-duplicate with MinHash), language identification, mixing domains, and the observation that data work dominates outcomes.

Alignment: supervised fine-tuning on instructions, preference data, direct preference optimization, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for reasoning; evaluation on benchmarks and its pitfalls; safety considerations.

b.s:
training FLOPs ≈ 6 · N_params · N_tokens
RMSNorm(x) = x / √(mean(x²) + ε) · g
memory ≈ params (2 bytes) + grads (2) + Adam states (8) + activations

items: Most of a language model is systems and data; the architecture is a small part.
Six times parameters times tokens is the compute; plan with it.
Deduplication and filtering move results more than most architectural changes.

b.s: Implement byte-level BPE training and encoding from scratch, train a 2000-token vocabulary on the repository's text, and measure the compression ratio against character-level tokens.

resources.title: What are Diffusion Models? (Weng, Lil'Log)

b.s: A long web post that explains how a computer can draw a picture by starting from noise and cleaning it up bit by bit.

Lilian Weng's blog post explains diffusion models, the method behind modern image generators: add noise to data step by step, train a network to undo one step, then generate by starting from noise. It compares diffusion with GANs and VAEs. Free; it is long and mathematical in places, so read it in two sittings.

Read the first sections (the forward and reverse processes and the training objective) and skim the later ones on speeding up sampling and on conditioning. Then implement a tiny diffusion model on one-dimensional data (daily speed profiles) to see the idea work.

The post derives the variational objective, the simplification to noise prediction, and the connection to score matching; it is a faithful and compact version of the original papers. The later sections on classifier-free guidance and on fast samplers track the field.
Weng's other posts (on attention, on self-supervised learning, on prompt engineering and on agents) are similarly careful surveys; her blog is a reliable index of a topic's literature.
A well-maintained survey post is often more useful than a review paper because it is revised; cite the papers, but read the post first.

Generative model families compared (GAN, VAE, flow, diffusion); the forward diffusion process (adding Gaussian noise over steps, the closed form at any step); the reverse process and its parameterization; the variational objective and its simplification to predicting noise (DDPM); connections to score-based generative modelling and stochastic differential equations; speeding up sampling (DDIM, progressive distillation, consistency models); latent diffusion; conditioned generation (classifier guidance, classifier-free guidance); model architecture (U-Net, diffusion transformers); and a quick summary.

items: Forward process: q(x_t | x_{t−1}) = N(√(1 − β_t) x_{t−1}, β_t I) for t = 1..T with a variance schedule; the closed form q(x_t | x_0) = N(√ᾱ_t x_0, (1 − ᾱ_t) I) with ᾱ_t = Π(1 − β_s), so any noisy version is one sample away.
Reverse process: p_θ(x_{t−1} | x_t) = N(μ_θ(x_t, t), Σ_θ) learned by a network; the true posterior q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0) is Gaussian with known mean, which lets the objective be written as KL terms.

Objective: the variational bound decomposes into per-step KL divergences; parameterizing the mean through predicted noise ε_θ gives the simplified loss L_simple = E‖ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε, t)‖², a regression from a noisy sample and a timestep to the noise.

Sampling: start from pure Gaussian noise and apply the learned reverse step T times, adding noise at each step except the last; DDIM makes a deterministic, faster sampler by changing the process without retraining; distillation and consistency models reduce steps to a few or one.
Score matching view: the noise predictor estimates the score ∇ log p(x_t); annealed Langevin dynamics and the SDE formulation unify diffusion models and score-based models.
Latent diffusion: run the diffusion in the latent space of an autoencoder to cut cost, which is how large image models work.

Conditioning: classifier guidance uses a classifier's gradient to steer sampling; classifier-free guidance trains with and without the condition and extrapolates between them at sampling with a guidance scale.
Architectures: U-Nets with attention and timestep embeddings; diffusion transformers operating on latent patches.

b.s:
q(x_t | x_0) = N(√ᾱ_t x_0, (1 − ᾱ_t) I)
L_simple = E_{t, x_0, ε} ‖ ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε, t) ‖²
classifier-free guidance: ε̃ = (1 + w) ε_θ(x_t, c) − w ε_θ(x_t)

items: Diffusion training is regression from a noisy input and a timestep to the noise; that simplicity is why it works.
Sampling is iterative denoising; most later work is about making it faster.
Guidance trades diversity for fidelity to a condition.

b.s: Implement DDPM on one-dimensional daily speed profiles (288 values) with a small MLP as the noise predictor, train on the Mac mini, sample new profiles, and compare their 5 pm distribution with real ones.

resources.title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders (fast.ai)

b.s: A free class where you train a real neural network on the very first day and only later learn all the details, like learning to ride a bike before studying how it works.

Jeremy Howard's course is top-down: you build working models first (on images, text and tables) and learn the theory as you need it. It uses the fastai library built on PyTorch. It is good for confidence and full of practical tricks that make training work.

Its tabular lessons (random forests first, then neural networks on tables) and its training tricks (a learning-rate finder, the one-cycle schedule) are directly usable in stage 9. The lesson on embeddings for categorical variables shows how to give station identity to a network, which is how the spatio-temporal net could learn per-station behavior.

The course's emphasis on iterating quickly and inspecting data is a counterweight to theory-first study, and its stated view that tree ensembles usually win on tabular data matches the evidence and this project's production choice. Its chapter on data ethics is short and worth the time for anyone whose model will issue alerts to drivers.

The fastai library's abstractions can hide details you need for a custom model such as the spatio-temporal network. Learn the ideas from the course, then implement in plain PyTorch. The course's lessons on collaborative filtering and on tabular embeddings are the clearest introduction to learned representations for categorical data.

fast.ai's research output (training-efficiency results, transfer learning for text) shows that practitioner-driven groups produce research results. Its philosophy of accessible deep learning shaped how many teams onboard engineers, and its lesson structure is a reasonable template for an internal course on this pipeline.

Lessons: getting started (a working image classifier in minutes, what ML is, transfer learning); deployment (data cleaning with the model, a web app); neural net foundations (from scratch: a linear model, then a network, SGD, the training loop); natural language (fine-tuning a language model then a classifier); from-scratch model (tabular, neural nets from foundations); random forests (bagging, out-of-bag, feature importance, partial dependence, tree interpretation); collaborative filtering (embeddings, dot products, biases, weight decay); convolutions (kernels, stride, padding, channels); data ethics; and the book's later chapters (ResNets, architecture details, training tricks, a CNN from scratch).

items: Top-down: train a state-of-the-art classifier first with a pretrained backbone and fine-tuning, then learn why it works; the argument that transfer learning is the default for images and text.

The training loop from foundations: parameters, predictions, loss, gradients (autograd), step, repeat; from a linear model on MNIST digits to a network with ReLU; mini-batches; the learning-rate finder (increase the rate until the loss explodes and pick a point before) and the one-cycle schedule.

Tabular: random forests as the first model (fast, robust, informative), out-of-bag error, feature importance by permutation, partial dependence plots, removing redundant features, extrapolation failure of trees and the test for out-of-domain data; then neural nets on tabular data with categorical embeddings; ensembling both.

Collaborative filtering: users and items as embeddings whose dot product plus biases predicts a rating; training with weight decay; interpreting embedding dimensions; the same idea gives station embeddings for the traffic net.
Text: tokenization, numericalization, language-model pretraining on the domain corpus, then fine-tuning a classifier (ULMFiT), which is the recipe for the incident headline classifier.

Convolutions: a kernel sliding over an image, stride and padding, channels, receptive fields, batch norm, and building a ResNet; the practical rules (start with a pretrained model, progressive resizing, test-time augmentation, mixup, label smoothing).
Ethics: feedback loops, bias, disinformation, and the responsibility of practitioners; checked in every project through questions about data provenance and affected people.

b.s:
learn = vision_learner(dls, resnet18, metrics=error_rate); learn.lr_find(); learn.fine_tune(3)
rating ≈ u_user · v_item + b_user + b_item

items: Start from a pretrained model whenever one exists; train from scratch only for tabular data or when you must.
The learning-rate finder and one-cycle schedule remove most guesswork from training.
Random forests are the fast, interpretable first model for tables; embeddings turn categories into geometry.

b.s: Fine-tune a pretrained ResNet on a small folder of your own photos with the learning-rate finder and one-cycle, then fine-tune a small pretrained language model on incident headlines for severity and compare with a bag-of-words baseline.

resources.lives: course · free · eight weeks · the vision and text lessons, with transfer learning throughout

items: Train a small convolutional network on a public digits dataset on MPS, then fine-tune a pretrained ResNet on a tiny set of your own photos.
Fine-tune a small pretrained encoder to predict 511 incident severity from headlines; compare with a bag-of-words logistic regression.

Run a quantized open language model locally, extract route, direction and severity from 50 headlines, and score exact match against hand labels; build a small retrieval-augmented question answerer over the repository's docs with a 30-question eval set.
Train an autoencoder on daily speed profiles and rank days by reconstruction error; train a conditional VAE that generates profiles given weekday and rain.
Pretrain a masked-step model on all Fremont stations and compare a linear probe with raw features on the slow-episode label.
A headline severity classifier with macro F1 and calibration next to the bag-of-words baseline.
An extraction accuracy number for the local LLM with an error analysis of its worst ten cases.
A generated-profile plot next to real ones, with a distribution comparison of the 5 pm speed.
Fine-tuning with a learning rate meant for training from scratch.
Trusting an LLM's output without an eval set.
Judging generative samples by eye alone.

items.title: Shipping it on one Mac mini: memory, scheduling, monitoring

b.s: Run the whole thing unattended on 16 GB, know when it is failing, and retrain without breaking what works.
Our helper has to run all by itself every five minutes on one small computer that must never fall asleep.
It also has to check its own work. If it starts guessing badly, someone should find out, and it should learn again from the new days.
Set a timer to water a plant every day. What happens if the phone with the timer runs out of battery? How would you notice?

The Mac mini has 16 GB of memory shared by everything: the screen, the browser, and our program. A year of Fremont data is about 10 million rows; as 60 columns of numbers that is about 2.5 GB, so it fits, but only if we store numbers compactly and never run two big jobs at once. The Chrome downloader alone takes a gigabyte.
Jobs are scheduled by macOS with launchd: ask 511 every 15 minutes, predict every 5 minutes, check accuracy weekly, retrain monthly.
Monitoring means comparing last week's predictions with what really happened once the PeMS file for those days arrives, and checking that the clues still look like the ones the model trained on.
Compute 10,000,000 rows × 60 columns × 4 bytes. Convert to gigabytes. How many years fit in 12 GB if nothing else is running?

The serving loop: load the three models and the calibration file once; every five minutes build the last 13 steps of features with the same code that built the training table, predict, calibrate, apply the thresholds, write a JSON file, and append to a log.

Memory rules: float32, categorical ids, monthly Parquet parts, one heavy job at a time, three gigabytes kept free. Scheduling rules: launchd plists with `StartInterval`, Energy settings set to never sleep, `caffeinate` around the long download.

Monitoring: population stability index per feature against the training distribution, and average precision recomputed over the last seven days when PeMS posts them. Retrain monthly, or sooner on a real drop. The known gap: there is no real-time speed feed yet, so the loop runs in replay mode on yesterday's file.
Write the launchd plist for the predictor with a 300-second interval, and explain in two sentences why cron is worse on a machine that sleeps.

Train-serve skew is the classic failure: a second implementation of the features drifts within weeks. The defense is one module imported by both paths plus a golden-file test that recomputes one stored day and compares bit for bit. Point-in-time correctness follows: serving must only see what was available at t, and so must the training table.

Operational mechanics: idempotent jobs, atomic model swaps (write to a temporary name, rename), predictions logged with the newest input timestamp they used, and delayed scoring once labels arrive a day later. Drift: PSI = Σ (p_i − q_i) ln(p_i / q_i) over bins; a shift of one standard deviation in a normal feature gives PSI near 0.5, well past the 0.2 alarm.
Memory on unified hardware: measure with `psutil` and `tracemalloc`, set `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, and treat swap as failure. Reproducibility: pinned requirements, seeds, and a manifest with content hashes.
Implement PSI with ten quantile bins from the training distribution and compute it for a feature shifted by 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 standard deviations. Where would you set the alarm?

Treat the pipeline as a reliability problem: service objectives for freshness and latency, alerts on missing data (silent failure is the default failure), canary evaluation of a retrained model on the most recent month before it replaces the champion, rollback, and a champion-challenger record.

Retraining is a control problem: frequency against drift speed against cost, with the risk of feedback loops once alerts change behavior. Continual learning without forgetting is unsolved in general; periodic full retrains with the newest month always in the window are the robust default.
Governance: raw immutable, derived reproducible, lineage in the manifest, and metric definitions versioned with the label so that a change in one is visible in the other.
Design the canary rule that decides when a retrained model may replace the old one, using a statistical test that respects temporal dependence, and state its false-promotion rate.

At scale the same stage becomes streaming feature pipelines with exactly-once semantics, online feature stores, model registries, shadow deployments and staged rollouts, and on-device deployment with privacy-preserving telemetry. The Mac mini is a faithful miniature of on-device budgets: memory, energy, thermal throttling, and no operator watching.

Research threads: performative prediction and feedback loops (next month's training data contains the effect of this month's alerts), monitoring without labels through uncertainty and density-ratio drift detectors, and continual learning with guarantees.
Propose how you would detect that the model's own alerts are changing the label distribution, and how you would correct the training data or the objective for it.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

The serving loop runs every five minutes and must compute features exactly as training did, so the feature code lives in one module, `features.py`, imported by both the training script and the predictor; `from features import build_features` loads that function. Loading the models: `lgb.Booster(model_file=...)` reads a saved LightGBM model; `joblib` is a library for saving and loading Python objects such as the isotonic calibrators; `json.load` reads the thresholds. The dictionary comprehension `{h: ... for h in (15, 30, 60)}` builds one entry per horizon.

`load_last_13_steps()` is your function that returns the most recent 13 five-minute rows per station (the 12 lags plus the current row); in replay mode it slices yesterday's Parquet at the current wall-clock slot, so the whole pipeline can be exercised without live PeMS. `build_features(buf).iloc[-N:]` computes the feature table and keeps the newest row per station. For each horizon the raw score is calibrated and compared with its threshold; `zip` pairs station ids with probabilities. `pd.Timestamp.utcnow().isoformat()` stamps the output with when it was made, and `input_ts` says how fresh the data was.

The last line is the atomic write: write to a `.tmp` file, then `os.replace` renames it over the real file in one step, so a reader never sees a half-written JSON. Any dashboard reads `output/predictions_latest.json`. (`import os` is needed; add it at the top.)
The serving loop's core, using the training feature module.

items: `from features import build_features` — the one feature implementation, shared with training
`models = {h: lgb.Booster(model_file=...) for h in (15, 30, 60)}` — the three saved models
`cal = json.load(...); isos = {h: joblib.load(...) ...}` — thresholds and calibrators
`buf = load_last_13_steps()` — the recent rows needed to compute every lag
`X = build_features(buf).iloc[-1 * N:]` — features for the newest row of each station
`q = isos[h].predict(m.predict(X[feats]))` — raw score, then calibrated probability
`out["rows"].append({..."alert": bool(p >= cal[str(h)]["tau"])})` — one record per station and horizon
`json.dump(out, open("...tmp", "w")); os.replace(tmp, real)` — write, then rename atomically

b.s: Drift is the slow change in the data after training: a new lane, a sensor replaced, a changed commute pattern. The Population Stability Index (PSI) is a single number comparing a feature's distribution now with its distribution in training. Cut the training values into ten equal-count bins (`np.quantile` at 0, 0.1, …, 1 gives the edges; setting the outer edges to −∞ and +∞ catches everything), count what share of training rows and of live rows fall in each bin (`np.histogram` counts, dividing by the count gives shares, `+ 1e-6` avoids dividing by or logging zero), and sum (p − q)·log(p / q) over bins.

The usual reading: below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 watch, above 0.25 the feature has moved and the model may be stale. Compute it weekly for the top ten features and log it; a rise in PSI is the earliest sign that retraining is due, long before the delayed scores of the next step confirm it.
Population stability index against the training distribution.

items: `edges = np.quantile(train_col.dropna(), np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)); edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf` — ten equal-count bins from training, open at both ends
`p = histogram(train) / n + 1e-6; q = histogram(live) / n + 1e-6` — share of rows per bin, then and now
`return float(np.sum((p - q) * np.log(p / q)))` — the index: zero if nothing moved

b.s: Truth arrives late: PeMS posts a day's data the next day, so a prediction can be scored only after that. The predictor should append every prediction it makes to `output/predictions_log.parquet` with the station, the input timestamp, the horizon and the probability. Delayed scoring joins that log to the truth once it exists. `target_ts` is the moment the prediction was about: input time plus horizon minutes, built with `pd.to_timedelta(log.h, "min")`.

The merge matches station and target moment against the cleaned table's `label` at that moment. `groupby("h").apply(lambda g: ap(g.label, g.p))` computes average precision per horizon on real live predictions, the number that finally answers 'is the model still good'. Compare it with the validation and test numbers from training; a steady fall means retrain.
Delayed scoring once PeMS posts the day.

log = pd.read_parquet("output/predictions_log.parquet"); truth = pd.read_parquet("data/pems_processed/2026-11.parquet")[["station_id", "timestamp", "label"]]
log["target_ts"] = log.input_ts + pd.to_timedelta(log.h, "min")
scored = log.merge(truth, left_on=["station_id", "target_ts"], right_on=["station_id", "timestamp"])
print(scored.groupby("h").apply(lambda g: ap(g.label, g.p)))

items: `log = pd.read_parquet("output/predictions_log.parquet"); truth = ...[["station_id", "timestamp", "label"]]` — what we said, and what happened
`log["target_ts"] = log.input_ts + pd.to_timedelta(log.h, "min")` — the moment each prediction was about
`scored = log.merge(truth, left_on=["station_id", "target_ts"], right_on=["station_id", "timestamp"])` — prediction beside outcome
`scored.groupby("h").apply(lambda g: ap(g.label, g.p))` — live average precision per horizon

b.s: launchd is macOS's built-in scheduler, the thing that runs programs at boot and on timers; it is the right way to run the predictor every five minutes on a Mac mini with no one logged in at the keyboard. A job is described by a plist, an XML file of keys and values, saved as `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.traffic1.predict.plist` and loaded once with `launchctl load` on that path.

The keys: `Label` names the job; `ProgramArguments` is the command as a list, and it must use the venv's own Python by full path (`/Users/you/Traffic1/.venv/bin/python`) so the right libraries are found, with the script's full path after it; `StartInterval` 300 runs it every 300 seconds; `WorkingDirectory` makes the relative `data/` and `models/` paths resolve; `StandardOutPath` and `StandardErrorPath` capture what the script prints and any error, which is where you look when it stops working. Replace `you` with your username. Make the `logs/` folder first. Check that it runs with `launchctl list | grep traffic1` and by watching the log file.
A launchd plist for the predictor.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.traffic1.predict</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key><array><string>/Users/you/Traffic1/.venv/bin/python</string><string>/Users/you/Traffic1/19_predict_live.py</string></array>
  <key>StartInterval</key><integer>300</integer>
  <key>WorkingDirectory</key><string>/Users/you/Traffic1</string>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/Users/you/Traffic1/logs/predict.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/you/Traffic1/logs/predict.err</string>
</dict></plist>

items: `<key>Label</key><string>com.traffic1.predict</string>` — the job's name
`<key>ProgramArguments</key><array>...venv python... ...19_predict_live.py...</array>` — run the predictor with the venv's Python
`<key>StartInterval</key><integer>300</integer>` — every five minutes
`<key>WorkingDirectory</key>...` — so relative paths inside the script work
`<key>StandardOutPath</key> / <key>StandardErrorPath</key>` — where output and errors go

b.s: Memory is the resource that kills a 16 GB machine silently: a stage that grows to 12 GB makes everything else swap. So every stage prints one structured line at the end with its name, its input, how long it took and its peak resident memory. `psutil` is a library for asking the operating system about processes (`pip install psutil`); `psutil.Process(os.getpid())` is the current process, and `.memory_info().rss` is its resident set size in bytes, the memory actually in RAM; dividing by 1e9 gives gigabytes.

`time.time()` is the current time in seconds; subtracting the start time gives the duration. The f-string formats with `:.1f` (one decimal) and `:.2f`. Writing `key=value` pairs makes the line easy to search with `grep` and to load into a table later. Keep these lines; a stage whose memory line creeps up week by week is a stage with a growing leak or a growing file.
A memory line in every stage's log.

import psutil, time, os
t0 = time.time(); proc = psutil.Process(os.getpid())
# ... stage work ...
print(f"stage=clean file={path} seconds={time.time()-t0:.1f} rss_gb={proc.memory_info().rss/1e9:.2f}")

items: `t0 = time.time(); proc = psutil.Process(os.getpid())` — start the clock and get a handle on this process
`print(f"stage=clean file={path} seconds={time.time()-t0:.1f} rss_gb={proc.memory_info().rss/1e9:.2f}")` — one searchable line: what ran, on what, how long, how much memory

b.q: Why write the JSON to a temporary name and rename?

a.s: A reader that opens the file mid-write sees half a file. Rename is atomic on the same filesystem, so readers see either the old file or the new one.

b.q: Why log the input timestamp with every prediction?

a.s: Scoring later needs to know what the model knew; and the gap between input time and generation time is the real latency a user experiences.

b.q: What is wrong with retraining every night automatically?

a.s: Nothing checks the new model before it replaces the old one. A bad day of data produces a bad model that ships at midnight. Canary first, then swap.

items: 'It works on my laptop, so it will run unattended.' Sleep, reboots, a changed login page and a full disk are the normal failures; none show up in a demo.
'Monitoring is accuracy.' Freshness and missing data fail first; accuracy is the last thing to notice.
'More memory would fix it.' Filtering at ingest, float32 and one job at a time fix it; memory would only hide the design.

items.title: APIs, containers and the cloud: serving a model beyond one Mac

b.s: Wrap a model in a service, package it so it runs anywhere, and know what changes when it leaves the Mac mini.
Right now the helper lives on one small computer. To let a phone app ask it questions, we give it a door with a doorbell: the app rings, asks 'is I-880 slow?', and the helper answers.
A container is a lunchbox with everything the helper needs packed inside, so it works on any computer.
Play doorbell: one person is the app, one is the helper. The app asks a question at the door and the helper answers. That is an API.

An API is an agreed way for programs to talk: the app sends a request (station, horizon) and gets a JSON answer (probability). A web framework such as FastAPI turns a Python function into that door. A container (Docker) packages the code, Python and libraries into one image that runs the same everywhere. The cloud is renting computers by the hour to run it.
Write a Python function `predict(station_id, horizon)` that returns the latest probability from `predictions_latest.json`. That function is the whole API before the door is added.

FastAPI: define request and response models, add an endpoint, run with a server, read the auto-generated docs. Docker: a Dockerfile lists the base image and install steps, `docker build` and `docker run` package and run it, `.dockerignore` keeps data out. Cloud basics: a virtual machine, object storage for files, a scheduler, secrets management, and logs. Batch versus online serving: this project's 5-minute batch writes a file; an online service answers on demand.
Security basics: never expose secrets, validate inputs, rate-limit, use HTTPS.
Wrap the predictor in a FastAPI endpoint, containerize it, run it on the Mac, and call it with `curl`. Then measure latency for 100 requests.

Service design: statelessness, health checks, versioned endpoints, timeouts and retries, idempotency, structured logging with request ids. Model serving patterns: model loaded once per process, warm-up, batching, shadow deployments, canary releases, rollback. Containers versus virtual machines; orchestration (Kubernetes) at a level of understanding; infrastructure as code. Cost and latency budgets as design inputs.
Data movement: object storage as the shared truth, caching, and the feature-consistency problem between batch and online paths.
Design the API contract (schemas, error codes, versioning) for the alert service and implement it with a golden test that replays a stored day through the endpoint.

Reliability engineering for ML services: service-level objectives, observability (metrics, traces, logs), load testing, graceful degradation (serve persistence when the model fails), and multi-region concerns. Edge deployment (on-device) versus cloud, and the privacy and latency trade-offs. Security threats specific to ML endpoints (model extraction, adversarial inputs).
Write the runbook for the alert service: what alerts fire, what the on-call does for each, and how to roll back a bad model in under five minutes.

Serving at scale is a systems research area: inference optimization, hardware-aware scheduling, multi-tenant model serving, and the economics of inference. On-device serving flips the constraints to energy, memory and privacy, which the M1 sandbox mimics. The organizational lesson: the model is a small part of the service, and the service is what users experience.
Compare cloud batch, cloud online and on-device serving for a traffic alert product on cost, latency, privacy and failure modes, and recommend one with a migration path.

b.q: What does a container solve?

a.s: Environment drift: the code, interpreter and libraries travel together, so the service runs the same on the Mac, a server or the cloud.

b.q: Why keep serving stateless?

a.s: Any instance can answer any request, which makes scaling, retries and rollbacks simple; state lives in storage, not in the process.

items.title: Scaling: GPUs, distributed training and mixed precision

b.s: Know why GPUs are fast, how training spreads across many of them, and what breaks when models and data outgrow one machine.

A GPU is a chip with thousands of tiny calculators that all work at once, so it can do the same small sum on a huge pile of numbers very fast. Big learning machines use many GPUs at once, like many cooks in one kitchen.
Have four friends each add up a quarter of a long list of numbers, then add their four answers. That is parallel computing.

GPUs do many identical arithmetic steps in parallel, which is what matrix multiplication needs. Training a big model splits the work: data parallelism gives each GPU different batches and averages their gradient updates; model parallelism splits the model itself across GPUs. Mixed precision uses smaller numbers (16-bit) where it is safe, doubling speed and halving memory.
The Mac mini's GPU shares memory with the CPU; there is no copying, but there is also no way to add more.
Time a matrix multiplication of two 4096 × 4096 matrices on the CPU and on MPS. How many times faster is the GPU?

Throughput versus latency; memory bandwidth as the usual bottleneck; batch size and learning-rate scaling; data loading as the hidden bottleneck. Data parallelism with all-reduce of gradients; gradient accumulation to simulate large batches; mixed precision with loss scaling. Checkpointing and resuming. Profiling to find the actual bottleneck before optimizing.
Profile the spatio-temporal net's training step on the M1 with the PyTorch profiler; report the share of time in data loading, forward, backward and optimizer, and speed up the largest.

Hardware: GPU architecture (streaming multiprocessors, memory hierarchy, tensor cores), roofline models, arithmetic intensity. Distributed training: data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, ZeRO-style sharding of optimizer state, communication costs and overlap, collective operations. Numerics: bfloat16 versus float16, loss scaling, numerically stable implementations.
Scaling laws and compute-optimal training as the principled way to size a model for a budget.
Compute the arithmetic intensity of the net's matrix multiplications and place them on a roofline for the M1 GPU; explain why small batches are bandwidth-bound.

Systems for large-scale training: schedulers, fault tolerance, elastic training, and the engineering of thousand-GPU runs; compilers and kernels (fused attention, custom kernels); inference optimization (quantization, KV caching, speculative decoding). The environmental and financial cost of scale as a research constraint.
Estimate the compute, memory and time to train a city-scale spatio-temporal transformer on a year of statewide PeMS data on one GPU versus eight, and identify the parallelism strategy.

Scale is the defining engineering fact of modern ML; the research frontier includes efficient architectures, training and inference at scale, and the science of scaling laws. The M1 sandbox teaches the discipline (profile, measure, budget) that transfers; the numbers do not.
Write a compute budget for a production traffic model at state scale (training, monthly retrains, inference), and argue where the cost actually lands.

b.q: Why are GPUs fast for neural networks?

a.s: Networks are mostly matrix multiplications, which are thousands of identical, independent multiply-adds that a GPU runs in parallel.

b.q: What does mixed precision risk?

a.s: Underflow and overflow in 16-bit numbers; loss scaling and keeping master weights in 32-bit are the standard fixes.

resources.title: CS 329S: Machine Learning Systems Design, lecture notes (Huyen, Stanford)

b.s: Free class notes about making a learning machine work in the real world day after day, written by someone who has done it.

Chip Huyen's Stanford course, with free lecture notes and slides: what an ML system is, data engineering, training data, feature engineering, model development, deployment, monitoring, continual learning, and the human side. It is the free version of her book and covers phase 9's ideas.

The notes on deployment (batch versus online), on monitoring and drift, and on continual learning map onto stages 12 and 13; the notes on data engineering and on training-serving skew explain the one-feature-module rule.

The course notes give vocabulary and checklists (feature stores, model registries, data validation) with case studies; pair with Made With ML for implementations and with the technical-debt paper for the why.
Its treatment of feedback loops and of testing in production is directly relevant to alerts that change traffic; the guest lectures (linked) cover industrial practice.
A free snapshot of the systems consensus; for a lead, the notes align a team's vocabulary before architecture discussions.

Lecture notes: understanding ML production (research versus production, the ML system's components); data engineering (data sources, formats, storage, processing, batch and streaming); training data (sampling, labelling, class imbalance, augmentation); feature engineering (missing values, scaling, encoding, crosses, positional features, leakage, importance, generalization); model development (selection, ensembles, experiment tracking, distributed training, AutoML); evaluation (baselines, calibration, slicing, perturbation, invariance, directional expectation, model calibration, confidence measurement); deployment (batch versus online prediction, model compression, edge); monitoring (data distribution shifts, detection, addressing); continual learning and test in production; infrastructure and tooling; the human side.

items: Production versus research: different objectives (business metrics, latency, cost), data that shifts, fairness and interpretability requirements; the ML system is data, features, model, serving, monitoring and the people around them.

Data engineering: first-party and third-party data, row-major versus column-major formats (CSV versus Parquet), text versus binary, relational versus NoSQL, ETL versus ELT, batch versus stream processing, and the dataflow of a feature pipeline.

Training data: sampling strategies (random, stratified, importance), labelling (hand labels, natural labels with delays, weak supervision, semi-supervision, active learning), class imbalance (metrics, resampling, cost-sensitive learning), augmentation.

Features: handling missing values (MCAR, MAR, MNAR), scaling, discretization, encoding categoricals (including hashing for unbounded categories), feature crossing, positional features, and leakage (from splitting time-correlated data randomly, from scaling before splitting, from imputation statistics, from duplicates, from group leakage); feature importance and generalization across time.

Model development: start simple, beware of state-of-the-art claims, tracking and versioning experiments and data, debugging, distributed training (data and model parallelism), AutoML; the six tips for model selection.

Evaluation: baselines (random, zero-rule, simple heuristic, human, existing solution), perturbation tests for robustness, invariance tests for fairness, directional expectation tests, calibration, confidence measurement, and slice-based evaluation to find groups where the model fails.

Deployment: batch prediction (periodic, cheap, stale) versus online prediction (on request, fresh, needs fast features), the unified pipeline for streaming and batch features, model compression (low-rank, distillation, pruning, quantization), and edge deployment with its constraints.

Monitoring and continual learning: natural causes of failure, covariate shift, label shift, concept shift; detection by statistics and two-sample tests over time windows; addressing by retraining; stateless retraining versus stateful fine-tuning; the four stages toward continual learning; test in production with shadow deployment, A/B tests, canaries, interleaving, bandits.

b.s: covariate shift: P(X) changes, P(Y|X) fixed;  label shift: P(Y) changes, P(X|Y) fixed;  concept drift: P(Y|X) changes

items: Leakage and imbalance are handled at the data and feature stages, not by the model.
Evaluate by slices, perturbations and baselines before believing an aggregate number.
Batch prediction is the right default until freshness is worth the complexity of online serving.

b.s: Run slice-based evaluation of the traffic model by station, hour and rain, add a perturbation test (jitter speeds by 2 mph) and an invariance test (shift timestamps by a week), and write up any slice where AP falls below persistence.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; the systems view, as lecture notes

resources.title: MLflow documentation

b.s: The manual for a tool that writes down every experiment you run: the settings, the score, and the model, so you can find them later.

MLflow is a free, open-source tool for tracking experiments (parameters, metrics, artifacts), packaging models and keeping a registry of versions. Its quickstart runs locally in minutes. Use it to log every training run in phase 9 instead of a JSON file, once the JSON file gets unwieldy.

Read the tracking quickstart and the model registry pages: log parameters and metrics from the LightGBM runs, store the model files as artifacts, and mark a version as production. Its local server shows runs in a browser.

Understand what a tracking server and an artifact store are, how runs and experiments are organized, and how the registry supports staging and rollback; then decide whether the project needs it or whether a manifest and a folder suffice.
MLflow is one of several tools for the same job; the concepts (runs, artifacts, registry, lineage) are what matter and transfer to any platform.
Experiment tracking is infrastructure for reproducibility; the research-relevant question is whether a result can be traced to code, data and parameters a year later, which the tool makes routine.

Components: tracking (runs, experiments, parameters, metrics, artifacts, tags, autologging, the tracking server and UI, backends and artifact stores), models (the MLmodel format, flavors for LightGBM, PyTorch and scikit-learn, signatures and input examples, logging and loading, `pyfunc` for custom models), the model registry (registered models, versions, aliases and tags, stage transitions and annotations), projects (packaging runs with dependencies), deployment (serving a model locally as a REST endpoint, batch inference), and evaluation utilities.

items: Tracking: `mlflow.set_experiment('traffic1')`; inside `with mlflow.start_run():` log `mlflow.log_params(params)`, `mlflow.log_metric('val_ap', ap, step=i)`, `mlflow.log_artifact('output/evaluation_report.json')`, tags for git commit and data hash; autologging for LightGBM and PyTorch captures most of it.
Storage: a local file store by default, a SQLite backend for a UI with search, an artifact directory; `mlflow ui` shows runs, compares parameters and metrics, and plots curves.

Models: `mlflow.lightgbm.log_model(model, 'model', signature=infer_signature(X, p))` records the model with its flavor, environment and input schema; `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(uri)` loads any flavor uniformly; custom `pyfunc` wrappers bundle preprocessing (the feature module) with the model, which is how training and serving share one artifact.

Registry: `mlflow.register_model(uri, 'traffic-h30')` creates a version; aliases (`champion`, `challenger`) point serving at a version; descriptions and tags record evaluation results; transitions are audited.
Serving and batch: `mlflow models serve -m models:/traffic-h30@champion` starts a REST endpoint; batch scoring with `mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf` or a loaded model over a DataFrame.
Reproducibility: log the code version, the data manifest hash and the environment (`conda.yaml` or `requirements.txt`) with every run; a run id names a result exactly.

b.s:
with mlflow.start_run(tags={'commit': sha, 'data': manifest_hash}):
    mlflow.log_params(params); model = lgb.train(...); mlflow.log_metric('val_ap', best)
    mlflow.lightgbm.log_model(model, 'model', signature=infer_signature(Xva, pva))
mlflow.register_model(f'runs:/{run_id}/model', 'traffic-h30'); client.set_registered_model_alias('traffic-h30', 'champion', version)

items: A run id plus logged code, data and environment names a result reproducibly.
A `pyfunc` model that bundles preprocessing is the cure for training-serving skew.
Aliases (champion, challenger) make promotion and rollback one command.

b.s: Log every training run of the three horizons with parameters, metrics, the evaluation report and a signed model; register them; point `champion` at the best; then roll back to the previous version and show the serving loop follows the alias.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; experiment tracking and a model registry

resources.title: Evidently, open-source ML monitoring documentation

b.s: The manual for a free tool that checks whether the data a learning machine sees today still looks like the data it learned from.

Evidently is an open-source Python library for monitoring: it compares current data with reference data and reports drift per feature, data quality issues, and model performance over time, as reports or dashboards. Its tutorials run locally. Use it in stage 13 to check drift weekly.

Read the tutorial on data drift and the one on classification performance: compute drift on the feature table against the training reference, and performance metrics on the scored predictions once labels arrive. Compare its drift tests with the PSI you implemented.

The library implements several statistical tests for drift; understand what each assumes and why a single number per feature is a screen, not a verdict. Its report format is a reasonable template for the weekly monitoring output.
Monitoring tools encode choices about what drift means; read the documentation's methodology pages critically and keep your own definition versioned.
Open-source monitoring made a piece of production practice inspectable; useful as a reference implementation when designing a team's own.

Concepts (reports, tests, metrics, presets; reference versus current data; column mapping), data drift (per-column statistical tests chosen by type and size, dataset drift share, embeddings drift), data quality (missing values, ranges, duplicates, correlations), regression and classification performance (metrics, error analysis, by segment), target drift, test suites with conditions for CI or scheduled checks, and monitoring dashboards over time (workspace, snapshots, panels).

items: Reference and current: monitoring compares a current window of data with a reference (the training set or a stable period); the column mapping declares target, prediction, numerical, categorical and datetime columns.

Drift detection: for numerical columns, Kolmogorov-Smirnov or Wasserstein distance (large data) and for categoricals chi-square or Jensen-Shannon; thresholds; the dataset-level share of drifted columns; PSI available; embeddings drift for learned representations; the caveat that drift is a signal to investigate, not a verdict.
Data quality: missing-value rates, out-of-range values, new categories, duplicates, constant columns, and correlation changes, which catch pipeline breakages before they reach the model.

Performance: classification reports with precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR curves, confusion matrices, class representation and probability distributions; regression with error distributions and error bias by feature; both by segment, which is slice-based evaluation.

Tests and conditions: a test suite states expectations (`TestShareOfDriftedColumns(lt=0.3)`, `TestColumnValueMin(column='speed', gte=0)`) and passes or fails, suitable for a scheduled job that writes a weekly file and alerts on failure.
Monitoring over time: snapshots stored per run, dashboards with panels of metrics over time, and comparisons across model versions.

b.s:
report = Report(metrics=[DataDriftPreset(), DataQualityPreset()]); report.run(reference_data=train_df, current_data=week_df); report.save_html('output/monitor/week.html')
suite = TestSuite(tests=[TestShareOfDriftedColumns(lt=0.3), TestColumnValueMin(column='speed', gte=0)])

items: Compare a current window with a reference; drift per column is a screen, the dataset share is the alarm.
Data quality tests catch pipeline breaks earlier than performance metrics can.
Test suites with thresholds turn monitoring into a pass-or-fail job.

b.s: Build a weekly Evidently test suite for the feature table (drift share, speed range, null rate, category checks) and a performance report once labels arrive; compare its drift verdicts with your PSI implementation.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; drift and performance reports

resources.title: The Turing Way

b.s: A free handbook about doing science with computers in a way that others can check and repeat.

A community-written handbook on reproducible, ethical and collaborative research with data: version control, environments, testing, documentation, data management, and project design. Free online. Read the reproducibility guide during phase 9.

The chapters on reproducible environments, on version control, on testing and on research data management are the scientific version of the engineering rules; its templates (README, project structure) are worth adopting.
Its treatment of the reproducibility spectrum (rerunnable, repeatable, reproducible, replicable) clarifies what the manifest and the golden test achieve, and its ethics chapters connect to phase 10.
A useful reference for the norms of open research and for collaboration practices; its community process is itself a model.
For a lab or team, the handbook is a ready-made standard for research practice and a source of onboarding material.

Guides: reproducible research (overview, open research, version control, licensing, research data management, reproducible environments, code reviewing, code testing, code quality, research compendia, notebooks, credit, continuous integration, risk assessment, case studies); project design (planning, communication, collaboration, data management plans); communication (writing, presenting, figures, making research accessible); collaboration (teams, maintainers, working remotely); ethical research (consent, data protection, algorithmic impact); and community handbook.

items: Reproducibility definitions: reproducible (same data, same analysis, same result), replicable (new data, same analysis), robust (same data, different analysis), generalizable (new data, different analysis); the crisis and the practices that address it.

Version control and environments: git for code with meaningful history; capturing computational environments with package managers, lock files, containers and images; why 'works on my machine' is not reproducible.

Research data management: FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable), data organization and naming, metadata, storage and backup, sharing and licensing, sensitive data handling, and data documentation (README, data dictionaries).

Code quality and testing: readable code, style guides, linters, documentation, testing (unit, integration, regression, smoke, runtime), continuous integration to run tests automatically, and code review as a practice.

Compendia and notebooks: a research compendium bundles data, code, environment and results; notebooks are for exploration and communication and should be converted to scripts for pipelines; version notebooks sensibly.
Ethics and impact: consent, privacy, data protection regulation, algorithmic impact assessments, and accessibility of outputs; credit and authorship.
Communication: writing clearly, figures that convey one message, presenting, and making research accessible to different audiences.

b.s: FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable

items: Reproducible means same data, same code, same environment give the same result; name each explicitly.
A compendium (data, code, environment, results) is the unit of reproducible work.
Documentation and licensing are part of the deliverable.

b.s: Turn the repository into a research compendium: a README that states how to reproduce the evaluation report, a data dictionary for the feature table, a lock file, a license, and a CI run that rebuilds from the fixture.

resources.lives: book · free · weeks · free; reproducible research as a handbook

resources.title: Site Reliability Engineering (Google), the free book

b.s: A free book about keeping big computer services running all the time, and what to do when they break.

Google's book on how they run services, free online: service level objectives, monitoring, being on call, handling incidents, postmortems, and avoiding overload. Read the chapters on monitoring, on service level objectives and on postmortems for the serving stage.

The chapters on monitoring distributed systems (the four golden signals), on service level objectives, on being on call and on blameless postmortems give the operating discipline for the alert service; write the runbook and the postmortem template from them.
Its treatment of error budgets, of toil, and of release engineering frames the retraining and rollback policies; the chapter on managing incidents is the procedure for a bad model in production.
Written for large services, the principles scale down; the exercise is deciding which practices a one-machine system needs and which are ceremony.
A foundational operations text; ML systems inherit all of its concerns plus data and model drift.

Part I, introduction (SRE's approach, the production environment). Part II, principles (embracing risk, service level objectives, eliminating toil, monitoring distributed systems, automation, release engineering, simplicity). Part III, practices (alerting from time-series data, being on call, effective troubleshooting, emergency response, managing incidents, postmortem culture, tracking outages, testing for reliability, software engineering in SRE, load balancing, handling overload, cascading failures, distributed consensus, cron at scale, data pipelines, data integrity, launches). Part IV, management (training, dealing with interrupts, operational load, communication). Part V, conclusions.

items: Risk and objectives: 100 % reliability is the wrong target; define service level indicators (latency, availability, freshness, correctness), objectives for them, and an error budget that balances reliability against change velocity.

Monitoring: the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation); symptoms versus causes; white-box and black-box; alerts must be actionable and rare; pages for urgent, tickets for the rest; avoid alerting on causes you cannot act on.

Toil and automation: repetitive, manual, automatable work should be automated; the hierarchy of automation from manual to self-healing; cron at scale and data pipelines as chapters directly relevant to scheduled jobs.
Alerting from time series: rules over aggregated metrics with rate and windowing; the pitfalls of thresholds on raw values; alerting on error budget burn rates.

On call and incidents: structured on-call with limits; troubleshooting as hypothesis testing (triage, examine, diagnose, test, treat); incident management with roles (commander, operations, communication); the postmortem as a blameless document with timeline, root cause, actions and lessons.

Release and testing: canaries, gradual rollouts, feature flags, rollback capability; testing for reliability (unit, integration, system, production tests, canary tests); simplicity as a reliability strategy.
Data pipelines and integrity: periodic pipelines' failure modes (thundering herd, moiré), workflow systems, and the principle that backups are useless unless restores are tested.

b.s:
error budget = 1 − SLO;  spend it on change, stop changes when it is exhausted
golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation

items: Set objectives and an error budget; they decide when to ship and when to stop.
Alert on symptoms that need action; page rarely.
Blameless postmortems with actions are how a system gets more reliable.

b.s: Write SLOs for the alert service (freshness under 10 minutes, availability, correctness proxy), a golden-signals dashboard spec, an alerting rule on freshness, an on-call runbook, and a postmortem template.

resources.lives: book · free · selected chapters, a week · free; SLOs, on-call and postmortems

resources.title: Hypothesis documentation (property-based testing)

b.s: The manual for a testing tool that makes up thousands of tricky examples for you and finds the one that breaks your code.

Hypothesis is a free Python library: instead of writing one test input, you describe what inputs look like (a list of speeds between 0 and 100) and it generates many, including nasty edge cases, and shrinks any failure to the smallest example. Its quickstart is short.

Use it on the parsers and feature code: properties such as 'cleaning never produces speeds outside 0 to 100', 'lag features of a shifted series equal shifted lag features', 'the profile of a constant series is that constant'. Read the pages on strategies and on shrinking.

Property-based testing finds bugs example-based tests miss (empty inputs, boundaries, unusual timestamps); its stateful testing extends to pipelines. Understand how to write good properties: invariants, round trips, comparisons with a reference implementation.
For data code, properties are often the only tractable specification; the technique is also a way to document assumptions executably, which the data-contract exercise needs.
Property-based testing is underused in ML engineering; adopting it for feature libraries is a cheap, high-yield practice.

Quick start, the `@given` decorator and strategies (integers, floats, text, lists, dictionaries, datetimes, `from_type`, `builds`, composite strategies, `sampled_from`, `one_of`, filtering, mapping), shrinking of failing examples, settings (max examples, deadlines, database of failures), stateful testing (rule-based state machines), the numpy and pandas extras (arrays, DataFrames with column strategies), health checks, and integration with pytest.

items: Property-based testing: instead of fixed inputs, describe the space of inputs with strategies and state a property that must hold for all; Hypothesis generates many cases, biased toward edge cases (empty, zero, NaN, boundaries), and reports a minimal failing example after shrinking.

Strategies: `st.integers(min_value, max_value)`, `st.floats(allow_nan=False, min_value=0, max_value=100)`, `st.lists(st.floats(...), min_size=1)`, `st.datetimes(timezones=...)`, `st.sampled_from(station_ids)`, `st.builds(Event, ...)`, `@st.composite` for structured inputs; `.filter` and `.map` to constrain or transform.

Properties worth stating for data code: invariants (cleaned speeds within bounds), round trips (write Parquet then read equals original), idempotence (cleaning twice equals once), comparisons with a reference implementation (numpy versus SQL lag), and metamorphic relations (shifting timestamps by a day shifts features accordingly).

Failures and reproducibility: failing examples are saved in a local database and replayed first next time; `@example` pins specific cases; `settings(max_examples=500, deadline=None)` for slow functions.
Stateful testing: define a state machine with rules (add rows, clean, compute features) and invariants checked after each step, which tests sequences of operations on the pipeline.
numpy and pandas extras: `arrays(dtype, shape, elements)` and `data_frames(columns=[column('speed', elements=st.floats(0, 100))])` to generate DataFrames that match the schema.
State properties, not examples; let the tool search for the counterexample.
Round trips, idempotence and reference comparisons are the properties data code has.
Shrunk failing examples are the best bug reports you will get.

b.s: Write five property tests for the cleaning and feature modules (bounds, idempotence, Parquet round trip, lag versus reference, timestamp-shift metamorphic), run them, and pin any failing example with `@example`.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; tests that invent their own edge cases

resources.title: Made With ML (Mohandas)

b.s: A free website that shows, with real code, how to build a learning machine the careful way, with tests and checks so it keeps working.

Goku Mohandas's course walks through an ML project end to end: data, modelling, and then the operational parts, testing, monitoring, pipelines and serving, all with code you can read. It is free. Follow the operational sections in phase 7.

Its testing lesson (data tests, model tests, behavioral tests) and its monitoring lesson (drift detection with statistical tests) are directly reusable in stage 13. Its pipeline lesson shows orchestration that you can scale down to launchd jobs on one Mac mini without losing the ideas.

Compare its tooling with a minimal setup: one Mac mini does not need Airflow or a feature store, but it needs the ideas (idempotent tasks, lineage, validation, versioning). Extract the principles and implement them in a few hundred lines rather than adopting the stack.

Its coverage of experiment tracking and model versioning gives the vocabulary to design a JSON-based registry for this project, and its lessons on scaling with Ray are for later, when the data outgrows one machine. The course's opinionated structure is itself a useful design for an internal curriculum.

A free, opinionated, code-first MLOps curriculum is rare. Use it to align a team on practices before choosing a platform, and note which of its practices survive the translation to a single-machine deployment: most of them, which says something about what MLOps actually is.

A course in lessons: design (setup, product and system design), data (preparation, exploration, preprocessing, distributed data), model (training, tracking, tuning, evaluation, serving), developing (scripting, command line, packaging, organization, logging, documentation, styling, pre-commit), testing (code, data, models), deploying (systems, serving, workflows), iterating (continual learning and monitoring), with a companion repository.

items: Product and system design: start from the user and the business objective, define the ML task, consider the data and the constraints, and plan the feedback loops; the design document template.

Data: exploratory analysis with intent, splitting (stratified, or by time and group), preprocessing (cleaning, feature engineering) that runs identically in training and inference, and distributed data loading.

Training and tracking: a baseline first, then increasing complexity; experiment tracking with MLflow (parameters, metrics, artifacts), tuning with a search library, and evaluation that is overall, per class, per slice, with behavioral tests (invariance, directional, minimum functionality).

Developing: moving from notebooks to scripts and packages, a command-line interface, organization (config, data, models, utilities), logging levels and handlers, documentation from docstrings, style (black, isort, flake8) and pre-commit hooks so checks run before every commit.

Testing: unit tests with pytest (fixtures, parametrization, markers, coverage), data tests with expectations (schema, ranges, uniqueness, null rates) run on every new batch, and model tests (behavioral tests, training tests such as overfitting a batch, inference tests).

Deploying: serving as a REST API with batch and online inference, packaging models with their preprocessing, containerizing, workflows and orchestration of the pipeline steps, scaling with a distributed framework.
Iterating: monitoring system health, data quality, drift (using statistical tests and drift libraries), and performance; retraining triggers; the continual-learning loop with human review.

b.s:
pre-commit hooks: black, isort, flake8, pytest -m 'not slow'
data test: assert df.speed.between(0, 100).all(); assert df.groupby('station_id').size().eq(288).all()

items: Notebooks to packages, with configs, logging and a CLI, is the transition that makes a project maintainable.
Test code, data and models; each catches different failures.
Behavioral tests on models (invariance, directional expectations) are cheap and revealing.

b.s: Convert the pipeline into a package with a CLI (`traffic clean`, `traffic features`, `traffic train`), add pre-commit hooks, and write three data tests and two behavioral model tests.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; testing, monitoring and pipelines with code

resources.title: Machine Learning Engineering (Burkov)

b.s: A short, plain book about the whole job of building learning machines, from getting the data to keeping them running.

Andriy Burkov's book, free to read online under a 'read first, buy later' model. It covers the project lifecycle: collecting data, building features, training, evaluating, deploying, and monitoring. It is concise, and each chapter reads like a checklist you can apply to a stage of this project.

Its chapters on data leakage, on evaluation and on deployment are the fastest reads on those topics. The leakage chapter lists exactly the traps lessons 4 to 6 cover: target leakage, temporal leakage, and contamination between train and test. Read it before building the feature table.

Burkov's earlier Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book is the companion for the math; together they are a compact reference set. Use the engineering book's checklists as review criteria for each stage: does stage 8 pass the leakage checklist, does stage 12 pass the deployment one.

It is opinionated and short. Where it disagrees with Huyen (for instance, on how much automation a small team needs), both positions are worth thinking through, and the disagreement itself is a useful prompt for deciding what this project's phase 7 should actually build.

A concise practitioner reference is useful for writing internal guidelines, and its brevity forces prioritization, which senior engineers need more than additional content. Its structure is a reasonable skeleton for an engineering-standards document for an ML team.

Chapters: introduction (what is ML engineering, when to use ML, the project lifecycle); before the project (prioritization, team, cost, integration, risks); data collection and preparation (questions about data, common problems, good data, data leakage, partitioning, imputation, augmentation, sampling, storage, versioning, documentation, reproducibility); feature engineering (properties of good features, techniques, leakage, standardization, discretization, missing values, stacking, dimensionality, storage and documentation); supervised model training (parts 1 and 2: baselines, algorithm selection, pipelines, hyperparameters, learning curves, evaluation, calibration, troubleshooting); model evaluation (offline, online, A/B tests, bandits); model deployment (patterns, serving, environments, monitoring, maintenance); model serving, monitoring and maintenance; a conclusion.

items: When ML: when rules are too complex or change too fast, when data exist, when errors are tolerable; the lifecycle from goal definition to maintenance; the team's roles.

Data problems: high cost, bad quality (noise, bias, low predictive power, outdated examples, outliers, leakage), and the properties of good data (informative, coverage, reflects real inputs, unbiased, not the result of the model's own feedback, consistent, big enough).

Leakage catalog: target leakage through features that contain the target or its consequences, contamination of the test set by preprocessing, duplicates across splits, time-series shuffling, and group leakage; detection by suspiciously high scores and by feature importance.
Partitioning and imputation: sizes of train, validation and test; stratification; imputation methods and indicator columns; augmentation for images and text; sampling strategies for imbalance.

Features: predictive, computable fast, reliable, uncorrelated with each other, unitary and stable across time; techniques (one-hot, binning, normalization, standardization, embeddings, hashing); handling missing values; feature stores and documentation; schemas.

Training: establish baselines, choose algorithms by data size and interpretability needs, build pipelines, tune hyperparameters with cross-validation appropriate to the data, read learning curves for bias and variance, evaluate with the right metrics, calibrate probabilities, troubleshoot (loss not decreasing, overfitting, underfitting) and version models with their data and code.

Evaluation and deployment: offline metrics, then online evaluation with A/B tests (statistical power, interference) or bandits; deployment patterns (static, dynamic on the server, on device, in the browser); serving modes (batch, streaming, on demand); monitoring for performance decay, data changes and pipeline failures; maintenance and retraining policies.

b.s:
good feature: predictive, fast, reliable, uncorrelated, unitary, stable
learning curve: plot validation error against training size; a gap that closes with data means variance

items: A leakage checklist applied before training saves the most embarrassment per minute of any practice.
Features have engineering properties (fast, reliable, stable) beyond predictive power.
Deployment is a choice of pattern and serving mode driven by freshness and cost.

b.s: Audit the traffic feature table against the book's leakage catalog and feature-property list, and write a one-page report of what passes, what fails and what you changed.

resources.lives: book · free · weeks · free to read online

resources.title: Full Stack Deep Learning

b.s: A free class about everything around a learning machine: getting data, keeping it working, and putting it inside a real app.

A free course (lectures and labs online) that covers the parts of a deep learning project that courses usually skip: data management, training infrastructure, testing, deployment, monitoring, and building a working product. Watch the deployment and monitoring lectures in phase 7.

Its labs build an end-to-end application (a text recognizer) with experiment tracking, tests, a web deployment and monitoring; the lectures on troubleshooting training and on data management are directly useful even for a tabular model. The lecture on deployment patterns frames the replay-mode choice.

The course's structure is the production ML lifecycle; its lectures on ethics, on project management and on team organization cover the non-technical failure modes. Compare its tooling choices with the minimal single-machine setup and extract principles.
Together with Huyen's book and Made With ML it forms the practical MLOps curriculum; its treatment of testing and troubleshooting neural network training is the most concrete of the three.
Its evolution across years is a snapshot of how industry practice changed; for a lead, it is the course to point engineers to when they move from research code to a product.

Lectures: when to use ML and how to set up projects; development infrastructure and tooling (software engineering, compute, resource management, frameworks, experiment management, all-in-one platforms); troubleshooting and testing (testing ML code, troubleshooting training, resource management); data management (sources, labelling, versioning, feature stores); deployment (serving patterns, edge, monitoring); continual learning; foundation models; ML teams and project management; ethics. Labs: a text-recognizer application built end to end with experiment tracking, tests, a web deployment and monitoring.

items: Project setup: ML projects fail when the problem is wrong (unclear value, infeasible, no data); prioritize by impact and feasibility; define the baseline and the metric; plan the lifecycle (planning, data, training, deployment) as a loop.

Tooling: version control, code review, continuous integration; compute options (local GPUs, cloud, spot instances) and cost; resource managers; frameworks (PyTorch) and their ecosystem; experiment tracking; the recommended stack for a small team.

Troubleshooting training: start simple, implement and debug (shape errors, casting, out-of-memory, loss not decreasing), evaluate against baselines, improve (tuning, bigger models, more data), the bug taxonomy and a systematic process; testing ML code with unit tests, data tests, training tests and integration tests; CI for ML.
Data management: data sources and pipelines, labelling tools and strategies (crowdsourcing, in-house, active learning, weak supervision), data versioning levels, feature stores and their tradeoffs.

Deployment: batch versus online, model-in-service versus model-as-service, REST APIs, serverless, model servers, edge deployment (quantization, distillation, hardware), and the decision matrix; monitoring (operational metrics, data drift, performance with delayed labels), alerting and dashboards.
Continual learning: the retraining loop, triggers, evaluation before promotion, and the organizational maturity ladder.
Foundation models and teams: using pretrained models, prompt engineering and fine-tuning as a development pattern; roles on ML teams, hiring, and managing projects that are inherently uncertain.

b.s: deployment matrix: batch | online × server | edge, chosen by latency, freshness, cost and privacy

items: Troubleshooting training is a process: simplify, verify shapes and losses, compare with baselines, then add.
Data labelling and versioning are engineering tasks with tools; plan them.
Deployment and monitoring decisions follow from latency, freshness, cost and privacy.

b.s: Set up continuous integration for the repository that runs the fast tests and a smoke training run on a fixture on every push, and document the deployment decision for the alert service using the lecture's matrix.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; the production lifecycle with labs

resources.title: Rules of Machine Learning (Zinkevich, Google)

b.s: A list of rules from an engineer who has built many learning machines, about what to do first and what mistakes to avoid.

A free document of 43 short rules from Google, such as 'do not be afraid to launch a product without machine learning', 'design and implement metrics first', and 'keep the first model simple'. Read it in an hour during phase 7; you will recognize this project in most of the rules.

Its phases (before ML, the first pipeline, feature engineering, slowed growth) match the course's phases. Rules about training-serving skew, about logging features at serving time, and about launching a simple model first are exactly the decisions in stages 12 and 13. Note which rules you have already broken.

The document encodes hard-won operational judgment: measure before modelling, prefer simple and debuggable, watch for silent failures, and treat feature logging as the foundation of everything later. Use it as a review checklist for the serving design.

Some rules are specific to large consumer products (ranking, human-in-the-loop labels) and do not transfer to a one-machine forecaster; identifying which is a useful exercise in generalizing engineering advice.
A primary source on how a large organization thinks about ML systems, written before MLOps was a word; read with Sculley's technical-debt paper as a pair.

Forty-three rules in four phases: before machine learning (launch without ML, design metrics first, choose ML over heuristics when it is complex); ML phase 1, the first pipeline (keep the first model simple, get the infrastructure right, test the infrastructure, separate the model from the serving logic, detect problems before exporting, watch for silent failures, give features owners); feature engineering (launch and iterate, start with observed features, explore with directly observed features, use meta-features, combine features, use human-understandable features, prefer features that generalize, clean up unused features); human analysis (measure the delta between models, choose utility measures that reflect user behavior, look for patterns in errors, quantify undesirable behavior, watch training-serving skew); ML phase 3, slowed growth (do not overthink the objective, keep ensembles simple, launch when plateaued, consider diversity and negative feedback).

items: Before ML: if a heuristic gives most of the value, ship it and collect data; design and implement metrics first so you can measure everything later; ML makes sense when the problem is complex and data exist.

First pipeline: choose a simple objective, build the end-to-end pipeline (data in, model out, predictions served) with simple features, and get it working; most gains come from pipeline and features, not the model; test the infrastructure independently of the model; separate the model from the serving policy.

Skew and silent failures: log the features at serving time and train on the logged features; monitor for feature drift and missing features; a table left stale for weeks is a silent failure; every feature has an owner and documentation.

Features: start with observed or reported features rather than learned ones; combine and modify features in human-understandable ways (discretization, crosses); the number of feature weights you can learn scales with the data you have; prefer features that generalize across contexts; remove features that are not used.

Analysis: measure the difference between models on held-out data and on real traffic; the utility of a model is what users do, so choose metrics that reflect behavior; look for patterns in errors and turn them into features; quantify undesirable behavior separately from the objective.
Skew, again: differences between training and serving pipelines, between training and serving data, and between the feedback loop and the model; the fix is one code path and logging.
