Late phase: complex ensembles rarely pay; when gains plateau, launch; diversity and negative feedback matter for long-term utility.

b.s: Rule: log features at serving time; train on logged features

items: Metrics and infrastructure before models; the first model is a pipeline test.
Training-serving skew is fought with one feature path and serving-time logs.
Human-understandable features that generalize beat clever learned ones early on.

b.s: Score the traffic pipeline against the 43 rules; for the five most violated, write the concrete change (for instance, logging serving-time features) and implement one.

resources.lives: docs · free · an hour · free; 43 rules from hard experience

resources.title: The ML Test Score (Breck, Cai, Nielsen, Salib, Sculley, 2017)

b.s: A checklist from engineers who ask: did you test your data, did you test your model, did you test the machine that runs it? You get points for each thing you checked.

A short free paper that gives a scoring rubric for how production-ready an ML system is: tests for data (is the schema right, are features useful), tests for model development (is the baseline beaten, are hyperparameters tuned), tests for infrastructure (can you roll back), and monitoring (is the model stale). Score this project against it in phase 7.

Each of the 28 items is a concrete test you could write for this pipeline: feature schema tests, a golden-day pipeline test, a check that serving features equal training features, a canary before model swap, alerts on data freshness. Turn the rubric into a `tests/` folder plan.

The rubric operationalizes the technical-debt paper; its scoring (points for manual checks, more for automated ones) encodes the principle that unautomated checks decay. Use it to prioritize what stage 13 automates first.
It predates data-validation tooling and drift libraries but defines what they should do; reading it explains why those tools exist and what they still miss (feedback loops, label delay).
A rare attempt to quantify production readiness; its limits (a checklist cannot weight items by risk) point toward risk-based test design, which is an open engineering problem in ML systems.

A rubric of 28 tests in four categories, features and data (7), model development (7), ML infrastructure (7) and monitoring (7), each scored by whether it is done manually or automated, with an overall score interpretation from 'more of a research project' to 'exceptional levels of automated testing and monitoring'.

items: Features and data: feature expectations are captured in a schema; all features are beneficial (measured by removal); no feature's cost outweighs its benefit; features adhere to meta-level requirements (privacy, policy); the data pipeline has appropriate privacy controls; new features can be added quickly; all input feature code is tested.

Model development: model specs are reviewed and versioned; offline and online metrics correlate; all hyperparameters have been tuned; the impact of model staleness is known; a simpler model is not better; model quality is sufficient on important data slices; the model is tested for considerations of inclusion.

Infrastructure: training is reproducible (determinism, seeds); model specs are unit tested (a training run on synthetic data reaches a target); the full pipeline is integration tested; model quality is validated before serving; the model is debuggable on single examples; models are tested via a canary before serving; models can be rolled back quickly.

Monitoring: dependency changes result in notification; data invariants hold in training and serving inputs; training and serving features compute the same values; models are not too stale; the model is numerically stable; the system has no dramatic regressions in training speed, latency, throughput or memory; the model has not regressed in prediction quality on served data.

Scoring: for each test, 0 if not done, 0.5 if done manually, 1 if automated and repeated; the category score is the sum; the overall score is the minimum over categories, which rewards balance; the paper's survey shows most teams score low on monitoring.

b.s: score = min over categories of Σ_tests {0, 0.5 manual, 1 automated}

items: Testing ML means testing data, model, infrastructure and monitoring, and the weakest category is the score.
Automated beats manual because manual checks decay.
Canary, rollback and training-serving feature equality are the infrastructure tests that matter most here.

b.s: Score the pipeline on all 28 tests honestly, then automate the three cheapest missing ones (schema check, golden-day feature equality, canary evaluation) and rescore.

resources.lives: paper · free · an hour · free; the production-readiness rubric

resources.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (Sculley et al., 2015)

b.s: A short paper by people who build big systems, saying: the learning part is small, and the messy parts around it are big and bite you later if you are not careful.

Ten pages, free. It lists the ways ML systems rot over time: tangled dependencies on data, glue code nobody owns, pipelines nobody understands, feedback loops where the model changes the data it learns from, and configuration mess. Read it once now and once after building phase 7, when every paragraph will sound familiar.

Its famous figure, a tiny box labelled ML code surrounded by large boxes of infrastructure, is a picture of this pipeline. Its warnings about correction cascades, undeclared consumers and data dependencies map to concrete rules here: one feature module, a manifest with hashes, versioned labels, and no script that silently reads another's output.

Treat each named debt as a checklist for the project: entanglement (changing one feature changes everything downstream), hidden feedback loops (alerts change traffic), pipeline jungles (stages 5 to 8 as separate scripts), dead experimental code paths, and configuration debt. Write one sentence per item about where it could appear here and what prevents it.

Later work, on ML test scores and on data-validation systems for production pipelines, operationalizes the paper's warnings; read it together with those follow-ups and with Huyen's chapter 8. The paper's concept of the CACE principle, changing anything changes everything, is the reason retraining needs a canary.

A foundational engineering paper whose legacy is the field of ML systems and MLOps. At your level the exercise is to separate which debts are inherent to ML (data dependencies, feedback) from which are ordinary software engineering, and to identify where research, rather than discipline, could reduce the inherent ones.

A paper arguing that ML systems carry all the maintenance problems of software plus ML-specific ones: complex models erode boundaries (entanglement, correction cascades, undeclared consumers); data dependencies cost more than code dependencies (unstable inputs, underutilized inputs, static analysis of data dependencies); feedback loops (direct and hidden); ML-system anti-patterns (glue code, pipeline jungles, dead experimental code paths, abstraction debt, common smells); configuration debt; dealing with changes in the external world (fixed thresholds, monitoring and testing); and other areas (data testing, reproducibility, process management, cultural debt).

items: Entanglement: changing anything changes everything (CACE); adding, removing or reweighting a feature changes the importance of all others, so features cannot be improved in isolation; mitigations include isolating models and monitoring prediction changes.

Correction cascades: a model built on top of another to correct it creates a dependency that makes both hard to improve; undeclared consumers use a model's outputs silently and break when it changes; access controls and service-level agreements help.

Data dependencies: unstable input signals (another system's output that changes qualitatively), underutilized dependencies (legacy, bundled, epsilon and correlated features that add little but cost), and the need for tooling to analyze data dependencies as static analysis does for code.
Feedback loops: direct (a model influences its own future training data) and hidden (two systems influence each other through the world); traffic alerts changing traffic is a direct loop.

Anti-patterns: glue code around packages, pipeline jungles from incremental data preparation, dead experimental branches, abstraction debt from lacking standard interfaces, and smells (plain-old-data types, multiple languages, prototypes in production).

Configuration debt: configurations are code; they need review, testing and versioning; the paper's list of configuration requirements (easy to specify a change, hard to make a mistake, easy to see the diff, assertable, detectable unused settings).

Changing world: fixed thresholds in dynamic systems, monitoring prediction bias, action limits, upstream producers; testing data and reproducibility; process management and cultural debt (rewarding deletion of features and complexity).

b.s: CACE: changing anything changes everything

items: ML debt is mostly data and dependency debt; treat features and inputs as owned, versioned dependencies.
Feedback loops are inherent when a model acts on the world; monitor for them.
Configuration and pipelines are code and deserve the same review and tests.

b.s: Draw the dependency graph of the pipeline (inputs, stages, outputs, consumers), mark unstable inputs and feedback loops, and list the configuration values that would silently change results if edited.

resources.lives: paper · free · an hour, twice · free; ten pages, read twice

resources.title: launchd.info and the pytest documentation

b.s: Instructions for two tools: one that makes the Mac run a program on a schedule by itself, and one that runs all your checks with a single command.

launchd.info explains macOS's scheduler: you write a small file called a plist saying what to run and how often, and macOS runs it even after a restart. The pytest documentation explains how to write and run tests. Read the getting-started page of each and try the smallest example.

launchd: `StartInterval` and `StartCalendarInterval`, `WorkingDirectory`, log paths, `launchctl load` and `unload`, and why it beats cron on a Mac (it handles sleep and wake, runs per user, and restarts jobs). pytest: fixtures, `parametrize`, `-k` to select tests, `-x` to stop early, `tmp_path` and `monkeypatch`, and `conftest.py` for shared fixtures.

Understand launchd agents versus daemons and the permission model (Full Disk Access for reading files, the keychain for secrets), because a job that works in the terminal and fails under launchd is almost always a permissions or environment problem. In pytest, fixture scoping and the plugin ecosystem (`pytest-cov`, `hypothesis`) are the next layer.

Scheduling is orchestration at small scale; know its failure modes (overlapping runs, missed intervals after sleep, environment differences) and their mitigations (lock files, idempotent jobs, explicit environment in the plist). For testing, property-based tests with hypothesis are the right tool for parsers and feature code, where the input space is large.

Tooling choices are context-dependent. The durable skill is specifying a job's contract, idempotence, timeout, alerting, and retry policy, independently of the scheduler, so that migrating from launchd to a cluster scheduler later is mechanical rather than a redesign.

launchd.info: what launchd is, agents versus daemons, property list files and their keys (Label, Program and ProgramArguments, StartInterval, StartCalendarInterval, RunAtLoad, KeepAlive, WorkingDirectory, EnvironmentVariables, StandardOutPath, StandardErrorPath, ThrottleInterval), the file locations, loading and unloading with launchctl, debugging, and a configuration reference. pytest: getting started, how-to guides (assertions, fixtures, marks, parametrize, temporary directories, monkeypatching, capturing output, skipping, doctests, plugins), configuration files, and the API reference.

items: launchd model: the system service manager starts jobs on demand, on a schedule or at load; user agents live in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` and run when the user is logged in; daemons in `/Library/LaunchDaemons` run as root at boot; a plist is an XML dictionary describing one job.

Scheduling keys: `StartInterval` runs every N seconds (missed runs while asleep are coalesced into one on wake, unlike cron which skips); `StartCalendarInterval` runs at specified minute, hour, day, weekday, month; `RunAtLoad` runs immediately when loaded; `KeepAlive` restarts on exit.

Environment: jobs run with a minimal environment; set `EnvironmentVariables` (PATH, secrets are better read from a file), `WorkingDirectory`, and full paths to the interpreter; log with `StandardOutPath` and `StandardErrorPath`.

Operations: `launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.traffic1.predict.plist` (or `bootstrap` on newer systems), `launchctl list | grep traffic1`, `launchctl unload`; `ThrottleInterval` prevents rapid restarts; permissions (Full Disk Access) apply to the executable.
pytest basics: test discovery (`test_*.py`, `test_*` functions), plain `assert` with introspection, running with `-q`, `-x`, `-k expr`, `-m marker`, `--lf` for last failed; exit codes for CI.

Fixtures: functions decorated with `@pytest.fixture` provide setup (and teardown with `yield`); scopes (function, module, session); `conftest.py` shares fixtures; built-in fixtures `tmp_path`, `monkeypatch` (set environment variables, patch attributes), `capsys`, `caplog`.

Parametrize and marks: `@pytest.mark.parametrize('case', [...])` runs one test over many inputs; custom markers (`slow`, `integration`) registered in configuration; `skip` and `xfail`; `pytest.raises` for exceptions; `pytest.approx` for floats.
Configuration and plugins: `pyproject.toml` `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` for paths and markers; `pytest-cov` for coverage; `pytest-xdist` for parallel runs; `hypothesis` as a plugin.

b.s:
<key>StartInterval</key><integer>300</integer>
@pytest.fixture
def day():
    return pd.read_parquet('tests/fixtures/one_day.parquet')

@pytest.mark.parametrize('col', ['speed', 'occ', 'flow'])
def test_bounds(day, col):
    assert day[col].dropna().between(0, 3000).all()

items: launchd coalesces missed runs after sleep and has no cron-like environment; set paths and logs explicitly.
Fixtures and parametrize are most of pytest; `conftest.py` is where shared setup lives.
Register markers and use `-m` so slow integration tests do not block quick feedback.

b.s: Write the four launchd plists and load them, confirm they run with `launchctl list` and the log files, and write a `conftest.py` with a one-day fixture used by three parametrized tests.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free

resources.title: FastAPI documentation

b.s: The manual for a tool that gives your program a door on the internet, so other programs can knock and ask questions.

FastAPI is a free Python framework for building web APIs. Its tutorial shows how to turn a function into an endpoint, define what requests and responses look like, and run a server, with automatically generated interactive documentation. The first ten tutorial pages are enough to wrap the predictor.

Read the tutorial through request bodies, path and query parameters, response models and error handling. Wrap the predictor: a request with station and horizon, a response with probability and alert. Try the automatic docs page and call the endpoint from the command line.

FastAPI is built on type hints and a validation library; understand how validation, serialization and documentation come from the same models, and how dependency injection structures shared resources such as a loaded model. Read the pages on background tasks and on testing with the test client.
Its async model and deployment guidance (workers, reverse proxies) are the practical side of serving; for batch-predict pipelines a web API is optional, for a dashboard it is the interface.
Framework choice matters less than the service contract; FastAPI's docs are also a good example of documentation that teaches the underlying concepts rather than only the library.

Tutorial: first steps, path parameters, query parameters, request body (Pydantic models), validations, multiple parameters, body fields, nested models, example data, extra data types, cookies and headers, response models, status codes, form data, file uploads, error handling, path operation configuration, JSON encoding, body updates, dependencies, security, middleware, CORS, SQL databases, bigger applications, background tasks, metadata and docs, static files, testing, debugging. Advanced guide and deployment (servers, workers, Docker, HTTPS).

items: First steps: `app = FastAPI()`; a function decorated with `@app.get('/path')` returns JSON; run with a server (`uvicorn` or `fastapi run`); the automatic interactive docs at `/docs` from the OpenAPI schema.

Parameters: path parameters typed in the signature (`station_id: int`) are validated and converted; query parameters are untyped path arguments with defaults; `Annotated` with `Query`, `Path` for constraints (`ge`, `le`, `max_length`).

Request and response bodies: Pydantic models declare fields and types; the body is parsed, validated and documented; `response_model` filters and validates output; nested models, lists, enums; status codes and `HTTPException` for errors with detail.

Dependencies: functions injected with `Depends`, used for shared resources (the loaded model), parameters, authentication; dependencies with `yield` for setup and teardown; app lifespan events to load the model once at startup.
Operations: middleware for logging and timing, CORS, background tasks for work after the response, static files, and settings via environment variables with a Pydantic settings class.
Testing: `TestClient` from Starlette calls the app in-process for tests; the golden test replays a stored day through the endpoint.

Deployment: run with multiple worker processes behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS; containerize with a slim image; health-check endpoints; the docs' deployment concepts (security, running on startup, restarts, replication, memory).
Type hints are the API contract; validation and docs come free.
Load the model once with lifespan or a cached dependency; never per request.
Test through `TestClient` with a golden day.

b.s: Wrap the predictor with a `/predict` endpoint and a `/health` endpoint, load models at startup, write a `TestClient` test that replays one stored day, and measure p50 and p99 latency for 100 requests.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; a door on the predictor in an afternoon

resources.title: Docker, Get started guide

b.s: Instructions for packing your program and everything it needs into one box that runs the same on any computer.

Docker packages code, its interpreter and libraries into an image that runs anywhere Docker runs. The Get Started guide walks through building an image from a Dockerfile, running it, keeping data outside the container, and sharing images. An afternoon is enough for this project's service.

Do the first parts of the guide (build, run, volumes), then write a Dockerfile for the prediction service: a slim Python base image, requirements installed, the code copied, the model files mounted from outside. Keep data and secrets out of the image.

Understand layers and caching (order your Dockerfile so dependencies are cached), image size, multi-stage builds, and the difference between an image and a container. Know what a container does not isolate (the kernel) and what that means for security.

Containers are the unit of deployment on orchestration platforms; the guide's later sections on Compose and on multi-container apps are the step toward a small stack (service, scheduler, monitoring). For Apple silicon, note multi-architecture images.

Containerization is the boundary that makes reproducibility and deployment mechanical; the research-relevant question is whether your experiment can be rerun from an image and a data hash a year later.

Overview (what a container is, images, registries), the getting-started workshop (containerize an application, update the application, share the application, persist data with volumes, use bind mounts, multi-container applications with Compose, image-building best practices), Dockerfile reference (FROM, RUN, COPY, WORKDIR, ENV, CMD, ENTRYPOINT), and guides on multi-stage builds and multi-platform images.

items: Concepts: an image is a read-only layered filesystem plus metadata; a container is a running instance with its own process namespace; a registry stores images; containers share the host kernel and are lighter than virtual machines.

Dockerfile: `FROM python:3.12-slim`, `WORKDIR /app`, `COPY requirements.txt .`, `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt`, `COPY . .`, `CMD ['python', '19_predict_live.py']`; order for cache efficiency (dependencies before code); `.dockerignore` to exclude data, `.env`, `.git`.

Building and running: `docker build -t traffic1:latest .`, `docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 traffic1`, `-e` for environment variables, `-v` for volumes; logs with `docker logs`; `exec` for a shell inside.
Data: containers are ephemeral; volumes persist data managed by Docker; bind mounts map a host directory (`-v $PWD/data:/app/data`) so models and data stay outside the image.
Compose: a YAML file describing several services (the API, a scheduler, a monitoring dashboard) with networks, volumes and environment; `docker compose up`.

Best practices: small base images, multi-stage builds to drop build tools, pin versions, run as a non-root user, one process per container, health checks, and multi-platform images for Apple silicon and x86 (`--platform`).
Security: never bake secrets into images; pass them at runtime; scan images; keep base images updated.

b.s:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ['uvicorn', 'serve:app', '--host', '0.0.0.0', '--port', '8000']
docker build -t traffic1 . && docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 -v $PWD/models:/app/models traffic1

items: Dependencies before code in the Dockerfile so rebuilds are fast.

Secrets are runtime inputs, never image layers.

resources.title: PyTorch distributed overview

b.s: The manual page about using many computers or chips at once to train one learning machine faster.

PyTorch's overview of distributed training explains the main options: data parallelism (every device gets different batches and they average their updates), and ways to split a model across devices when it is too big for one. It points to tutorials for each. Read it to understand what you would need if the model outgrew the Mac mini.

Read the overview and the DistributedDataParallel tutorial to see the pattern: one process per device, a shared training script, gradients averaged with an all-reduce. You cannot run it meaningfully on one Mac, but reading it prepares you for any cloud GPU.

Understand process groups, collective operations, the cost model of gradient synchronization, and the fully sharded variant that partitions optimizer state and parameters. The tutorials on checkpointing and on elastic training cover the operational side.

Distributed training is where systems knowledge (communication, memory hierarchy) meets ML; the overview links the pieces you will meet in the ultra-scale playbook and in any large-model paper's training section.

The distributed stack is a research area in itself (compilers, sharding strategies, fault tolerance); for a lead, the practical question is which parallelism a model needs and what it costs in engineering time.

The overview page maps PyTorch's distributed features: the `torch.distributed` communication package (process groups, collectives, backends NCCL and Gloo), data-parallel training (`DistributedDataParallel`), model-parallel and sharded training (`FullyShardedDataParallel`, tensor parallel, pipeline parallel), the launcher (`torchrun`), elastic training, and pointers to tutorials for each.

items: Process groups and collectives: each device runs one process; `init_process_group(backend)`; collectives `all_reduce`, `broadcast`, `all_gather`, `reduce_scatter`; NCCL for GPUs, Gloo for CPUs; rank and world size.

DistributedDataParallel: replicate the model on every process, give each a different shard of data (`DistributedSampler`), run forward and backward locally, and all-reduce gradients so every replica updates identically; gradient bucketing overlaps communication with backward computation; use it instead of the older `DataParallel`.

Fully sharded data parallel: shard parameters, gradients and optimizer state across processes and gather parameters just in time per layer, cutting memory per device at the cost of communication; mixed precision and CPU offload options; checkpointing sharded state.

Tensor and pipeline parallelism: split individual layers' matrices across devices (tensor parallel) or assign layers to devices in sequence with micro-batches (pipeline parallel); combined with data parallelism for large models.
Launching and resilience: `torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py` sets ranks and environment; elastic training restarts on failure with a changed world size; checkpoint regularly and resume.
Debugging and profiling: `TORCH_DISTRIBUTED_DEBUG`, timeouts, deadlocks from mismatched collectives, and the profiler's view of communication versus compute.

b.s:
dist.init_process_group('nccl'); model = DDP(model.to(rank), device_ids=[rank]); sampler = DistributedSampler(ds)
torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py

items: DDP is gradient all-reduce across replicas; FSDP shards state to fit bigger models.
One process per device, and every process must run the same collectives in the same order.
Checkpoint and resume; large runs fail.

b.s: Read the DDP tutorial and write the modifications the spatio-temporal net's training script would need to run on eight GPUs (sampler, wrapper, launcher), even though you cannot run them on the Mac; then explain where FSDP would become necessary.

resources.title: The Ultra-Scale Playbook: Training LLMs on GPU Clusters (Hugging Face)

b.s: A free online book about training gigantic language models on hundreds of chips at once, with pictures of how the work is split up.

Hugging Face's playbook explains how large language models are trained across many GPUs: splitting data, splitting the model, splitting the layers, and keeping all the chips busy. It reports thousands of experiments. It is advanced; read the introduction to see how much engineering scale involves.

Read the sections on data parallelism and on memory (activations, optimizer state) to understand why a model's memory is several times its parameter count, and how mixed precision and gradient accumulation help. The interactive figures make the trade-offs concrete.

The playbook is the current practical reference on parallelism strategies (data, tensor, pipeline, context), on overlapping communication with computation, and on choosing a configuration for a given cluster. Its benchmarks are reproducible and its code is open.
Compare with the academic papers on sharding and pipeline parallelism; the playbook's contribution is measurement across configurations. For anyone planning a large training run, it is the checklist.
Open, measured engineering knowledge of this kind is rare; the playbook is both a reference and a model of how to publish systems results.

Sections: a high-level overview of training on one GPU (memory usage of parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations; activation recomputation; gradient accumulation; profiling); data parallelism (all-reduce, overlapping communication, bucketing, gradient accumulation with DP, ZeRO stages 1 to 3); tensor parallelism (sharding matrix multiplications, sequence parallelism); context parallelism (ring attention); pipeline parallelism (schedules: all-forward-all-backward, one-forward-one-backward, interleaved, zero-bubble); expert parallelism; combining strategies and finding the best configuration; GPU internals (kernels, fused kernels, FlashAttention, mixed precision); and benchmarks from thousands of runs.

items: Memory on one GPU: in mixed precision, parameters (2 bytes) plus gradients (2) plus Adam states in fp32 (8) plus master weights (4) give about 16 bytes per parameter, before activations, which scale with batch, sequence length, hidden size and layers; activation recomputation trades compute for memory; gradient accumulation simulates a larger batch.

Data parallelism: replicas average gradients with all-reduce; overlap communication with the backward pass by bucketing; ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, ZeRO-2 also gradients, ZeRO-3 also parameters (this is FSDP), with all-gather and reduce-scatter replacing all-reduce.

Tensor parallelism: split a linear layer's weight by columns or rows across GPUs so each computes part of the matrix multiply, with an all-reduce (or all-gather) to combine; attention heads split naturally; sequence parallelism shards the non-matmul parts (layer norm, dropout) along the sequence.
Context parallelism: for very long sequences, shard the sequence across GPUs and pass keys and values around a ring (ring attention) so attention over the full sequence is computed piecewise.

Pipeline parallelism: assign consecutive layers to GPUs; micro-batches fill the pipeline; the bubble (idle time) depends on the schedule; one-forward-one-backward and interleaved schedules cut it; zero-bubble schedules split backward into two parts.

Expert parallelism and combinations: mixture-of-experts layers place experts on different GPUs; a 5-D parallelism space (data, tensor, sequence/context, pipeline, expert); rules of thumb for choosing (fit the model, then fit the batch, then optimize throughput), and the playbook's benchmark tables.

GPU internals: streaming multiprocessors, memory hierarchy, arithmetic intensity, kernel fusion, FlashAttention's tiled computation avoiding the n² matrix, mixed precision (bf16 compute, fp32 master), and profiling with traces.

b.s:
memory per parameter (mixed precision, Adam) ≈ 2 + 2 + 8 + 4 = 16 bytes
training FLOPs ≈ 6 · N · D;  throughput = FLOPs / (time × peak FLOP/s) = MFU

items: Fit first (sharding, recomputation), then fill (batch), then optimize (overlap, kernels).
Every parallelism trades memory for communication; overlap hides it.
Model FLOP utilization is the number to report for a training system.

b.s: Compute the memory footprint of a 1-billion-parameter model under mixed precision with Adam, with and without ZeRO-3 across 8 GPUs, and estimate its training time for 20 billion tokens at 40 % utilization on a stated GPU.

resources.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (Kaplan et al., 2020)

b.s: A paper that found that bigger models trained on more text get better in a very predictable way, like a line on a graph.

Researchers trained language models of many sizes and found that the loss falls smoothly and predictably as model size, data and compute grow, following power laws. That predictability is why companies can plan enormous training runs. Read the introduction and the main figures.

Look at the figures relating loss to parameters, tokens and compute; note that architecture details mattered less than scale. Later work (compute-optimal training) revised how to split a budget between model size and data. The lesson for any project: measure how your metric changes with data size before assuming a bigger model will help.

The paper's methodology (fit power laws across orders of magnitude, hold other factors fixed) is a template for empirical scaling studies; its revision by compute-optimal analyses shows the importance of tuning learning rates per scale. Apply the method to the traffic model: skill against months of data.

Scaling laws organize much of current research on large models; their limits (task-specific behavior, data quality, emergence claims) are active debates. For forecasting, the analogous question is whether more stations and years keep improving skill.
Understanding scaling is now part of research strategy; the open questions include what scales with what, and where data quality dominates quantity.

Empirical power laws for language-model loss as a function of model size (non-embedding parameters), dataset size and compute, over several orders of magnitude; the weak dependence on architectural details (depth versus width); the sample-efficiency of large models; the overfitting law relating model and data size; training curves and their predictability; the compute-optimal allocation (train very large models and stop before convergence); and transfer to other distributions.

items: Setup: decoder-only transformers trained on WebText2 with next-token cross-entropy in nats; sweep parameters N from 768 to 1.5 billion (excluding embeddings), tokens D from 22 million to 23 billion, and compute C.

Power laws: with enough data and compute, L(N) ≈ (N_c/N)^{α_N} with α_N ≈ 0.076; with a fixed model and limited data, L(D) ≈ (D_c/D)^{α_D} with α_D ≈ 0.095; with limited compute at optimal allocation, L(C) ≈ (C_c/C)^{α_C} with α_C ≈ 0.050; straight lines on log-log plots across six orders of magnitude.
Architecture matters little: at fixed N, varying depth, width, heads and feed-forward ratio changes loss only mildly within a broad range; the total parameter count dominates.
Overfitting: a joint law L(N, D) shows that data must grow sublinearly with model size (D ∝ N^{0.74}) to avoid an overfitting penalty; the paper's fitted expression combines both terms.
Sample efficiency and training curves: larger models reach a given loss with fewer tokens and steps; the loss curve L(N, S) is predictable early; critical batch size grows as loss falls.

Compute-optimal training: for a compute budget, the best strategy is a very large model trained on relatively little data and stopped well before convergence; most compute should go to model size, with data growing slowly (a conclusion later revised by compute-optimal analyses that found data should grow proportionally).
Generalization: loss on other text distributions tracks training loss with a constant offset, so improvements transfer.
Loss follows power laws in size, data and compute; extrapolation is a legitimate planning tool.
Architecture details matter far less than scale in this regime.
The compute-optimal allocation depends on methodology; later work corrected the data share.

b.s: Fit a power law of validation log loss against training months for LightGBM and for the spatio-temporal net on the traffic data, and use it to predict the gain from a second year of data.

resources.lives: paper · free · an evening or two · free; measure before assuming bigger helps

resources.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Hoffmann et al., 2022)

b.s: A paper that found that many big models had been trained on too little text, and that a smaller model trained on more text can be better.

Researchers trained many models with different sizes and amounts of data and found the best balance for a fixed compute budget: model size and data should grow together. Their model, Chinchilla, beat bigger models trained on less data. Free; read it after the scaling-laws paper.

Read the method (three approaches to fitting the trade-off) and the main result (tokens should scale roughly with parameters); compare with Kaplan's earlier conclusions and note how a methodological change (tuning learning-rate schedules per run) changed the answer.

The paper is a lesson in experimental methodology: the earlier scaling result depended on a confound, and fixing it moved the optimum substantially. Apply the same skepticism to any scaling claim, including your own data-size curves.
Later work refines the trade-off for inference cost and data quality; the paper's fitted laws remain the reference point for planning training runs.
Together with its predecessor it defines how the field reasons about compute allocation; for research strategy, it is the argument for data over parameters.

A study of how to split a fixed compute budget between model size and training tokens, using three approaches (fix model size and vary tokens; IsoFLOP profiles; fit a parametric loss function), finding that models had been under-trained and that parameters and tokens should scale roughly equally; training Chinchilla (70 billion parameters, 1.4 trillion tokens) with the same compute as Gopher (280 billion) and showing it is better; and downstream evaluations.

items: Three approaches: (1) for each model size, train with several token counts and find where loss is minimized for each compute level; (2) for fixed compute (IsoFLOP curves), vary model size and find the minimum; (3) fit L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β and minimize under the constraint C ≈ 6ND; all three agree that N and D should scale about equally with compute.

Correction to earlier laws: the previous scaling analysis used a fixed learning-rate schedule length regardless of training length; setting the cosine schedule to match each run's actual length changed the fitted exponents and the conclusion.

Chinchilla: 70 billion parameters trained on 1.4 trillion tokens outperforms Gopher (280 billion, 300 billion tokens) and other larger models on language modelling and downstream tasks, with a smaller inference cost.
The rule of thumb: about 20 tokens per parameter at compute-optimality; later work notes that when inference cost matters, training smaller models on more tokens than compute-optimal is better still.
Data implications: compute-optimal training of large models needs trillions of high-quality tokens, which makes data collection and filtering the binding constraint.

b.s:
L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β;  minimize subject to C = 6ND
compute-optimal: N_opt ∝ C^{0.5}, D_opt ∝ C^{0.5};  roughly 20 tokens per parameter

items: Under a fixed budget, grow data and parameters together.
A methodological detail (schedule length) reversed a headline conclusion; check methodology before believing a law.
Inference cost argues for smaller models trained longer than compute-optimal.

b.s: Using the fitted form L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β with the paper's constants, compute the optimal N and D for three compute budgets and plot the IsoFLOP curves.

phases.lives: Everything this asks for has been explained above: the lessons and topics for the ideas, the walkthroughs for the code, the books and courses for depth. The glossary at the end defines any word that is still new.

phases.title: Beyond supervised learning
phases.meta: weeks 60–70 · ≈70 h · builds an alert-policy analysis, a fairness audit, a dashboard ranker

b.s: What changes when a model's output is a decision: reinforcement learning, causal inference, fairness, privacy and ranking.

items: Markov decision processes, value functions, Q-learning and policy gradients; bandits; off-policy evaluation from logged data; where RL fits in traffic control.
Potential outcomes, confounding, causal diagrams, randomization; adjustment, instruments, difference-in-differences; interference; performative prediction.
Fairness definitions and their conflicts; measuring disparity by slice; differential privacy; documentation (model cards, datasheets); governance.
Recommenders and ranking: collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, learning to rank, ranking metrics, exposure bias and feedback loops.

items.title: Reinforcement learning: agents, rewards, bandits and policies

b.s: Understand learning by acting: the setup, the core algorithms, and where it fits (and does not fit) in a traffic system.

Some learning happens by trying things and seeing what happens: touch the hot stove once and you learn. A computer can learn a game the same way, getting points for good moves and losing points for bad ones.
Teach a friend a simple game only by saying 'good' or 'bad' after each move, never explaining the rules. Do they figure it out?

In reinforcement learning an agent sees a state, picks an action, gets a reward, and the world moves to a new state. It learns a policy, a rule for choosing actions, that collects the most reward over time. The hard part is that rewards may come late, and that trying new actions (exploration) costs something.
A bandit is the simplest case: one decision, repeated, like which of three alert messages drivers respond to most. Traffic lights and ramp meters can be controlled by reinforcement learning.
Play with a bandit on paper: three slot machines with hidden payout rates; keep choosing, track averages, and decide when to stop exploring.

Markov decision processes: states, actions, transitions, rewards, discounting. Value functions and the Bellman equation; Q-learning and policy gradients as the two families; exploration versus exploitation; deep RL (a network for the value or policy). Bandits: epsilon-greedy, upper confidence bound, Thompson sampling. Simulators are usually required because trying actions in the real world is expensive or unsafe.
For traffic: ramp metering and signal timing are natural RL problems; alerting is closer to a bandit with delayed feedback.
Implement Q-learning on a small grid world in numpy, then Thompson sampling for a three-arm bandit; plot regret over time.

Dynamic programming (value and policy iteration), temporal-difference learning, function approximation and its instability (the deadly triad), policy gradient theorem and actor-critic methods, off-policy evaluation from logged data (importance sampling), and the sample-inefficiency problem. Contextual bandits as the practical middle ground for decisions with immediate feedback.
Offline RL and off-policy evaluation are what a system with logged alerts and outcomes could actually use; online RL on live traffic is rarely acceptable.
Formulate the alerting policy as a contextual bandit with delayed reward, propose an off-policy estimator for a new policy from logged data, and state its assumptions.

Model-based RL with learned or physical simulators (traffic microsimulation as an environment), multi-agent RL for networks of intersections, safe RL with constraints, and the evaluation problem (simulator-to-real gap). Connections to control theory and to causal inference (policies as interventions).
Design a ramp-metering controller for one Fremont on-ramp trained in a traffic simulator, and the validation that would justify a field trial.

RL in products is mostly bandits and offline evaluation; full RL succeeds where a faithful simulator exists (games, some control). The research frontier includes sample efficiency, offline RL with guarantees, RL from human feedback for language models, and safe deployment. For transport, learned control of signals and meters is an active applied area with real deployments.

Write the evaluation protocol for an RL-controlled corridor: metrics, baselines (fixed-time, actuated), safety constraints, and how you would attribute changes to the controller rather than to demand shifts.

b.q: What distinguishes RL from supervised learning?

a.s: There are no correct labels, only rewards, and the agent's actions change the data it sees.

b.q: Why are bandits the practical case?

a.s: Immediate feedback and no state transitions make evaluation and safety tractable; most product decisions look like that.

items.title: Causal inference: from correlation to intervention

b.s: Ask what would happen if you acted, and know what data can and cannot tell you about it.
Ice cream sales and sunburns go up together, but ice cream does not cause sunburn; the sun causes both. Finding the real cause is harder than noticing things go together.
Think of two things that happen together in your life but where one does not cause the other. What causes both?

Correlation is when two things move together; causation is when changing one changes the other. Confounders are hidden causes of both. The cleanest way to find a cause is an experiment: randomly do the thing to some and not others, then compare. When you cannot experiment, you need assumptions and careful methods.
For traffic: incidents and slowdowns go together, but reporting an incident also depends on congestion; and an alert that changes driver behavior changes the outcome it predicted.
Design a fair test of whether an alert makes drivers reroute: who gets the alert, who does not, and how you decide.

Potential outcomes: each unit has an outcome with and without treatment; the effect is the difference; you only ever see one. Randomization makes the groups comparable. Without it: adjust for confounders (regression, matching, weighting), use natural experiments (instruments, discontinuities, differences-in-differences), and draw the causal diagram (DAG) to decide what to adjust for and what not to (colliders).
A/B tests are randomized experiments; interference (one driver's reroute affects others) breaks the usual analysis.
Draw the DAG for incident, congestion, reporting, rain and alert. Which variables should you adjust for to estimate the effect of an incident on speed, and which must you not?

Identification conditions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency), the back-door and front-door criteria, do-calculus at a reading level, estimators (outcome regression, inverse probability weighting, doubly robust), instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences and synthetic controls. Causal machine learning: double machine learning and causal forests for heterogeneous effects.
Interference and spillovers, which are the rule in traffic; cluster-randomized and switchback designs.
Estimate the effect of rain on the probability of a slow episode with inverse probability weighting on hour and weekday, and compare with a naive difference; explain the gap.

Time-varying treatments and g-methods for sequential policies (alerting is one); mediation; sensitivity analysis to unmeasured confounding; causal discovery and its limits; causal representation learning. Performative prediction as a bridge between causal inference and ML deployment.
Design a switchback experiment for alerts across days and routes that respects interference, and the analysis that estimates the effect on travel time.

Products that act on predictions are causal systems, and evaluating them requires experimental design or credible quasi-experiments; the research frontier includes experimentation under interference, off-policy evaluation, and causal effects of algorithmic systems on populations. Traffic is an unusually good testbed because interventions are visible and physical.
Write the causal question, identification strategy and analysis plan for 'do alerts reduce total delay on I-880 in the evening peak?'

b.q: Why does adjusting for a collider cause bias?

a.s: Conditioning on a common effect of two variables induces an association between them that does not exist causally.

b.q: What does randomization buy?

a.s: Treated and untreated groups are comparable on everything, measured or not, so the difference in outcomes is the causal effect on average.

items.title: Fairness, privacy and ethics: what a model owes people

b.s: See where a traffic model can treat people unequally or expose them, and know the tools and the limits of technical fixes.
A helper should be fair: it should not warn some neighborhoods and forget others. And it should not tell anyone where a particular person drove.
If a helper only worked for one street, who would be left out? How would they feel?

Fairness: a model's mistakes can fall more on some groups, for example if detectors are worse in some neighborhoods, alerts there are worse. Privacy: data about where people go is sensitive; even aggregated speeds can reveal a single car at 3 am. Ethics also covers being honest about what the model can do and who is accountable when it is wrong.
Look at the station map. Which parts of Fremont have few detectors? What does that mean for whom the alerts help?

Fairness definitions and why they conflict: equal error rates across groups, calibration within groups, demographic parity; you cannot have all at once. Measuring: slice every metric by area and time. Privacy: anonymization fails against linkage; differential privacy adds calibrated noise with a provable guarantee; aggregation thresholds and k-anonymity are weaker but common. Ethics in practice: documentation (datasheets, model cards), stating limits, and a person accountable for decisions.
For this project: detector coverage is uneven; probe data would raise privacy questions the loop data do not.
Compute recall and false-alarm rate per station and plot them on the map. Which areas get worse service, and why?

Formal fairness criteria (independence, separation, sufficiency) and impossibility results; sources of disparity (measurement, representation, label, deployment); mitigation methods (reweighting, constraints, post-processing) and their costs. Differential privacy: definition, composition, the privacy budget, DP-SGD; federated learning and its limits. Governance: impact assessments, audits, and regulation as constraints on design.
Prediction versus decision: fairness lives in the policy (who gets alerts) as much as in the model.
Implement a DP release of hourly average speeds per station with Laplace noise; plot utility against epsilon and decide the smallest epsilon the product could tolerate.

The limits of technical fairness (measurement of groups, contested definitions, distributional versus procedural justice); long-term dynamics of fair decisions; privacy attacks on models (membership inference, extraction) and defenses; the tension between transparency and gaming. Participatory design and the role of affected communities in defining harms.
Audit the alert policy for disparate impact across neighborhoods under two fairness definitions, show they conflict on this data, and write the memo that explains the choice to a city council.

Responsible ML at scale is organizational: review processes, documentation, red-teaming, monitoring for disparate impact after deployment, and legal compliance. The research frontier includes fairness under distribution shift and feedback, privacy-preserving learning with useful guarantees, and evaluation of societal impact. Transport systems allocate a public good, which raises the stakes.
Design the governance for a public traffic-alert system: what is measured, who reviews it, what triggers a pause, and how the public can contest a decision.

b.q: Why can a model be calibrated for every group and still have unequal error rates?

a.s: Calibration and equal error rates are different criteria, and when base rates differ across groups they cannot all hold at once.

b.q: What does differential privacy guarantee?

a.s: That any single person's data changes the released output's distribution by at most a bounded factor, whatever else an attacker knows.

items.title: Recommender systems and ranking

b.s: Rank things for people from their behavior, evaluate a ranking, and see the feedback loops that ranking creates.
When a video app shows you what to watch next, it guessed from what you and people like you watched before. That guessing is a recommender.
Our helper ranks roads too: the ones most likely to jam go to the top of the list.
Make a list of your friend's favorite games ranked from most to least. What did you use to guess?

Recommenders learn from clicks, plays and ratings. Collaborative filtering says: people who liked what you liked will like this; matrix factorization learns a few hidden traits per person and per item. Content-based methods use item features. Ranking systems score candidates and order them; evaluation asks whether the good items are near the top.
Ranking the top-risk segments per route for a dashboard is a small ranking problem with the same metrics.
Rank ten stations by predicted probability of a slow episode. If only three actually became slow, how many were in your top three? That is precision at 3.

Matrix factorization with implicit feedback, nearest-neighbor methods, and modern two-tower models that embed users and items; candidate generation then ranking; ranking losses (pointwise, pairwise, listwise). Metrics: precision at k, recall at k, mean average precision, NDCG. Offline evaluation is biased by what was shown (exposure), which is the central difficulty.
Feedback loops: what is recommended gets clicked, which trains the next model; popularity bias and filter bubbles follow.
Implement matrix factorization by alternating least squares on a small public ratings dataset and report NDCG at 10 against a popularity baseline.

Learning to rank (LambdaMART, which is gradient boosting for ranking), embedding retrieval with approximate nearest neighbors, position bias and unbiased learning to rank, off-policy evaluation of rankers from logged data (inverse propensity scoring), and exploration in recommendation. Cold start and side information. Multi-objective ranking (relevance, diversity, freshness).
For the dashboard: rank segments by calibrated risk times exposure (traffic volume), and evaluate with NDCG against realized episodes.
Train a LightGBM ranker (lambdarank) to order stations by risk each 5 minutes using the classifier's features, and compare NDCG at 5 with sorting by calibrated probability.

Recommendation as a causal and sequential problem: exposure bias, interference between users, long-term effects, and the alignment of optimization targets with user welfare. Large-scale systems (retrieval, ranking, re-ranking stages) and their latency budgets. Evaluation through online experiments and interleaving.
Propose an off-policy evaluation of a new segment-ranking policy for the dashboard from logged views and outcomes, and the propensity model it needs.

Recommenders are the most deployed ML systems and the most studied for societal effects; research spans sequential recommendation, causal recommendation, fairness of exposure, and generative retrieval. The methodological core, ranking under partial feedback, transfers to any system that shows people a prioritized list, including a traffic dashboard.
Design the ranking objective for a public traffic dashboard that balances predicted delay, number of affected drivers and fairness of coverage, and say how you would evaluate it.

b.q: Why is offline evaluation of a recommender biased?

a.s: Logged feedback exists only for items that were shown; items never shown have no data, and the log reflects the old policy's choices.

b.q: What does NDCG reward?

a.s: Putting relevant items near the top, with a discount that makes the first positions count most.

resources.title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (Sutton, Barto)

b.s: The classic free book about learning by trial and reward, by two of the people who invented the field.

Sutton and Barto's textbook, free online, explains reinforcement learning from bandits through Markov decision processes, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference methods, to function approximation and policy gradients. Part 1 is readable with basic probability. It is the standard first book.

Read chapters 1 to 6 (bandits, MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, temporal-difference learning) and implement the small examples (grid worlds, the cliff walk). Chapter 13 on policy gradients is the bridge to deep RL. The exercises are excellent and the answers are checkable by simulation.

The book's careful treatment of the Bellman equations, of on-policy versus off-policy learning, and of the deadly triad (function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy) is what you need to read deep RL papers critically. Chapter 11 on off-policy methods with approximation is the relevant one for learning from logged alert data.

Its coverage of eligibility traces, of planning with learned models, and of the psychology and neuroscience connections gives the field's intellectual context; the second edition's case studies show what worked and why.
The canonical reference; its authors' later essays on the field's direction are worth reading alongside. For a lead, it is the book to require before anyone proposes RL for a control problem.

Part I, tabular methods: the k-armed bandit (action values, epsilon-greedy, optimistic initial values, UCB, gradient bandits); finite Markov decision processes (agent-environment interface, returns, policies, value functions, Bellman equations, optimality); dynamic programming (policy evaluation, policy improvement, policy iteration, value iteration, generalized policy iteration); Monte Carlo methods (prediction, estimation of action values, control, off-policy with importance sampling); temporal-difference learning (TD(0), Sarsa, Q-learning, expected Sarsa, double learning); n-step bootstrapping; planning and learning with tabular models (Dyna, prioritized sweeping, MCTS). Part II, approximate methods: on-policy prediction with function approximation (gradient MC, semi-gradient TD, linear methods, feature construction), on-policy control (semi-gradient Sarsa, average reward), off-policy methods and the deadly triad, eligibility traces (TD(lambda)), policy gradient (REINFORCE, actor-critic). Part III: psychology, neuroscience, applications (TD-Gammon, Atari, AlphaGo), frontiers.

items: The problem: an agent chooses actions, receives rewards and new states, and seeks to maximise expected discounted return; learning from evaluative (not instructive) feedback creates the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

MDPs and Bellman equations: the state value v_pi(s) is the expected return from s under policy pi; it satisfies a recursive consistency equation; the optimal value v* satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, and a greedy policy with respect to v* is optimal.

Dynamic programming assumes a known model: policy evaluation iterates the Bellman equation to a fixed point; policy improvement acts greedily; alternating them (generalized policy iteration) is the pattern behind almost every RL algorithm.

Monte Carlo learns from complete episodes without a model by averaging returns; off-policy learning reweights returns from a behaviour policy with importance-sampling ratios, at the price of variance.

Temporal difference learns from incomplete episodes by bootstrapping: update the estimate toward reward plus discounted estimate of the next state. Sarsa is on-policy (uses the action actually taken); Q-learning is off-policy (uses the max); double Q-learning removes maximisation bias.
n-step methods and eligibility traces interpolate between MC (high variance, no bias) and TD(0) (low variance, bias); TD(lambda) averages all n-step returns with weights (1-lambda) lambda^(n-1).
Planning uses a model to simulate experience; Dyna interleaves real and simulated updates; MCTS builds a search tree from rollouts guided by value estimates.

Function approximation: with large state spaces, values are parameterised (linear in features, or a network) and updated by semi-gradient TD; combining bootstrapping, off-policy learning and function approximation (the deadly triad) can diverge.

Policy gradient methods parameterise the policy directly; the policy gradient theorem gives an unbiased gradient estimate from sampled returns (REINFORCE); a learned baseline or critic reduces variance (actor-critic).

b.s:
return: G_t = R_{t+1} + gamma R_{t+2} + gamma^2 R_{t+3} + ...
Bellman: v_pi(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a) [r + gamma v_pi(s')]
TD(0): V(S_t) <- V(S_t) + alpha [R_{t+1} + gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)]
Q-learning: Q(S,A) <- Q(S,A) + alpha [R + gamma max_a Q(S',a) - Q(S,A)]
policy gradient: grad J(theta) = E_pi[ G_t grad log pi(A_t|S_t, theta) ]

items: Generalized policy iteration (evaluate, then improve) is the skeleton of every RL method.
TD learning bootstraps; MC does not; the choice trades bias for variance.
Function approximation plus off-policy plus bootstrapping can diverge, so read Chapter 11 before trusting a deep RL result.

b.s: Implement tabular Q-learning and Sarsa on a small gridworld and on a signal-timing toy (a queue that grows with arrivals and drains when the light is green); plot learning curves and show that Q-learning finds the shorter but riskier path in the cliff-walking example.

resources.lives: book · free · a semester · free; the standard first book

resources.title: David Silver's Reinforcement Learning course (UCL, DeepMind)

b.s: Video lectures by a scientist who helped build a computer that beat the best human at the board game Go, explaining how machines learn from rewards.

Ten free lectures that follow Sutton and Barto: Markov decision processes, planning, learning without a model, function approximation, policy gradients, and games. Watch them alongside the book; the lectures make the equations feel inevitable.

Lectures 1 to 5 cover the foundations used in the RL topic; lecture 6 on value function approximation and lecture 7 on policy gradients are the bridge to deep RL. Do the book's exercises after each lecture.

Silver's derivations (the Bellman equations, the policy gradient theorem) are clear and complete; his lecture on exploration and on integrating learning and planning is a compact treatment of the ideas behind model-based RL.
The course predates much of deep RL; pair it with Spinning Up for algorithms and with recent surveys for offline RL. Its value is conceptual clarity.
A widely used lecture series that defines the shared vocabulary of the field; useful as a common reference when a team discusses control problems.

Ten lectures: introduction to RL; Markov decision processes; planning by dynamic programming; model-free prediction (MC and TD); model-free control (on-policy and off-policy); value function approximation (incremental methods, batch methods, DQN); policy gradient methods (finite difference, Monte Carlo policy gradient, actor-critic, natural gradient); integrating learning and planning (model-based RL, Dyna, simulation-based search, MCTS); exploration and exploitation (bandits, optimism, Thompson sampling, information state search); case study of classic games (Backgammon, checkers, chess, Go, poker).

items: The RL problem is framed by reward hypothesis, history and state, the Markov property, and the three agent components (policy, value function, model); the distinction between prediction (evaluate a policy) and control (find the best one) organises the course.
MDP lecture: Markov processes, reward processes, decision processes; the Bellman expectation and optimality equations in matrix and recursive form; the existence of a deterministic optimal policy.
Dynamic programming: iterative policy evaluation, policy iteration and value iteration are contraction mappings, so they converge; asynchronous and prioritised sweeps.

Model-free prediction: MC averages returns, TD bootstraps; the bias-variance argument; TD(lambda) with forward (lambda-return) and backward (eligibility trace) views, which are equivalent for offline updates.
Model-free control: on-policy MC and Sarsa with GLIE exploration; off-policy Q-learning; the role of importance sampling and why Q-learning avoids it.
Function approximation: incremental gradient methods with linear and nonlinear features; batch methods (least-squares, experience replay with fixed targets as in DQN) stabilise learning.
Policy gradient: score function, the policy gradient theorem, REINFORCE, reducing variance with a critic and with baselines, compatible function approximation, natural policy gradient.
Model-based RL and search: learn a model from experience, plan with it; Dyna; forward search; MCTS with UCT and its success in Go.
Exploration: regret, optimism in the face of uncertainty (UCB), probability matching (Thompson sampling), information-state MDPs; contextual bandits.

b.s:
UCB: A_t = argmax_a [ Q_t(a) + c sqrt( ln t / N_t(a) ) ]
lambda-return: G_t^lambda = (1-lambda) sum_n lambda^(n-1) G_t^(n)
actor-critic update: theta <- theta + alpha grad log pi(a|s) Q_w(s,a)

items: Prediction and control are separate problems and every algorithm is a pairing of one evaluation method with one improvement rule.
Off-policy learning lets one dataset evaluate many policies, which is why Q-learning and DQN are so widely used.
Exploration is a statistical problem (regret) with principled solutions (UCB, Thompson) that beat epsilon-greedy.

b.s: Watch lectures 1 to 5 alongside Sutton and Barto chapters 1 to 6, then reproduce the lecture's gridworld DP demo in NumPy, and implement UCB and Thompson sampling on a bandit that chooses which of three ramp-meter rates to use.

resources.lives: video · free · ten lectures, two weeks · free lectures alongside the book

resources.title: Spinning Up in Deep RL (OpenAI)

b.s: A free website that teaches modern trial-and-reward learning with clear notes and code you can run.

Spinning Up is an educational site with an introduction to deep reinforcement learning, a list of key papers, and clean implementations of the main algorithms. It was written for people who know some deep learning and want to do RL properly. Read the introduction and run one algorithm on a simple simulated task.

Read the three-part introduction (key concepts, kinds of algorithms, the policy-gradient derivation) and study the code for one algorithm (PPO or DQN). The exercises and the 'spinning up as a researcher' essay are practical advice.

Its implementations are readable references for the standard algorithms and their tricks; the key-papers list is a curated syllabus for the field. Use it to reproduce a result on a simulated control task before attempting a traffic-control simulator.

It reflects the state of deep RL around its writing; later methods (offline RL, RL from human feedback) are covered elsewhere. Its clarity about what makes RL hard (sample efficiency, instability, reward design) remains accurate.
A useful teaching resource and a reminder that reproducible baselines were a problem the field had to solve deliberately.

An introduction (key concepts and terminology; kinds of RL algorithms; intro to policy optimization with derivations), a list of key papers by topic (model-free, exploration, transfer, hierarchy, memory, model-based, meta-RL, scaling, safety, imitation, reproducibility), and clean, single-file implementations with documentation of VPG, TRPO, PPO, DDPG, TD3 and SAC, plus exercises and advice on doing RL research.

items: Terminology: states and observations, action spaces, policies (deterministic and stochastic, with log-probability computation for categorical and diagonal Gaussian policies), trajectories, reward and return, the RL objective, value functions and advantage functions.
Taxonomy: model-free versus model-based; within model-free, policy optimisation (on-policy, stable) versus Q-learning (off-policy, sample-efficient but less stable); hybrids (DDPG, SAC).

Policy gradient derivation: the log-derivative trick turns the gradient of an expectation into an expectation of gradients; reward-to-go and baselines reduce variance without bias; the general form with advantage estimates.
Vanilla policy gradient: collect trajectories, estimate advantages with a value network (generalized advantage estimation), take one gradient step; simple and on-policy.

Trust region and PPO: limit each policy update so performance does not collapse; TRPO by a KL constraint solved with conjugate gradient; PPO by a clipped surrogate objective that is simpler and works nearly as well.

Off-policy actor-critic: DDPG learns a deterministic policy and Q function with replay and target networks; TD3 adds twin critics, target smoothing and delayed policy updates; SAC maximises entropy-regularised return with a stochastic policy.
Research advice: read for breadth, reproduce results, run many seeds, measure with learning curves, and tune one thing at a time; RL results are noisy and easy to fool yourself with.

b.s:
log-derivative: grad E[R(tau)] = E[ sum_t grad log pi(a_t|s_t) R(tau) ]
PPO clip: L = E[ min( r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_t ) ], r_t = pi_theta(a|s)/pi_old(a|s)
GAE: A_t = sum_l (gamma lambda)^l delta_{t+l}, delta_t = r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)

items: Policy gradient is one derivation; every on-policy algorithm is that derivation plus a variance-reduction and a step-size control.
PPO's clipped objective is the practical default for on-policy learning; SAC for continuous control off-policy.
Run several seeds; a single learning curve in deep RL proves nothing.

b.s: Implement VPG from the pseudocode on CartPole with a value baseline, then swap in the PPO clip, and plot five-seed learning curves for each; write one paragraph on what the clip changed.

resources.lives: docs · free · a week · free; clean algorithms and a reading list

resources.title: Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Cunningham)

b.s: A free book about telling causes from coincidences, written in a friendly voice with lots of examples from real life.

Scott Cunningham's book, free online, teaches the methods economists use to find causes in data without experiments: comparing groups over time, using cut-offs, using instruments, and matching. It explains directed graphs (pictures of cause and effect) early and uses them throughout. Code is included.

Read the chapters on directed acyclic graphs, on potential outcomes, on matching, and on difference-in-differences. Then draw the DAG for incidents, congestion and reporting and decide what you can estimate from the archive.

The Mixtape is the applied-economics complement to Hernán and Robins: more on quasi-experimental designs (instruments, regression discontinuity, synthetic control), less on time-varying treatments. Its worked examples with code are the fastest way to see each method fail and succeed.

Its treatment of difference-in-differences includes the recent literature on staggered adoption, which is relevant to evaluating roadwork or policy changes across corridors. Read it alongside the causal machine-learning literature.
A free, current, applied causal-inference text; for a product team asking what an alert causes, it is the accessible primer before the formal one.

Chapters: introduction; probability and regression review; directed acyclic graphs; potential outcomes causal model (physical randomisation, randomisation inference, Fisher's sharp null); matching and subclassification (exact matching, approximate matching, propensity scores, coarsened exact matching); regression discontinuity (sharp, fuzzy, bandwidth, density tests, placebo tests); instrumental variables (LATE, weak instruments, heterogeneous effects); panel data (fixed effects); difference-in-differences (the 2x2, parallel trends, event studies, staggered adoption and the Bacon decomposition, Callaway-Sant'Anna); synthetic control; with Stata, R and Python code throughout.

items: Potential outcomes: each unit has Y(1) and Y(0); the individual effect is their difference and is never observed; the average treatment effect requires assumptions (SUTVA, ignorability) to identify from data; randomisation makes treatment independent of potential outcomes.

DAGs: draw the assumed causal structure; the backdoor criterion says which variables to condition on to block confounding paths; conditioning on a collider opens a path and creates bias (selection bias).

Matching and propensity scores: under conditional independence given X, compare treated to similar controls; the propensity score p(X) = P(D=1|X) reduces dimensionality; check overlap (common support) and balance; inverse probability weighting.

Regression discontinuity: when treatment is assigned by a cutoff on a running variable, units just above and below are comparable; estimate with local linear regression on each side, test for manipulation with a density test at the cutoff, run placebo cutoffs.

Instrumental variables: an instrument affects treatment but affects the outcome only through treatment; two-stage least squares; the estimate is a local average treatment effect for compliers; weak instruments bias toward OLS.

Difference-in-differences: compare the change in the treated group to the change in the control group; parallel trends is the identifying assumption; event-study plots check pre-trends; with staggered adoption the two-way fixed effects estimator can be badly biased because it uses already-treated units as controls.
Synthetic control: build a weighted combination of untreated units that matches the treated unit's pre-period trajectory; inference by placebo permutation across donor units.

b.s:
ATE = E[Y(1) - Y(0)];  naive difference = ATE + selection bias + heterogeneity bias
DiD: (E[Y_T,post] - E[Y_T,pre]) - (E[Y_C,post] - E[Y_C,pre])
2SLS: first stage D = pi Z + X gamma + v, second stage Y = beta D_hat + X delta + u
propensity weighting: E[Y(1)] = E[ D Y / p(X) ]

items: Identification comes from assumptions and design, not from the size of the dataset.
Draw the DAG before the regression; it says what to control for and what never to control for.
For policy questions about roads (a new ramp meter, a lane closure), difference-in-differences on nearby untreated segments is the natural design.

b.s: Take a real or simulated change on one Fremont segment (a new signal timing), pick control segments, run a difference-in-differences with an event-study plot, and test the parallel-trends assumption with pre-period leads.

resources.lives: book · free · selected chapters, two weeks · free; applied causal methods with code

resources.title: Causal Inference: What If (Hernán, Robins)

b.s: A free book about telling the difference between 'these two things happen together' and 'this one causes that one', which is harder than it sounds.

A textbook by two epidemiologists, free as a PDF, about answering causal questions from data: what would have happened if we had done something else. Part 1 is readable with basic statistics and uses simple examples. Read it in the final phase when you ask what an alert actually causes.

Part 1 introduces counterfactuals, randomized experiments, confounding, and the diagrams (DAGs) that make assumptions explicit. Apply it to the project: does an incident cause the slowdown, or does congestion cause the incident to be reported? The book gives the tools to state that question precisely.

Its treatment of exchangeability, positivity and consistency as the conditions for causal identification, and of methods (standardization, inverse probability weighting, g-methods), is the rigorous base for causal questions in ML. Part 2 covers models; part 3 covers time-varying treatments, which is where traffic interventions live.

Read alongside Pearl's structural approach (the Book of Why for the story, Causality for the math) and the modern causal ML literature (double machine learning, causal forests). The time-varying-treatment chapters are directly relevant to sequential alerting policies.

The epidemiological tradition of causal inference is the most careful one about assumptions; for a product that intervenes (alerts that change traffic), it is the framework for saying what you can and cannot learn from logged data.

Part I, causal inference without models: definition of causal effect (individual and average effects, randomisation, counterfactuals); randomised experiments (conditional randomisation, standardisation, inverse probability weighting); observational studies (identifiability conditions, exchangeability, positivity, consistency); effect modification; interaction; graphical representation (DAGs, d-separation, backdoor); confounding; selection bias; measurement bias; random variability. Part II, causal inference with models: why models, IP weighting and marginal structural models, standardisation and the parametric g-formula, g-estimation of structural nested models, outcome regression and propensity scores, instrumental variables, causal survival analysis, variable selection. Part III, time-varying treatments: treatment-confounder feedback, g-methods for time-varying treatments, target trial emulation.

items: The three identifiability conditions: exchangeability (treated and untreated would have had the same outcome distribution had they received the same treatment), positivity (every covariate stratum has some treated and some untreated), consistency (the observed outcome under the received treatment equals the counterfactual).

Standardisation and IP weighting are two ways to use conditional exchangeability given L: compute stratum-specific risks and average over the population, or reweight each unit by 1/P(A|L) to create a pseudo-population without confounding; they give the same answer nonparametrically.

DAGs encode the assumptions: d-separation determines which independencies hold; confounding is an open backdoor path; selection bias is conditioning on a collider or a descendant of one; measurement bias comes from mismeasured variables.

With many covariates, models are needed: the marginal structural model fits a model for the causal effect using IP weights; the parametric g-formula models the outcome given treatment and covariates and standardises; doubly robust estimators combine both.

Instrumental variables need four conditions (relevance, exclusion, exchangeability of the instrument, and monotonicity or homogeneity for point identification); the IV estimate is the ratio of reduced-form to first-stage effects.

Time-varying treatments with treatment-confounder feedback break conventional regression: adjusting for a time-varying confounder that is also affected by earlier treatment blocks part of the effect and opens collider paths; the g-methods (IP weighting, g-formula, g-estimation) handle this.

The target trial: specify the randomised trial you would run (eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment, follow-up, outcome, causal contrast, analysis), then emulate each component with observational data; this discipline prevents most design errors.

b.s:
standardisation: E[Y^a] = sum_l E[Y | A=a, L=l] P(L=l)
IP weight: W^A = 1 / f(A | L);  stabilised: f(A) / f(A|L)
IV: E[Y^{a=1}] - E[Y^{a=0}] = (E[Y|Z=1]-E[Y|Z=0]) / (E[A|Z=1]-E[A|Z=0])

items: Every causal claim from observational data rests on exchangeability, positivity and consistency; state them explicitly.
Standardisation and IP weighting are the same estimand computed two ways; doubly robust estimators hedge the modelling risk.
Time-varying treatments (traffic interventions that respond to congestion they then affect) need g-methods, not regression.

b.s: Write the target trial for 'does activating ramp metering at 6 am reduce bottleneck probability by 7 am?', list eligibility, strategies, outcome and the contrast, then implement IP weighting with a logistic model for metering given the previous hour's state.

resources.lives: book · free · part 1, three weeks · free; the rigorous base, part 1 now

resources.title: Introduction to Causal Inference (Brady Neal), course and book draft

b.s: A free online class and book about telling causes from coincidences, taught from the very beginning with pictures of arrows.

Brady Neal's free course (video lectures) and book draft introduce causal inference from a machine-learning perspective: potential outcomes, causal graphs, confounding, adjustment, and the main methods. It assumes only basic probability. It is the free entry point for the causal topic.

Chapters 1 to 4 (motivation, potential outcomes, the flow of association and causation in graphs, causal models) give the vocabulary and the diagrams; chapters on identification and on instruments give the methods. Draw the traffic DAG after chapter 3.
