Neal presents Pearl's graphical approach and the potential-outcomes framework together and shows their correspondence, which the specialized books do less well; its later chapters connect to machine learning (causal discovery, counterfactuals).

Read it as the bridge between the Mixtape's applied methods and Hernán and Robins's rigor; its treatment of the estimand and of identification is a clean template for writing your own causal question.
A free, ML-oriented causal course is the right shared reference for an engineering team beginning to ask what a system's outputs cause.

Course videos and a book draft: motivation (Simpson's paradox, correlation is not causation, what is causation); potential outcomes (individual and average effects, the fundamental problem, ignorability, exchangeability, conditional exchangeability, positivity, no interference, consistency, adjustment formula); the flow of association and causation in graphs (chains, forks, colliders, d-separation, Markov assumption); causal models (structural causal models, interventions, the backdoor adjustment); randomised experiments; nonidentifiability; frontdoor adjustment and do-calculus; estimation (COM estimators, propensity scores, IPW, doubly robust, matching, double machine learning, causal forests); unobserved confounding (bounds, sensitivity analysis); instrumental variables; difference-in-differences; causal discovery (from observational and interventional data); transfer learning and transportability; counterfactuals and mediation.

items: Simpson's paradox shows that the right answer depends on the causal structure, not the data alone: whether to condition on the subgroup variable depends on whether it is a confounder or a mediator.

Potential outcomes and the identification assumptions; the adjustment formula turns a causal quantity into a statistical one under conditional exchangeability and positivity; the positivity-unconfoundedness trade-off as you condition on more variables.
Graphs: association flows along chains and forks and is blocked at colliders; conditioning reverses each; d-separation gives the full rule; the backdoor criterion selects adjustment sets.
Structural causal models: variables as functions of parents and noise; interventions replace an equation (do-operator); the difference between conditioning and intervening.
Beyond backdoor: the frontdoor criterion identifies effects through a mediator even with unobserved confounding; do-calculus gives three rules that are complete for identification.

Estimation: conditional-outcome models plug a fitted regression into the adjustment formula (S-learner, T-learner, X-learner), propensity-based methods reweight, doubly robust estimators combine, and double ML orthogonalises to use flexible learners; causal forests estimate heterogeneous effects.
Unobserved confounding cannot be tested; sensitivity analysis (how strong would a confounder need to be to explain the effect away) and bounds are the honest response.
Causal discovery attempts to learn the graph from data: constraint-based (PC), score-based, and functional (additive noise) methods, each with strong assumptions.

b.s:
adjustment: E[Y | do(t)] = E_W[ E[Y | t, W] ]
frontdoor: P(y|do(t)) = sum_m P(m|t) sum_t' P(y|t',m) P(t')
doubly robust (AIPW): tau = mean[ mu1(X) - mu0(X) + T (Y - mu1(X))/e(X) - (1-T)(Y - mu0(X))/(1-e(X)) ]

items: Conditioning is not intervening; the do-operator makes the distinction precise.
Chains and forks transmit association; colliders block it, and conditioning on them opens it.
Flexible ML can estimate causal effects only inside a design (adjustment sets, orthogonalisation) that justifies the estimand.

b.s: Draw the DAG for rain, time of day, upstream flow, metering and bottleneck; find a valid backdoor set; estimate the metering effect with a T-learner (two LightGBM models) and with AIPW, and compare.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; causal inference for ML people, from zero

resources.title: Fairness and Machine Learning (Barocas, Hardt, Narayanan)

b.s: A free book about making sure learning machines treat different groups of people fairly, and about how hard it is to even agree on what fair means.

A textbook, free online, about fairness in machine learning: how models can treat groups differently, the different definitions of fairness and why they conflict, how discrimination is understood in law and philosophy, and what can be done. It is readable with basic statistics.

Read the chapters on classification (the fairness criteria and the impossibility of satisfying them all), on causality, and on the legal background. Then audit the alert policy across neighborhoods using two criteria and see them disagree.

The book's formal treatment (independence, separation, sufficiency; the trade-offs; measurement issues) is the rigorous base; its chapters on the limits of technical fixes and on broader questions are unusually honest for a technical text.
It connects to causal inference (counterfactual fairness), to long-term dynamics of decisions, and to measurement of protected attributes; the bibliography is a map of the field.
The standard graduate text; for a lead deploying a public system, its framing of fairness as a socio-technical question, not a metric, is the one that survives contact with real decisions.

Chapters: introduction (demographic disparities, the machine-learning loop, the state of society, the trouble with measurement, from data to models, the pitfalls of action, feedback loops, getting concrete with a toy example); when is automated decision-making legitimate; classification (formal setup, group fairness criteria: independence, separation, sufficiency; incompatibilities; calibration; scoring, ROC, trade-offs); relative notions of fairness (individual fairness, distance, counterfactuals); causality (causal models, counterfactual fairness, path-specific effects, the trouble with causal reasoning about race); understanding United States anti-discrimination law; testing discrimination in practice (audits, testing, observational studies, adversarial testing); a broader view of discrimination; datasets (histories, benchmarks, harms of datasets); and a chapter on the limits of fairness through the lens of the book's arguments.

items: Disparities enter through the loop: what the world is like, what is measured (the target variable as a construct), how the data are sampled, how the model is fitted, and how decisions feed back into the world.

Three group criteria for a score R, attribute A, outcome Y: independence (R independent of A), separation (R independent of A given Y: equal error rates), sufficiency (Y independent of A given R: calibration by group); any two are incompatible except in degenerate cases.

Classification with a threshold: ROC curves per group show what is achievable; equalised odds may require different thresholds per group; the COMPAS debate is a sufficiency-versus-separation disagreement.

Individual fairness: similar individuals treated similarly under a task-specific metric; counterfactual fairness: the decision would not change had the protected attribute been different, which requires a causal model.

Causal reasoning about protected attributes is fraught (what does it mean to intervene on race); path-specific effects distinguish legitimate from illegitimate pathways but need justification for each path.
Legal frameworks (disparate treatment versus disparate impact, the four-fifths rule, business necessity) constrain what interventions are allowed and do not map cleanly onto statistical criteria.
Testing discrimination: audit studies, correspondence tests, algorithmic audits with synthetic inputs, observational comparisons and their pitfalls (conditioning on post-decision variables).
Datasets have histories; benchmark culture shapes what gets built; datasets can cause harm through representation, privacy and downstream use.

b.s:
independence: P(R | A=a) = P(R | A=b)
separation: P(R | Y=y, A=a) = P(R | Y=y, A=b)  (equal TPR and FPR)
sufficiency: P(Y | R=r, A=a) = P(Y | R=r, A=b)  (calibration by group)

items: Fairness criteria conflict, so a choice among them is a value judgement that must be made explicitly.
Measurement is where most unfairness enters: the target variable is a proxy for a construct.
For a traffic model, the relevant groups are geographic: corridors and neighbourhoods; check error rates per station group.

b.s: Compute AP, calibration and false-negative rate per station group (north versus south of the interchange, or by neighbourhood income if joined to census tracts); write one page on which criterion matters for whom and why.

resources.lives: book · free · three weeks · free; the graduate text

resources.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (Dwork, Roth)

b.s: A book about adding a little randomness to shared numbers so that nobody can tell whether any one person's information was used.

Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth's monograph, free from the authors, defines differential privacy: a way of releasing statistics with noise so that each person's data has a bounded effect on the result. It explains the basic mechanisms and how privacy loss adds up. The first chapters are readable; the rest is for specialists.

Read chapters 1 to 3 (the promise, the definition, the Laplace and exponential mechanisms, composition) and implement a private release of hourly average speeds. Plot how accuracy changes with the privacy parameter.

The monograph's treatment of composition, of sensitivity, and of the exponential mechanism is the foundation for private learning (DP-SGD) and for private data release. Understand what the guarantee does and does not cover (it protects individuals, not groups; it says nothing about the data being wrong).

Later work covers private deep learning, local differential privacy (as used on devices), and privacy accounting; the monograph is the base for reading it. Its examples of failed anonymization are the argument for the definition.

Differential privacy is deployed at scale in operating systems and statistical agencies; the research frontier is utility at practical privacy budgets and privacy under continual release, which is exactly what a streaming traffic system does.

Chapters: the promise of differential privacy; basic terms (the model of computation, randomised response, the definition, its properties: post-processing, group privacy, composition); basic techniques and composition (randomised response, the Laplace mechanism, the exponential mechanism, composition theorems, the sparse vector technique); releasing linear queries with correlated error (SmallDB, private multiplicative weights, iterative constructions); generalisations (mechanisms via alpha-nets, the iterative construction mechanism, connections to learning); boosting for queries; when data are drawn from a distribution (query release via Gaussian noise, generalisation); lower bounds and separation results; differential privacy and computational complexity; differential privacy and mechanism design; differential privacy and machine learning (SQ learning, private PAC learning, empirical risk minimisation); additional models (local, pan-private, continual observation); reflections.

items: Definition: a mechanism M is (epsilon, delta)-differentially private if for all neighbouring databases x and y and all output sets S, P(M(x) in S) <= exp(epsilon) P(M(y) in S) + delta; the guarantee is about the mechanism, not the data, and it holds against any auxiliary information.

Properties: immunity to post-processing (no further computation can weaken it), group privacy (k changes cost k epsilon), sequential composition (epsilons add), parallel composition (disjoint data does not add), and advanced composition (roughly sqrt(k) growth for k mechanisms with a delta).

Laplace mechanism: add Laplace(Delta f / epsilon) noise to a numeric query with L1 sensitivity Delta f; Gaussian mechanism for (epsilon, delta) with L2 sensitivity; sensitivity is computed over neighbouring databases.
Exponential mechanism: choose an output with probability proportional to exp(epsilon u(x, r) / (2 Delta u)), for any utility function u; the general tool for non-numeric outputs.
Sparse vector technique: answer only queries whose noisy value exceeds a noisy threshold, paying privacy only for the answers above threshold; the basis of many adaptive algorithms.

Releasing many queries: for a database of size n and k linear queries, error can scale like sqrt(log k) per query for the synthetic-data approaches (SmallDB, multiplicative weights), far better than independent noise.
Learning privately: SQ-learnable classes are privately learnable; private ERM by output perturbation, objective perturbation or noisy gradient descent (the ancestor of DP-SGD).
Local model: each user randomises their own data before sending (randomised response is the prototype); more private, much noisier (error scales like sqrt(n) instead of constant).

b.s:
(eps, delta)-DP: P[M(x) in S] <= e^eps P[M(y) in S] + delta for neighbours x, y
Laplace mechanism: M(x) = f(x) + Lap(Delta_1 f / eps)
Gaussian mechanism: sigma >= sqrt(2 ln(1.25/delta)) Delta_2 f / eps
randomised response (p=1/2 truth): eps = ln 3

items: Privacy is a property of the algorithm that releases the output, and it composes: every release spends budget.
Sensitivity is the key computation; bounding it (clipping) is what makes noise calibrated.
Traffic counts per station per five minutes are a query with sensitivity one per vehicle; the noise needed is small at the aggregate and large at the individual level.

b.s: Implement the Laplace mechanism for hourly counts at one station with eps in {0.1, 1, 10}, plot the noisy series against the true one, then implement sequential composition tracking for a day of hourly releases.

resources.lives: book · free · weeks · free from the authors; chapters 1 to 3

resources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting (Mitchell et al., 2019) and Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2018)

b.s: Two papers that say every learning machine and every pile of data should come with a label, like food has ingredients and warnings.

Two short papers proposing standard documentation: a model card describes what a model is for, how it was evaluated, on whom, and where it fails; a datasheet describes how a dataset was collected, what it contains and how it should and should not be used. Both are free and have templates you can fill in.
Fill in a datasheet for the Fremont PeMS and 511 data and a model card for the LightGBM alert model, using the papers' question lists. You will find questions you cannot answer; those are the gaps.
The papers' value is the questions; they operationalize accountability without prescribing a metric. Compare with later documentation standards and with regulatory requirements for high-risk systems.
Documentation is part of the technical-debt story (Sculley) and of governance (fairness book); the research question is whether documentation changes behavior, which later studies examine.
Model and data documentation are now expected in responsible deployment; for a lead, they are the artifacts a review board or regulator will ask for first.

Model cards: motivation, the proposed sections (model details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, quantitative analyses with disaggregated results, ethical considerations, caveats and recommendations) and two worked examples (a smile detector and a toxicity classifier) with intersectional evaluations. Datasheets: motivation from electronics datasheets, questions grouped by stage (motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing and labelling, uses, distribution, maintenance), and worked examples.

items: A model card states who built the model and why, what it is for and not for, which factors (groups, instruments, environments) affect performance, which metrics and thresholds are used, and how it performs across those factors, so users can judge fitness for their use.
Disaggregated evaluation is the core: report metrics per relevant group and intersections, with confidence intervals; a single aggregate hides the failures that matter.
Ethical considerations and caveats document known risks, sensitive data, and the conditions under which results should not be trusted.

A datasheet answers, for every dataset, why it was created, what is in it (instances, labels, missing data, sensitive attributes, splits), how it was collected (who, mechanism, timeframe, consent), how it was processed, what it has been used for and should not be used for, how it is distributed and licensed, and who maintains it and how errata are handled.
Both documents are meant to be written by the people who made the artefact, at creation time, and to travel with it; they shift accountability from users guessing to makers stating.

b.s:
model card sections: details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, quantitative analyses, ethics, caveats
datasheet stages: motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses, distribution, maintenance

items: Documentation that travels with the artefact is part of the artefact.
Disaggregated metrics with intervals are the heart of a model card.
Write the datasheet for the PeMS extract once, and every later user of the data starts from the right assumptions.

b.s: Write a model card for the LightGBM bottleneck predictor (with AP per station, per hour bucket and per weather condition) and a datasheet for the cleaned PeMS-plus-511 dataset, each two pages, and commit them next to the model.

resources.lives: paper · free · an evening or two · free; documentation you will actually fill in

resources.title: Google's Recommendation Systems course

b.s: A free class from Google about how apps guess what you might like next.

A short free course covering how recommendation works: candidate generation (finding possible items), scoring, and re-ranking; collaborative filtering and matrix factorization; embeddings; and the problems of cold start and bias. With small exercises in a notebook.
Do the sections on collaborative filtering, matrix factorization and retrieval; then apply the ranking metrics (precision at k, NDCG) to the traffic dashboard's ordering of segments.

The course is a compact tour of an industrial recommender's stages and their trade-offs; read it as architecture, then the papers for the methods (matrix factorization, two-tower retrieval, learning to rank).
It is introductory and Google-flavored; the research literature on exposure bias, off-policy evaluation and fairness in ranking is where the hard questions live.
A useful shared reference for the structure of ranking systems; for a lead, its staged architecture is the design pattern for any system that shows people an ordered list.

Modules: introduction (what recommendations are, terminology: items, queries, embeddings; the common architecture: candidate generation, scoring, re-ranking); candidate generation (content-based filtering, collaborative filtering, matrix factorisation, objective choice, weighted matrix factorisation, SGD versus WALS, pros and cons, deep neural network models, softmax training, negative sampling, folding, and retrieval with approximate nearest neighbours); scoring (why a separate model, choosing the objective, positional bias); re-ranking (freshness, diversity, fairness); with a Colab on matrix factorisation for MovieLens.

items: The pipeline: candidate generation narrows millions of items to hundreds cheaply, scoring ranks those with a richer model, and re-ranking applies constraints (freshness, diversity, policy).
Content-based filtering represents items by features and recommends items similar to what a user liked; it does not need other users but cannot expand tastes.

Collaborative filtering uses the interaction matrix; matrix factorisation learns user and item embeddings whose dot product predicts the interaction; the unobserved entries need a weight (weighted MF) or the model predicts everything as observed.
Solving MF: SGD is flexible but slow to converge; weighted alternating least squares alternates closed-form solves and parallelises well.

DNN models generalise MF: item towers and query towers with side features; softmax over items as a classification objective, trained with sampled negatives; folding is the failure mode where unrelated groups of embeddings land near each other.
Retrieval: with embeddings, nearest-neighbour search (exact or approximate) returns candidates in milliseconds.

Scoring uses a separate model with more features and the right objective (click, watch time, satisfaction) and corrects for positional bias; re-ranking adds freshness and diversity and enforces fairness constraints.

b.s:
MF objective: sum_{(i,j) observed} (A_ij - U_i . V_j)^2 + w0 sum_{(i,j) unobserved} (U_i . V_j)^2 + lambda (||U||^2 + ||V||^2)
softmax over items: p(j | x) = exp(psi(x) . V_j) / sum_k exp(psi(x) . V_k)

items: Retrieval then scoring then re-ranking is the architecture; each stage has its own objective and budget.
Unobserved interactions are not negatives; weight them or sample them, or the model degenerates.
The same two-tower and nearest-neighbour idea applies to any 'find similar' problem, including similar stations or similar days.

b.s: Build a day-similarity retriever: embed each day of Fremont data with a small autoencoder or with its hourly speed profile, retrieve the ten nearest days for a held-out day, and use their outcomes as a k-NN forecast; compare to LightGBM.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; the architecture of ranking systems

resources.title: Recommender Systems chapter, Dive into Deep Learning

b.s: A free chapter, with code, about how apps guess what you might like next.

The recommender-systems chapter of Dive into Deep Learning covers matrix factorization, autoencoders for ratings, implicit feedback, sequence-aware recommendation, feature-rich models and click-through prediction, each with runnable code. It replaces the paywalled matrix-factorization article with a free, complete treatment.

Read the sections on matrix factorization and on implicit feedback (personalized ranking), and run their code on a small public ratings dataset; then compute precision at k and NDCG as the ranking topic asks.

The chapter's coverage of Bayesian personalized ranking and of click-through models is the practical core of ranking with implicit feedback; its factorization machines section connects to the tabular models of phase 4.
Its treatment is method-centric; pair with the exposure-bias and off-policy-evaluation literature for the evaluation problems, which the chapter does not solve.
A free, runnable reference for the classical recommender methods; useful as the baseline set when a team proposes something new.

Sections: overview (collaborative filtering, explicit and implicit feedback, recommendation tasks); the MovieLens dataset (loading, statistics, splitting); matrix factorisation (model, implementation, training, evaluation); AutoRec (rating prediction with autoencoders); personalised ranking (Bayesian personalised ranking loss, hinge loss); neural collaborative filtering (NeuMF); sequence-aware recommendation (Caser); feature-rich recommender systems (click-through rate prediction and the Criteo dataset); factorisation machines; deep factorisation machines.

items: Explicit feedback (ratings) versus implicit (clicks, views); rating prediction versus ranking; evaluation with RMSE for ratings and with hit rate and AUC for ranking.
Matrix factorisation with user and item biases, trained by minimising squared error on observed ratings; a clean implementation in a few dozen lines.
AutoRec reconstructs a user's or item's rating vector with an autoencoder, masking unobserved entries in the loss.
Personalised ranking: BPR maximises the probability that an observed item ranks above an unobserved one for the same user; pairwise losses fit implicit feedback better than pointwise regression.
NeuMF combines a generalised MF branch and an MLP branch on concatenated embeddings; sequence-aware models (Caser) apply convolutions over the embeddings of the last L items.

Feature-rich CTR prediction: sparse categorical features one-hot encoded at scale; factorisation machines model pairwise feature interactions with low-rank factors in linear time; DeepFM adds an MLP over shared embeddings.

b.s:
MF with biases: r_hat_ui = p_u . q_i + b_u + b_i + mu
BPR: maximise sum ln sigma(r_hat_ui - r_hat_uj) - lambda ||theta||^2 for observed i, unobserved j
FM: y_hat = w0 + sum_i w_i x_i + sum_{i<j} (v_i . v_j) x_i x_j

items: Implicit feedback needs pairwise ranking losses, not regression on missing entries.
Factorisation machines are the bridge between recommenders and general tabular models with interactions.
The chapter's implementations are short enough to read fully; do so before using a library.

b.s: Implement matrix factorisation and BPR on MovieLens-100k from the chapter, then adapt FM to predict bottleneck probability from one-hot station, hour and weekday features, and compare to LightGBM on the same features.

resources.lives: book · free · weeks · free; matrix factorization to ranking, with code

resources.title: Hugging Face Deep RL course

b.s: A free online class where you train little agents to play games and land a rocket, and see them get better.

Hugging Face's free reinforcement-learning course: the foundations, Q-learning, deep Q-networks, policy gradients, actor-critic methods, and multi-agent settings, with hands-on units where you train agents in simulators and share them. It pairs practice with Sutton and Barto's theory.

Do units 1 to 4 (introduction, Q-learning, deep Q-learning, policy gradient) alongside the RL topic; the hands-on notebooks run on a free cloud GPU or, with small settings, on the Mac. The unit on evaluation and on the reproducibility of RL results is short and important.

The course uses standard libraries (Stable-Baselines3, Gymnasium) so you learn the practical stack; understand what the libraries hide (replay buffers, target networks, advantage estimation) by reading Spinning Up's implementations alongside.
It is practice-first; its coverage of offline RL and of off-policy evaluation, which the alerting problem needs, is thin, so read those from the literature.
A free, maintained practical course; a good calibration of what a working RL baseline looks like before proposing a control experiment.

Units: introduction to deep RL (the RL framework, exploration, two approaches, tasks); Q-learning (value-based methods, Bellman, MC and TD, Q-learning implementation for FrozenLake and Taxi); deep Q-learning (DQN, experience replay, fixed targets, double DQN, Atari); policy gradient (REINFORCE with CartPole and Pixelcopter); actor-critic (A2C, robotics environments); multi-agent RL and self-play; PPO (theory, implementation from scratch, Unity ML-Agents and VizDoom); with bonus units on Godot, Sample Factory, Optuna, and decision transformers; with hands-on notebooks and a leaderboard.

items: The framework: agent, environment, state or observation, action, reward; episodic and continuing tasks; exploration-exploitation; policy-based and value-based methods; the notebooks use Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3.
Q-learning from scratch: a Q-table, epsilon-greedy with decay, the TD update; the two tabular environments make the algorithm concrete before any network.

DQN: a network approximates Q; experience replay breaks correlation between consecutive samples; a fixed target network stabilises the regression target; double DQN decouples selection and evaluation of the max; frame stacking gives temporal context.
REINFORCE: sample episodes, compute returns, take a gradient step on log-probability weighted by return; high variance, no bootstrapping.
Actor-critic (A2C): the critic's value estimate replaces the return, and the advantage reduces variance; synchronous parallel environments for throughput.

PPO: the clipped surrogate objective and the implementation details that matter (advantage normalisation, value clipping, entropy bonus, multiple epochs over the batch, learning rate annealing); implemented from scratch in the unit.
Multi-agent RL: self-play, cooperative and competitive settings; the ML-Agents SoccerTwos environment; the difficulty of non-stationarity when other agents learn.

b.s:
DQN loss: (r + gamma max_a Q_target(s', a) - Q(s, a))^2
double DQN target: r + gamma Q_target(s', argmax_a Q(s', a))
A2C advantage: A = r + gamma V(s') - V(s)

items: Value-based methods learn a Q function and act greedily; policy-based methods learn the policy directly; actor-critic uses both.
Replay and target networks are what made deep Q-learning work; their absence is why naive DQN diverges.
PPO's implementation details are as important as the objective; the unit's from-scratch build is the way to learn them.

b.s: Complete units 2 and 4 (Q-learning and REINFORCE), then write a Gymnasium environment for a single ramp meter with a queue and mainline density, and train PPO with Stable-Baselines3 on the M1 to reduce total delay.

resources.lives: course · free · four weeks · free; train agents hands-on

resources.title: Gymnasium documentation

b.s: The manual for a set of practice worlds where a learning agent can try things safely, like a cart balancing a pole.

Gymnasium is the maintained version of OpenAI Gym: a standard interface for reinforcement-learning environments (observe, act, reward, done) and a set of classic tasks. Its documentation explains the interface and how to build your own environment, which is what a traffic-control simulator would need.

Read the basic usage page and the guide to making a custom environment; implement a tiny ramp-metering environment (state: queue and mainline occupancy; action: meter rate; reward: negative delay) and train a bandit or Q-learning agent on it.
The environment API is the contract between algorithms and simulators; understand observation and action spaces, episode termination versus truncation, and vectorized environments for throughput.
Wrapping a traffic simulator (SUMO) as a Gymnasium environment is the standard path to RL experiments in transport; the documentation's custom-environment guide is the template.
A shared interface made RL research comparable; the same lesson applies to any experimental platform you build.

Basic usage (creating an environment, the step and reset loop, observation and action spaces, seeding), the Env API (step returns observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info; render modes; close), spaces (Box, Discrete, MultiDiscrete, MultiBinary, Text, Tuple, Dict, Sequence, Graph), wrappers (observation, action and reward wrappers, TimeLimit, RecordEpisodeStatistics, FrameStack, normalisation, vectorised wrappers), vector environments (sync and async), environment creation (writing a custom Env, registration, checking with the environment checker), the built-in environments (classic control, Box2D, toy text, MuJoCo, Atari via ALE), and migration notes from Gym.

items: The interaction loop: reset returns the first observation and info; step takes an action and returns observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info; terminated means the MDP ended, truncated means a time limit cut it, which matters for bootstrapping.
Spaces describe valid observations and actions, with sampling and containment checks; a Dict space packages multiple inputs; Box handles continuous vectors with bounds.
Wrappers modify environments without changing their code: normalise observations, clip actions, stack frames, record episode returns, enforce time limits; compose them in order.
Custom environments implement reset, step, render and the spaces; registration lets gym.make find them; the passive environment checker validates the API contract.
Vector environments run many copies for throughput; automatic resets and the final-observation convention need care.
Seeding for reproducibility: seed on reset and seed the action space; determinism still depends on the underlying simulator.

b.s:
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0);  obs, r, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(a);  done = terminated or truncated
bootstrapping rule: if truncated and not terminated, target = r + gamma V(s')

items: Terminated and truncated are different, and confusing them biases value estimates.
Write the environment as a plain class first, then register it; check it with the environment checker before training anything.
Wrappers are the right place for normalisation and time limits, not the environment itself.

b.s: Implement a ramp-meter environment: state is (queue length, mainline density, time of day), action is metering rate from a Discrete(4), reward is negative total delay; wrap with TimeLimit(288) and RecordEpisodeStatistics, and run the checker.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; the environment interface, and how to build one

resources.title: SUMO, Simulation of Urban MObility, documentation

b.s: The manual for a free program that simulates a whole city's traffic, car by car, so you can test ideas without touching real roads.

SUMO is an open-source traffic simulator from the German Aerospace Center: road networks, vehicles with realistic car-following, traffic lights, ramp meters, and a Python interface to control and observe the simulation. Its tutorials build a small network and run it.

Do the beginner tutorials (a simple network, adding vehicles, viewing the simulation), then import a piece of Fremont's road network from OpenStreetMap and simulate a rush hour with an incident. The Python interface (TraCI) lets you read speeds like PeMS would and change signals.

SUMO is the environment for the traffic-control RL exercise and a source of synthetic data for stress-testing the forecaster; understand its car-following models (Krauss, IDM) and its calibration limits before trusting its numbers.

Simulator-to-reality gaps are the central issue: calibrate demand and driver parameters against PeMS counts, and evaluate any learned controller under demand shifts. The documentation on calibration and on the TraCI interface is the practical reference.
Open simulators are where counterfactual questions about alerts and routing become answerable; SUMO with a learned forecaster and a control policy is a complete research platform on one machine.

User documentation: installation, the tutorials (Hello SUMO, quick start, OSM web wizard, driving in circles, public transport, TraCI examples), networks (importing from OpenStreetMap with netconvert, generating with netgenerate, editing with netedit, edges, lanes, junctions, connections, traffic lights), demand (trips, routes, flows, calibrators, randomTrips, duarouter, marouter, origin-destination matrices, vehicle types and car-following models), simulation (sumo and sumo-gui, outputs: trips, edge data, lane data, detectors, FCD, emissions), TraCI (the control interface with Python bindings, and libsumo for speed), traffic lights (static, actuated, and controlled through TraCI), and tools (visualisation, calibration, detector import).

items: A SUMO scenario is a network (nodes, edges, lanes, connections, signals), a demand (vehicles with types and routes over time) and a configuration; the OSM web wizard produces all three for any real area, including the I-880 and I-680 corridors.
Car-following models (Krauss, IDM, Wiedemann) determine microscopic behaviour; lane-changing models determine weaving; parameters such as desired headway and acceleration shape the emergent capacity.

Demand can be trips (origin, destination, departure) routed by duarouter, flows with rates, or calibrated to match detector counts; getting demand right is most of the work in matching a real corridor.
Detectors in the simulation (induction loops, lane area, multi-entry-exit) produce outputs that look like PeMS data: counts, occupancy, speed per interval; this is how simulated and real data align.

TraCI lets a Python program step the simulation and read or write state each step: vehicle positions and speeds, detector values, signal phases; this is the bridge to RL and to closed-loop control experiments.
Traffic lights can be static programs, actuated by detectors, or set by TraCI; ramp meters are traffic lights on on-ramps in this model.
Outputs: aggregated edge and lane data, per-vehicle trip information (delay, time loss), floating car data for trajectories; use them for evaluation.

b.s:
run: sumo -c fremont.sumocfg --tripinfo-output trips.xml
TraCI loop: traci.start(cmd); while traci.simulation.getMinExpectedNumber() > 0: traci.simulationStep(); ...
IDM desired gap: s* = s0 + v T + v dv / (2 sqrt(a b))

items: Simulation gives labelled counterfactuals (what if metering changed) that observational data never can; it is also only as good as its demand calibration.
Simulated detectors produce PeMS-shaped data, so the same feature and model code can run on both.
TraCI plus Gymnasium is the path to RL on a realistic corridor.

b.s: Use the OSM web wizard to build the I-880 segment through Fremont, add induction loops at the real station locations, calibrate a morning-peak demand so that simulated speeds roughly match PeMS, and write a TraCI script that reads loop speeds every five minutes.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; a city's traffic, car by car

resources.title: Fairlearn user guide

b.s: The manual for a free tool that checks whether a learning machine treats different groups of people fairly, and helps fix it.

Fairlearn is an open-source Python library from Microsoft for assessing and improving fairness: metrics computed per group, dashboards, and algorithms that reduce disparities under constraints. Its user guide explains the fairness definitions it implements and their trade-offs.

Read the user guide's sections on assessment (metric frames by group) and on mitigation, then compute recall and false-alarm rate per neighborhood for the alert policy and try one mitigation; see what it costs in overall precision.

The guide's careful discussion of which fairness metric fits which harm, and of the limits of technical mitigation, is a practical companion to the fairness book; its implementations are correct references for the definitions.
Fairness tooling encodes choices; use the library for measurement and treat its mitigations as experiments to be evaluated, not fixes to be applied.
A maintained open-source reference for fairness assessment; useful for standardizing audits across a team's models.

User guide: fairness in machine learning (harms, group fairness, the sensitive-feature concept, fairness metrics and constraints, limitations); assessment (MetricFrame for disaggregated metrics with grouping, intersections, aggregations such as difference and ratio; plotting; common fairness metrics such as demographic parity and equalised odds differences); mitigation (preprocessing with correlation remover; reductions approach with exponentiated gradient and grid search for constraints such as demographic parity, equalised odds, true-positive-rate parity, bounded group loss; postprocessing with threshold optimiser); with an API reference and worked examples.

items: Fairness is about harms (allocation, quality of service) to groups defined by sensitive features; the library helps assess and mitigate, but choosing the criterion is a human decision.
MetricFrame computes any metric overall and per group (and intersections) and reports difference, ratio, min and max across groups; this is disaggregated evaluation as a data structure.
Constraints as objects: demographic parity (selection rates equal), equalised odds (TPR and FPR equal), true-positive-rate parity, error-rate parity, bounded group loss for regression.

Reductions: exponentiated gradient reduces constrained classification to a sequence of cost-sensitive problems solved by any base learner, producing a randomised classifier; grid search produces a deterministic one from a grid of relabelings.

Postprocessing: threshold optimiser picks per-group thresholds (possibly randomised) on a fitted scorer to satisfy a constraint while maximising an objective; requires the sensitive feature at prediction time.
Preprocessing: correlation remover linearly removes correlation between features and sensitive features; a blunt tool with clear limits.
Limitations section: metrics assume the sensitive feature is measured well, group definitions are contestable, and satisfying a metric does not make a system fair.

b.s:
demographic parity difference: max_a P(h=1|A=a) - min_a P(h=1|A=a)
equalised odds difference: max over y of max_a P(h=1|Y=y,A=a) - min_a P(h=1|Y=y,A=a)
MetricFrame(metrics={'ap': average_precision_score}, y_true=y, y_pred=s, sensitive_features=group)

items: MetricFrame is the reusable piece: any metric, any grouping, differences and ratios in one object.
Mitigation methods trade accuracy for a constraint; measure the trade-off rather than assuming it is small.
The library's own limitations page is required reading; the numbers are not a certificate.

b.s: Wrap the bottleneck model's validation predictions in a MetricFrame grouped by station group and hour bucket, report AP and FNR differences, then run a threshold optimiser for equal FNR across station groups and show what it costs in overall AP.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; fairness assessment and mitigation in code

resources.title: Programming Differential Privacy (Near, Abuah)

b.s: A free online book that teaches how to add just enough randomness to shared numbers, with code you can run, so nobody can be picked out.

A free book, written as runnable notebooks, that teaches differential privacy by doing: the Laplace mechanism, sensitivity, composition, private counts and averages, and private machine learning, all in Python on a real dataset. It is the practical companion to Dwork and Roth.

Work through the chapters on the Laplace mechanism, on sensitivity and on composition, then release the hourly speed averages privately and plot accuracy against the privacy parameter as the topic asks. The chapter on differentially private gradient descent shows private model training.

The book's worked examples make the definitions concrete and its exercises are checkable; its treatment of local differential privacy and of synthetic data connects to on-device settings and to the generative-model topic.
Read it alongside the theory monograph: the book shows what the mechanisms do to real data, which is where the practical privacy-utility trade-off lives.
A free, executable textbook is the right onboarding for engineers who will implement private releases; its examples are a starting point for a team's own privacy library.

Chapters: introduction; de-identification and its failures (linkage attacks, aggregation, differencing attacks); k-anonymity; differential privacy (the definition, the Laplace mechanism, counting queries); properties (sequential and parallel composition, post-processing); sensitivity (global, local, clipping for unbounded attributes); approximate differential privacy (the Gaussian mechanism, vector-valued queries); local sensitivity and smooth sensitivity (propose-test-release, sample and aggregate); Rényi and zero-concentrated DP; the exponential mechanism; the sparse vector technique; machine learning with DP (noisy gradient descent, gradient clipping, private logistic regression); local differential privacy (randomised response, unary encoding); synthetic data; with Python code and exercises in every chapter.

items: De-identification fails because auxiliary data enable linkage; aggregate statistics leak through differencing attacks; k-anonymity is fragile under homogeneity and background knowledge.
The definition and the Laplace mechanism, applied in code to counting queries on a census dataset; the noise is tiny relative to the count and the privacy is formal.
Composition and post-processing in practice: a loop that answers k queries spends k epsilon; disjoint histogram bins spend epsilon once; any transformation of a private output is free.

Sensitivity: counts have sensitivity one; sums of bounded values have the bound as sensitivity; unbounded values must be clipped to a chosen bound, which costs accuracy and must be chosen without looking at the data (or privately).
Gaussian mechanism and vector queries with L2 sensitivity; approximate DP variants (Rényi DP, zCDP) give tighter composition for many iterations, which matters for training.
Noisy gradient descent: clip each example's gradient to norm C, sum, add Gaussian noise with scale proportional to C, average, step; account for the total privacy spent over epochs; this is DP-SGD.
Local DP: each participant randomises before sending; unary encoding for histograms; error is much larger than in the central model.
Synthetic data: release a private histogram or marginals and sample from them; usable for low-dimensional queries.

b.s:
Laplace counting query: count + np.random.laplace(loc=0, scale=1/eps)
clipped sum sensitivity: b for values clipped to [0, b]
DP-SGD step: g = sum_i clip(g_i, C) + N(0, sigma^2 C^2 I); theta <- theta - eta g / n
sequential composition: total eps = sum_i eps_i

items: Code the mechanisms yourself once; the concepts become concrete when noise is a line of NumPy.
Clipping bounds sensitivity and is the main knob in private learning.
Accounting (how much epsilon a whole pipeline spends) is where real systems fail; track it from the first query.

b.s: Work through the chapters on sensitivity and DP-SGD, then train a private logistic regression for bottleneck-in-15-minutes on the features with eps = 1 over the whole training run, and report AP versus the non-private model.

resources.lives: book · free · weeks · free; privacy mechanisms as runnable notebooks

resources.title: Performative Prediction (Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner, Hardt, 2020)

b.s: A paper about what happens when a prediction changes the thing it predicted, like telling everyone a road will be slow so everyone avoids it and it is not slow after all.

When a model's predictions influence the world, the data it learns from next time are shaped by its own past predictions. This paper names that situation and studies when retraining still settles down to a sensible model. Traffic alerts are a textbook case.

Read the introduction and the examples; then the definition of a performatively stable model (one that stays optimal on the data it induces) and the conditions under which repeated retraining converges to one. Ask what it means for stage 13's monthly retrain.

The framework formalizes feedback loops as a distribution map from model to data; the results relate convergence to how sensitive the distribution is to the model. It is the theory behind the practical warning in lessons 6 and 12.

Subsequent work covers strategic behavior, optimization methods for performative risk, and connections to causal inference and reinforcement learning; for traffic, the open question is estimating the distribution map from logged alerts.
A foundational framing for any system that acts on its predictions; a research program on alerting policies would start here and with the causal-inference literature.

The paper: motivation (predictions that influence the outcomes they predict, such as traffic forecasts that change routes); the framework (a distribution map from model parameters to a data distribution; performative risk; performative stability and performative optimality as solution concepts); repeated risk minimisation and repeated gradient descent (retraining on the induced distribution); convergence results under strong convexity, smoothness and a sensitivity condition on the distribution map; the gap between stable and optimal points; connections to strategic classification, causal inference and RL; experiments on a credit-scoring simulation.

items: Performativity: deploying a model theta changes the distribution D(theta) of the data; the loss that matters is the performative risk, the expected loss under the distribution the model induces, not under the training distribution.

Two solution concepts: a performatively optimal model minimises performative risk; a performatively stable model is optimal for the distribution it induces (a fixed point of retraining); stable points are what retraining converges to, and they are not optimal in general.

Repeated risk minimisation (retrain on the data your model produced) converges to a stable point at a linear rate when the loss is strongly convex and smooth and the distribution map is epsilon-sensitive with epsilon small relative to the strong convexity over the smoothness; otherwise it can oscillate or diverge.
Repeated gradient descent with a small step behaves similarly with weaker requirements per step.

The gap between stable and optimal grows with the sensitivity of the distribution map; when the model strongly affects behaviour, retraining is not enough, and one must model the feedback (or optimise the performative risk directly, which later work does).

Applications: strategic classification (agents change features to be classified favourably) is a special case; traffic prediction is the canonical example, since forecasts reroute drivers and change congestion.

b.s:
performative risk: PR(theta) = E_{Z ~ D(theta)} l(Z; theta)
stable: theta_PS = argmin_theta E_{Z ~ D(theta_PS)} l(Z; theta)
convergence condition for repeated risk minimisation: eps < gamma / beta (sensitivity, strong convexity, smoothness)

items: A deployed forecast changes what it forecasts; the training distribution is not the deployment distribution by construction.
Retraining converges to a stable point, which is not the best model, and can fail to converge when feedback is strong.
For a public bottleneck predictor, expect the predictions to shift departure times and routes, and log deployment-era data separately from pre-deployment data.

b.s: Simulate a simple performative loop: drivers shift departures earlier by an amount proportional to the predicted bottleneck probability, regenerate the outcome, retrain the model, repeat ten times; plot the AP and the predicted rate over rounds and find the step where it stabilises or oscillates.

resources.lives: paper · free · an evening or two · free; the theory of alerts that change traffic

items: Q-learning on a grid world and Thompson sampling on a three-arm bandit; formulate alerting as a contextual bandit and write the off-policy estimator.
Draw the DAG for incidents, congestion, reporting, rain and alerts; estimate the effect of rain on slow episodes with inverse probability weighting; design a switchback experiment for alerts.

Audit recall and false alarms per station on the map under two fairness definitions; release hourly speeds with differential privacy and plot utility against epsilon; fill in a model card and a datasheet.
Train a LightGBM ranker to order segments by risk for the dashboard and evaluate NDCG against realized episodes.
A memo on what the logged data can and cannot say about the effect of alerts, with the experiment that would settle it.
A fairness audit map and a filled model card.
A ranked dashboard with NDCG next to sorting by probability.
Adjusting for a collider.
Treating feature importance as a causal claim.
Believing one fairness metric settles the question.

phases.lives: Everything this asks for has been explained above: the lessons and topics for the ideas, the walkthroughs for the code, the books and courses for depth. The glossary at the end defines any word that is still new.

phases.title: Depth
phases.meta: weeks 70–76, then onward · open-ended · builds papers, PEMS-BAY, Bayesian models, write-ups

b.s: From 'can build this' to 'can design the next one and say why it works'. Rotate the tracks; each is months, not weeks.

items: Uncertainty: quantiles, Bayesian thinking, conformal prediction, adaptive conformal inference; risk control for alerts.
Theory: generalization, bias-variance properly, convexity, margins, double descent; what breaks under shift.
Bayesian machine learning: hierarchical models, MCMC and variational inference, Gaussian processes, Bayesian optimization.
Reading and reproducing: DCRNN, STGCN, Graph WaveNet on PEMS-BAY at reduced scale; ablations; write-ups.
Practice and communication: two competitions written up honestly, one open-source contribution, one public write-up of the traffic model, one talk.

items.title: Uncertainty: quantiles, Bayesian thinking, conformal prediction

b.s: Say how sure the model is, with guarantees you can defend.
Sometimes the honest answer is 'probably between 20 and 40 minutes', not one number. A good helper says how sure it is and gives a range.
Guess how many candies are in a jar as a range you are pretty sure about. Was the true number inside your range?

A single number hides how wrong it might be. A range ('between 20 and 45, nine times out of ten') is more useful. You can get one by predicting quantiles directly, or by conformal prediction: check on held-out data how wrong the model usually is and widen the range until it covers 90 % of cases.
For ten past predictions, compute the errors, find the ninth largest, and use it as a plus-or-minus width. Check how many of the ten it covers.

Quantile regression with the pinball loss; prediction intervals versus confidence intervals. Bayesian thinking: a prior belief updated by data into a posterior. Conformal prediction: calibrate a score on held-out data, take its (1 − α) quantile, and get guaranteed coverage with almost no assumptions, provided calibration and test data are exchangeable. For time series that assumption is stretched, and adaptive methods exist.
Build a 90 % interval for the 30-minute speed with LightGBM quantile objectives at 0.05 and 0.95, and measure coverage on the test split.

Aleatoric versus epistemic uncertainty; calibration of intervals; Bayesian logistic regression with a Laplace approximation; Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles as approximate posteriors; split conformal and conformalized quantile regression with their coverage proof; risk control for binary alerts.
Prove split-conformal coverage from exchangeability of the calibration and test scores.

Conformal prediction under shift (weighted conformal, adaptive conformal inference for time series), risk-controlling prediction sets, conditional coverage and its impossibility results, hierarchical Bayesian models for per-station effects with partial pooling, and decision-making under uncertainty.
Implement adaptive conformal inference on the rolling predictions and plot realized coverage week by week.

Uncertainty in products: what users do with intervals, communicating probability, alert budgets enforced with guarantees, and the research frontier of distribution-free inference under dependence and feedback, Bayesian deep learning at scale, and calibration under performative shift.
Propose a coverage guarantee that survives the feedback loop in which alerts change the traffic they predicted.

b.q: What does 90 % coverage mean?

a.s: Over many predictions, about 90 % of intervals contain the truth. It does not mean one specific interval has a 90 % chance.

b.q: Why does conformal need held-out data?

a.s: It measures how wrong the model is on data it did not fit. Training errors are optimistic.

items.title: Theory: why learning works at all

b.s: Know what generalization is, why more capacity is not always better, and what assumptions every guarantee rests on.
If you practice a game on one level only, you might get great at that level and bad at new ones. Learning that works means being good on new levels too.
Learn a card trick with one deck, then try it with a different deck. Does it still work?

A model can memorize its training rows (overfitting) or be too simple to fit them (underfitting). The goal is doing well on new data. More data helps, simpler models overfit less, and checking on held-out data tells you where you are.
Draw eight points. Fit a straight line and a wiggly curve through them. Which guesses a ninth point better?

Training error versus test error; the bias-variance trade-off; complexity (leaves, depth, layers) and regularization; cross-validation to estimate test error, forward-only for time series. The no-free-lunch idea: assumptions, called inductive bias, are what let a model generalize.
Plot validation average precision against `num_leaves` from 7 to 511 and find where it peaks.

Empirical risk minimization; the bias-variance decomposition for squared loss; uniform convergence, VC dimension and Rademacher complexity as intuition; regularization as constraining the hypothesis space; convexity and tractable optimization; margin theory for boosting. Bounds are loose, but they explain the shape of learning curves.
Derive the bias-variance decomposition and identify each term for a k-nearest-neighbors model as k changes.

Modern puzzles: interpolating models that generalize, double descent, the implicit regularization of stochastic gradient descent, benign overfitting; PAC-Bayes and information-theoretic bounds; and how distribution shift (covariate, label, concept) breaks every bound unless an invariance assumption restores it.
Reproduce a double-descent curve on a small synthetic regression problem and explain the peak.

Theory as engineering guidance: which knobs matter (data quality over model size for tabular problems), scaling laws and where they fail, the theory-practice gap in deep learning, and the open problems relevant here: learning under dependence and feedback, and transfer across road networks.
State precisely what assumption would let a model trained on Fremont transfer to San Jose, and design the test that would falsify it.

b.q: Why does a bigger model not always win?

a.s: Variance. It fits noise unless data or regularization constrains it.

b.q: What is inductive bias?

a.s: The assumptions built into a model class. Without any, nothing generalizes.

items.title: Reading papers and reproducing benchmarks

b.s: Turn a paper into a change you could make to stage 9, and know whether its claim is real.
Scientists write down what they tried and what happened so others can try it too. Reading their notes and redoing their experiment is how you learn the newest tricks and check they are real.
Follow a recipe exactly. Then change one thing and see what happens.

A paper has an abstract (the summary), a method, experiments with tables, and a conclusion. Read the abstract and the tables first and ask: what did they compare with? Reproducing means running their code, or rewriting it, on the public data and getting close to their numbers.
Find the DCRNN paper online. Write down its three horizons and its best number at 60 minutes.

Three passes: title, abstract, figures and conclusion; then method and experiments with attention to baselines and datasets; then re-derive the key equations and read the code. For traffic, METR-LA and PEMS-BAY are the standard datasets, PEMS-BAY being Bay Area PeMS with 325 sensors, and the metrics are MAE, RMSE and MAPE at 15, 30 and 60 minutes. On the M1, reduce epochs, hidden size and batch, but keep the evaluation protocol identical.
Run the public DCRNN code on PEMS-BAY with a reduced configuration and compare your numbers with the paper's table.

Evaluating claims: is the baseline tuned, is the split honest, is the gain within seed-to-seed noise, and what does it cost in compute? Reproduction discipline: pin versions, record seeds, log everything, report variance. A reproduction report has method, deviations, results and a judgment.
Write a one-page reproduction report of STGCN with a table of the paper's numbers against yours.

The reproducibility literature shows many published gains vanish under fair baselines. Ablations isolate what matters. A benchmark score is not a deployable model. Read with a question: what would this change in my stage 9? Graph WaveNet and later transformer models are the next reads; understand adaptive adjacency versus a physical graph.
Run an ablation on your spatio-temporal net: remove neighbor mixing and quantify the change in average precision at 60 minutes.

Research practice: choosing problems where data is the bottleneck, designing experiments whose failure would be informative, reviewing, and the ethics of claims. For traffic forecasting the open questions are transfer, non-stationarity, causal intervention and coupling with routing, and product impact often comes from data and evaluation rather than architecture.
Write the related-work paragraph a paper on this Fremont model would need: the three papers it must cite and the gap it fills.

b.q: What is the first thing to check in a results table?

a.s: The baselines, and whether persistence or a simple model is among them.

b.q: Why reproduce with a reduced configuration?

a.s: To verify the pipeline and the protocol on your hardware. The absolute number scales with compute you can add later.

items.title: Bayesian machine learning and Gaussian processes

b.s: Treat parameters as uncertain, update beliefs with data, and use models that come with their own error bars.
Before you look, you have a guess. After you look, you have a better guess. Bayesian thinking is keeping track of how sure you are and changing it a little with every new clue.
Guess how many marbles are in a jar. Now someone tells you it is more than 50. Change your guess. Someone says fewer than 80. Change it again.

Bayes' rule updates a prior belief with data into a posterior. A Bayesian model does that for its parameters: instead of one best weight, it keeps a whole distribution of plausible weights, so its predictions come with uncertainty. A Gaussian process is a Bayesian model over functions: it predicts a curve and a band around it, wide where data are scarce.
Plot ten (time, speed) points for one station and sketch by hand a smooth curve with a band that is narrow near the points and wide between them.

Priors, likelihoods and posteriors; conjugate examples (Beta-Binomial for a station's slow rate); posterior predictive distributions; Bayesian linear and logistic regression; hierarchical models sharing strength across stations. Gaussian processes: a kernel defines similarity, predictions are closed-form with variance, cost grows as the cube of the data size, so they suit small data and hyperparameter tuning.
Computation: exact for conjugate cases, otherwise Markov chain Monte Carlo or variational inference (PyMC, Stan, or NumPyro).
Fit a Beta-Binomial model of each station's slow-episode rate with a shared prior, and compare the shrunken estimates with the raw rates for stations with few data.

Bayesian decision theory; model comparison and the marginal likelihood; MCMC (Metropolis, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) and diagnostics; variational inference and the ELBO; Laplace approximation; Gaussian processes in depth (kernels, hyperparameter learning by marginal likelihood, sparse approximations). Bayesian optimization as the workhorse of hyperparameter tuning.
Bayesian neural networks and their approximations (dropout, ensembles, last-layer Laplace) for uncertainty in deep models.

Implement a Gaussian process regression for one station's daily profile with a periodic kernel and learn the hyperparameters by maximizing marginal likelihood; compare its predictive band with the bootstrap interval.

Scalable Bayesian inference (stochastic variational inference, inducing points), Bayesian nonparametrics, probabilistic programming, calibration of Bayesian predictive distributions under model misspecification, and the relation between Bayesian and conformal guarantees. Hierarchical spatio-temporal models as a classical alternative to graph networks.

Build a hierarchical Bayesian model of slow-episode rates with station and hour effects in a probabilistic programming language, check convergence, and compare its calibration with the boosted trees'.

Bayesian methods underlie modern uncertainty quantification, experimental design, and Bayesian optimization at scale; the research frontier includes scalable inference for deep models, decision-making under uncertainty, and combining Bayesian and frequentist guarantees. For products, the practical value is honest uncertainty and principled pooling across sparse groups.
Argue, with a small experiment, whether a Bayesian hierarchical model or isotonic calibration on a boosted model gives better-calibrated per-station probabilities with three months of data.

b.q: What does a prior do when data are scarce?

a.s: It dominates: the posterior stays near the prior until data accumulate, which is exactly the shrinkage that helps stations with few observations.

b.q: Why do Gaussian processes suit hyperparameter tuning?

a.s: They model a smooth unknown function with uncertainty from few evaluations, which is what Bayesian optimization needs to choose the next trial.

resources.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction (Murphy)

b.s: A very big free book that explains almost all of machine learning using the language of chance.

Kevin Murphy's book, free as a PDF, about a thousand pages. It is a reference, not a read-through: look up a topic (logistic regression, decision trees, calibration, neural networks) and read that section. Its pictures are excellent and its examples are consistent from chapter to chapter.

Use its chapters on probability and statistics (2 to 5), on linear models (9 to 11) and on trees and ensembles (18) as the rigorous version of ISLP. Its notation is consistent, and its habit of connecting every method to a likelihood shows that lessons 7, 8 and 9 are the same idea with different function classes.

This is the graduate-level unification: every model as a probabilistic model, every loss as a negative log-likelihood, Bayesian and frequentist views side by side. Read the chapters on generalization, on optimization, and on calibration; its treatment of decision theory frames the alert threshold of lesson 11 properly.

The second volume, Advanced Topics, covers inference, generative models and causality; between the two they are the modern reference set. Its treatment of Gaussian processes and Bayesian neural networks is the background for the uncertainty track of phase 8, and its chapters on time series connect state-space models to recurrent networks.

Murphy's books are the field's encyclopedia. Cite them for standard results and use them to find the original references quickly; for research, their breadth is what lets you place a new idea in the landscape in an afternoon rather than a week.

Part I foundations: introduction; probability (univariate and multivariate models, Bayes' rule, exponential families, transformations, Monte Carlo); statistics (MLE, MAP, Bayesian and frequentist statistics, bias-variance); decision theory (Bayesian decision theory, ROC, hypothesis testing, calibration); information theory (entropy, relative entropy, mutual information); optimisation (first-order, second-order, stochastic, constrained, proximal, bound optimisation and EM). Part II linear models: linear discriminant analysis, logistic regression, linear regression, generalised linear models. Part III deep networks: MLPs, CNNs, RNNs and transformers. Part IV nonparametric: exemplar methods (k-NN, kernel density), kernel methods (Mercer kernels, GPs, SVMs), trees, forests, bagging, boosting. Part V beyond supervised: dimensionality reduction (PCA, autoencoders, manifolds), clustering, recommender systems, graph embeddings; appendix on notation.

items: Everything is a probabilistic model: a joint or conditional distribution with parameters; learning is inference about parameters (MLE, MAP, Bayesian) and prediction is inference about outputs; this framing unifies regression, classification, deep learning and unsupervised learning.
Exponential families, sufficient statistics and conjugate priors give closed forms for the Gaussian, Bernoulli, categorical and gamma cases; most of applied ML is a special case.
Decision theory separates the model (probabilities) from the action (a threshold chosen to minimise expected loss); calibration and proper scoring rules evaluate the probabilities themselves.
Information theory links compression, likelihood and learning: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood, KL is the excess coding cost, mutual information measures dependence.
Optimisation chapter covers gradient descent, momentum, Adam, second-order methods, constrained optimisation with Lagrangians and KKT, proximal methods for sparsity, and EM as bound optimisation.
Linear models are treated fully: logistic regression with its Hessian and IRLS, regularisation, Bayesian linear regression with predictive distributions, GLMs with link functions.

Deep networks chapters give the standard architectures and training recipes with an eye to what they compute probabilistically (softmax outputs as categorical likelihoods, dropout as approximate inference).
Nonparametric methods: kernels and GPs, SVMs as margin maximisers, trees and ensembles (with the bias-variance explanation of bagging and the functional gradient view of boosting).
Unsupervised chapters: PCA as a linear Gaussian latent model, mixture models with EM, and the beginnings of deep generative models.

b.s:
Bayes: p(theta | D) = p(D | theta) p(theta) / p(D)
cross-entropy = H(p) + KL(p || q)
logistic regression Hessian: H = X^T diag(mu (1 - mu)) X
GP posterior mean: K_*^T (K + sigma^2 I)^{-1} y

items: One vocabulary (likelihood, prior, posterior, predictive, decision) covers every model in the book, which is why the book is worth reading front to back.
Calibration and proper scoring rules are part of the model, not an afterthought.
Chapters 4, 5, 8 and 10 alone (statistics, decision theory, optimisation, logistic regression) fill most of the gaps that practice leaves.

b.s: Read chapters 4 through 6 and 10, then write the bottleneck classifier as an explicit probabilistic model (features, Bernoulli likelihood, prior), derive the gradient and Hessian of the log posterior, and fit it with Newton's method on a subsample.

resources.lives: book · free · reference · free PDF; the modern reference

resources.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning (Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman)

b.s: A famous, hard, free book by three statisticians who invented many of the methods it describes.

The graduate version of ISLP, free as a PDF, with proofs and depth. Read a chapter when you have met the topic in ISLP and want to know why it works: chapter 7 on judging models, chapter 10 on boosting, chapter 15 on random forests. Expect to read slowly and to reread.

Chapter 10 is the origin story of gradient boosting written by its inventor, and it explains why fitting small trees to residuals works. Chapter 7 is the honest treatment of bias, variance and cross-validation, including why the test error estimate from cross-validation is itself uncertain. Chapter 15 explains why random forests work through variance reduction.

ESL's derivations (boosting as additive modelling in function space, the bias-variance decomposition, effective degrees of freedom, shrinkage) are the background every ML PhD assumes. Work the exercises for chapters 7 and 10; they are the ones that make the later literature readable.

Its coverage predates deep learning's rise and the modern boosting libraries, but its statistical framing (estimators, degrees of freedom, shrinkage, model selection) is what explains why those tools work. Pair chapter 10 with the XGBoost and LightGBM papers to see the second-order approximation that made boosting fast.

Still the canonical citation for many methods, and its authors' later work on sparsity and the lasso is the natural continuation. For a paper, its notation for loss functions and additive models is safe to adopt, and its chapter 7 remains the reference for arguing that a reported gain is within noise.

Chapters: introduction; overview of supervised learning (least squares and nearest neighbours, statistical decision theory, the curse of dimensionality, bias-variance); linear regression (subset selection, ridge, lasso, least angle regression, derived directions); linear classification (LDA, logistic regression, separating hyperplanes); basis expansions and regularisation (splines, wavelets, smoothing splines, RKHS); kernel smoothing; model assessment and selection (bias-variance decomposition, optimism, AIC, BIC, MDL, VC dimension, cross-validation, bootstrap); model inference and averaging (bootstrap, Bayesian, EM, MCMC, bagging, stacking, bumping); additive models, trees and related methods (GAMs, CART, PRIM, MARS); boosting and additive trees (AdaBoost as forward stagewise additive modelling, gradient boosting, the right-sized tree, regularisation, interpretation); neural networks; support vector machines and flexible discriminants; prototype methods and nearest neighbours; unsupervised learning (association rules, clustering, SOMs, PCA, ICA, MDS, spectral clustering); random forests; ensemble learning; undirected graphical models; high-dimensional problems.

items: Supervised learning is function estimation under squared or 0-1 loss; the Bayes-optimal predictor is the conditional mean or mode, and every method is an approximation to it with a bias-variance trade-off governed by its effective degrees of freedom.

Shrinkage: ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero smoothly (a Gaussian prior), lasso shrinks and selects (a Laplace prior); least angle regression traces the lasso path; the geometry of the constraint regions explains the difference.
Basis expansions: splines with knots, smoothing splines as penalised regression with a roughness penalty, and the reproducing-kernel view that connects them to kernel methods and Gaussian processes.

Model selection: the optimism of the training error equals twice the covariance between fitted and observed values over n; AIC, BIC and cross-validation estimate test error differently and select differently; the bootstrap estimates variability of anything.
Trees are partitions with piecewise-constant fits, grown greedily and pruned by cost-complexity; they are interpretable, handle mixed data, and are unstable, which bagging and forests fix.

Boosting as forward stagewise additive modelling: AdaBoost minimises exponential loss stagewise; gradient boosting generalises to any differentiable loss by fitting trees to negative gradients; shrinkage and subsampling regularise; tree depth sets interaction order; partial dependence and relative importance interpret the ensemble.
Random forests decorrelate bagged trees by random feature subsets at each split; out-of-bag error is a free cross-validation; variable importance by permutation.
SVMs maximise margin with a kernel; the hinge loss puts them in the same family as logistic regression with a different loss; flexible discriminants generalise LDA.

Unsupervised: clustering as prototype fitting, PCA as the best rank-k reconstruction, spectral clustering from the graph Laplacian; high-dimensional chapter covers regularised discriminants, feature screening and multiple testing.

b.s:
bias-variance: E[(y - f_hat(x))^2] = sigma^2 + Bias^2(f_hat(x)) + Var(f_hat(x))
ridge: beta = (X^T X + lambda I)^{-1} X^T y;  df(lambda) = trace(X (X^T X + lambda I)^{-1} X^T)
gradient boosting step: fit tree to r_i = -dL(y_i, f(x_i))/df(x_i), then f <- f + nu sum_j gamma_j 1(x in R_j)
optimism: E[Err_in] - E[err_train] = (2/N) sum_i Cov(y_hat_i, y_i)

items: Chapter 7 (assessment) and chapter 10 (boosting) explain why LightGBM works and how to tune it; read those first.
Effective degrees of freedom is the concept that unifies ridge, splines, trees and boosting.
Every method is a bias-variance position; knowing where a method sits tells you what to try next.

b.s: Read chapters 7 and 10, then reproduce figure 10.2 style experiments on the Fremont data: AP versus number of boosting rounds for tree depths 1, 2, 4 and 6, with and without shrinkage 0.1, and identify the interaction order the problem needs.

resources.lives: book · free · reference · free PDF

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms (Shalev-Shwartz, Ben-David)

b.s: A free math book that asks: why can a machine that learned from old examples be right about new ones? And it proves the answers.

A university textbook, free as a PDF, about the theory of learning: what it means to learn, when it is possible, and how much data you need. It is hard, and it is the right book when you want proofs rather than pictures. For the final phase.

The first part (the PAC learning framework, VC dimension, bias-complexity trade-off) is the formal version of the theory ladder. Read chapters 2 to 6 slowly, doing the exercises; they make the words overfitting and generalization precise.

Its coverage of uniform convergence, Rademacher complexity, regularization and stability, and convex learning gives the tools to read generalization bounds in papers. The chapters on boosting and on stochastic gradient descent connect the theory to the algorithms of phases 4 and 6.

It is the standard reference for classical learning theory; modern questions (overparameterization, implicit bias) build on it and are covered in recent lecture notes and papers rather than textbooks. Read it with Boyd's convex optimization for the optimization side.
The base layer for theoretical work; its exercises are qualifying-exam material, and its treatment of stability is the entry point to the generalization theory of SGD.

Part I foundations: a gentle start (ERM, overfitting, finite hypothesis classes); a formal learning model (PAC, agnostic PAC, the realisability assumption); learning via uniform convergence; the bias-complexity trade-off (no free lunch, error decomposition); the VC dimension (shattering, the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, Sauer's lemma); nonuniform learnability (structural risk minimisation, MDL, Occam's razor); the runtime of learning (computational complexity, hardness). Part II from theory to algorithms: linear predictors (halfspaces, perceptron, linear regression, logistic regression); boosting (weak learnability, AdaBoost, its VC dimension); model selection and validation; convex learning problems; regularisation and stability; stochastic gradient descent; support vector machines; kernel methods; multiclass, ranking and complex prediction; decision trees; nearest neighbour; neural networks. Part III additional models: online learning, clustering, dimensionality reduction, generative models, feature selection. Part IV advanced theory: Rademacher complexities, covering numbers, proof of the fundamental theorem, multiclass learnability, compression bounds, PAC-Bayes.

items: PAC learning formalises 'learning from examples': a class is learnable if some algorithm, with enough samples, outputs a hypothesis whose error is within epsilon of the best in the class with probability 1 - delta; the sample complexity of finite classes is log|H| / epsilon^2.
Uniform convergence: if empirical risks are close to true risks for all hypotheses simultaneously, ERM works; finite classes and finite VC dimension classes have uniform convergence.

The fundamental theorem: for binary classification, PAC learnability, agnostic PAC learnability, uniform convergence and finite VC dimension are equivalent; the sample complexity is proportional to VC dimension over epsilon squared.

No free lunch: without restricting the hypothesis class, no learner beats chance on all distributions; prior knowledge (inductive bias) is necessary; the error decomposition into approximation and estimation error.
